EBRUARY  23-24,  1882. — Reconnaissance  to  Pea  Ridge  Prairie,  Mo.,  and 

skirmish. 

Report  of  Capt.  John  M.  Richardson , Missouri  Cavalry  Militia . 

> 

Springfield,  Mo.,  February  26,  1862. 
Sir  : On  Friday,  22d  instant,  I was  ordered  by  Lieutenant-Colonel 
ills,  commanding  this  post,  to  proceed  with  my  command  to  Mount 
ernon  and  there  wait  the  arrival  of  Captain  Mudgett.  I started  at 
1.30  o’clock  on  the  morning  of  the  22d  with  41  of  my  Mountain  Rangers, 
te  others  being  sick  and  on  detached  service.  At  10  o’clock  p.  m.  of 
le  same  day  we  reached  Mount  Vernon,  having  marched  33  miles, 
n arriving  i received  an  order  from  Captain  Mudgett  to  be  at  Gullet’s 
rm,  8 miles  below  Mount,  Vernon,  by  daylight  next  morning.  We 
Earted  at  3 o’clock,  and  were  there  by  the  time  required.  After  con- 
ning with  Captain  Mudgett  he  determined  for  me  to  proceed  north  of 
bring  River  and  disperse  the  rebels  congregated  there. 

Having  rested  my  command  two  hours  we  started,  marched  down 
bring  River  on  the  north  side  to  the  old  Booneville  Ford,  crossing  there 
id  traveling  in  a northwestern  direction  to  a point  where  the  road 
ading  from  Oregon,  or  Bower’s  Mills,  to  Greenfield  enters  the  Pea 
idge  Prairie.  At  that  point  I directed  Sergeant  Butcher  with  8 men 
> proceed  up  the  prairie  on  its  south  side,  to  arrest  all  persons  running 
om  the  north,  to  search  certain  houses  for  arms,  and  to  keep  a good 
>okout  for  the  rebels. 

With  the  balance  of  the  command  I proceeded  to  the  north  side  of 
le  prairie,  then  changing  my  course  east  towards  Bell’s,  where  we 
xpected  to  find  the  enemy.  X had  traveled  up  the  prairie  but  a short 
istance  when  Sergeant  Breshers,  stationed  on  a high  point  of  the 
rairie,  made  the  signal  the  enemy  had  been  found.  Sergeant  Butcher 
ad  marched  up  the  south  side  of  the  prairie  one  mile  and  a half,  when 
band  of  rebels  formed  near  a point  of  timber  to  oppose  his  progress, 
le  marched  steadily  forward,  and  on  nearing  them  they  retired  behind 
le  point  of  timber,  where  the  sergeant  and  his  party  charged  them, 
le  result  of  which  was  a running  fight  for  3 miles.  In  the  action  my 
icn  killed  3 rebels,  wounded  1,  and  killed  1 horse.  We  had  1 horse 
hot,  and  the  sergeant  rode  his  down  in  the  chase.  We  captured  3 
risoners  and  3 horses.  The  sergeant  and  his  party  were  engaged  with 
•om  12  to  15  rebels,  and  had  it  not  been  that  my  full  command  made 
s appearance  so  promptly  on  the  south  side  of  the  prairie  he  would 
ave  brought  on  an  action  with  from  40  to  50,  who  were  posted  in  the 
rush,  but  retired  as  the  command  marched  across  the  prairie. 

It  affords  me  great  pleasure  to  commend  Sergeant  Butcher  and  his 
len  in  the  highest  terms  for  their  gallant  conduct  on  the  field.  Any 
fiicer  would  be  proud  to  command  such  men. 

From  the  scene  of  action  I sent  Sergeant  Breshers  with  10  men  to  the 
orth  side  of  the  prairie,  and  with  the  balance  I marched  up  the  south 
ide,  the  two  divisions  meeting  at  John  Colly’s.  Breshers  rendered 
aluable  services.  We  gave  the  neighborhood  a good  scouring,  driving 


72 


OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARIv.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chap.  XVIII. 


the  secessionists  before  us.  We  were  in  a section  of  country  infested 
with  a band  of  bad  men — secessionists.  We  alarmed  them  greatly,  and 
rendered  good  service  to  the  Union  cause.  They  had  come  to  the  con- 
clusion our  troops  would  not  visit  them,  and  were  depredating  on  the 
property  of  loyal  citizens.  The  3 prisoners  we  took  were  engaged  in 
the  attempt  to  rob  the  house  of  John  Gullet  of  a lot  of  boots  and  shoes 
on  the  evening  of  the  19th  instant. 

On  the  evening  of  this  hard  day’s  work  we  reached  the  plantation  of 
Price  Anderson.  Tra  veling  without  tents  and  camp  equipage,  we  were 
preparing  to  take  our  rest  on  the  ground  without  shelter,  when  Mr. 
Anderson  invited  the  company  to  take  shelter  in  his  large  and  commo- 
dious residence.  Having  reason  to  believe  an  enemy  in  front  of  us,  the 
command  laid  on  its  arms  during  the  night. 

On  the  morning  of  the  24th  I divided  the  command,  sending  half 
of  it,  under  Sergeant  Butcher,  up  Stall’s  Creek,  and  from  thence  to 
Mallard’s  still  house,  in  the  Turnlack  timber  north  of  the  prairie,  with 
directions  to  destroy  Pennington’s  still-house  and  the  one  at  Mallard’s, 
and  to  come  to  my  assistance  if  he  heard  firing.  With  half  the  com- 
mand I crossed  the  prairie  to  Daniels’  farm,  where  it  was  represented 
the  rebels  had  a strong  picket.  Not  finding  them,  I marched  to  Mal- 
lard’s still-house  from  the  northwest.  The  rebels  had  lied  before  us, 
and  I returned  to  Mount  Yernon,  and  on  the  25th  came  to  this  city. 
There  were  two  reasons  for  destroying  those  still-houses : First,  they 
were  places  of  rendezvous  for  the  forming  secession  bands  for  plunder; 
secondly,  bad  men  would  get  drunk  there,  and  go  to  Union  men’s  houses 
and  expose  their  naked  persons  to  Union  women.  I hope  you  will,  and 
1 know  every  good  woman  in  the  State  will,  indorse  the  destruction — 
the  burning  of  those  still-houses.  They  were  each  worth  almost  $150. 

Since  my  company  was  mustered  into  the  service  I have  been  con- 
stantly in  the  field  and  am  behind  with  my  property  reports,  but  will 
make  them  out  at  the  earliest  convenient  moment. 

I am,  sir,  very  respectfullv,  vour  obedient  servant, 

‘ JOHN  M.  RICHARDSON, 
Captain  Mountain  Bangers,  Mo.  8.  M. 

Col.  Chester  Hardinq, 

Adjutant- General , Missouri. 


FEBRUARY  23-25,  1862. — Reconnaissance  from  Greenville,  Mo.,  and  skir- 
mish near  Saint  Francisville. 

Report  of  Col.  Albert  Jackson , Twelfth  Missouri  Cavalry  Militia. 

y Greenville,  Mo.,  February  27,  1862.  ] 

Sir  : On  the  23d  instant  there  was  a scouting  party  sent  out  from 
this  post  by  the  commandant,  Colonel  Alexander,  of  about  200  men. 
The  troops  composing  this  party  consisted  of  parts  of  two  companies  of 
the  First  Indiana  Cavalry,  Captain  Ha  wkins’  company  Missouri  Volun- 
teers, and  Captain  Beeper’s  company  Missouri  State  Militia,  all  under 
command  of  Major  Clendenning,  of  the  First  Indiana  Cavalry.  On 
Tuesday,  the  25th  instant,  they  were  surprised  by  a party  of  rebels, 
variously  estimated  at  from  2,000  down  to  80  men,  the  true  number, 
from  best  accounts,  not  being  less  than  80  nor  over  200  men.  That  our 
men,  or  at  least  the  largest  portion  of  them,  made  an  unnecessary

[af.XVHI.]  SKIRMISH  NEAR  SAINT  ERANCISVILLE,  MO. 

arnpede  and  inexcusable  retreat  there  can  be  no  question.  The  fault 
’ it  is,  I believe,  universally  attributed  to  the  officer  in  command  of 
ie  expedition,  whether  justly  or  not  I do  not  pretend  to  say.  I wish, 
jwever,  to  represent  the  case  so  far  as  to  do  justice  to  Captain  Leeper 
id  a part  of  his  company,  who  by  their  dauntless  courage  and  heroic 
induct  on  the  occasion  prevented  our  force  from  being  involved  in  the

When  the  surprise  was  made  our  whole  force  was  just  mounted  and 
bout  to  make  a forward  movement.  Captain  Leeper  immediately  ordered 
is  men  to  dismount  and  form,  which  was  done  by  most  of  his  men,  and  im 
Mediately  engaged  the  enemy.  By  orders  of  the  commanding  officer  the 
:her  troops  moved  a few  yards  in  advance  of  the  position  which  they 
bcupied,  and  instead  of  their  forming  and  charging,  as  they  had  a good 
jiance  to  do,  and  by  which  movement,  too,  they  would  have  secured 
very  one  of  the  rebels  as  prisoners,  they  turned  around  and  broke  back 
irougk  the  lane  where  Captain  Leeper  and  his  men  were  fighting,  run- 
ling  over  and  breaking  that  line,  thereby  causing  part  of  keeper’s  men 
i join  in  the  stampede  (panic  they  call  it),  and  leaving  him  with  only 
bout  25  men  with  which  to  contend  against  the  enemy.  Leeper  stood 
is  ground  with  the  few  men  left  him  and  prevented  the  enemy  from 
ursuing  the  fugitives ; and  at  last,  when  the  enemy  turned  back  and 
jft,  he  followed  on  after  our  men,  gathering  up  some  of  their  arms  and 
lothing  which  they  had  disencumbered  themselves  of  in  their  flight, 
[e  left  1 killed  and  2 wounded  on  the  field  and  lost  6 taken  prisoners, 
he  prisoners  taken  were  those  of  Captain  keeper’s  men,  who  had  been 
nocked  down  and  run  over  by  Major  Clendenning  and  his  men  as  they 
irned  and  fled  from  the  enemy,  they  not  being  able  to  recover  before 
ie  enemy  got  up  that  far — which  was  as  far,  too,  as  he  ever  advanced, 
japtain  Leeper  feels  a little  sore  under  this  defeat,  but  every  one  who 
oticed  Captain  keeper’s  conduct  on  the  field  of  combat  does  him  the 
'istice  to  say  that  he  acted  bravely  and  as  co©lly  as  if  no  fight  was 
oing  on,  giving  his  orders  to  his  men  and  seeing  that  they  were  as 
ell  disposed  as  they  could  be,  and  also  calling  to  the  fugitives  to  come 
ack ; that  they  could  whip  them  if  they  would  come  back ; and  he 
ow  says  that  if  only  the  whole  of  his  own  company  had  remained  they 
ould  have  been  the  conquerors  instead  of  the  vanquished. 

It  is  not  my  place  to  write  a report  of  this  transaction  ; that  is  the 
uty  of  the  proper  officer.  I only  want  to  have  justice  done  to  an 
ffieer  who  under  so  unfavorable  circumstances  did  his  whole  duty ; 
nd  as  Captain  keeper’s  company  is  a part  of  the  Missouri  Militia,  of 
hich  you  have  the  chief  command,  I thought  it  would  not  be  con  si  fi- 
red out  of  place  for  me  in  this  way  to  bring  his  acts  to  your  notice, 
'aptain  Leeper,  I have  no  doubt,  is  wishing  to  merit  and  obtain  a 
igher  command  than  he  now  holds,  and  it  is  the  opinion  of  all  who 
now  how  bravely  and  honorably  he  did  his  duty  on  the  occasion,  and 
etting  off  with  so  small  a loss  (1  killed  and  2 wounded),  that  he  has 
hown  himself  worthy  of  the  confidence  of  those  who  have  bestowed 
pon  him  the  office  he  now  holds. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

ALBERT  JACKSOX. 
General  John  M.  Schofield,  Saint  Louis.

Report  of  Brig.  Gen.  Samuel  R.  Curtis , U.  S.  Army.

Camp  Halleclc , February  27,  1862. 

Captain  : A cavalry  force  of  Texas  Rangers  turned  my  flank  and 
surprised  Captain  Montgomery  at  Keetsville,  killing  2 men,  taking 
60  or  70  horses,  and  burning  some  5 sutler  wagons.  The  enemy’s

Arkansas  seem  quite -willing  to  rally  under  the  old  flag;  but  they 
fear  the  united  forces  of  Price,  Van  Dorn,  McCulloch,  and  Pike  may 
return  and  force  them  to  be  secessionists  as  before.

No.  2. 

Report  of  Col.  Clad:  Wright , Sixth  Missouri  Cavalry. 

Headquarters  Sixth  Missouri  Cavalry, 

Cassville , Mo.,  February  27,  1862. 

General  : I left  Camp  Halleck  at  10  o’clock  a.  m.,  and  pressed  for- 
ward in  the  direction  of  Keetsville  by  forced  marches.  I learned, 
however,  before  reaching  there  that  500  Texas  Rangers  had  attacked 
Captain  Montgomery.  I still  pressed  forward,  and  on  my  arrival  there 
learned  that  the  captain  had  fallen  back  on  Cassville,  and  that  that 
point  was  threatened  It  was  after  dark,  but  I at  once  determined  to 
join  the  forces  at  this  place,  where  I arrived  at  9 o’clock  p.  m.  last 
night.  The  particulars  of  the  attack  1 learn  from  the  captain  to  be  as 
follows : I 

About  11  o’clock  on  the  night  of  the  25th  some  500  mounted  men, 
well  armed,  supposed  to  be  Texas  Rangers,  made  a descent  upon  their 
camp  from  the  right  and  left  through  the  brush,  riding  down  the  picket 
and  guards,  and  commenced  a general  fire  upon  the  men  asleep  in  camp. 
The  captain  rallied  his  force  on  foot  and  a general  fight  ensued.  A 
portion  of  our  men,  however,  were  cut  off*,  but  the  remainder  stood 
their  ground  and  three  times  repulsed  the  enemy.  After  about  twenty 
minutes,  however,  the  enemy’s  superior  force  being  about  to  surround 
our  force,  the  captain  fell  back  under  cover  of  the  brush  and  main- 
tained his  position  and  held  the  town,  the  enemy  retiring. 

On  yesterday  morning,  after  the  enemy  had  all  left,  our  men  found 
that  the  enemy  had  cut  loose  and  stampeded  some  40  of  their  horses. 
The  captain  and  a portion  of  his  men  fell  back  to  Cassville  for  assist- 
ance, leaving  Lieutenant  Montgomery  and  the  remainder  of  the  men

New  Madrid,  Mo.,  April  9,  1862. 

The  canal  across  the  peninsula  opposite  Island  No.  10,  and  for  tin 
idea  of  which  I am  indebted  to  Gen.  Schuyler  Hamilton,  was  completed 
by  Colonel  Bissell’s  Engineer  Regiment,  and  four  steamers  broughi 
through  on  the  night  of  the  6th.  The  heavy  batteries  I had  throwi 
up  below  Tiptonville  completely  commanded  the  lowest  point  of  the 
high  ground  on  the  Tennessee  shore,  entirely  cutting  off  the  enemy7* 
retreat  by  water.  His  retreat  by  land  has  never  been  possible  througl 
the  swamps. 

On  the  night  of  the  4th  Captain  Walke,  of  the  Navy,  ran  the  enemy7* 
batteries  at  Island  No.  10  with  the  gunboat  Carondelet  and  reportec 
to  me  here.  On  the  night  of  the  6th  the  gunboat  Pittsburgh  also  rar 
the  blockade. 

Our  transports  were  brought  into  the  river  from  the  bayou,  wherd 
they  had  been  kept  concealed,  at  daylight  on  the  7th,  and  Paine’s  divisj 
ion  loaded.  The  canal  has  been  a prodigiously  laborious  work.  II 
was  12  miles  long,  6 miles  of  which  were  through  heavy  timber,  which 
had  to  be  sawed  off  by  hand  4 feet  under  water.  The  enemy  has  lined 
the  opposite  shore  with  batteries,  extending  from  Island  No.  10  tc 
Tiptonville,  Meriwether  Landing,  to  prevent  the  passage  of  the  riven 
by  this  army.  I directed  Captain  Walke  to  run  down  with  the  two 
gunboats  at  daylight  on  the  7th  to  the  point  selected  for  crossing,  and 
silence  the  enemy’s  batteries  near  it.  He  performed  the  service  gal 
lantly,  and  I here  bear  testimony  to  the  thorough  and  brilliant  mannei 
in  which  the  officer  discharged  liis  difficult  duties  with  me,  and  to  tin 
hearty  and  earnest  zeal  with  which  $t  all  hazards  he  co-operated  wit! 
me. ' 

As  soon  as  he  signaled  me  the  boats  containing  Paine’s  divisioi 
moved  out  and  commenced  to  cross  the  river.  The  passage  of  this 
wide,  furious  river  by  our  large  force  was  one  of  the  most  magnificent 
spectacles  I ever  witnessed.  By  12  o’clock  that  night  (the  7th)  all  the 
forces  designed  to  cross  the  river  were  over,  without  delay  or  accident 
As  we  commenced  to  cross,  the  enemy  began  to  evacuate  Island  No.  1C 
and  his  pontoons  along  the  shore.  The  divisions  w ere  pushed  forw  ard 
to  Tiptonville  as  fast  as  they  landed,  Paine’s  leading.  The  enemy  was 
driven  before  him,  and  although  they  made  several  attempts  to  form 
line  of  battle  and  make  a stand,  Paine  did  not  once  deploy  his  column. 
The  enemy  was  pushed  all  night  vigorously,  until  at  4 a.  m.  he  was 
driven  back  upon  the  swamp  and  forced  to  surrender. 

Three  generals,  seven  colonels,  seven  regiments,  several  battalions 
of  infantry,  five  companies  of  artillery,  over  100  heavy  siege  guns,  24 
pieces  of  field  artillery,  an  immense  quantity  of  ammunition  and  sup 
plies,  and  several  thousand  stand  of  small-arms,  a great  number  oi 
tents,  horses,  w agons,  &c.,  have  fallen  into  our  hands. 

Before  abandoning  Island  No.  10  the  enemy  sunk  the  gunboat  Gram  j 
pus  and  six  of  his  transports.  These  last  I am  raising  and  expect  t<J 
have  ready  for  service  in  a few  days.  The  famous  floating  battery  waei 


; hap.  XVIII.]  NEW  MADRID,  MO.,  AND  ISLAND  NO.  10,  BTC.  79 

scuttled  and  turned  adrift,  witli  all  her  guns  aboard.  She  was  captured 
and  run  aground  in  shoal  water  by  our  forces  at  New  Madrid. 

Our  success  is  complete  and  overwhelming.  Our  troops,  as  I expected, 
jehaved  gloriously.  I will  in  my  full  report  endeavor  to  do  full  justice 
:o  all. 

Brigadier- Generals  Paine,  Stanley,  and  Hamilton  crossed  the  river 
md  conducted  their  divisions  with  untiring  activity  and  skill.  I am 
especially  indebted  to  them. 

General  Paine,  fortunate  in  having  the  advance,  exhibited  unusual 
rigor  and  courage,  and  had  the  satisfaction  to  receive  the  surrender  of 
die  enemy. 

Of  Colonel  Bissell,  Engineer  Regiment,  I can  hardly  say  too  much. 
Full  of  resource,  untiring  and  determined,  he  labored  night  and  day, 
md  completed  work  which  will  be  a monument  of  enterprise  and  skill. 

We  have  crossed  this  great  river  with  a large  army,  the  banks  of 
ivhich  were  lined  with  batteries  of  the  enemy  to  oppose  our  passage  ; 
jave  pursued  and  captured  all  his  forces  and  material  of  war,  and  have 
aot  lost  a man  nor  met  with  an  accident. 

JNO.  POPE,  Major-General. 

Major-General  Halleck. 


Preface  to  report  of  Brig.  Gen.  John  Pope  of  operations  which  resulted  in 
the  capture  of  Ne  w Madrid .* 

At  this  time  the  rebel  armies  in  the  West  occupied  a line  of  fortified 
positions  from  Bowling  Green  to  Columbus,  Ky.  This  line  was  broken 
by  General  Grant  at  Forts  Henry  and  Donelson  by  the  16th  of  Feb- 
ruary, 1862.  His  operations  compelled  the  evacuation  of  Columbus, 
>n  the  east  bank  of  the  Mississippi  River,  which  place,  though  strongly 
fortified,  was  turned  by  the  advance  of  Grant  up  the  Tennessee  and 
Cumberland  Rivers.  This  result  had  been  for  some  time  foreseen  by 
rhe  rebel  generals,  and  General  Beauregard,  who  had  been  assigned 
to  command,  selected  Island  No.  10,  60  miles  below  Columbus,  as  the 
strong  place  where  the  possession  of  the  Mississippi  River  was  first  to 
oe  contested.  The  place  was  strongly  fortified,  mounted  with  150 
pieces  of  heavy  artillery,  and  garrisoned  by  about  9,000  men.  I do 
not  mean  that  the  island  itself  contained  this  garrison  and  these  guns, 
but  that  they  were  disposed  in  the  system  of  defenses  for  the  island, 
m and  around  it,  on  both  banks  of  the  Mississippi  River. 

New  Madrid  was  manifestly  the  weak  point  of  this  system,  and 
against  that  place  our  first  operations  were  to  be  directed. 

I was  recalled  to  Saint  Louis  from  Central  Missouri  on  the  14th  of 
February,  1862,  and  on  the  18th  General  Halleck  pointed  out  to  me 
the  situation  at  New  Madrid  and  Island  No.  10,  and  directed  me  to 
organize  and  command  a force  for  their  reduction. 

On  the  19th  I left  Saint  Louis  for  Cairo,  111.,  which  was  then  believed 
to  be  threatened  from  Columbus,  with  orders  to  assume  command  at 
that  place  in  case  any  movement  against  it  was  made  by  the  enemy, 
but  as  soon  as  apprehension  of  such  a movement  was  at  an  end  to  pro- 
ceed with  my  operations  against  New  Madrid. 

On  the  21st  of  February,  finding  that  the  fear  of  an  advance  upon 
Cairo  was  groundless,  I left  that  place  on  a steamboat,  with  a guard  of

the  river  between  Saint  Louis  and  Helena,  in  Arkansas,  and  was  on 
that  account  selected  as  a base  of  operations  against  New  Madrid 
from  which  place  it  is  distant  by  laud miles.  The  bluff's,  how- 

ever, retreat  directly  to  the  west  from  Commerce,  leaving  an  alluvial 
swampy  bottom  land,  at  least  30  miles  wide,  along  the  river  below 
that  place.  A dismal  and  almost  impassable  swamp,  known  as  tin 
Great  Mingo  Swamp,  extends  all  the  way  from  Commerce  to  New 
Madrid.  At  that  season  of  the  year  the  banks  of  the  Mississippi 
were  overflowed,  and  the  river  spread  out  for  miles  on  both  sides 
beyond  its  bed.  The  whole  country  tor  30  miles  west  of  the  river  was 
under  water.  At  many  places  the  water  was  8 or  10  feet  deep  and 
everywhere  from  1 to  5 feet  deep.  An  old  embankment,  upon  wliicl 
a corduroy  road  had  been  built,  extended  part  of  the  way  to  New 
Madrid,  but  the  road  had  not  been  repaired  for  years,  and  was  in  i 
very  bad  condition,  and  in  many  places  entirely  impassable.  Tin 
weather  was  cold  and  wet.  A drizzling  snow  and  rain  was  falling 
upon  us,  and  adding  to  our  almost  insuperable  difficulties  from  tin 
time  we  marched  from  Commerce  until  we  reached  New  Madrid.  3 
can  only  account  for  the  fact  that  the  enemy  attempted  no  oppositioi 
to  our  march  by  their  belief  that  the  country  at  that  season  of  over- 
flow was  entirely  impracticable. 

I landed  at  Commerce  on  the  night  of  the  21st  of  February,  1862,  will 
the  small  escort  I have  mentioned.  Regiments  were  sent  me  rapidh 
from  Saint  Louis,  from  Cincinnati,  and  from  Cairo ; most  of  them  en 
tirely  raw,  having  had  their  arms  first  placed  in  their  hands  when  tbej 
embarked  on  the  steamer  to  join  me.  Few  of  them  had  ever  served  a 
all,  and  as  they  had  never  served  together  or  been  even  brigaded,  I was 
forced  to  make  a complete  organization  of  them  at  Commerce.  In  tliii 
difficult  task  I was  so  ably  assisted  by  Generals  Schuyler  Hamilton 
Stanley,  Palmer,  and  Granger  that  within  one  week  of  the  day  I landet 
almost  alone  at  Commerce  we  began  our  march  to  New  Madrid.  This 
organization  was  the  nucleus  of  the  corps  afterwards  designated  tin 
Army  of  the  Mississippi,  widely  known  and  greatly  distinguished  ii 
the  West  for  its  discipline,  its  gallantry,  and  its  effectiveness,  and  fo 
the  soldierly  and  cordial  good  feeling  which,  characterized  both  officer; 
and  men. 

It  is  not  only  proper,  but  it  is  my  duty,  to  say  here  that  during  nn 
whole  experience  in  this  war  I have  never  seen  troops  which  woul( 
compare  with  this  little  army.  Of  the  mobility  and  esprit  de  corps , o 
courage  in  battle  and  patience  and  fortitude  under  exposure,  labor,  am 
privation,  and  of  the  cordial  harmony  which  existed  among  the  officer 
and  men,  from  the  highest  to  the  lowest,  the  services  and  the  reputatioi 
of  this  little  army,  from  the  beginning  to  the  end  of  the  war,  whet  he: 
acting  together  or  separated  and  serving  in  other  organizations,  ar< 
sufficient  evidence.  I cannot  at  this  day  think  of  them  and  recall  my 
association  with  them  as  their  commander  without  emotions  whicl 
could  not  be  expressed  in  such  a paper  as  this.  As  long  as  I live 
shall  never  cease  to  remember  them,  nor  fail  to  acknowledge  the  deei 
and  lasting  gratitude  I owe  them  for  the  cordial  support  they  gave  m< 
while  I served  with  them,  and  for  their  earnest  sympathy  and  unfalter 
ing  confidence  during  the  most  trying  and  darkest  period  of  my  life] 
1 esteem  it  the  highest  honor  to  have  belonged  to  this  little  army,  and 
regard  every  officer  and  soldier  connected  with  it  as  a personal  lrieud| 
from  whom  neither  time  nor  circumstances  can  ever  estrange  me.

After  incredible  labor  and  exposure,  wading  through  the  swamps,  and 
l many  places  dragging  wagons  and  artillery  by  hand,  we  appeared 
efore  New  Madrid  on  the  3d  of  March,  and  at  once  drove  in  the  pickets 
ad  outposts  of  the  enemy  and  closely  invested  the  place.

[adrid,  the  reports  of  division  and  brigade  commanders,  and  my  official 
arrespondence  with  General  Halleck  by  letter  and  telegraph.  I also 
btach  hereto  a return  of  the  force  engaged,  which  exhibits  in  detail  its 
atire  organization  and  every  regiment  of  which  it  was  composed.

General  : I have  the  honor  to  submit  for  the  information  of  the

I arrived  before  the  town  with  the  forces  under  my  command  on 
[onday,  the  3d  instant.  I found  the  place  occupied  by  five  regiments 
f infantry  and  several  companies  of  artillery.  One  bastioned  earth- 
ork,  mounting  14  heavy  guns,  about  a half  a mile  below  the  town, 
ad  another  irregular  work  at  the  upper  end  of  the  town,  mounting  7 
ieces  of  heavy  artillery,  together  with  lines  of  intrenchments  between 
lem,  constituted  the  defensive  works.  Six  gunboats,  carrying  from  4 
) 8 heavy  guns  each,  were  anchored  along  the  shore  between  the  upper 
ad  lower  redoubts.  The  country  is  perfectly  level  for  miles  around 
le  place,  and  as  the  river  was  so  high  that  the  guns  of  the  gunboats 
•oked  directly  over  the  banks,  the  approaches  to  the  town  for  several 
ales  were  commanded  by  direct  and  cross-fire  from  at  least  60  guns  of 
eavy  caliber.  It  would  not  have  been  difficult  to  carry  the  intrench- 
lents,  but  it  would  have  been  attended  with  heavy  loss,  and  we  should 
ot  have  been  able  to  hold  the  place  half  an  hour  exposed  to  the  destruc- 
ve  fire  of  the  gunboats. 

As  there  seemed  no  immediate  hope  of  the  appearance  of  our  gun- 
aats,  it  became  necessary  to  bring  down  a few  heavy  guns  by  land  to

round  and  into  several  parts  of  the  town.  Some  brisk  skirmishes

as  found  impossible  to  induce  them  to  trust  any  considerable  force  of 
leir  infantry  outside  of  their  intrenchments.  As  soon  as  I found  it 
ouid  be  necessary  to  await  the  arrival  of  our  heavy  guns  I deter- 
ined  to  occupy  some  point  on  the  river  below,  and  establish  our  small 
uns,  if  possible,  in  suclrposition  as  to  blockade  the  river,  so  far  as 
■ansports  were  concerned,  and  to  cut  off  supplies  and  re-enforcements 
>r  the  enemy  from  below.  Point  Pleasant,  12  miles  below,  was  se- 
eted  as  being  in  a rich  agricultural  region,  and  being  the  terminus  of 
le  plank  road  from  the  interior  of  Arkansas.  I accordingly  threw 
•rward  Colonel  Plummer,  Eleventh  Missouri,  to  that  point,  with  three

sland  No.  10  lies  at  the  bottom  of  a great  bend  of  the  Mississippi,

m Island  No.  10  to  Tiptonville  is  5 miles,  while  by  water  it  is  27. 
Commencing  at  Hickman,  a great  swamp,  which  afterwards  becomes 
Afoot  Lake,  extends  along  the  left  bank  of  the  Mississippi  and  dis- 
trges  its  waters  into  the  river  40  miles  below  Tiptonville,  leaving  the

ee  sides  and  Eeelfoot  Lake  and  the  great  swamps  which  border  it 
the  other.  A good  road  leads  from  Island  No.  10  along  the  west 
lk  of  Eeelfoot  Lake  to  Tiptonville.  The  only  means  of  supply,  there- 
3,  for  the  forces  at  and  around  Island  No.  10  in  this  peninsula  were 
the  river.  When  the  river  was  blockaded  at  New  Madrid  supplies

neck  of  the  peninsula  by  land.  There  was  no  communication  with

At  8 or  9 o’clock  that  night  (the  7th)  the  small  force  abandoned  on

he  divisions  were  pushed  forward  to  Tiptonville  as  fast  as  they  were

mes  near  that  place,  but  Paine  did  not  once  deploy  his  columns.  By 
lidnight  all  our  forces  were  across  the  river  and  pushing  forward  rap- 
ily  to  Tiptonville. 

The  enemy,  retreating  before  Paine  and  from  Island  No.  10,  met  at 
iptonville  during  the  night  in  great  confusion,  and  were  driven  back

ntly  unable  to  resist,  they  laid  down  their  arms  and  surrendered  at 
iscretion.  They  were  so  scattered  and  confused  that  it  was  several 
ays  before  anything  like  an  accurate  account  of  their  number  could

Meantime  I had  directed  Col.  W.  L.  Elliott,  of  the  Second  Iowa  Cav-

ossibly  could.  He  reached  there  before  sunrise  that  morning,  the  8th, 
n d took  possession  of  the  encampments,  the  immense  quantities  of 
tores  and  supplies,  and  of  all  the  enemy’s  batteries  on  the  main  land,

aking  possession  of  the  steamers  not  sunk  or  injured  he  remained 
ntil  the  forces  from  the  flotilla  landed.  As  Colonel  Buford  was  in

nd  proceeded  to  scour  the  country  in  the  direction  of  Tiptonville,  along 
teelfoot  Lake,  as  directed.

of  small-arms,  tents  for  12,000  men,  several  wharf-boat  loads  of  provis- 
ions,  an  immense  quantity  of  ammunition  of  all  kinds,  many  hundred 
horses  and  mules,  with  wagons  and  harness,  &c.,  are  among  the  spoils. 
Very  few,  if  any,  of  the  enemy  escaped,  and  only  by  wading  and  swim- 
ming through  the  swamps.  1 

The  conduct  of  the  troops  was  splendid  throughout,  as  the  results  ot 
this  operation  and  its  whole  progress  very  plainly  indicate.  We  haver 
crossed  this  great  river,  the  banks  of  which  were  lined  with  batteries! 
and  defended  by  7,000  men.  We  have  pursued  and  captured  the  whole 
force  of  the  enemy  and  all  his  supplies  and  material  of  war,  and  have 
again  recrossed  and  reoccupied  the  camps  at  New  Madrid,  without  los- j 
ing  a man  or  meeting  with  any  accident.  Such  results  bespeak  effi- 
ciency.  good  conduct,  high  discipline,  and  soldierly  deportment  of  the 
best  character  far  more  conclusively  than  they  can  be  exhibited  m 
pitched  battle  or  the  storming  of  fortified  places.  Patience,  willing  | 
labor,  endurance  of  hardship  and  privation  for  long  periods,  cheertul  ! 
and  prompt  obedience,  order  and  discipline,  bravery  and  spirit,  are  the 
qualities  which  these  operations  have  developed  in  the  forces  under  my  i 
command,  and  which  assure  for  them  a brilliant  and  successful  career 
in  arms.  It  is  difficult  to  express  the  feeling  which  such  conduct  has 
occasioned  one  fortunate  enough  to  be  the  commander  of  such  troops. 
There  are  few  material  obstacles  within  the  range  of  warfare  which  a 
man  of  courage  and  spirit  would  hesitate  to  encounter  with  such  a force. 

To  the  division  and  brigade  commanders,  whose  reports  I transmit,  I 
leave  the  grateful  privilege  of  designating  in  detail  the  forces  engaged 
in  these  operations.  Generals  Paine,  Stanley,  Hamilton,  and  Plummer 
crossed  the  river,  together  with  a portion  of  General  Granger’s  cavalry 
division,  under  Col.  W.  L.  Elliott,  Second  Iowa  Cavalry.  To  all  these 
officers  I am  deeply  indebted  for  their  efficient  and  cordial  aid  in  every 
portion  of  our  operations.  They  conducted  their  divisions  with  eminent 
skill  and  vigor,  and  to  them  I am  largely  indebted  for  the  discipline 
and  efficiency  of  this  command. 

General  Paine,  fortunate  in  having  the  advance,  exhibited  conspicu- 
ous gallantry  and  vigor,  and  had  the  satisfaction  to  receive  the  sur- 
render of  the  enemy.  General  Palmer  vras  posted  ten  days  before  the 
final  operations  in  support  and  in  charge  of  the  battery  below  Tipton- 
ville.  Throughout  he  was  prompt  and  active  in  the  discharge  of  his 

duties.  . , „ 

Of  Colonel  Bissell,  Engineer  Regiment,  and  his  regiment  1 can  hardly 
say  too  much.  Untiring  and  determined,  no  difficulties  discouraged 
them  and  no  labor  was  too  much  for  their  energy.  They  have  con- 
ducted and  completed  a work  which  will  be  memorable  in  the  history 
of  this  war. 

My  own  personal  staff — Major  Butler,  assistant  ad  jutant-general  j 
Major  Morgan  and  Captain  Marshall,  aides-de-camp;  Maj.  J.  M.  Corse, 
inspector-general,  and  Surg.  O.  W.  Nixon,  medical  director — rendered 
me  important  service,  and  were  in  all  respects  zealous  and  efficient. 

Our  success  was  complete  and  overwhelming,  and  it  gives  me  pro- 
found satisfaction  to  report  that  it  was  accomplished  without  loss  of  life. 

I am,  general,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

’ ’ JNO.  POPE, 

Major- General , Commanding . 

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

Commanding  Department  of  the  Mississippi , Saint  Louis , Mo.

Report  of  Surg.  0.  W.  Nixon , IT.  8.  Army , Medical  Director . 

New  Madrid,  March  16,  1862. 

General  : I have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  list  of  killed  and 
wounded  of  your  command  in  the  recent  action  with  the  enemy  in- 
trenched at  New  Madrid.*  The  wounds,  with  two  or  three  exceptions, 
were  severe.  Two  died  in  a few  hours  after  receiving  their  injuries 
and  two  others  the  next  day.  The  wounded  are  carefully  nursed,  and 
every  comfort  at  our  command  lias  been  given  them. 

The  different  division  and  regimental  surgeons  have  lost  no  opportu- 
nity, both  on  the  held  and  in  the  hospital,  of  ministering  to  the  comfort 
of  the  wounded. 

I am,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

O.  W.  NIXON, 

Maj.  Gen.  John  Pope.  Acting  Medical  Director.

OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chap.  XVIII. 


No.  5. 

Report  of  Capt.  Joseph  A.  Mower , First  United  States  Infantry , com.- 

manding  siege  train. 

Camp  before  New  Madrid, 

March  15,  1862. 

Major  : I have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  compliance  with  orders  from 
General  Pope,  I took  command  of  the  siege  train  on  the  evening  of  the 
12th  instant,  and  proceeded  with  it  to  the  position  that  had  been  assigned. 
I had  under  my  command  Companies  A and  H,  First  United  States 
Infantry.  I placed  Company  H in  the  battery  on  the  left  (Battery  No. 
1),  in  which  were  one  8-inch  howitzer  and  one  24-pounder,  and  Company 
A in  the  battery  on  the  right  (Battery  No.  2).  This  battery  had  two 
24-pounders.  I put  this  battery  under  the  immediate  command  of  Lieu- 
tenant Fletcher,  commanding  Company  A.  Lieutenant  Beeder  was! 
also  with  this  company.  I was  directed  by  General  Stanley  to  open 
fire  on  the  enemy  at  daylight  on  the  13th,  which  I did  from  both  bat-; 
teries.  Our  fire  was  briskly  replied  to  by  the  fort,  which  was  in  front,; 
and  the  gunboats,  which  took  position  both  in  front  and  towards  oui 
left  flank.  They  threw  rifled  shot,  shell,  and  round  shot.  At  about  10 
o’clock  a.  m.  a round  shot  struck  one  of  the  guns  in  Battery  No.  1,  break  ! 
ing  a piece  out  of  it,  and  killing  1 man  and  wounding  6.  In  the  after- 
noon the  gunboats  withdrew  from  our  front,  and  taking  position  beyond 
the  reach  of  our  guns,  kept  up  a steady  fire,  with  occasional  intermis 
sions,  until  sundown. 

On  the  morning  of  the  14th  I was  preparing  to  open  fire  again,  when] 
I received  an  order  from  General  Hamilton  not  to  fire,  as  a flag  of  truce] 
was  approaching.  Shortly  after  General  Hamilton  arrived  at  the  bat 
teries,  and  desired  me  to  take  20  men  of  my  company  and  ascertain 
whether  or  not  the  fort  had  been  abandoned.  Having  no  colors  belong 
ing  to  the  First  Infantry,  I was  furnished  with  the  regimental  colors  ol 
a regiment  of  volunteers  to  raise  upon  the  fort.  I proceeded  to  the 
fort  and  found  that  the  enemy  had  deserted  it.  I raised  the  flag  upon 
the  ramparts  and  took  possession  of  the  works.  I found  that  two  oJ 
the  enemy’s  guns  had  been  dismounted  and  another  struck  and  badly 
injured  by  our  fire.  I am  unable  to  say  what  damage  was  done  to  th(j 
gunboats.  Lieutenants  Fletcher  and  Beeder  displayed  great  zeal  am 
activity  during  the  whole  engagement,  although  they,  as  well  as  tin 
whole  command,  were  nearly  exhausted  by  fatigue  and  exposure.  1 
regret  to  have  to  state  that  Lieutenant  Beeder,  after  having  exhibitei 
so  much  zeal  in  the  performance  of  his  duty,  was  unfortunately  wounded 
by  the  accidental  discharge  of  his  revolver,  and  was  consequently  de 
prived  of  the  opportunity  of  entering  the  enemy’s  works  with  his  com 
pany.  Sergeants  Connelly  and  Downey,  of  Company  A,  Corporal  Young  i 
man  and  Privates  Morgan  and  Burke,  of  Company  H,  performed  theft! 
duty  at  the  guns  with  great  coolness  and  skill ; First  Sergeant  Libby 
of  Company  H,  was  very  attentive  to  his  duties,  and  deserves  mucl 
credit,  as  do  all  of  the  men  of  the  two  companies. 

I inclose  herewith  a list  of  the  killed,  wounded,  and  missing.* 

I am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOS.  A.  MOWER, 

Captain,  First  Infantry , Commanding  Siege  Train . I 

Maj.  Speed  Butler, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General. 

* Nominal  list  omitted  shows  1 killed,  6 wounded,  and  1 missing.

No.  6. 

Report  of  Map  Warren  L.  Lothrop , First  Missouri  Light  Artillery, 


Headquarters  Artillery, 

Camp  near  New  Madrid , Mo.,  March  10,  1802. 

Sir  : I liave  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  the  opera- 
ions  of  the  artillery  under  my  command  during*  the  investment  and 
vacuation  of  New  Madrid.  Having  been  ordered  by  the  general  com- 
uanding  to  make  a reconnaissance  of  the  enemy’s  works  and  select  a 
>osition  to  plant  a siege  battery,  I went  down  on  the  11th  instant,  with 
"apt.  L.  H.  Marshall,  First  Infantry,  and  a squadron  of  dragoons,  within 
bbout  a half  mile  of  the  enemy’s  works.  From  this  position  (northwest 
rom  the  town)  I could  see  distinctly  their  gunboats  and  lower  fort.  I 
letermined  at  once,  from  my  observation,  where  to  plant  the  battery, 
nd  on  the  12th  instant  w ent  to  the  same  point  again,  in  company  with 
Colonel  Bissell,  of  the  Engineers,  and  Captain  Marshall,  to  satisfy  my 
elf  that  I was  not  mistaken  in  the  selection  of  the  ground.  Colonel 
lissell  and  Captain  Marshall  thought  the  position  to  be  a good  one. 
-he  same  evening,  at  dusk,  Colonel  Bissell  and  myself,  with  Colonel 
[organ’s  brigade,  the  Tenth  and  Sixteenth  Illinois  Regiments,  went 
lown  within  about  500  yards  in  rear  of  the  position  wiiere  the  battery 
fas  to  be  established.  At  this  point  one  regiment  was  deployed  as 
kirmishers  and  the  other  furnished  with  spades  and  shovels.  The 
kirmishers  advanced  about  50  yards  in  front  of  the  men  in  rear  with 
pades  and  shovels,  until  the  latter  arrived  on  the  ground  w here  the 
•attery  was  to  be  established.  In  a few  moments  the  work  was  laid 
ut  and  the  men  put  to  work.  At  daylight  the  work  was  completed, 
nd  three  24-pounder  siege  guns  and  one  8-inch  howitzer  put  in  posi- 
ion.  This  work  was  undoubtedly  completed  before  the  enemy  had 
ny  knowledge  of  it.  At  daylight  in  the  morning  the  enemy’s  fort& 
nd  gunboats  opened  upon  our  battery  and  kept  up  a constant  can- 
onading  until  about  12  o’clock  m.  After  this  they  continued  to  firer 
t intervals  until  sundown.  Captain  Mower,  of  the  First  Infantry 
nd  Lieutenant  Reeder,  with  Companies  A and  H,  served  the  gunsr 
nd  all  conducted  themselves  in  the  most  gallant  and  creditable  man- 
er.  Captain  Mower  remained  in  the  battery  until  the  town  was  evac- 
ated  by  the  enemy,  and  then  placed  our  siege  guns  in  the  enemy’s* 
>rt. 

During  the  investment  of  New' Madrid,  Capt.  A.  M.  Powell,  First  Mis- 
3uri  Light  Artillery ; Capt.  Henry  Hescock,  same  regiment ; Capt.  N.. 

Spoor,  Second  Iowa  Light  Artillery,  Captain  Sands,  Eleventh  Ohio* 
ight  Artillery  j and  Lieutenant  Darling’s  battery,  Company  F,  Second 
artillery,  U.  S.  Army,  were  frequently  under  the  enemy’s  tire,  and  all 
ehaved  in  a very  creditable  manner. 

Captain  Powell,  a few  days  after  our  arrival  in  front  of  New  Madrid, 
as  detached  from  the  command  and  went  to  Point  Pleasant  with  Col- 

nel  Plummer. 

I am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  L.  LOTHROP, 

Major , First  Missouri  Light  Artillery , Commanding  Artillery. 

Maj.  Speed  Butler, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General.

OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chap.  XVIII. 


No.  7. 

Report  of  Brig.  Gen.  David  S.  Stanley,  TJ.  S.  Army , commanding  First 

Division. 

Headquarters  First  Division, 

April  20,  1862. 

Major  : In  reporting  upon  the  part  taken  by  the  First  Division  of 
this  army  in  compelling  the  surrender  of  Island  No.  10  I have  the  honor 
to  state  that  I was  assigned  the  command  of  the  division  on  the  4th 
day  of  March,  and  on  the  same  night  a detachment  of  500  men,  com- 
manded by  Col.  J.  L.  Kirby  Smith,  Forty- third  Ohio  Volunteers,  made 
a reconnaissance  in  force,  and  after  cannonading  the  town  and  forts  for 
half  an  hour  retired  to  their  camp  without  loss.  Upon  the  6th  of  the 
same  month  my  entire  division,  consisting  of  the  First  Brigade,  Colonel 
Groesbeck  commanding,  and  the  Second  Brigade,  Col.  J.  L.  Kirby  Smith 
commanding,  by  the  order  of  the  major-general  commanding,  pushed 
our  way  into  the  town  of  New  Madrid  to  within  700  yards  of  the  upper 
fort,  driving  the  enemy’s  infantry;  but  at  this  point,  finding  ourselves 
under  a cross-fire  of  seven  gunboats  and  the  guns  of  both  the  forts, 
I deemed  it  proper  to  withdraw  my  troops.  We  were  for  half  an 
hour  under  a fierce  cannonade,  and,  strange  to  say,  suffered  only  in  3 
wounded.  J 

The  operations  of  the  13th  March,  in  which  my  division  had  the 
honor  to  bear  an  important  part,  have  already  been  reported  to  your 
office.*  The  time  elapsing  between  the  13th  of  March  and  the  7th  ol 
April  was  occupied  in  instructing  the  division  in  the  duties  of  outposts 
and  the  drill  of  the  battalion  and  brigade.  In  all  these  I am  happy  te- 
leport decided  progress. 

On  the  7th  my  division,  accompanied  by  Captain  Dees’  Michigan 
battery,  crossed  the  Mississippi  from  the  upper  fort  immediately  aftei 
the  crossing  of  General  Paine’s  division.  Waiting  for  the  head  ol 
General  Hamilton’s  division,  we  took  up  the  march  immediately  upon 
his  arrival,  and  moved  by  the  river  route  toward  Tipton ville.  Deserted 
camps  and  abandoned  artillery  indicated  a flying  enemy.  Night  com 
ing  on  very  dark  and  our  guide  being  uncertain  of  the  route,  the  com 
mand  was  bivouacked  until  morning,  when  a contraband  informed  me 
the  enemy  had  surrendered  to  General  Paine.  Subsequently  the  same 
day  we  crossed  the  New  Madrid  Bend  to  Island  No.  10.  Covering  the 
country  for  7 miles  perpendicular  to  the  main  road  with  skirmishers 
we  picked  up  about  40  prisoners.  All  the  houses  were  found  full® 
the  enemy’s  sick,  and  cannon,  ammunition,  tents,  wagons,  and  various 
material  of  war  were  found  scattered  through  the  bend.  These  we  liac 
no  means  to  move.  The  major-general  has  already  been  apprised  o 
these  facts.  _ A 

I transmit  inclosed  the  reports  of  Colonels  Groesbeck  and  Smith 
brigade  commanders. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  S.  STANLEY,

Captain  : I liave  the  honor  to  report  to  the  general  commanding 
be  First  Division  the  part  taken  in  the  late  action  before  New  Madrid 
y the  brigade  under  my  command,  consisting  of  the  Twenty- seventh 
nd  Thirty-ninth  Begiments  Ohio  Infantry. 

On  the  afternoon  of  the  12th  instant  I detailed  Companies  A and  F, 
wenty-seventh,  and  I and  H,  Thirty -ninth  Ohio,  to  drive  in  the  pick- 
bs  of  the  enemy,  hold  an  advanced  position,  and  cover  the  parties  de- 
nied to  plant  our  heavy  artillery.  He  drove  in  the  pickets,  and  took 
le  position  assigned  him  within  800  yards  of  the  enemy’s  gunboat  and 
rincipal  fort. 

At  3 o’clock  on  the  morning  of  the  13th  I moved  forward  with  my 
rigade  and  took  position  on  the  right  of  the  battery.  The  enemy’s 
kirmishers  immediately  commenced  firing  upon  us,  but  without  doing 
uy  injury.  A few  minutes  afterwards  our  artillery  opened  the  engage- 
icut,  and  the  brigade  was  ordered  to  fall  back  about  200  yards,  which 
did  in  good  order,  under  a heavy  fire  of  shot  and  shell  from  the  guns 
f the  fort.  While  lying  there  five  companies  of  the  Twenty-seventh 
hio  were  detached  to  take  a position  several  hundred  yards  to  the 
‘ft,  on  a road  leading  past  the  enemy’s  fort,  to  guard  against  any  flank 
lovement.  I then  moved  the  brigade  300  yards  to  the  left  and  took 
osition  within  easy  supporting  distance  of  the  battery,  where  the  slop- 
tg  bank  of  a bayou  afforded  considerable  protection  to  the  men,  who 
imained  thus  placed  during  the  rest  of  the  day.  The  firing  ceased 
bout  sunset.  Having  thrown  out  an  additional  company  of  pickets  in 
ont  of  the  extreme  left,  the  men  remained  in  their  position  till  day- 
ght,  when  I was  relieved. 

I take  pleasure  in  mentioning  the  good  conduct  of  my  command.  It 
shaved  with  great  coolness,  although  exposed  to  heavy  fire  the  whole 
ay. 


Considering  the  closeness  and  rapidity  of  the  firing,  the  casualties 
ere  remarkably  few,  viz,  1 killed,  3 severely  wounded  of  Twenty-sev- 
lth  Ohio,  and  1 very  slightly  wounded  of  Thirty -ninth  Ohio. 

I am,  captain,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOHN  GEOESBECK,

Headquarters  Second  Brigade,  First  Division, 

April  17,  1862. 

Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  the  move- 
ments of  this  brigade  at  the  capture  of  the  rebel  position  at  and  near 
Island  No.  10: 

The  brigade,  consisting  of  the  Forty-third  Ohio  Infantry,  Lieut.  Col. 
Wager  Swayne,  and  the  Sixty -third  Ohio  Infantry,  Col.  J.  W.  Sprague,! 
crossed  the  river  on  the  morning  of  the  7th  instant,  embarking  at  the 
upper  fort  at  New  Madrid,  and  landing  at  the  site  of  the  three-gun  rebel 
battery  just  captured  by  our  gunboats,  and  having  been  formed  in  line 
of  battle,  moved  forward  a half  mile  from  the  landing,  and  took  a posi- 
tion in  a wood  near  an  abandoned  rebel  encampment  of  two  regiments, 
apparently  quite  recently  evacuated.  A guard  of  20  men  was  placed 
over  the  property  here,  and  over  a few  prisoners,  who,  being  sick  or  in 
toxicated,  had  failed  to  escape  with  the  enemy.  A company  was  sent 
back  to  the  landing  to  render  assistance  and  support  to  the  rifle  battery 
of  Captain  Dees,  which  had  crossed  with  us.  We  remained  at  this  point 
about  an  hour,  until  joined  by  the  other  brigade  of  the  division  (the 
First,  Colonel  Groesbeck),  and  then  moved  in  the  direction  of  Tipton 
ville  to  the  support  of  General  Paine,  whose  division  was  in  advance.] 
The  brigade  bivouacked  about  an  hour  after  dark  at  a point  near  the] 
bank  of  the  river,  and  about  8 miles  below  the  point  where  the  landing] 
had  been  made. 

The  march  to  Tiptonville  was  resumed  in  the  morning  and  the  brigade] 
reached  there  about  noon.  The  enemy  had  already  surrendered,  with- 
out fighting,  to  the  advance  of  our  army,  and  the  brigade  was  placed  in  I 
position  as  part  of  the  guard  of  the  prisoners.  Two  hours  later  the! 
brigade  was  put  in  march  for  the  late  position  of  the  enemy  opposite 
Island  No.  10.  On  the  march  thither  the  country  between  the  road  and  1 
the  river  was  thoroughly  beaten  up  by  a strong  line  of  skirmishers 
under  Lieutenant- Colonel  Swayne,  and  several  prisoners  taken.  The] 
brigade  bivouacked  opposite  Island  No.  10  about  5 p.  m.  On  the  morn 
ing  of  the  9th  instant  the  brigade  was  moved,  with  the  rest  of  the  division, 
by  transport,  to  New  Madrid,  and  resumed  its  former  encampment. 

Very  respectfullv,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  L.  KIRBY  SMITH,

Report  of  Col.  John  W.  Sprague , Sixty -third  Ohio  Infantry. 

Headquarters  Sixty-third  Eegiment  O.  Y.  I., 

Camp  near  New  Madrid , Mo.,  March  14,  1862. 
Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  report  that  the  Sixty-third  Eegiment  O.  Y.  I., 
nder  my  command,  in  obedience  to  your  order,  left  camp  about  3 o’clock 
hursday  morning,  the  13th  instant,  and  marched  about  3 miles  to  a 
oint,  say,  southwest  of  the  town  of  New  Madrid,  and  distant  about  1 
tile,  and  was  there  deployed  in  line  of  battle  along  the  road,  by  your 
rder,  as  a part  of  the  support  of  a battery  planted  by  our  troops,  say, 
ne  hundred  rods  in  advance  of  our  line. 

Almost  immediately  after  taking  this  position  the  guns  of  our  bat- 
ales  opened  fire  upon  the  fort  and  gunboats  of  the  enemy,  to  which 
ley  replied  with  shot  and  shell.  As  soon  as  the  enemy’s  gunboats  got 
do  their  chosen  positions  it  was  found  that  the  position  of  the  regi- 
ent  under  my  command  was  exposed  to  the  cross-fire  of  at  least  one 
unboat  and  the  lower  or  principal  fort  of  the  enemy.  By  your  order 
moved  my  regiment  forward  about  25  rods  in  line  of  battle  and 
ilted  along  the  base  of  a very  slight  elevation.  While  this  new  posi 
on  did  not  remove  my  command  from  exposure  to  the  cross-fire  before 
entioned,  the  elevation  before  mentioned  afforded  a partial  protection, 
uring  the  forenoon  a few  shovels  were  procured,  and  in  a few  hours  a 
ench,  say  4 feet  wide  and  from  2 to  3 feet  deep,  was  excavated,  which 
lorded  increased  protection.  The  fire  of  the  enemy  continued  during 
le  entire  day,  with  occasional  intermissions.  At  night  the  fire  of  the 
iemy  ceased,  but  about  midnight  we  were  visited  by  a terrific  storm 
* rain,  accompanied  by  thunder  and  lightning.  Our  little  trench  irnme- 
ately  filled  with  water  and  all  were  soaked  by  the  falling  rain. 

At  daylight  next  morning  we  were  relieved,  having  occupied  the 
isition  over  twenty-four  hours,  exposed  to  a galling  fire  and  the  in- 
emency  of  the  weather. 

I have  no  casualties  to  report.  One  man,  Private  Thomas  King,  of 
ampany  IT,  Captain  Jackson,  was  sent  to  the  rear,  and  was  afterwards 
en  a short  distance  from  the  regiment  on  his  way  to  rejoin  his  com- 
my,  but  did  not  do  so ; he  is  still  missing. 

In  conclusion,  I beg  leave  to  say  that  every  officer  and  man  under  my 
mmand  behaved  with  coolness  and  courage ; not  a word  of  complaint 
as  made  of  hardship  or  fatigue. 

Every  order  given  by  me  was  promptly  obeyed  and  executed,  not- 
itlistanding  the  harassing  fire  of  the  enemy. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JOHN  W.  SPEAGUE, 

Colonel  Sixty-third  Regiment  0.  V.  I. 

Col.  J.  L.  Kirby  Smith,

o atttack  the  town  of  New  Madrid,  Mo.,  on  the  north. 

Throwing  out  my  skirmishers,  I advanced  upon  and  engaged  the 
memy’s  pickets  about  400  yards  north  of  the  town  plat,  in  a large  corn

fiosely  upon  them,  and  seeing  that  they  were  supported  by  400  or  500 
nfantry  and  a piece  of  light  artillery,  I sheltered  my  men  behind  a

or  a length  of  time,  I sent  word  to  Colonel  Granger  by  one  of  his  aides

urn to  camp.

As  commander  of  the  column  mentioned  within,  which  moved  upon 
few  Madrid  yesterday,  it  affords  me  much  satisfaction  to  more  than 
orroborate  every  statement  of  the  modest  but  gallant  Major  Robertson. 
Iis  officers  and  men,  under  a terrific  fire  of  round  shot  and  shell  for 
ome  two  hours,  behaved  like  veterans,  and  quite  surprised  me  by  their 
oolness  and  indifference  to  the  danger  which  surrounded  them. 

Major  Robertson  was  especially  conspicuous,  never  dismounting  from 
iis  horse,  although  their  sharpshooters  tried  their  best  to  pick  him  off.

On  Board  Steamboat  City  op  Alton,

Sir  : In  pursuance  of  Special  Orders,  No.  11,  I have  the  honor  to 
report  as  follows : 

The  Tenth  Begiment  Iowa  Volunteers  and  Twenty-sixth  Begiment 
Missouri  Volunteers  formed  the  Second  Brigade  of  your  division,  then 
in  camp  near  New  Madrid.  On  the  12th  of  March  the  Second  Division 
had  been  ordered  out  in  the  morning  at  5 o’clock,  and  took  position  in 
the  center  of  the  line  of  battle  formed  by  the  whole  army  towards  New 
Madrid,  the  Second  Brigade  in  the  second  line.  At  3 o’clock  p.  m.  the 
Second  Division  had  been  ordered  back  to  camp.  The  13th,  at  3 o’clock 
in  the  morning,  we  marched  to  the  right  of  New  Madrid,  to  relieve  the 
division  of  General  Stanley,  and  had  to  protect  our  batteries  operating 
against  the  lower  fort  of  the  rebels.  The  Second  Brigade  was  drawn 
up  in  a corn  field,  a small  wooded  land  separating  them  from  the  rebel 
batteries.  According  to  your  orders,  a company  as  skirmishers  had 
been  thrown  forward  under  Captain  Bandleman,  who  at  7 o’clock  a.  m. 
reported  that  2 men  had  come  to  them  with  a flag  of  truce,  asserting 
that  New  Madrid  and  all  its  forts  had  been  evacuated  the  night  pre- 
vious by  the  rebels.  I reported  the  case  'to  you,  and  received  your 
orders  to  send  a field  officer  and  20  men  to  New  Madrid,  that  he  may 
inquire  if  the  statement  be  true.  I detailed  Major  McCalla,  accord- 
ingly, who  entered  the  rebel  forts,  found  them  deserted,  and  reported 
to  this  effect.  You  then  ordered  four  companies,  one  from  each  regi- 
ment of  your  division,  to  occupy  the  town  and  the  forts,  which  being 
accomplished,  the  Second  Brigade  was  ordered  back  into  camp. 

On  the  7th  of  April  the  Second  Brigade,  with  the  rest  of  your  divis- 
ion, marched  to  New  Madrid,  went  on  board  steamboat,  and  was  dis- 
embarked towards  evening  about  3 miles  below  New  Madrid.  The  line! 
of  march  having  been  ordered,  we  marched  about  4 miles  in  the  wakel 
of  the  troops  which  preceded  us,  and  bivouacked  in  the  woods. 

April  8,  in  the  morning,  renewed  our  march  at  9 o’clock  a.  m.  Bel 
eeived  the  news  of  the  evacuation  of  Island  No.  10  at  12  o’clock  m.J 
received  the  news  of  the  surrender  of  the  rebel  forces  to  General  Pope] 
at  2 o’clock  p.  m.  Arrived  at  Tipton ville,  encamped  there,  and  returned! 
April  10  to  our  camp  near  New  Madrid. 

The  men  and  officers  behaved  all  very  well.  The  greatest  order  was! 
sustained  throughout  the  whole  operations.  All  had  been  ready  andl 
expected  to  encounter  the  enemy,  and  I do  not  think  it  boastful  to  assert! 
that  the  Second  Brigade  of  your  fine  division  would  not  have  been  miss-1 
ing  in  the  hour  of  deadly  conflict. 

I am,  sir,  yours,  respectfully, 


N.  PEBOZEL, 

Col.,  Comdg.  Second  Brig.,  Second  Div .,  Army  Mississippi.

as  embarked  on  steamboats,  with  intrenching  tools,  with  a view  to

b the  landing,  and  under  cover  of  the  gunboats  my  division  crossed, 
ich  regiment  landing  in  succession,  amid  the  cheers  of  the  men,  and

reastworks,  it  being  apparent  that  success  in  capturing  the  flying

orks.

f the  Tenth  Illinois  Regiment,  commanded  by  Lieut.  Col.  John  Tillson, 
ad  the  Sixteenth  Illinois  Regiment,  commanded  by  Col.  R.  F.  Smith,

ois  Regiment,  commanded  by  Lieutenant-Colonel  Bradley,  followed, 
itli  orders  to  send  small  parties  upon  the  road  leading  from  our  line

nel  Boberts,  of  the  Forty-second  Illinois  Begiment.  The  five  boats 
amprising  the  expedition  were  in  charge  of  First  Master  J.  T.  Johnson, 
f the  Saint  Louis,  assisted  by  Fourth  Master  G.  P.  Lord,  of  the  Ben-

Flag-Steamer  Benton, 

Off  Island  No.  10,  April  6,  1862. 

General  : I inclose  several  papers  in  relation  to  our  operation 
here.  I have  written  Commodore  Porter  that,  in  consideration  of  m 
having  authority  to  modify  the  Eastport,  now  preparing  for  a gunboa 
at  Mound  City,  into  a ram,  and  the  two  boats  you  refer  to  as  beiu 
built  also  for  that  purpose,  he  had  better  not  attempt  to  fit  out  th 
steamer  Choctaw,  at  Saint  Louis,  as  he  proposes,  into  a ram,  but  ti 
confine  himself  to  fitting  out  and  getting  the  Essex  ready  to  join  id 
as  soon  as  possible.  If  under  your  authority  you  wish  Commodoil 
Porter  to  fit  out  the  Choctaw,  he  will  of  course  do  it  under  your  dire*j 
tions.  I have  no  authority  to  act  in  the  matter  except  what  may  I 
authorized  and  directed  by  you. 

As  you  will  perceive  by  the  accompanying  papers,  there  is  so  mucl 
hazard  in  running  the  blockade  with  our  badly-protected  gunboat.1] 
and  the  rebels  being  so  much  on  the  alert,  I consider  it  injudicious  tj

U.  S.  Gunboat  Carondelet,  April  7,  1862. 

Sir  : Agreeably  to  your  instructions  of  the  6th  instant,  I proceeded 
Lown  the  Mississippi  about  6.30  this  morning.  Attacked,  silenced,  and 
piked  all  the  guns  of  the  rebel  batteries  opposite  your  batteries.  The 
ower  one  made  a desperate  resistance.  It  consisted  of  two  64-pounder 
Lowitzers  and  one  32-pounder  gun.  Two  were  dismounted  and  the 
>ther  disabled  by  our  shots.  I then  took  and  spiked  temporarily  a 64- 
>ounder  howitzer  about  half  a mile  above,  and  a quarter  of  a mile  above 
hat  found  a 64-pounder  spiked.  I took  on  board  a man  who  reported 
limself  to  me  as  a spy,  whom  I send  to  you.  The  rebels  had  set  fire  to 
t house  on  the  shore. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  WALKE, 
Commander , U.  8.  Navy. 

Maj.  Gen.  John  Pope, 

Commanding  TJ.  8.  Forces , New  Madrid. 


No.  23. 

Reports  of  Thomas  A.  Scott , Assistant  Secretary  of  War. 

Near  Island  No.  10,  Mississippi  River, 

April  2,  1862. 

Dear  Sir  : I returned  to  this  point  Monday  afternoon  and  found  all 
luiet,  but  there  were  several  small  matters  in  progress,  all  of  which 
rave  proved  successful. 

Before  leaving  for  Cairo  on  Saturday  night  Colonel  Buford,  in  com- 
aand  of  infantry  forces,  consulted  Commodore  Foote  and  myself  in  re- 
Card  to  the  propriety  of  making  a dash  upon  Union  City,  to  break  up 
he  rebel  encampment  there,  which  it  was  believed  consisted  of  one 
egiment  of  infantry  and  one  of  cavalry.  It  was  left  with  Colonel  Bu- 
ord,  as  commander,  to  act  as  in  his  judgment  seemed  proper. 

He  left  Sunday  morning  by  steamers  to  Hickman  with  1,050  infantry, 


124 


OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chap,  xvni.l 


one  company  of  artillery,  four  guns,  and  three  companies  of  cavalry 
total  force,  1,350.  Made  a splendid  movement,  arriving  within  4 miles 
of  the  the  rebel  camps  by  8 p.  m.  Moved  again  at  daybreak  and  made 
the  attack.  At  7 a.  m.  opened  with  his  battery  upon  their  cavalrfl 
which  was  formed  in  line  of  battle ; broke  their  ranks  twice,  and  the 
whole  camp  finally  fled  in  great  confusion.  Their  camps,  baggage! 
stores,  &c.,  were  all  burned.  About  100  horses  and  mules,  with  12 
wagons,  were  brought  off,  along  with  such  papers  and  trophies  as  theirs 
transportation  would  admit  of. 

Troops  returned  to  Hickman  in  excellent  order,  having  made  thei 
march  of  30  miles  and  completely  routing  the  enemy  all  within  twenty- 
four  hours.  It  was  a very  successful  and  gallant  affair.  Great  credit 
is  due  to  Colonel  Buford  and  his  officers  and  men. 

Yesterday  morning  I went  out  to  find  Colonel  Bissell,  with  his  foui 
steamers  and  barges,  which  are  now  in  his  canal  in  the  woods  on  theii ! 
way  to  General  Pope,  at  New  Madrid,  by  a new  channel,  which  Colonel 
Bissell,  with  a regiment  of  mechanics,  is  cutting  through.  It  is  a her 
culean  job,  but  will  be  successful  by  Thursday  evening,  requiring  more 
time  than  was  expected. 

Pope  cannot  be  ready  before  Sunday  to  cross  his  forces,  and  the  cap 
ture  of  [Island]  No.  10  may  be  delayed  until  then.  It  will  be  made  a 
certainty. 

Yesterday  a little  expedition  was  agreed  on  for  last  night,  to  capture! 
sentinels  and  spike  all  the  guns  in  the  upper  fort  of  the  enemy  on  Ten 
nessee  shore.  Ifc  was  intrusted  by  Colonel  Buford,  commanding,  tc 
Colonel  Roberts,  of  the  Forty-second  Illinois,  with  40  picked  men  oi 
his  regiment.  Commodore  Foote  furnished  five  small  boats,  with  crews  < 
from  gunboats  to  row  them.  They  left  the  Benton  at  6 p.  m.,  and  re 
mained  among  the  timber  in  neighborhood  of  fort  until  about  11  p.  in., 
when  they  came  into  the  river  in  front  of  the  fort  and  moved  righl 
upon  it,  driving  away  sentinels,  who  fled  in  the  darkness  after  first  fire 
Colonel  Roberts  and  his  men  spiked  with  files  all  the  guns  in  position 
and  left  without  the  loss  of  a man;  a capital  success  and  most  valui 
able  to  the  flotilla  for  coming  operations,  as  the  position  of  the  fort  was^ 
difficult  to  reach,  and  contained  some  heavy  84-pounders.  We  shall 
probably  have  some  cannonading  to-day  at  Fort  No.  2.  Will  report* 
to-morrow.  I will  make  another  excursion  among  the  cottonwood  to 
morrow,  to  see  Bissell  and  his  command  working  their  way  in  new  chan 
nel  for  transportation. 

Yours,  very  respectfully, 

THOMAS  A.  SCOTT, 
Assistant  Secretary  of  War. 

Hon.  E.  M.  Stanton, 

Secretary  of  War , Washington  City.

night  Colonel  Travis’  Tennessee  regiment.  I will  try  and  maintain  this 
work.  I have  sent  no  more  troops  to  New  Madrid,  for  the  reason  that 
more  troops  would  mask  the  fire  of  the  gunboats.  The  country  being 
perfectly  level,  I can  re-enforce  from  this  place  in  one  hour. 

What  I fear  most  is  that  the  enemy’s  gunboats  may  pass  this  place 
unless  they  give  me  a few  days  to  prepare  for  them.  The  guns  and 
ammunition  arrived  here  in  the  greatest  confusion.  I shall  mount  guns 
and  throw  up  breastworks  afterwards.  If  the  gunboats  pass  and  defeat 
Hollins,  New  Madrid  must  fall.  If  New  Madrid  fall,  I can  be  perfectly 
besieged  by  their  occupation  of  Tipton.  I have  here  under  my  com- 
mand ten  regiments  and  three  small  battalions,  in  all  about  5,000  in- 
fantry. I have  not  half  force  enough  to  fight  in  any  other  way  thani 
behind  my  trenches  on  the  river  shore  with  any  certainty  of  success. 
I have  two  batteries,  one  opposite  No.  10  and  the  other  at  Madrid.  Ii 
forces  could  be  massed  at  Madrid,  that  force  could  be  destroyed,  but 
should  their  gunboats  pass,  the  force  would  be  cut  off  from  Tennessee. 
I will  fight  the  gunboats  as  long  as  they  desire,  but  I fear  they  will  try 
the  Port  Eoyal  game  on  me.  Unless  I have  time,  I fear  they  may  suc- 
ceed. However,  I hope  after  they  pass  that  I may  turn  them  over  tc 
Commodore  Hollins  in  a shattered  condition.  Commodore  Hollins  has 
five  gunboats,  four  at  New  Madrid  and  one  here. 

I wish  the  general  was  here.

Headquarters, 
Madrid  Bend , March  31,  1862.  I 

Colonel  : At  midnight  on  the  night  of  February  25  I was  directed 
by  Major-General  Polk  to  proceed  to  this  point.  I arrived  here  early 
on  the  morning  of  February  26  and  proceeded  to  examine  the  position, 
including  New  Madrid  and  Island  No.  10. 

I found  no  guns  or  works  on  the  island.  On  the  main-land,  opposite 
the  island,  Batteries  Nos.  1 and  5 were  constructed  and  partially  armed 
No  magazine  constructed  for  No.  5,  and  the  one  for  No.  1 was  over- 
flowed.* 

New  Madrid  was  defended  by  Fort  Thompson,  a small  work,  and  well 
armed  with  cannon.  This  work  was  garrisoned  by  the  Eleventh  and 
Twelfth  Arkansas  Regiments  and  Captains  Stewart’s  and  Upton’s  com 
panics  of  artillery,  under  the  command  of  Col.  E.  W.  Gantt,  of  the 
Twelfth  Arkansas.

March  6,  the  enemy  planted  a battery  at  Point  Pleasant,  and  by  a 
liite  flag  induced  Captain  Dunnington  (Pontchartrain)  to  near  the 
ore,  when  she  was  fired  into  by  musketry,  killing  and  wounding 
veral.  Picket  skirmishing  all  day. 

March  7,  a strong  advance  of  the  enemy  was  driven  back  by  the 
*e  from  our  gunboats,  Captain  Bankhead’s  battery,  and  Capt.  R.  A. 
swart’s  Parrott  guns.  The  gunboats  failed  to  silence  the  battery  at 
)int  Pleasant,  which  attempt  was  renewed  on  the  8th  and  9th  with  a 
:e  result,  Capt.  R.  A.  Stewart  driving  the  enemy’s  infantry  from  the 
ore  at  that  point  with  his  Parrott  guns. 

March  10,  heavy  picket  skirmishing  all  day. 

March  11,  I placed  two  24-pounder  siege  pieces  opposite  Point  Pleas- 
it. 

March  13,  the  enemy  planted  some  batteries  during  the  night,  with 
le  pits  supporting  the  batteries.  They  opened  fire  upon  our  trans- 
rts,  hitting  all  that  approached  Fort  Thompson.  The  enemy’s  guns 
ire  24-pounders  and  one  8-inch  gun.  Commander  Hollins,  from  his 
nboats,  and  we  with  our  guns  from  the  works,  returned  the  fire,  re- 
Ising  one  heavy  advance  upon  the  fort  at  the  mouth  of  the  bayou. 

By  a careful  examination  of  their  works  I became  satisfied  that  they 
ire  making  regular  approaches  to  cut  off  communication  with  the 
ver  fort  (Fort  Thompson).  I was  also  convinced  that  our  gunboats 
uld  not  stand  against  their  land  batteries,  and  that  unless  the  fleet 
apped  below  Point  Pleasant  it  would  be  cut  off.  Commander  Hollins 
d General  Stewart  concurring  in  this  opinion,  I ordered  the  evacua- 
»n  of  New  Madrid. 

1 directed  General  Stewart  to  take  the  immediate  direction  of  the 
acuation  of  Fort  Thompson,  placing  at  his  disposal  the  steamer  Louis- 
le,  a large  wharf-boat  lying  at  the  fort,  and  two  gunboats ; and  to 
aieral  L.  M.  Walker  that  of  the  work  at  the  mouth  of  the  bayou, 
icing  at  his  disposal  the  steamer  De  Soto  and  one  gunboat,  and  I 
lered  the  steamers  Winchester  and  Ohio  Belle  to  report  to  General 
alker.  The  captain  of  the  Winchester  did  not  obey  the  order.

At  11  o’clock  a heavy  rain-storm,  that  lasted  all  night,  impeded  the 
work.  All  the  field  guns  were  brought  off;  the  heavy  guns  were  spiked 
and  some  of  the  carriages  injured;  the  ammunition  all  saved,  except  f 
few  shot  and  the  ammunition  in  caissons  and  limbers  of  Captain  Bank 
head’s  battery.  These  caissons  and  limbers,  with  their  contents,  wer( 
thrown  into  the  river.  No  commissary  stores  were  left  that  I am  aware 
of.  Several  wagons  were  left  at  Fort  Thompson.  The  remaining 
wagons  and  artillery  horses  were  removed  to  Madrid  Bend. 

I send  inclosed  Colonel  Gantt’s  report  of  the  evacuation  of  For 
Thompson,  and  as  soon  as  I can  procure  reports  from  Generals  Stewar 
and  Walker  I shall  forward  them.  The  gunboat  fleet  and  transport* 
dropped  down  to  Tiptonville,  retaining  only  such  as  were  necessary  fo] 
water  boats,  transports,  and  hospitals.  The  bad  weather  and  exposur( 
had  increased  our  sick  to  an  alarming  extent. 

So  harassing  was  the  duty  at  New  Madrid,  that  I on  several  occasion: 
ordered  Colonel  Neely,  Fourth  Tennessee,  and  Colonel  Scott’s  Twelitl 
Louisiana  Begiments  to  that  point  for  twenty-four  hours  to  do  guarc 
and  picket  duty.  Several  men  and  one  officer  were  left  at  Fort  Thomp 
son,  having  hid  themselves  to  avoid  work  or  to  shelter  themselves  fron 
rain.

ously  wounded.

March  14,  disposed  my  force  so  as  to  prevent  a crossing  of  the  enemy

Reports  of  Brig.  Gen.  William  W.  Mackall , C.  8.  Army , commandim

Macon,  Ga.,  August  21,  1862. 1 

General  : I have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  ml 
late  command  of  Madrid  Bend  : 

In  obedience  to  the  order  of  General  Beauregard,  given  at  Corintll 
I proceeded  to  Madrid  Bend  by  the  first  opportunity,  and  reached  til 
headquarters  of  Major-General  McCown  on  the  morning  of  March  31 
and  assumed  command  on  the  afternoon  of  the  same  day.  On  that  dal 
Major-General  McCown,  General  Trudeau,  chief  of  artillery,  an  officJ 
in  the  service  of  the  State  of  Virginia,  the  chief  quartermaster,  anl 
chief  commissary  left  the  command,  and  every  record  of  the  post  wil 
carried  away  with  General  McCown,  except  six  or  seven  letters  froil 
the  headquarters  of  Generals  Beauregard  and  Polk  and  two  partid 
returns  of  troops  of  different  dates.  The  information  given  to  me  li 
General  McCown  was  to  the  effect  that  the  gunboats  could  do  no  injuri 
that  the  enemy  had  30,000  troops  opposite  to  me,  and  that  their  bal 
teries  extended  on  the  opposite  side  of  the  river  from  New  Madrid  to  I 
point  several  miles  below  our  lowest  battery,  which  was  planted  immj 
diately  above  Tipton ville;  that  they  were  endeavoring  to  cut  a can] 
across  the  opposite  peninsula  for  the  passage  of  transports,  in  order  i 
land  below  the  bend ; that  they  would  fail,  and  that  the  position  w<j 
safe  until  the  river  fell  and  no  longer. 

The  concurring  testimony  of  the  commanders  of  regiments  was  l 
the  effect  that  their  men  were  broken  down  by  hard  labor,  dispirited  d 
two  recent  evacuations,  and  impressed  with  the  idea  that  the  post  wl 
untenable  and  its  defense  hopeless.  Examination  by  Captain  Shelihl 
my  engineer,  on  April  1 and  2,  showed  that  the  works  of  defense  col 
sisted  of  a naval  fioating  battery,  and  of  water  batteries  mountiil 
about  fifty  guns,  on  a coast  of  25  miles  in  extent,  without  a single  ina| 
azine,  and  the  guns  of  far  less  range  than  those  of  the  enemy.  Satisfil 
that  the  post  was  only  tenable  so  long  as, the  forces  of  the  enemy  coul 
not  cross,  and  that  with  the  troops  at  my  disposal  I could  not  secure  til 
batteries  from  a land  force,  I devoted  myself  to  increasing  my  batterij 
and  establishing  order  among  the  troops  and  system  in  the  staff  <1 
partmcnt. 

On  the  night  of  April  1 the  enemy  stormed  our  upper  batteries,  cl  I 
fended  by  a guard  of  the  First  Alabama  Regiment,  and  spiked  til 
guns.

General:  Agreeably  to  your  orders,  I left  Corinth  on  March  24  and 
lemphis  on  the  following  day  by  steamboat  for  Island  No.  10.  In

company  with  Major  Meriwether  and  others  we  were  landed  about  7 
miles  below  Tiptonville,  on  the  Tennessee  shore  of  the  Mississippi  River.j 
There  were  four  gunboats  lying  at  the  same  point,  under  the  command, 
of  Commodore  Hollins.  On  presenting  myself  to  that  officer  and  inform- 
ing him  of  my  mission,  he  courteously  offered  our  party  the  use  of  a 
gunboat,  which  under  cover  of  the  night  safely  passed  the  enemy’s  bat- 
tery at  Riddle’s  Point,  and  was  landed  safely  at  Tiptonville  before 
dawn. 

Early  in  the  morning  I commenced  an  examination  of  the  defenses 
in  Madrid  Bend  and  on  Island  No.  10.  Rucker’s  battery  (No.  1),  about 
2 miles  above  the  settlements,  composed  of  rifled  32-pounders,  defends 
the  right  flank  of  the  position  ; but,  owing  to  the  high  water,  it  cannot 
be  now  manned,  and  is  only  accessible  iu  boats.  A guard,  however,  is 
always  kept  there  to  deceive  the  enemy  as  to  utility.  Two  miles  lowei 
down  are  four  tine  batteries  of  32  rifled  0-inch  and  8-incli  guns  and 
howitzers.  These,  with  a few  isolated  heavy  guns,  three  batteries  or 
Island  No.  10,  together  with  the  floating  battery  there,  constitute  the 
defenses  against  the  gunboats  of  the  enemy,  which  would  seem  quite 
adequate  for  this  purpose  should  he  attempt  to  reduce  the  batteries 
before  passing  them.  But  it  is  not  impossible  that  the  frequent  sue 
cess  which  has  attended  our  gunboats  in  their  passage  across  his  bat 
teries  may  suggest  to  the  enemy  the  propriety  of  a similar  essay  in  from 
of  our  batteries  in  the  obscurity  of  some  stormy  night. 

Unless  he  can  do  this,  the  high  water  must  prove  a successful  barriei 
against  the  enemy’s  efforts  to  obtain  a foothold  in  the  bend.  On  tin 
east  Reelfoot  Lake  is  impassable  to  either  flats  or  rafts.  Between  tin 
batteries  and  the  point  marked  A on  the  annexed  map  it  is  impossible 
for  him  to  cross  with  steam  power.  Between  A and  B the  country  it' 
submerged,  and  does  not  admit  of  a landing.  Between  B and  Tipton 
ville  flats  may  be  landed;  but  a few  batteries  judiciously  planted  on  the 
shore  could  effectually  prevent  a disembarkation.  An  iron-clad  gun 
boat  running  between  these  points  could  answer  the  same  purpose 
The  country  below  Tiptonville  is  under  water,  and  no  landing  can  bij 
made  there".  It  seems  to  be  certain,  then,  that  unless  the  enemy  cai 
put  boats  below  the  Madrid  batteries  the  forces  at  Island  No.  10  anc 
Madrid  Bend  are  secure  against  assault  until  the  water  falls  at  leas 
5 feet,  and  even  then  a few  guns  could  prevent  a landing. 

The  garrison  was  supplied  with  ammunition,  although  I regret  hi 
say  the  most  of  it  was  very  much  exposed,  being  kept  in  tents  on  th«j 
island,  which  was  daily  bombarded  from  the  enemy’s  mortar  boat! 
above.  The  commanding  officer  had  promised  to  have  it  magazined  a I 
soon  as  possible.  I 

There  were  at  the  post  about  2,000  effective  men  and  about  1 ,351 
on  the  sick  report.  These  last  were  scattered  over  the  bend  and  in  pri 
vate  houses.  The  sickness  was  abating ; the  principal  disease  bowej 
complaint  and  fever,  resulting  from  exposure. 

There  was  at  the  post  flour  enough  to  last  twenty-one  days,  bacon 
enough  for  thirty  days,  18  sacks  of  coffee  (165  pounds  each),  100  bushel 
of  rye,  and  about  three  months’  supply  of  the  small  rations.  In  th  | 
bend  could  have  been  obtained  about  50,000  pounds  of  bacon  and  abou ; 
250,000  bushels  of  corn.  A grist-mill  was  employed,  and  furnished  abou 
70  bushels  of  meal  per  day.  Some  of  the  commissary  stores  were  with  A 
out  shelter. 

My  examination  of  the  lake  satisfied  me  that  it  was  impossible  to  gc 
a steamboat  into  it,  and  that  it  afforded  no  means  of  re-enforcing  o,. 
retiring  an  army.
