Bend  Peninsula,  for  preventing  the  enemy’s  landing  from  the  opposite 
or  Missouri  side  of  the  Mississippi.  No  guns  have  replaced  the  siege 
cannon  on  the  island,  but  the  naval  floating  battery  New  Orleans,  carry- 
ing eight  8-inch  columbiads  and  one  32-pounder  rifled  gun,  is  located] 
there,  so  as  to  command  the  north  channel. 

Several  batteries  are  now  ready,  facing  the  batteries  of  the  enemy 
below  New  Madrid,  and  two  heavy  guns  (8-inch  columbiads  and  32- 
pounders)  will  be  in  position  on  each  side  of  the  peninsula  to  open  upon 
the  enemy,  as  well  as  to  prevent  the  passing  up  or  down  of  any  boat 
which  may  possibly  force  itself  through  the  canal  being  cut  into  John’s 
Bayou. 

I have  located  the  batteries  as  near  the  end  of  the  peninsula  as  the  j 
overflow  will  admit  of,  say  one  and  a half  miles  from  Port  Thompson  on  ( 
the  west  side,  and  about  the  same  distance  from  the  mouth  of  John’s 
Bayou  on  the  east  side.  I 

The  canal  being  cut  by  the  enemy  is  nearly  opposite  Island  No.  8, 1 
below  the  mouth  of  the  James  Bayou,  and  is,  probably,  1 mile  long  j 
from  the  Mississippi  into  a small  lake  which  connects  with  the  John’s  I 
Bayou.  Tugs  and  flat-boats  or  barges  may  possibly  get  through  such  j 
a canal,  provided  the  river  remains  up  at  its  present  high  stage.  It  is  I 
now  on  a stand  and  may  fall.  A very  rapid  fall  of  the  water  through  j 
it  might  prevent  the  use  of  John’s  Bayou,  and  may  prove  fatal  to  our  j 
defenses  by  leaving  our  right  flank  unprotected.  It  is  not  to  be  ex- 1 
pected  that  the  river  can  go  down  sufficient  to  enable  the  enemy  tol 
move  with  artillery  through  the  bottoms  in  front  and  to  the  right  of] 
the  cremaillere  line  of  the  redan  battery ; but  it  does  subside  very! 
rapidly  at  times,  and  the  utmost  attention  and  vigilance  will  be  required! 
to  watch  and  repair  our  right-flank  works  and  build  new  ones.  Asl 
long  as  the  water  remains  up  we  are  secure  in  this  direction,  and  ourl 
chief  attention  should  be  given  to  the  present  left  flank,  which  is  below! 
Island  No.  10,  and  on  the  west  side  of  the  peninsula. 

A proper  distribution  of  3,000  or  4,000  men,  with  the  guns  and  am-j 
munition  at  hand,  might  enable  Island  No.  10  to  hold  itself  as  it  now] 
is  against  the  overwhelming  force  threatening  it;  but  it  will  require! 
every  resource  of  mind  and  the  physical  as  well  as  mental  energies  oil 
every  man  now  in  this  bend.  Any  misjudgment  or  mistakes  made  now, 
such  as  have  been  witnessed  from  the  planking  of  the  streets  of  Mem-j 
phis  to  the  sad  errors  of  Columbus,  in  the  last  eight  months,  will  cost! 
the  Confederacy  an  irreparable  injury. 

If  a gunboat  were  placed  a mile  below  Tiptonville,  she  would  effect- j 
ually  prevent  any  landing  by  the  enemy  if  he  should  strike  across  from] 
Point  Pleasant  or  Kiddle’s  Point.  The  only  landing  that  could  be  made] 
by  the  enemy  to  effect  anything  below  Point  Pleasant  must  be  had  in 
this  distance  of  4 miles. 

Between  Point  Pleasant  and  Andy  Riddle’s  (the  lowest  battery  of  I 
the  enemy)  a gunboat  can  lay  without  molestation  from  the  enemy’s  I 
batteries,  nor  could  they  place  a gun  between  Riddle’s  Point  and  their  I 
battery  at  Andy  Riddle’s.  The  same  may  be  said  of  the  section  be-i 
tween  the  enemy’s  battery  at  Dr.  Martin’s  and  his  battery  at  Point! 
Pleasant.  A gunboat  could  lay  on  our  side  entirely  out  of  the  reach  t 
of  the  enemy’s  guns,  and  by  keeping  up  a little  steam  nights  only  could  ] 
be  ready  to  destroy  any  expedition  attempted  by  the  enemy  across  the] 


:uav.  XVIII.]  NEW  MADRID,  MO.,  AND  ISLAND  NO.  10,  ETC.

•iver  from  John’s  Bayou  at  New  Madrid  to  their  lowest  battery  at 
Indy  Kiddle’s,  and  at  the  same  time  not  be  exposed  to  any  injurious 

ire. 

If  it  became  absolutely  necessary  at  any  time  these  two  gunboats 
lould  pass  the  blockade  in  the  night,  as  is  proven  they  can  do,  though 
it  some  little  risk.  The  well  drilled  and  disciplined  crews  of  these 
mats,  with  their  vigilance  at  night  and  shell  guns  ready  at  a moment’s 
lotice,  would  render  our  position  at  Island  No.  10  (with  a judicious  dis- 
ribution  of  our  own  troops  and  guns  and  watchfulness)  secure,  1 feel 
atisfied. 

The  placing  of  two  of  those  gunboats  now  below  Kiley’s  at  the  posi- 
ions  I have  indicated  I believe 'to  be  of  vital  importance,  however  dis- 
agreeable it  may  be  to  their  crews;  but  inconvenience  and  risks  all  of 
is  must  be  subject  to.  Two  full  regiments  could  not  be  as  effective  as 
wo  gunboats  on  the  west  side  of  the-  peninsula.  As  now  located,  to 
>e  signalized  to  by  the  uncertain  explosion  of  rockets,  &c.,  and  move 
ip  in  the  dark,  must  prove  abortive,  if  the  enemy  have  the  slightest 
nergy  and  strategy,  which  must  be  accorded  to  them.

Report  of  Capt.  D.  B.  Harris , C.  S.  Engineers. 

Island  No.  10,  March  9,  1862. 

Colonel  : I have  the  honor  to  inform  the  general  that  there  a 
now  mounted  at  this  point  thirty-four  heavy  guns ; twenty-four  of  the; 
guns,  of  which  nine  are  rifled  32s,  five  8-inch  columbiads,  and  ten  smoot 
bore  32s,  are  distributed  in  five  different  batteries  on  the  main  land.  T] 
other  ten  guns,  composed  of  the  Belmont  rifled  gun,  one  8-inch  Columbia 
and  seven  smooth-bore  32s,  are  in  two  batteries  on  the  head  of  the  islan 
These  guns  are  protected  by  good  parapets,  are  all  in  barbette  on  centt 
pintle  carriages,  and,  with  the  exception  of  Battery  No.  1,  are  in  go< 
fighting  condition ; that  battery,  consisting  of  six  guns,  is  now  ov€ 
flowed  a few  inches  above  the  platforms,  and  cannot  of  course  be 
much  service  until  the  river  falls.  The  floating  battery,  consisting 
one  rifled  32  and  eight  8-inch  columbiads,  has  been  moved  from  the  poi 
tion  indicated  on  the  map  which  Captain  Gray  sent  by  Major  Me: 
wether  to  the  general  to  the  north  side  of  the  island  for  the  better  pi 
tection  of  the  channel  of  the  river  on  that  (the  Missouri)  side.  Anoth 
battery  of  five  guns  on  the  island  will  soon  be  ready  for  use. 

The  banks  of  the  river  are  caving  in  very  fast,  and  we  will  be  und 
the  necessity  of  erecting  new  batteries  in  rear  of  two,  if  not  more, 
those  already  constructed,  and  we  will  be  fortunate  if  we  do  not  lo 
any  of  the  guns,  if  what  we  hear  is  true  in  regard  to  the  land-slid 
that  sometimes  occur  on  the  Mississippi. 

The  banks  of  the  river  both  on  the  main  land  and  island  being  gem 
ally  as  high  as  anywhere  else  makes  it  necessary  to  locate  our  hi 
teries  too  near  the  river  for  permanence  or  even  safety.  The  upp 
portion  of  the  island  is  covered  by  a growth  of  heavy  timber,  which  i 
terferes  with  and  retards  the  construction  of  our  batteries  there, 
very  much  regret  the  general  has  not  been  able  to  make  a personal  i 
spection  of  this  position  and  give  Captain  Gray  and  myself  the  bene 
of  his  suggestions  in  regard  to  the  best  mode  of  defending  it.  We  st 
indulge  the  hope  he  may  yet  do  so. 

After  the  necessary  batteries  are  constructed  we  think  it  would 
advisable  to  turn  our  attention  to  the  eremaillere  lines  and  postpo 
the  construction  of  the  redoubts  which  the  general  contemplated  in  1 
plan  of  defense  on  the  main -land  and  the  island  till  those  lines  are  co 
pleted. 

It  is  very  important  as  soon  as  the  river  falls  to  complete  the  li 
already  commenced  by  Captain  Gray  from  the  river  to  the  lake.  J 
timber  has  yet  been. cut  on  the  Missouri  side  of  the  river ; it  is  ve 
heavy,  and  if  necessary  to  be  cut  with  expedition  will  require  a lar 
number  of  axmen.  Captain  Gray  and  myself  do  not  think  it  advisalj 
to  spend  much  labor  in  that  way  at  this  time,  there  being  a belt 
cleared  land  from  one-half  to  three-fourths  of  a mile  in  width  opposj 
the  island,  which  would  give  us  a good  view  of  the  enemy  should 
attempt  an  approach  in  that  quarter,  which  is  impracticable,  Capts 
Gray  says,  at  the  present  high  stage  of  the  river,  and  not  easy  j 
accomplish  at  any  time. 

There  are  no  very  commanding  positions  on  the  island  or  main-lai 
The  banks  of  the  river  on  the  island  and  this  shore  are,  however,  10 
15  [feet]  higher  than  those  on  the  opposite  shore. 

I spoke  to  General  McCown  several  days  since  in  regard  to  the  c<j 
struction  of  a redoubt,  as  directed  by  the  general,  near  New  Madr

id  tendered  him  my  services  in  that  or  any  other  way  they  might  be 
eded  at  that  point. 

The  general  said  he  thought  the  redoubt  would  be  in  the  way  of  the 
mboats,  if  it  were  practicable  to  construct  it  in  the  presence  of  the 
emy,  and  there  was  no  need  of  my  services  at  New  Madrid  at  that 
ne.  My  attention  has,  therefore,  been  confined  to  the  works  at  this 
*int  in  concert  with  Captain  Gray.  There  has  been  no  addition  to  our 
boring  force  since  you  were  here ; it  consists  of  about  200  negroes, 
8 Irishmen,  and  Captain  Wintters’  very  efficient  company  of  Sappers 
d Miners,  numbering  about  40  men.  These  are  aided  by  daily  details 
soldiers  in  the  construction  of  the  works,  but  here,  as  elsewhere, 
ey  are  not  very  efficient  with  the  spade.  Should  a larger  force  be 
at  here,  we  will  need  wheelbarrows,  axes,  spades,  and  shovels  in  pro- 
rtion  to  the  number  sent,  say  for  1,000  laborers  300  axes,  500  wheel- 
rrows,  200  spades  and  shovels,  in  addition  to  what  we  now  have. 
Captain  Gray  thinks  it  would  be  advisable  to  send  a special  messen- 
r from  your  headquarters  to  Memphis  to  see  that  we  are  supplied 
th  the  above-mentioned  implements,  if  it  is  contemplated  to  work  a 
•ge  force  here.  Barrows,  he  says,  can  only  be  procured  from  railroad 
ntractors  at  Memphis  or  from  houses  that  furnish  the  contractors 
th  them. 

Yours,  very  respectfully, 

D.  B.  HARRIS, 

Captain  Engineers.

-companies  of  heavy  artillery  under  my  command  had  arrived  alread

(now  Johnston’s)  siege  battery,  the  Southern  Guards.  Captains  IJumei 
Fisher,  and  Jones  had  been  already  ordered  by  General  McCown  t 
the  island  : the  other  companies  were  encamped  in  the  rear  of  Battei 
No.  5. 

1 was  struck  with  a painful  amazement  upon  my  arrival  at  findin 
that  the  post  we  were  about  to  occupy  was  in  no  measure  fortified,  an 
that  unless  we  had  some  days  of  respite  given  us  we  were  in  no  coi 
dition  to  stop  the  gunboats  on  their  way  down  the  river.  We  had  thn 
•64-pounders  mounted  upon  navy  carriages,  three  32s  and  five  smootl 
bores  (32s)  on  the  bend  on  the  island.  The  Belmont  gun,  mounted  i 
haste,  had  to  be  put  in  battle  order  by  setting  the  traverse  circle,  an 
one  8-inch  columbiad. 

Acting  in  obedience  to  your  orders  and  with  all  possible  dispatch 
began  immediately  to  prepare  against  any  emergency  by  commencin

THE  ENGAGEMENT  WITH  THE  ENEMY’S  GUNBOATS. 

A little  after  daylight  on  the  morning  of  the  15th  instant  firing  of 
*annon  was  heard  up  the  river,  immediately  followed  by  four  long 
vhistles  from  our  scout  steamer,  the  Grampus,  which  was  soon  seen 
coming  down  the  river  under  a full  head  of  steam.  Following  close 
pehind  came  the  enemy’s  gun  and  mortar  boats,  consisting  of  light 
pmboats,  five  tugs,  towing  as  many  mortar  boats,  and  several  large 
ransports. 

At  a distance  of  4 miles  some  of  the  gunboats  opened  fire,  firing 
;hot  and  shell  slowly,  and  directing  their  fire  at  various  points  in  the 
)end,  evidently  feeling  for  batteries.  At  the  first  alarm  I had  immedi- 
itely  repaired  to  Captain  Sterling’s  battery  and  had  the  four  alarm  guns 
ired  and  the  guns  of  all  the  smooth  bores  shotted.  The  rifled  pieces 
vere  ordered  to  be  loaded  with  cartridges  and  the  shot  to  be  placed  in 
he  guns  in  case  of  an  attack  only.  I signaled  Captain  Humes,  on 
he  island,  to  do  the  same,  and  at  7.30  o’clock  I reported  to  the  major- 
general  all  ready  for  action. 

The  enemy  continued  firing  slowly  during  the  day  from  the  gun- 
>oats.  In  the  evening,  seeing  several  tugs  in  front  of  his  battery,  Cap- 
ain  Eucker  opened  upon  them  with  shot  and  shell,  but  with  no  per- 
ceptible effect,  the  distance  being  too  great  for  the  range  of  our  guns, 
fhe  gun  detachments  were  ordered  to  remain  at  their  pieces  during  the 
light,  the  First  Alabama  Eegiment  relieving  our  gunners  from  mid- 
light  until  daylight. 

At  9 p.  m.  Captain  Cummings,  of  the  signal  service,  went  to  Battery 
^o.  1 and  established  there  a signal  station,  which  proved  of  great  serv- 
ce  during  the  various  engagements. 

The  captains  of  the  batteries  were  notified  at  the  same  time  that  at 
.2  p.  m.  the  steamboat  Winchester  would  be  sunk  by  the  engineers 
n the  wash-channel  on  the  Missouri  shore.  All  went  on  quietly  that 
light,  and  the  obstruction  of  the  channel  was  successfully  performed 
vithout  attracting  the  enemy’s  notice. 

On  the  16th  gunboats  came  from  behind  the  point  on  the  Missouri 
chore,  where  most  of  the  fleet  lay  during  the  night. 

About  11  a.  m.  they  formed  a line  of  battle,  which  was  beautifully 
cept  all  day,  the  mortar  bofits  on  the  wings,  fastened  to  the  shore,  at  a 
*ange  of  4,200  yards,  the  gunboats  forming  the  center  and  the  trans- 
ports fastened  behind  the  point,  out  of  harm’s  way. 

At  11.30  o’clock  the  fire  was  opened  from  three  13-inch  mortar  boats 
ind  from  two  gunboats,  a fourth  mortar  (a  10-inch)  opening  towards 
evening.  Shells  were  thrown  in  Battery  No.  1,  around  the  bend,  and 
)n  the  island ; but  the  fire  seemed  especially  directed  towards  those 
wo  points.  The  range  was  short  and  pointing  inaccurate. 

Towards  9 o’clock  that  morning  I received  a report  from  the  officer 
>f  the  day  that  Captain  Eucker  was  making  signals  of  distress  or  else 
|:hat  he  had  shown  the  white  flag  from  his  battery.  Amazed  and  mor-

tilled,  I ordered  a skiff,  and  proceeded  to  the  battery,  up  the  river. 
Upon  nearing  it  I discovered  a white  flag  moving  in  various  directions, 
and  a steam-tug  from  the  enemy,  bearing  also  a white  flag,  steering 
upon  the  battery.  Captain  Rucker  was  not  aware  that  his  signal  flag 
•could  be  construed  into  a flag  of  distress  either  by  us  or  by  the 
enemy.  It  was  too  late  to  stop  the  tug;  she  reached  the  battery  as 
soon  as  I did.  An  officer,  a lieutenant  in  the  Navy,  informed  Captain 
Rucker  that  he  had  seen  his  signal  and  had  come  to  inquire  if  he 
wished  to  communicate  with  the  fleet,  to  which  a negative  answer  was 
given.  I explained  the  mistake,  and  told  him  that  the  flag  would  be 
changed,  and  he  left  without  landing.  This  occurrence  is  much  to  be 
regretted,  as  it  gave  the  enemy  a chance  of  seeing  the  condition  of  our 
battery,  all  under  water,  with  its  ammunition  on  the  parapet,  and  also 
perhaps  a good  view  of  our  other  batteries ; but  it  was  unavoidable,  as 
well  as  unexpected. 

The  bombardment  was  kept  up  during  the  whole  day,  the  guns  firing 
8-inch  and  rifled  42-pounder  shells,  and.  the  mortars  pouring  incessantly 
a shower  of  13-inch  shell  in  every  direction. 

I opened  fire  from  the  island  towards  1 o’clock  that  day  from  the 
Belmont  gun  upon  some  of  the  enemy  at  work  on  the  Missouri  shore, 
with  the  effect  of  stopping  their  proceedings  altogether.  Subsequent 
reports  show  that  we  disabled  one  gun  and  killed  and  wounded  several 
men.  During  the  night  the  bombardment  was  kept  up  steadily  at  an 
interval  of  thirty  minutes,  with  no  casualty. 

On  the  morning  of  the  17th  Major- General  McCown  ordered  Col- 
onel Neely’s  Fourth  Tennessee  Regiment  and  Colonel  Brown’s  Fifty- 
fifth  Tennessee  Regiment  to  report  to  me  for  duty,  he  being  apprehen- 
sive that  the  enemy  might  attempt  a landing,  which  was  evidently  his 
intention.  I placed  Colonel  Brown’s  regiment  on  the  end  of  the  cr6- 
maillere  line,  each  man  having  60  rounds  of  buck  and  ball  cartridges. 
Colonel  Neely’s  was  placed  in  reserve  at  my  headquarters  in  rear  of 
Battery  No.  3.  Colonel  Steedman  was  ordered  to  send  two  detach- 
ments, of  15  men  each,  under  command  of  Lieutenants  Owens  and 
Sandford,  from  his  regiment  and  to  keep  in  front  of  my  headquarters — 
all  the  rest  of  his  forces,  not  detailed  in  the  batteries,  as  a reserve  of 
infantry. 

On  Monday  morning,  the  17th  instant,  the  enemy  having  placed  two 
gunboats  alongside  of  their  four  mortar  boats,  on  the  Missouri  side,  and 
one  13-inch  and  one  10-inch  in  the  bend  above,  on  the  Tennessee  side, 
began  to  form  their  line.  Their  large  boats  were  lashed  together  and 
•dropped  down  slowly  upon  Battery  No.  1.  At  2 miles  above  them  they 
formed  a second  line  with  their  transports,  seven  in  number,  loaded 
with  soldiers.  The  tugs  kept  busy  steaming  from  one  boat  to  another. 

At  10.30  or  11  o’clock  the  enemy  opened  fire  on  Battery  No.  1 with 
their  gunboats  lashed  together,  their  boats  lying  behind  the  point  called 
Willow  Point,  and  all  their  mortars.  Their  fire  was  slow  at  first  but 
increased  in  rapidity  and  precision,  and  was  kept  up  until  dark  with 
great  vigor  and  regularity,  the  enemy  being  well  in  range — 2,000  yards. 

1 signaled  Captain  Rucker  to  commence  firing,  and  at  the  same  time 
I ordered  Colonel  Steedman  to  proceed  to  the  battery  with  my  aide,

The  result  of  our  fire  on  that  day  could  not  be  exactly  ascertained  ji 
but  subsequent  information  places  beyond  a doubt  that  one  of  their 
gunboats  sank  that  night  before  reaching  Hickman ; another  one  was

The  number  of  killed  and  wounded  on  their  side  has  not  been  ascer- 
tained. 

The  effect  of  the  enemy’s  fire  upon  the  batteries  on  the  bend  and 
upon  the  island  has  been  without  any  result.  No  damage  of  any  kind 
done,  except  to  the  redan  fort,  upon  which  he  seemed  to  have  concen- 
trated all  his  efforts.  It  presented  the  most  appalling  picture  of  ruin 
and  desolation.  The  parapet  was  plowed  up  in  every  direction  and 
torn  to  pieces.  The  water  from  the  river  washed  into  the  battery,  filling 
it  with  mud.  Trees  were  hacked  down  and  torn  to  shreds  by  the  heavy 
shells  and  the  rifled  cannon,  and  yet  only  1 man  was  killed  in  this  ter- 
rific contest. 

I must  now  beg  leave  to  call  the  attention  of  the  major-general 
commanding  to  the  heroic  feats  of  bravery  of  the  devoted  little  band 
and  earnestly  request  that  those  who  sit  in  the  councils  of  the  nation 
should  take  such  steps  as  they  deem  proper  to  reward  the  heroism  oi 
my  small  command.  All  brave,  all  gallant,  all  would  have  done  what 
a portion  of  them  have  been  called  upon  to  do  on  the  17th  instant. 

The  artillery  has  saved  the  valley  of  the  Mississippi.  Let  its  in- 
habitants show  their  gratitude  for  the  eminent  service  rendered  the 
cause.  In  the  name  of  my  officers  and  men  I request  that  a small 
marble  tablet  be  placed  on  the  contested  battery;  that  under  it  the  re- 
mains of  our  brother  at  arms  William  M.  Clark  should  be  placed,  and 
that  the  names  of  the  officers  and  men  who  were  present,  and  who  con- 
tributed in  the  defense  of  the  battery,  should  be  recorded. 

Besides  the  artillery  officers  already  mentioned,  who  were  conspicu- 
ous for  their  bravery  and  utmost  coolness  under  the  most  galling  fire,

dangers  of  those  around  him  ; to  Colonel  Brown,  of  the  Fifty-fifth  Ten- 
nessee Regiment,  who  remained  all  day  with  his  men  on  the  cremaillere ,

Captain  Rucker  behaved  throughout  the  day  with  cool  judgment  and 
discretion.  I say  nothing  of  the  bravery  he  displayed  on  that  day. 
Captain  Rucker  is  a hero  and  behaved  like  one.  I propose  to  you  to 
bring  his  name  for  promotion  before  the  general  commanding-in-chief 
in  the  Army  of  the  Mississippi.  No  braver  heart,  no  better  man  could 
be  selected  for  that  distinction  on  March  17.  Captain  Rucker  has  won 
imperishable  laurels. 

The  engagement  of  the  17th  instant  is  one  of  the  most  brilliant  ex- 
ploits of  this  war.  The  enemy  admits  it,  and  claims  to  have  killed 
1,000  of  our  men.  Yes,  it  required  1,000  men  to  perform  what  150  men 
did  on  that  day.  I do  not  know  one  single  instance  on  record  that 
can  be  compared  with  it.  Its  results  are  incalculable.  By  that  victory 
we  have  shown  the  enemy  the  superiority  of  our  land  batteries  over 
their  iron-clad  gunboats.  We  have  effectually  closed  against  him  the 
gates  of  the  Thermopylae  of  the  South,  and  we  have  gained  time  and 
also  confidence  in  ourselves. 

Herewith  is  appended  document  B,*  containing  the  names  of  the 
non-comission ed  and  commissioned  officers  who  have  served  in  the 
battery  during  that  memorable  action. 

The  French  soldiers  prided  themselves  upon  the  battle  of  the  Pyra- 
mids, and  glory  and  honor  was  bestowed  upon  them  who  could  say, 
“I  was  present  at  the  battle  of  the  Pyramids.’7  Before  many  months 
elapse  it  will  be  deemed  not  the  less  glorious  among  us  to  be  able  to 
show  a name  on  the  list  of  the  heroes  of  March  17,  and  say,  “I  was 
present  at  the  attack  upon  the  redan  fort  at  Madrid  Bend.77 

With  much  respect,  general,  I submit  this  report  for  your  considera- 
tion, and  remain,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  TRUDEAU,

command  of  the  post  of  Madrid  Bend  to  me  as  ranking  officer  there, 
and  instructed  me  to  hold  the  place  as  long  as  possible,  and  when  I

the  post,  and  that  he  thought  it  advisable  to  evacuate  the  island,  an<

that  time  he  supposed  Captain  Humes,  in  command  of  heavy  ar tiller;

A few  minutes  after  this  Lieutenant  Averett,  commanding  the  floating

A few  minutes  after  this — not  being  able  to  get  any  communicatio: 
or  instructions  from  General  Mackall,  though  a messenger  had  bee. 
dispatched,  and  knowing  the  enemy  to  be  in  the  immediate  vicinit

which  could  be  brought  to  bear  upon  any  point  in  the  rear  of  the  bal

Acordingly  the  command  left  the  post  at  about  2.30  p.  m.,  and  afte

ferry  the  next  day  about  noon,  and  after  much  labor,  difficulty,  an<!

on  the  8th  instant.  We  proceeded  thence  to  Dyersburg,  where  the  cilj 
izens  received  us  very  hospitably. 

We  left  the  next  day,  after  the  stragglers  had  come  up,  for  Bell’J 
Station,  on  the  Memphis  and  Ohio  Bailroad,  and  arrived  there  on  thj 
11th  instant,  where  we  remained  two  days  for  stragglers  to  come  ivl 
and  for  orders.

General  : In  compliance  with  your  order  I submit  the  following 
eport  of  the  occurrences  at  Battery  No.  1 (the  redan  fort)  during  the 
)ombardment  by  the  enemy  since  the  15th  instant,  while  commanding 
aid  battery : 

On  the  morning  of  Saturday,  March  15,  the  Federal  fleet  appeared 
□ sight,  coming  down  the  Seven-Mile  Reach  above  the  fort  at  11  a,  m. 
Tie  enemy’s  advance,  consisting  of  several  gun  and  mortar  boats, 
eemed  to  be  examining  for  a position  to  commence  an  attack.  Shortly 
fter  several  shot  and  shell  were  fired  at  the  battery  and  at  intervals 
luring  the  day. 

At  5 p.  m.,  observing  several  tugs  nearly  in  front  of  my  battery,  re- 
onnoitering  a slough  just  above  the  sand  bar,  and  with  transports  seem- 
ng  to  locate  at  this  point  two  mortar  boats,  I opened  fire  upon  them, 
hrowing  several  shells,  some  falling  short  and  others  ranging  beyond, 
.he  transports  immediately  moved  away,  when  the  gunboats  and  mor- 
ars  replied  to  the  fire. 

At  9 p.  m.  Captain  Cummings,  of  the  Signal  Corps,  came  up  to  my 
attery  to  establish  a signal  station.  He  reported  to  me  that  a large 
teamboat  would  be  sunk  in  the  slough  during  the  night,  which  was 
one  by  Captain  Gray,  of  the  Engineers,  at  about  2 o’clock  Sunday

morning,  thus  effectually  preventing  the  passage  of  the  enemy  throng

Sunday  morning,  the  16th,  I observed,  as  soon  as  it  was  light,  the 
the  enemy  had  in  position  four  mortar  boats,  with  which  they  kej 
up  a slow  but  constant  fire  on  my  battery.

The  contest  now  became  general  from  five  gunboats  and  four  mort 
boats.  This  was  at  11  a.  m.,  the  17th.  Our  batteries,  from  No.  1 to  tl 
island,  inclusive,  now  engaged  also  in  the  defense.  From  their  great 
distance  they  ceased  to  fire  after  a while,  when  the  enemy  turned  tin

tars  and  broadsides  from  rifled  cannon  of  the  heaviest  caliber.  Th 
terrible  cannonading  lasted  until  7 o’clock  in  the  evening,  when  t’ 
enemy  hauled  off,  evidently  having  the  appearance  of  being  crippled 

During  this  engagement  only  three  guns  (8-inch  columbiads)  we 
used  by  me.  They  were  mounted  upon  kon  carriages,  constructed

make  the  complement  of  six  guns  in  Battery  No.  1. 

At  about  4 o’clock  on  the  17th  I had  the  sad  misfortune  to  lose  i

I am  gratified  to  say  that,  notwithstanding  our  Artillery  Corps  had

A gun  managed  by  W.  H.  Toler,  of  Captain  Upton’s  company,  by  its

oming  on,  our  men  slept  on  their  arms  in  the  fort. 

About  10  a.  m.  I received  orders  from  General  Stewart  to  evacuate 
le  fort.  I was  not  surprised  at  this,  as  without  receiving  re-enforce- 
tents  we  could  not  iiossibly  hold  the  place,  the  enemy  numbering,  as 
e had  learned,  eighty  regiments,  with  seventy  pieces  of  artillery, 
hile  our  whole  force  in  both  forts  could  not  exceed  3,500.  I was  sat- 
;fied  that  the  order  was  made  because  such  re-enforcements  could  not 
e obtained,  and  because  there  was  no  reason  to  sacrifice  a force  whose 
lose  proximity  to  another  point  would  render  them  invaluable,  and 
here  a sacrifice  of  them,  if  necessary,  would  have  an  inconceivable 
loral  effect.  I think  the  enemy  intended  no  immediate  assault.  His 
lan  evidently  was  to  throw  around  us  at  night  new  batteries,  sup- 
orting  them  with  a force  larger  than  our  entire  garrison,  thus  com- 
elling  us,  at  the  loss  of  the  co-operation  of  the  gunboats  and  guns 
om  the  forts,  to  go  out  to  meet  him,  or  to  be  reduced  by  the  increased 
trength  of  our  [his]  artillery  and  ultimately  and  speedily  overwhelmed. 
Ve  dared  not  go  out  to  meet  him.  There  was  no  time  when  we  could 
ave  done  so  or  even  harassed  him  on  his  march.  His  cavalry  force 
lone  was  as  large  as  the  garrison  at  Fort  Thompson,  and  his  advance 
uard  outnumbered  all  the  Confederate  troops  at  that  time  on  the 
lississippi  River  above  Memphis,  or,  as  I am  advised,  which  could 
ossibly  have  been  spared  to  us.

The  evacuation  was  conducted  and  accomplished  in  good  order. 
With  the  aid  of  transports  we  could  have  succeeded  in  bringing  ofl 
our  tents,  camp  equipage,  wagons,  and  teams;  but  the  bringing  oi 
transports,  and  it  already  garrisoned,  could  not  have  been  mistaken 
by  the  enemy.  The  undertaking  of  an  evacuation  in  sight  and  hearing 
of  overwhelming  numbers,  hazardous  and  delicate  in  itself,  might,  1 
feel  safe  in  saying,  have  been  defeated  by  the  bringing  of  transports: 
or,  if  not  defeated,  accompanied  with  great  destruction  of  life  and  the 
entire  loss  of  our  stores  and  other  property.  As  it  is,  we  have  sucj 
eeeded  in  saving  our  military  stores,  small-arms,  and  the  clothing  and! 
baggage  of  the  soldiers.  The  guns  in  the  fort  were  spiked,  and  the 
carriages  of  most  of  them  cut  and  left  behind.  It  was  utterly  impossi 
ble  to  save  them.  Except  them,  our  loss  is  trifling. 

Our  loss  in  killed  was  2,  wounded  1,  and  missing  13.  These  last  art 
principally  from  the  Eleventh  Arkansas  Regiment,  who  left  the  rifld 
pits  during  the  storm,  and,  seeking  shelter  near  some  of  the  unoccu 
pied  tents,  fell  asleep  and  were  left  behind.  We  had  no  means  oil 
ascertaining  the  enemy’s  loss.  Ambulances  were  seen  several  timea 
to  go  and  return  from  their  batteries.

’ort  Bankhead,  Avhich  was  commanded  by  me  : 

On  Thursday,  March  13,  at  about  8 p.  m.,  I was  ordered  to  report  to 
reneral  McCown,  commanding,  and  received  from  him  a verbal  order 
> evacuate,  and  the  steamer  De  Soto  assigned  to  me  for  that  purpose, 
ly  command  consisted  of  three  regiments  of  infantry,  one  of  which 
mtaiiied  twelve  companies,  and  one  battery  of  light  artillery.  My  first 
bep  was  to  place  three  companies  of  infantry  on  duty  at  the  parapet, 
i addition  to  the  picket  guard  of  180  men.  I informed  the  command 
lg  officers  of  regiments  and  battery  to  proceed  to  evacuate,  and  speci- 
ed  the  manner  in  which  it  was  to  be  done. 

I placed  the  steamer  under  command  of  Col.  Alpheus  Baker,  First 
labama,  Tennessee,  and  Mississippi  Begiment,  the  next  highest  in

uard  and  police  guard ; also  the  three  above-mentioned  companies,

‘moving  on  board  the  fixed  ammunition  of  the  32-pounders,  of  which 
>e  fort  contained  four. 

All  was  going  on  under  my  personal  superintendence  as  far  as  I was

New  Madrid , February  28,  1862. 

Dear  Sir  : I inclose  you  General  Thompson’s  letter.  Since  he  wrote 
it  the  enemy’s  cavalry  have  got  in  his  rear,  they  being  at  Sikeston  and 
tie  beyond.  Can  you  send  us  cavalry?  The  entire  force  of  the  enemy, 
20,000  strong,  is  at  Benton.  The  troops  at  Cape  Girardeau,  with  six 
pieces  of  artillery,  are  with  the  command.  Could  you  come  down  tor 
a few  hours  ? I do  not  fear  for  the  general,  but  would  like  to  have  the 
cavalry,  if  possible. 

In  haste,  vour  obedient  servant, 

E.  W.  GANTT,

Sikeston,  February  28,  1862. 

(Friday,  4 a.  m.) 

General  John  P.  McCown,  New  Madrid  : 

Dear  General  : The  enemy  returned  beyond  the  swamp  before 
night  yesterday.  There  was  but  the  one  squadron  (125).  I remained 
here  to  recruit  the  horses,  but  will  start  in  a few  minutes  for  Jones’ 
and  Hunter’s  Fords,  which  I will  endeavor  to  make  impassable  to-day. 
1 will  then  remain  up  here  as  long  as  I can  keep  my  numbers  secret. 
1 have  only  65  men  all  fold,  and  it  will  take  considerable  talent  to  hold 
20,000  in  check  more  than  a few  days.  They  report  a large  force  of 
cavalry,  which  might  possibly  overrun  me.  Should  any  horsemen 
arrive  at  New  Madrid,  send  them  up  to  support  me.

Gayosa  House,  Memphis,  Tenn., 

March  28,  1862—7  p.  m 

General:  Your  favor  of  the  26th  instant  is  at  hand.  I have  not 
been  at  New  Madrid  since  March  3,  at  4 p.  m.,  and  could  only  repeat 
rumor  of  the  conduct  of  affairs  at  that  place  after  that  time  5 but  as  I 
think  the  most  serious  mistakes,  if  any,  which  have  been  committed 
were  prior  to  that  time,  I will  report  what  came  under  my  observation 
after  my  leaving  you  at  Columbus  on  February  26. 

Upon  my  arrival  at  New  Madrid  I found  the  citizens  terribly  fright- 
ened at  rumored  reports  of  the  approach  of  the  eneniy.  I could  hear 
nothing  definite  as  to  his  whereabouts,  and  as  the  Missouri  Legislature 
was  to  meet  at  New  Madrid  on  March  3,  and  as  it  was  very  important 
that  the  session  should  be  punctually  held,  I proposed  that  I would  go 
with  a few  volunteers  to  discover  his  whereabouts,  and,  if  possible,  to 
prevent  his  coming  too  near  Madrid. 

I will  beg  leave  here  to  digress  a moment  and  state  Avhy  I desired  lie 
should  not  come.  You  will  probably  remember  that  I never  was  111 
favor  of  works  at  New  Madrid,  and  only  assisted  in  building  such  as  j 
were  ordered,  aud  did  not,  upon  my  suggestion,  finish  the  work  which 
was  called  Fort  Bankhead,  because  I believed  the  proper  front  to  defend  | 
the  position  was  the  causeway  known  as  Jones’  Ford  (Moore’s  Ford), 
believing  that  any  work  could  be  turned  from  the  nature  of  the  country,  | 
and  nothing  but  numbers  could  command  the  country  after  the  enemy 
had  crossed  the  fords  above  mentioned.  While  I consulted  with  Colonel ! 
Gantt,  commandant  at  this  post,  and  Brigadier-General  McCown,  and 
thev  approved  of  my  expedition,  I must  here  again  remark,  for  the  truth 
of  history,  that  General  McCown  remarked  to  me  that  I might  go  to 
see  where  the  enemy  was,  but  that  I must  parley  ; not  to  count  on  him 
to  frighten  him  away  j to  tole  him  in.  I remarked  that  after  Wednes- 
day he  might  come  as  soon  as  he  pleased,  as  by  that  time  the  Legisla- 
ture would  adjourn,  and  you  had  ordered  me  to  report  to  General  V an 
Dorn  after  that  time ; but  that  they  must  be  kept  away  until  then  if 

possible.  ... 

I left  New  Madrid  at  noon  on  Thursday,  July  [February]  27,  with 
66  volunteers,  some  of  whom  were  Confederate  volunteers,  some  Mis- 
souri State  Guards,  and  some  amateurs.  That  night  we  stopped  at 
Sikeston,  where  wre  found  a supper  prepared  for  the  Federals,  who  had 
been  expected  the  same  night,  which  supper  we  ate.  I was  informed 
that  1,000  had  been  expected  there  that  night. 

On  the  morning  of  July  [February]  28  we  started  for  o ones  Ford, 
which  is  30-odd  miles  from''  New  Madrid.  Wre  reached  the  place  early 


Chap.  XVIII.]  NEW  MADRID,  MO.,  AND  ISLAND  NO.  10,  ETC.  173 

in  the  day,  and  sending  a vedette  towards  Benton  (where  we  knew  the 
enemy  to  be),  we  commenced  burning  the  bridges  and  chopping  down 
trees  across  the  road.  I went  with  a small  party  to  the  Sumter  Ford, 
some  miles  distant,  and  threw  the  plank  off  the  bridges  into  the  water 
to  float  away.  I had  scarcely  returned  to  Jones’  Ford  before  a courier 
arrived,  in  hot  haste,  to  inform  me  that  the  enemy  had  reach  Sikeston 
in  large  force  by  the  railroad,  and  were  preparing  to  cut  off  my  retreat. 
I immediately  ordered  my  men  to  retreat  by  a swamp  road  known  only 
to  the  guides,  and  to  await  at  a specified  safe  position  for  my  orders. 
L,  with  4 men,  passed  down  towards  the  enemy,  and  avoiding  him  at 
Sikeston,  came  into  the  road  2 miles  below.  I here  met  Lieutenant 
Grant,  of  the  Twelfth  Arkansas,  who  had  charge  of  the  picket.  Lieu- 
tenant Grant  informed  me  that  a messenger  had  been  sent  to  New 
Madrid,  informing  the  officer  there  that  I was.  surrounded,  and  that 
Colonel  Kitchen,  with  a considerable  force  of  my  old  brigade,  now  Con- 
federate soldiers,  and  others,  would  be  up  that  evening  to  relieve  me. 

I at  once  sent  a courier  to  my  men  in  the  swamp  to  meet  me  at 
that  spot  in  the  morning  early.  In  the  mean  time  I sent  into  Sikeston 
to  see  the  enemy’s  force,  and  was  credibly  told  that  there  were  but 
300  infantry  and  100  cavalry  in  the  town.  I then  started  to  New  Mad- 
rid, expecting  at  each  moment  to  meet  the  relieving  party  ; but  after 
dark,  and  immediately  at  the  town,  I met  20  of  my  men  to  relieve  me. 

Hearing  from  citizens  that  nothing  had  been  done  towards  sending 
re-enforcements,  and  it  being  late  at  night,  I did  not  report  to  the  officer 
commanding;  but  after  a short  rest  I started  before  day  to  join  my 
men.  They  were  promptly  at  the  point  designated  and  in  plain  sight 
of  the  enemy;  fed  our  horses  and  waited  on  him.  Then  I concluded 
to  attack  them  in  that  form.  Finding  me  south  of  them  instead  of 
north,  as  they  expected,  that  I might  confuse  and  probably  whip  them, 
I opened  one  of  my  small  cannon  at  them,  and,  to  my  astonishment, 
Keller’s  [Kellogg’s]  cavalry  and  the  cavalry  of  Hamilton’s  brigade  de- 
ployed before  me.  I immediately  ordered  my  men  to  push  for  New 
Madrid,  or  until  they  met  support,  as  fast  as  possible,  while  I and  a 
dozen  selected  men  attracted  the  attention  of  the  enemy. 

1 answered  them  for  thirty  or  forty  minutes,  when  they  discovered 
my  men  and  charged  them.  For  16  miles  the  run  was  kept  up  by  the 
enemy,  overtaking  and  capturing  three  of  my  little  cannon. 

Upon  my  arrival  at  New  Madrid  I reported  that  the  cavalry  of  the 
Federals  was  within  4 miles,  but  that  the  infantry  had  not  crossed 
Jones’  Ford,  and  advised  an  attack  upon  him.  Nothing  was  done. 

On  Sunday,  2d  instant,  about  noon,  the  enemy  appeared  immediately 
on  the  outskirts  of  New  Madrid.  Bankhead’s  battery  was  sent  to  the 
saw-mill,  and  a regiment  (I  think  Walker’s)  was  sent  through  the  park 
to  meet  them.  A few  rifle  shots  had  been  fired  by  the  enemy  at  some 
of  my  men  in  the  road,  when  Bankhead  threw  a shell  among  them, 
when  they  retired.  All  of  ours,  as  far  as  I could  learn,  returned  to 
I quarters. 

On  Monday,  3d  instant,  the  whole  force  was  reported  as  approaching, 
and  at  noon  the  gunboats  commenced  firing  shell  over  the  town  and 
among  them.  I saw  that  it  had  been  determined  to  await  an  attack  be- 
hind the  defenses,  and  having  with  me  about  200  men,  many  of  whom 
were  my  brigade  officers,  and  as  the  Legislature  had  failed  to  meet,  I 
asked  permission  of  General  McCown  to  take  my  men  to  the  plank 
road,  at  the  west  end  of  which  most  of  my  men  were  stationed.  Gen- 
eral McCown  approved  of  my  course,  and  at  sundown  I started. 

We  halted  near  Point  Pleasant  for  a few  hours,  and  early  in  the 


174

morning  pushed  ahead  for  tlic  plank  road,  which  place  we  had  not

number  of  stragglers  and  citizens.  I still  have  possession  of  the  plank

Since  the  before-mentioned  time  I have  not  been  m -New  Madrid, 
and  therefore  can  give  no  information  as  to  the  subsequent  events. 
When  I left,  on  Monday,  the  23d,  I supposed  that  the  7,000  men  who

had  arrived  from  Bird’s  Point  via  Sikeston.  There  were  reported  to

number  of  General  Pope’s  command  at  20,000. 

I will  beg  leave  here  to  remark  that  I have  always  contended  that 
without  aline  of  works  from  the  river  westward  to  the  swamps  (be 
tween  0 and  7 miles)  the  holding  of  New  Madrid  was  useless  as  t 
river  defense,  and  without  these  works  a large  number  of  men  would 
be  required ; and  after  the  enemy  made  his  approach  before  the  foit 
that  was  built  a dogged  and  determined  resistance  would  have  only 
proved  our  valor  and  not  our  wisdom,  and  after  it  was  found  that  oui 
gunboats  could  not  defend  the  river  bank  the  evacuation  of  the  place 
was  a military  necessity. 

Yours,  most  respectfully, 

’ M.  JEFF.  THOMPSON, 

Brigadier -Genera],  Missouri  State  Guard.

Report  of  Col.  J.  G.  W.  Steedman , First  Alabama  Infantry. 


Hdqrs.  First  Regiment  Alabama  Volunteers,  ^ - 

Island  No.  10,  Mississippi  River , March  28,  1862. 

Sir  : I beg  leave  to  report  that  on  the  17th  instant  two  detachments, 
of  15  men  each,  under  command  of  Lieutenants  Owens  and  Sanford, 
from  the  First  Alabama  Regiment,  constituted  a portion  of  the  gain 
son  of  Battery  No.  1. 

At  12  in.,  in  obedience  to  orders  from  General  Trudeau,  1 went  t< 
the  battery  in  person.  The  battery  had  not  yet  opened  fire  on  the  gun 
boats,  three  of  which  previously  (a  half  hour)  had  dropped  down  within 
a mile  of  the  battery  and  opened  fire  upon  it.  Upon  reaching  the  bat 
tery  and  finding  the  gunboats  in  full  range,  I ordered  the  battery  t< 
open  at  once.  The  men  received  the  order  with  loud  cheers  and  went 
into  the  action  most  gallantly. 

In  the  course  of  an  hour  their  shots  were  telling  well  on  the  enemy, 
we  having  but  three  guns  (8-inch  ship  guns)  which  could  reach.  1 
would  remark  that  the  battery  was  in  miserable  condition,  the  men 
standing  to  their  knees  in  mud  and  water  to  serve  the  guns.  1 he  watei 
having  just  receded  from  an  overflow  of  the  whole  battery,  it  required 
20  men  to  work  one  gun.  We  had  no  magazine,  our  ammunition  being 
set  on  the  parapet  to  keep  it  out  of  water. 

In  two  hours  the  first  detachment  from  my  regiment  and  Captai* 
Rucker’s  company  were  exhausted.  Colonel  Brown’s  Tennessee  regi 
ment  being  near  at  hand,  I called  upon  him  for  assistance  until  I coul< 
get  artillerists  from  the  other  batteries.  Forty  men  came  cheerfully 
and  served  the  guns  until  relief  came  from  General  Trudeau,  consist 
ing*  of  detachments  from  the  various  artillery  companies  near  his  head

quarters.  With  the  assistance  of  this  relief  and  the  original  garrison 
be  battery  was  manfully  served  until  darkness  had  rendered  further 
aring  unadvi  sable. 

When  darkness  came  the  battery  was  almost  a wreck ; the  parapet 
orn  in  many  places,  one  gun  dismounted,  another  badly  injured,  and 
ill  working  exceedingly  hard  ; our  men  were  exhausted. 

During  the  action  one  lieutenant  (Clark),  of  Captain  Rucker’s  com- 
jany,  was  killed  by  a shot  passing  through  the  parapet.  Five  men 
rom  the  same  company  were  wounded,  but  none  of  them  seriously. 

The  detach mept  from  my  regiment  acted  as  gallantly  as  men  could 
ict.  Lieutenants  Owens  and  Sanford  I refer  to  especially  as  gallant 
md  efficient. 

I cannot  speak  in  terms  of  too  great  praise  concerning  the  whole  of 
lie  artillery  force  engaged  at  Battery  No.  1 on  that  day;  they  stood 
mmoved  for  eight  hours  in  a terrific  fire  from  at  least  twenty  rifled 
runs  and  four  13-inch  mortars,  all  at  almost  point-blank  range. 

The  damage  since  reported  by  the  enemy  himself  shows  with  what 
efficiency  the  battery  was  served. 

I refer  with  especial  emphasis  to  the  gallant  conduct  of  Captain 
Rucker  during  the  whole  action. 

I am,  sir,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  G.  W.  STEEDMAN, 
Colonel  First  Regiment  Alabama  Volunteers.

No.  40. 

Report  of  Lieut.  Col.  W.  D.  8.  Cook , Twelfth  Arkansas  Infantry. 

Memphis,  Tenn.,  April  13,  1802. 

Having  to-day  arrived  in  this  city  from  Island  No.  10,  all  the  field 
md  general  officers  recently  at  that  point,  except  myself,  having  fallen 
into  the  hands  of  the  enemy,  I deem  it  my  duty  to  make  a brief  state- 
ment of  the  manner  in  which  the  place  was  lost  to  us. 

1 had  for  about  two  weeks,  with  my  regiment,  been  stationed  in 
Madrid  Bend,  on  the  Kentucky  shore,  to  guard  it  against  the  landing 
of  troops  and  protect  our  batteries  there.  We  were  here  engaged  day 
and  night  in  mounting  guns  and  digging  rifle  pits,  under  the  fire  con- 
stantly kept  up  from  the  batteries  of  the  enemy  on  the  opposite  shore. 
Three  several  regiments,  commanded  by  Colonels  Smith,  Clark,  and 
Henderson,  were  assigned  to  share  the  labors  and  dangers  of  the  posi- 
tion. 

O11  the  evening  of  the  4th  instant  I was  ordered  by  General  Mackall 
to  move  with  my  command,  without  delay,  to  Island  No.  10.  We  ar- 
rived at  night,  in  the  midst  of  a severe  storm,  during  which,  as  we 
could  see  by  the  constant  flashes  of  lightning,  one  of  the  enemy’s  large 
gunboats  passed  our  batteries.  Guns  were  fired  from  nearly  all  of  them, 
but,  owing  to  the  intense  darkness  intervening  the  lightning,  could  not 
be  so  pointed  as  to  disable  her. 

On  the  morning  of  the  6th  I was  ordered  to  relieve  Colonel  Brown’s 
Tennessee  regiment,  then  performing  guard  duty  on  the  island,  being 
assured  that  I should  be  in  turn  relieved  the  following  morning. 

During  the  day  and  the  early  part  of  the  night  we  placed  and  mounted 
a gun  on  the  north  side  of  the  island.  In  the  afterpart  of  the  night  it 


176 


OPERATIONS  LN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chap.  XVIII 

became  exceedingly  dark  and  stormy,  the  rain  falling*  in  torrents,  llie 
enemy,  taking  advantage  of  this  favorable  opportunity,  ran  down 
another  of  his  large  gunboats,  which  passed  the  island  under  the  inef 
fectual  fire  of  the  batteries,  both  on  the  main  land  and  on  the  island. 

I caused  the  musketry  to  fire  as  it  arrived  opposite,  in  order  to  indicate 
its  position  and  aid  in  directing  the  fire  ot  the  guns,  but  the  darkness 
was  too  great  to  point  them  with  accuracy,  and  she  passed  unharmed; 

On  the  morning  of  the  7th  (my  men  drenched  with  rain,  worn  down 
with  fatigue  and  with  fasting),  while  anxiously  expecting  to  be  relieved, 
I received  an  order  from  General  Mackall,  placing  me  in  command  of  the 
island,  and  Captain  Jackson,  of  the  artillery,  in  command  of  the  main 
land.  I then,  for  the  first  time,  learned  that  General  Mackall  had  gone, 
in  the  early  part  of  the  night,  with  all  the  remaining  infantry  and  light 
artillery,  to  join  Brigadier-General  Gantt  in  Madrid  Bend,  to  dispute 
the  landing  of  the  enemy  there. 

During  the  day  messengers  came  and  assured  me  that  the  enemy  was 
landing  in  force;  had  captured  and  spiked  our  guns;  had  driven  oui 
friends  back  to  Tipton ville,  and  occupied  the  ground  between  us.  Latex 
in  the  evening  his  cavalry  came  within  about  1 mile  of  the  lower  point 
of  the  island,  captured  a gun  mounted  at  Harris’  Meadow,  and  came  up 
in  rear  of  the  floating  battery.  On  their  approach  those  in  charge  sunt 
the  battery  and  attempted  to  escape.  Some  succeeded,  others  were 
killed,  and  others  fell  into  the  hands  of  the  enemy.  The  number  oi 
each  I am  not  able  to  report. 

In  the  mean  time  my  officers  were  importunate  that  I should  order  the 
evacuation  of  the  island.  I would  not  consent  to  do  so  until  I had  con- 
sulted Captain  Jackson,  who  commanded  the  land  forces,  which  I did. 
as  also  Captain  Humes,  in- charge  of  the  batteries  on  the  island.  All 
concurred  in  the  expression  of  the  conviction  that  it  was  impossible  tc 
hold  the  place  against  the  enemy  should  he  have  effected  a landing  on 
the  main-land  below,  --as  we  were  assured  he  had  done.  j 

There  were  no  guns  mounted  intended  to  be  used  against  a land 
attack  except  one  or  two  small  pieces  upon  the  new  fort  just  erected 
above  the  island.  There  was  literally  nothing  to  oppose  the  ascent  of 
gunboats  up  the  channel  on  the  Tennessee  side  of  the  island  except  my 
little  command,  at  that  time  but  little  exceeding  300  effective  men,  ex-1 
elusive  of  thpse  left  at  camp  on  the  main-land. 

We  therefore  determined  to  evacuate  at  an  early  hour  in  the  evening, 
leaving  tents  standing,  that  our  movements  might  not  be  discovered  to 
the  enemy.  It  was  agreed  between  Captain  Jackson  and  Captain 
Humes  that  the  former  should  send  up  two  rockets  as  a signal  for  mov- 
ing ; but  on  my  suggesting  the  impropriety  of  the  course,  Captain  Jackj 
son  failed  to  give  the  signal.  Of  this  I had  Captain  Humes  advised 
by  Mr.  Clagget,  of  the  Signal  Corps. 

While  I was  off  the  island  making  arrangements  for  the  evacuation 
the  officers  of  my  regiment  moved  their  several  companies  away  in  good 
order,  but  rather  earlier  than  I intended.  I rode  back  to  the  boat  land- 
ing, opposite  the  batteries  on  the  island,  and  ordered  the  steamer  De 
Soto  over  to  bring  away  Captain  Humes  and  his  command. 

There  was  some  delay,  as  the  captain  told  me,  for  want  of  the  Bn 
gineers.  I remained,  however,  until  the  De  Soto  landed  on  the  island, 
where  the  Champion  already  lay,  subject  to  Captain  Humes’  orders 
This  done,  I turned  away  to  overtake  my  regiment,  then  on  the  march 

1 have  no  positive  knowledge  of  the  fate  of  that  gallant  officer  Cap 
tain  Humes,  but  fear  that  he  and  his  whole  command  are  in  the  hands 
of  the  enemy.

ith  the  most  vigorous  exertions  on  the  part  of  those  already  over,  by 
on  or  soon  after  my  whole  command  was  over,  though  many  of  them

With  but  little  rest  or  sleep,  after  five  days  of  almost  unparalleled 
fifering  and  exposure,  we  arrived  at  Bell’s  Station,  and  are  now  here. 
To  the  credit  of  those  under  my  immediate  command  I must  be  per-

ose  just  from  the  hospital,  are  better  armed  to-day  than  ever  before, 
ving  secured  better  arms  abandoned  by  others.  We  are  not  able  to 
e these  arms  now.  We  are  without  clothing,  tents,  and  other  com- 
;ts,  but  hope  soon  to  be  able  to  take  the  field  again.

caped  with  me,  but  I have  lost  sight  of  them.

>ir  : In  compliance  with  an  order  of  the  major-general,  requiring 
to  transmit  immediately  to  division  headquarters  a report  of  the 
jion  of  myself  and  command  on  the  17th  instant,  during  the  terrific 
ick  of  the  enemy’s  Mississippi  flotilla  on  Battery  No.  1,  I submit 
following : 

>n  the  morning  of  the  17th  I received  the  following  order: 

Headquarters,  Madrid  Bend,  Mo.,  March  17,  1862. 
>lonel  Brown  : The  major-general  commanding  directs  me  to  say  that  you  will  move 
' regiment  according  to  previous  arrangements,  holding  it  in  readiness  to  support 

«ry  No.  1. 

B.  N.  MATHIS, 

Acting  Assistant  Adjutant-General.

Almost  simultaneously  with  the  receipt  of  the  above  General  Ti 
deau,  chief  in  command  of  artillery  at  this  place,  rode  hurriedly  up 
mv  quarters  and  gave  me  to  understand  that  he  had  every  reason 
apprehend  an  attack  on  our  battery  by  an  infantry  force  from  the  re; 
and  directed  me  to  proceed  with  all  possible  haste  to  prevent  the  cc 
summation  of  such  a plan.  A few  moments  only  elapsed  before  i 
regiment  was  in  rapid  march  for  Battery  No.  1,  a mile  and  a half 
two  miles  distant,  the  greater  portion  of  the  way,  owing  to  the  flush 
condition  of  the  river,  being  from  2 to  3 feet  deep  in  water.  My  m 
plunged  this  with  an  alacrity  which  bespoke  hearts  filled  with  the  hi 
resolve  to  meet  the  enemy  in  whatever  manner  or  on  whatever  eleme 

he  dare  present  himself.  0 , _ , , 

By  the  time  we  reached  the  battery,  between  8 and  9 a.  m.,  the  enei 
had  already  opened  a brisk  fire  from  their  gun  and  mortar  boats  on  o 
battery,  and  the  shot  and  shell  were  now  falHng  thickly  around  l 
Despite  this  we  pressed  on  unwaveringly  forward,  and  amid  the  w 
whistle  of  rifle  shot  and  terrific  explosion  of  enormous  shells,  the  ir£ 
ments  of  which  fell  like  hail  around,  I formed  my  regiment  along  t 
cremaillere  line  on  the  right  of  Battery  No.  1,  there  to  await  the  anti 
pated  attempt  of  the  enemy  on  our  battery  by  assault. 

From  this  time  the  enemy’s  fire  grew  fiercer  and  fiercer,  the  ent 
fleet  having  taken  position  about  2,000  yards  distant,  with  the  view 
concentrating  their  fire  upon  this,  our  weakest  battery,  intending 
doubt  to  silence  it  before  making  a demonstration  upon  any  ot  t 
other  lower  batteries. 

Our  battery  did  not  at  first  respond,  hoping  by  silence  to  entice  t 
enemy’s  fleet  within  a more  destructive  range;  but  failing  in  this,  a 
finding  our  battery  was  beginning  to  sustain  considerable  damage  tr< 
the  enemy’s  rifle  shot,  Captain  Bucker,  in  command  of  the  battery, 
length  opened  a slow  fire  on  them.  This  seemed  to  provoke  the  enei 
to  a more  determined  effort  to  silence  the  battery,  and  by  this  time- 
o’clock— the  conflict  had  assumed  a most  terrific  aspect.  The  enem  i 
heavy  shot  and  shell,  aimed  with  almost  unerring  accuracy  maul 
against  the  battery  on  our  left,  poured  an  almost  incessant  volu]j 
upon  our  meager  earthwork,  riddling  the  parapet  in  front  of  our  gin, 
plowing  up  the  earth  in  every  direction,  and  tearing  down  unmet! 
trees  in  a manner  baffling  description.  The  scene  was  the  most  tern: 

conceivable.  _ „ _ , , A 

The  conflict  continued  to  rage  with,  if  possible,  augmented  tu 
until  3 p.  m.,  when  the  darkest  hour  of  the  day  was  upon  us.  It  v 
at  this  time — when  the  enemy  poured  their  most  destructive  fire  up 
our  poorly-protected  battery;  when  their  128-pound  shot  and  13-m 
shells  had  completely  riddled  our  earthwork ; when  Lieutenant  Ola 
was  killed  by  a shot  penetrating  the  parapet  and  his  entire  deta< 
ment  disabled ; when  the  cannoneers  were  completely  exhausted, 
long-continued  exertion,  and  when  everything  seemed  to  yield  ben 
the  pressure  of  the  storm  which  poured  forth  its  iron  shafts  arou 
us,  save  an  unwavering  determination  never  to  surrender  the  batter} 
I learned  through  Colonel  Steedman,  of  the  First  Alabama  Begimc 
(who  had  been  gallantly  aiding  in  defense  of  the  battery),  of  the  o 
tressing  condition  of  the  artillerists,  who  had  up  to  that  time  ^c 
serving  their  guns  without  intermission,  and  saw  at  once  that  unn 
immediate  relief  was  rendered  them  the  battery  would  necessarily 
silenced,  if  not  abandoned.  I immediately  laid  the  facts  before  i 
men  and  called  upon  them,  by  all  that  was  dear  and  sacred  to  the 
never  to  let  that  battery  be  silenced.  But  little  time  had  elaps 


181 


P.  XVIII.]  NEW  MADRID,  MO.,  AND  ISLAND  NO.  10,  ETC. 

ore  the  requisite  number  had  laid  aside  their  guns  and  cartridge- 
's and  were  ready,  with  no  other  qualifications  for  the  service  they 
v proposed  rendering  save  their  strong  arms  and  resolute  hearts,  to 
er  the  battery.  It  was  a spectacle  worthy  of  the  highest  admira- 
n to  see  men,  in  the  face  of  such  terribly  adverse  circumstances, 
h almost  certain  destruction  overshadowing  their  pathway,  reso- 
ely  enter  where  the  missiles  of  death  fell  as  thickly  as  hail,  with  no 
Section  against  them,  to  perform  a service,  too,  with  which  they 
re  totally  unacquainted.  Such  determination  pointed  unmistakably 
the  issue  of  this  day’s  contest. 

n this  manner  the  firing  was  constantly  kept  up  for  several  hours, 
bil  a relief  of  experienced  artillerists,  under  Lieutenant  Finnie, 
ched  us  from  below. 

Che  engagement  continued  to  rage  with  unabating  fury  until  after 
;ht,  when  the  enemy’s  fleet  drew  off,  our  battery  giving  the  last  shot, 
e victory  being  ours,  wet  and  worn  down  by  exhaustion  we  began 
dously  to  look  for  relief,  which  did  not  reach  us  until  12  o’clock, 
en  Colonel  [John  M.]  Clark  came  with  his  regiment  to  relieve  us. 

At  this  late  hour,  shivering  with  cold  and  almost  famished  with 
ager,  we  took  up  our  line  of  march  for  camp,  where  we  arrived  in  a 
>rt  time,  after  traversing  our  watery  path,  with  fully  as  much  eager- 
5S  as  we  had  the  morning  before,  well  satisfied  with  the  issue  of  the 
y’s  work  for  our  side. 

t affords  me  great  pleasure  to  offer  my  hearty  acknowledgments  to 
I officers  and  men  of  my  command  for  distinguished  bravery  and 
ermination  which  characterized  their  conduct  under  these  most 
ing  circumstances,  and  to  express  the  confident  hope  that  they  may 
jr  act  with  the  same  spirit  when  similarly  situated, 
tespectfullv  submitted. 

ALEX.  J.  BEOWN,

No.  44. 

Reports  of  Flag-Officer  George  N.  Hollins , C.  S.  Navy. 

Flag-ship  McEae, 
Tiptonville , Tenn .,  March  15,  1862. 

General:  I deem  it  proper  to  communicate  with  you  direct  ; 
regards  the  position  of  my  command  in  this  vicinity.  My  force  co 
sists  of  six  gunboats ; two  of  them  are  ironed  over  their  engines,  whi( 
protects  them  from  small-arms  and  light  artillery,  but  affording  litt 
protection  against  heavy  guns;  all  the  others  are  very  vulnerable, 
feel  that  the  preservation  of  these  boats  are  of  the  last  importance 
our  country,  and  am  therefore  unwilling  to  risk  their  loss  or  beir 
crippled  by  the  guns  of  the  land  forces  of  the  enemy  except  in  the  la 
extremity. 

If  the  gunboats  should  pass  No.  10  I will  do  the  best  I can  to  stc 
them ; in  that  case  I will  of  course  run  the  risk  of  loss  or  capture  i 
keep  them  back.  Nearly  all  the  guns  at  New  Madrid  were  left  behir 
(as  you  will  have  heard  from  the  general  commanding)  when  that  plai 
was  evacuated;  though  they  were  spiked,  still  my  impression  is  th: 
they  could  be  rendered  useful  in  twenty-tour  hours,  if  not  less  time.  ( 
this  you  will  be  a better  judge  than  myself.  I think  if  the  gunboa 
do  not  or  cannot  pass  No.  10  I will  fall  back  below  the  lowest  poi 
that  the  enemy  can  fortify  below  this  place,  should  they  attempt  it, 
we  are  unable  to  prevent  it.  Our  gunboats  can  and  have  driven  tl 
enemy  from  the  banks  of  the  river,  but  as  soon  as  they  cease  their  fi] 
they  return  and  lire  into  the  transports  as  they  come  up  and  dow: 
This  they  did  at  Point  Pleasant,  and  may  continue  to  do  down  son 
miles  below  this  place,  when  they  will  be  stopped  by  the  nature  of  tl 

country.  „ _ . 

The  Manassas  has  been  ordered  back  to  New  Orleans,  as  you  r 
quested,  though  from  some  injury  received  from  a “ snag”  I fear  she  wi 
be  detained  some  days  in  Memphis  to  repair. 

I am  not  overburdened  with  ammunition  in  any  of  the  gunboats,  i 
you  may  suppose,  and  do  not  wish  to  throw  it  away  without  son 
return  from  the  enemy  for  it.  My  crews  are  all  short.  I have  bee 
kindly  furnished  by  General  McCown  with  some  from  his  command, 
merely  state  these’to  let  you  see  the  difficulties  under  which  I am  wor 
ing.  Any  suggestions  from  you  will  meet  with  all  attention,  and  n 
co-operation  will  be  hearty  and  to  the  extent  of  my  ability. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

’ G.  N.  HOLLINS, 

Flag-Officer , Commanding  Naval  Forces  on  the  Mississippi. 

General  G.  T.  Beauregard, 

Commanding  Confederate  Armies  on  the  Mississippi. 


Flag-ship  McEae,  March  30,  1862. 

General  : Your  letter  of  the  27th  instant,  asking  for  information  h 
regards  the  necessity  of  evacuating  New  Madrid,  has  been  receive* 
It  was  my  opinion,  from  the  manner  in  which  the  enemy  progressed  l 
their  work  under  the  fire  of  the  gunboats  and  Fort  Thompson,  that  i 
twenty-four  hours  more  Fort  Thompson  would  be  cut  oft  from  comim 
nication  with  the  upper  fort  entirely,  and  that,  if  a necessity  arose  fi 


185 


jap.  XVIII.l  NEW  MADRID,  MO.,  AND  ISLAND  NO.  10,  ETC. 


bancloning  the  works  later,  it  would  be  impossible  to  take  off  the  com- 
mand at  that  point.  I had  been  assured  by  all  who  appeared  to  know 
le  character  of  the  country  that  no  heavy  guns  could  be  brought  to 
ew  Madrid ; but  found  that  they  opened  with  24-pounders,  and  they 
ad  an  8-inch ; one  shell  of  that  caliber  was  thrown  into  our  works.  I 
slieved,  therefore,  that  if  the  evacuation  was  to  take  place  it  should 
3 done  at  once.  Generals  McCown  and  Stewart  were  both  present  at 
us  consultation.  General  Stewart  remarked  that  the  artillerymen 
the  fort  were  worn  out  already,  and  the  only  chance  of  relieving 
tern  was  by  taking  men  from  No.  10,  and  they  would  have  to  be  sent 
lere  and  the  others  taken  away  under  fire  of  the  enemy,  which  to 
ly  vessel  that  had  approached  the  fort  during  the  day  had  been  more 
lan  dangerous. 

The  enemy  were  throwing  up  works  on  the  lower  part  of  the  fort,  as 
as  proved  by  their  opening  fire  the  next  morning  from  that  side, 
ifilading  the  entire  camp  and  position,  and  it  would  have  rendered  it 
lpossible  to  send  transports  to  the  post  at  all.  Their  force  was  too 
rong  for  the  small  force  we  had  at  Madrid  in  the  works  erected  there 
hold  out  very  long  under  any  circumstances,  particularly  if  regular 
>proaches  were  made,  which  to  my  mind  evidently  was  their  inten- 
m.  Our  fire  had  not  seemed  to  stop  their  progress,  though  our  shot 
id  shell  appeared  to  do  great  execution,  as  we  could  see  their  arnbu- 
nces  going  continually.  Whenever  their  columns  appeared  on  the 
>en  field  we  could  disperse  them  and  drive  them  back ; but  in  their 
enches  I doubt  if  we  were  as  successful  ; at  least  we  did  not  appear 
stop  their  works. 

Under  these  circumstances  I thought  if  our  force  was  not  strong 
iough  to  stop  their  work  intrenching  we  had  better  evacuate.  It  was 
y opinion,  and  so  expressed  to  both  generals;  and  that  if  it  was  to  be 
me,  the  sooner  it  was  done  the  better,  and  that  it  ought  to  be  accom- 
ished.  What  the  facilities  were  for  moving — I told  General  McCown 
at  three  of  the  gunboats  would  give  such  assistance  as  would  be  re- 
ared. I ordered  the  Livingston,  Commander  Pinkney ; the  gunboat 
)lk,  Lieutenant-Commander  Carter ; and  the  Pontchartrain,  Lieu- 
nant-Cominander  Dunnington,  to  that  duty.  The  Pontchartrain 
is  employed  at  the  upper  fort;  the  other  two  vessels  at  Fort  Thomp- 


I was  not  myself  on  shore  during  the  embarkation  of  the  troops  nor 
e dismantling  of  the  forts,  but  will  refer  you  for  all  this  information 
the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  to  whom  I inclosed  the  reports 
their  movements  on  that  night.  I would  be  unwilling  to  say  what 
ght  or  could  be  done  under  the  circumstances,  not  having  been 
esent;  but  I believe  much  more  might  have  been  saved  if  stricter 
scipline  had  been  maintained  among  the  troops ; but  from  my  own  ob- 
rvation  I doubt  the  possibility  among  volunteers,  raised  and  officered 
many  of  our  regiments  are. 

I remain,  general,  your  obedient  servant, 


Maj.  Gen.  Leonidas  Polk, 

Corinth , Tenn. 


GEO.  N.  HOLLINS, 

Flag-Officer.

MARCH  3-7,  1862.— Reconnaissance  to  Berry ville,  Ark. 

Report  of  Col,  Galvin  A.  Fllis , First  Missouri  Cavalry. 

Headquarters  First  Missouri  Cavalry, 

Gamp  on  Sugar  Greek , Ark .,  March  9,  1862. 

General  : In  obedience  to  your  order  of  the  2d  instant,  to  procec 
to  Keetsville  and  send  forward  a commissary  train  reported  to  be  the. 
and  then  to  make  a reconnaissance  of  the  country  east  of  the  positu 
occupied  by  our  forces,  I marched  with  140  men  on  the  morning  ol  t 
3d,  accompanied  by  Colonel  Pease,  of  your  staff,  to  Keetsville,  and  o 
warded  the  train  as  directed.  I then  proceeded  east  to  the  Koani 
River,  and  north  8 miles  northeast  of  Cassville,  Mo.,  and  finding  i 

* Original  says  “in  latter  part  of  February,  1862.” 


Chap.  XVIII.l  LACLEDE,  WRIGHT,  AND  DOUGLAS  COUNTIES,  MO.  187 

appearance  of  the  enemy,  bivouacked  for  the  night.  At  daylight  of 
the  morning  of  the  4th  I again  moved  forward  in  the  direction  of  Mor- 
ris’ Mill,  on  White  Eiver,  where  a camp  of  the  rebels  was  reported  to 
be  in  that  vicinity.  I reached  the  mills  about  4 p.  m.  Finding  no  enemy 
there,  I at  once  moved  forward  in  the  direction  of  Berryville,  over  the 
most  broken  country  it  is  possible  to  conceive,  crossing  the  White  ltiver 
six  times  in  traveling  8 miles.  At  10  p.  m.,  having  found  forage  for  our 
horses,  I camped  for  the  night,  and  again,  at  daylight  of  the  5th,  moved 
forward  on  the  road  to  Berryville.  When  about  2 miles  I arrested  two 
men  of  suspicious  appearance,  and  from  them  obtained  information 
that  a company  was  organizing  at  Berryville  to  leave  on  the  following 
morning. 

Moving  forward  as  rapidly  as  the  nature  of  the  ground  would  admit 
I soon  came  to  the  suburb  of  the  town,  and  observed  a body  of  horse- 
men moving  north  on  the  road  leading  in  that  direction.  Taking  two 
companies  I went  in  pursuit ; Colonel  Pease,  with  the  balance  of  the 
command,  in  the  mean  time  surrounded  the  town,  taking  some  50  pris- 
oners, 22  horses,  and  50  stand  of  arms. 

My  horses  being  much  worn,  I was  unable  to  overtake  those  that  had 
Left,  and  after  destroying  three  wagons  partially  loaded  with  stores 
belonging  to  the  enemy,  I returned  to  King’s  Eiver  and  bivouacked. 

At  early  dawn  next  morning  the  command  was  ordered  to  saddle,  and 
rs  men  and  horses  were  exhausted  and  a snow  storm  prevailing  I con- 
3luded  upon  returning  to  camp,  which  I reached  at  2 a.  m.  on  the  morn- 
ing of  the  7th.  I found  forage  exceedingly  scarce,  failing  to  secure 
sufficient  over  the  whole  region  I scoured  in  that  direction  to  supply 
the  immediate  wants  of  my  command. 

I would  respectfully  state  that  I had  neither  field  officer  nor  captain 
ind  but  three  lieutenants  with  the  command,  and  take  this  opportunity 
:o  return  my  acknowledgment  to  your  aide-de-camp,  Col.  Henry  Pease, 
or  his  valuable  co-operation  and  encouragement  to  my  men,  and  his 
gallantry  and  bravery,  displayed  in  their  presence  on  this  and  other 
occasions  of  more  perilous  adventure. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  A.  ELLIS, 

Colonel , Commanding  First  Missouri  Cavalry. 

Brig.  Gen.  Jeff.  C.  Davis, 

Commanding  Third  Division. 


ftARCH  4-11, 1862. — Scout  through  Laclede,  Wright,  and  Douglas  Counties, 
Mo.,  including  skirmishes  at  Fox  Creek  (March  7)  and  Mountain  Grove 
(March  9). 

Report  of  Col.  George  E.  Waring , jr .,  Fourth  Missouri  Cavalry. 

Headquarters  of  Post, 

Lebanon , Mo .,  March  12,  1862. 

General  : I have  to  respectfully  report  that  the  patrol  of  cavalry 
mder  Captain  Ludlow  (Company  E),  of  my  regiment,  consisting  of  42 
aen,  which  left  here  on  the  4th  instant,  and  which  was  re-enforced  by 
>0  cavalry,  under  Captain  Heiden  (Company  F),  accompanied  by  Cap- 
am  Wuerpel,  assistant  provost-marshal,  returned  to  this  post  last 
veiling,  after  an  extended  scout  in  Laclede,  Wright,  and  Douglas 
counties,  bringing  in  21  prisoners. 


188  OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  LChap.  XVIII. 


On  the  morning  of  the  7th  instant,  just  at  daybreak,  the  detachment 
under  Captain  Ludlow,  which  was  encamped  at  Fox  Creek,  Douglas 
County,  7 miles  southeast  of  Yera  Cruz,  was  attacked  by  a body  of 
riflemen  concealed  in  the  bush.  Five  of  our  men  were  wounded  (one 
mortally)  and  several  horses  killed.  The  detachment  formed  under  a 
continued  fire,  and  made  a charge  upon  the  enemy,  who  eluded  the 
cavalry  bv  retreating  through  the  wood  trails.  Captain  Ludlow  then 
fell  back 'upon  Hartville,  where  he  was  joined  in  the  evening  by  the 
re-enforcements  under  Captain  Heiden.  This  latter  body  I had  dis- 
patched on  the  7th  instant,  having  received  information  of  the  presence 
of  a considerable  body  of  marauders  at  Yera  Cruz  or  its  vicinity.  The 
wounded  were  sent  back  from  Hartville,  and  the  next  day  occupied  in 
scouting  the  country  southward  from  Hartville.  ~ . 

On  this  day  (the  8th)  my  men  were  joined  by  some  Home  Guard 
scouts,  and  about  18  of  Bowen’s  cavalry,  under  Lieutenant  Flint,  from 
the  post  at  Marshfield.  During  the  day  information  was  had  of  a body 
of  men  (supposed  to  be  the  same  party  which  had  attacked  Lap  tain 
Ludlow  on  Fox  Creek)  being  at  a place  called  Mountain  Grove,  2 miles 
west  of  Montreal,  on  the  borders  of  Texas  and  Wright  Counties.  Dis- 
position was  made  to  surround  this  place,  and  after  a most  fatiguing 
march  over  rough  mountain  roads,  in  the  mid^t  of  a terrible  storm,  the 
settlement  (lying  on  the  summit  of  the  hill)  was  reached  about  noon  of 
the  9th.  As  the  cavalry  was  surrounding  the  principal  buildings  a ^ 
sharp  fire  was  opened  on  it  from  a small  blacksmith  shop.  The  enemy  j 
broke  for  the  bush  and  for  a tavern  building  near  by.  All  those  who 
did  not  gain  the  tavern  were  killed  by  the  cavalry,  except  one,  who  I 
escaped  on  his  horse.  Fire  was  then  opened  on  our  men  from  the] 
tavern,  but  it  was  speedily  taken  after  a sharp  fight.  Notwithstanding 
the  enemy  were  armed  with  rifles  and  protected  by  the  buildings  none 
of  our  men  were  killed  and  but  a few  trifling -flesh  wounds  received.] 
Eleven  of  the  marauders  were  killed  j 6 wounded,  2 of  these  mortally  j 
and  the  rest,  21  in  number,  taken  prisoners. 

Being  satisfied  that  the  band  was  thus  thoroughly  broken  up  the 
command  returned  to  Lebanon,  and  the  prisoners  are  now  safely  con-; 
fined  in  the  jail  here.  Previous  to  their  return  there  had  been  sent  m 
here  at  different  times  19  other  prisoners  who  had  been  taken  during 
the  week.  Over  30  horses  were  captured  and  as  many  rifles  and  guns, 
which  last  were  turned  over  to  Union  citizens,  who  are  at  once  organ- 1 
izing  a company  to  keep  down  any  further  attempt  to  make  up  their  j 

In  the  upper  story  of  the  tavern  were  found  saddles  and  an  overcoat 
lost  in  the  attack  at  Fox  Creek.  On  the  person  of  one  of  the  prisoners 
(J.  C.  Campbell,  a justice  of  the  peace  in  Wright  County)  was  found 
a document  of  which  the  following  is  a copy: 


[Special  authority.]

te  Indian  forces.  They  shot  arrows  as  well  as  rifles,  and  tomahawked

Headquarters  Trans-Mississippi  District, 

Van  Buren , ArZr.,  March  14,  1862. 

eneral  Samuel  R.  Curtis: 

General  : I am  instructed  by  Major-General  Van  Dorn,  commanding 
is  district,  to  express  to  you  his  thanks  and  gratification  on  account 
the  courtesy  extended  by  yourself  and  the  officers  under  your  com- 
and  to  the  burial  party  sent  by  him  to  your  camp  on  the  9th  instant. 
He  is  pained  to  learn  by  your  letter  brought  to  him  by  the  command- 
g officer  of  the  party  that  the  remains  of  some  of  your  soldfers  have 
en  reiiorted  to  you  to  have  been  scalped,  tomahawked,  and  otherwise 
utilated. 

lie  hopes  you  have  been  misinformed  with  regard  to  this  matter,  the 
dians  who  formed  part  of  his  forces  having  for  many  years  been  re- 
i-rded  as  civilized  people.  He  will,  however,  most  cordially  unite  with 
n in  repressing  the  horrors  of  this  unnatural  war,  and  that  you  may 
-operate  with  him  to  this  end  more  effectually  he  desires  me  to  in 
rm  you  that  many  of  our  men  who  surrendered  themselves  prisoners 
war  were  reported  to  him  as  having  been  murdered  in  cold  blood  by 
eir  captors,  who  were  alleged  to  be  Germans. 

The  general  commanding  feels  sure  that  you  will  do  your  part,  as  he 
11,  in  preventing  such  atrocities  in  future,  and  that  the  perpetrators 
them  will  be  brought  to  justice,  whether  German  or  Choctaw. 

The  privileges  which  you  extend  to  our  medical  officers  will  be  recip- 
cated,  and  as  soon  as  possible  means  will  be  taken  for  an  exchange  of 
isoners. 

I am  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

DABNEY  H.  MAURY, 

Assistant  Adjutant-  General.

hours,  our  loss  was  some  25  killed  and  wounded.  The  enemy  must  have) 
suffered  more,  as  our  artillery  had  telling  effect  along  the  road,  and  thei 
rebel  graves  in  considerable  numbers  bear  witness  of  the  enemy’s  loss.) 

The  firing  having  ceased,  I sent  back  other  troops  that  had  joined! 
the  movement  and  designated  the  positions  on  the  right,  which  werei 
promptly  occupied  by  the  First  and  Second  Divisions.  Our  men  rested! 
on  their  arms,  confident  of  hard  work  before  them  on  the  coming  day.i 
The  accompanying  map  of  the  battle  ground  will  fully  illustrate  the] 
positions  then  and  subsequently  assumed.*  In  my  front  was  the  deep,: 
broad  valley  of  Sugar  Creek,  forming  the  probable  approaches  of  the 
enemy,  our  troops  extending  for  miles,  and  generally  occupying  the' 
summits  of  headlands  on  Sugar  Creek.  In  my  rear  was  a broken  plateau 
called  Pea  Bidge,  and  still  farther  in  my  rear  the  deep  valley  of  Big 
Sugar  Creek,  or  Cross  Timber.  My  own  headquarters  and  those  of 
Generals  Sigel,  Asboth,  and  other  commanders  of  divisions  were  near 
Pratt’s  house.  The  lines  A,  B,  and  C show  the  different  fronts  assumed 
during  the  progress  of  the  battle. 

The  approach  by  Bentonville  brought  the  enemy  to  my  extreme  right, 
and  during  the  night  of  the  5th  and  6th  he  began  a movement  around 
my  flank  by  the  road  before  mentioned,  which  crosses  Pea  Bidge  some 
3 miles  northwest  of  the  main  Telegraph  road.  I ascertained  in  the

great  skill,  energy,  and  gallantry  each  day  of  the  battle. 

The  change  of  front  thus  directed  reversed  the  order  of  the  troops, 
placing  the  First  and  Second  Divisions  on  the  left,  their  left  still  rest- 
ing on  Sugar  Creek,  Osterhaus  and  the  Third  Division  in  the  center,

plaining the  proposed  movement  to  commanders  and  Colonel  Osterhaus
