senger brought  me  intelligence  that  my  picket,  commanded  by  Major 
Weston,  of  the  Twenty -fourth  Missouri,  had  been  attacked  by  infantry. 
This  was  at  Elkhorn  Tavern,  where  the  new  right  was  to  rest.  Colonel 
Carr  being  present,  he  was  ordered  to  move  into  position  and  support 
the  major  as  soon  as  possible. 

This  was  the  commencement  of  the  second  day’s  fight.  It  was  about 
10.30  o’clock,  and  the  officers  separated  to  direct  their  several  com- 
mands. The  fire  increased  rapidly  on  the  right  and  very  soon  opened 
in  the  center.  After  visiting  the  right,  where  I perceived  the  enemy 
was  making  a vigorous  attack,  and  finding  Colonel  Carr,  under  a brisk 
fire  of  shot  and  shell,  coolly  locating  and  directing  the  deployment,  I re- 
turned to  my  central  position  near  Pratt’s  house,  and  sent  orders  to 
Colonel  Davis  to  move  near  to  Colonel  Carr,  to  support  him.  In  the 
mean  time  Colonel  Osterhaus  had  attacked  the  enemy  and  divided  his 
forces  5 but  he  was  soon  pressed  with  greatly  superior  numbers,  that 
drove  back  our  cavalry  and  took  our  flying  battery,  which  had  advanced 
with  it.  The  colonel,  however,  was  well  supported  by  his  infantry,  and 
soon  checked  a movement  that  threatened  to  intercept  the  deployment 
of  other  forces.  I considered  the  affair  so  imminent  that  I changed  my 
order  to  Colonel  Davis,  and  directed  him  to  move  to  the  support  of  the 
center,  which  was  his  proper  place  according  to  my  order  for  the  change 
of  front.  My  new  line  was  thus  formed  under  the  enemy’s  fire,  the 
troops  generally  moving  in  good  order  and  gallant  bearing.  Thus 
formed,  the  line  was  not  continuous,  but  extended  entirely  across  Pea 
Eidge,  the  divisions  in  numerical  order  from  left  to  right,  Colonel  Os- 
terhaus remaining  in  command  of  a detachment  and  operating  with 
Colonel  Davis  in  resisting  McCulloch  and  McIntosh,  who  commanded 
the  enemy’s  foroes  in  the  center.  I did  not  err  in  sending  Colonel  Davis 
to  tin's  point,  although  Colonel  Carr,  on  the  right,  also  needed  re-enforce- 
inents. 

The  battle  raged  in  the  center  with  terrible  fury.  Colonel  Davis  held 
the  position  against  fearful  numbers,  and  our  brave  troops  nobly  stood 
or  charged  in  steady  lines.  The  fate  of  the  battle  depended  on  success 
against  this  flank  movement  of  the  enemy,  and  here  near  Leetown  was 
the  place  to  break  it  down.  The  fall  of  Generals  McCulloch,  McIntosh, 
and  other  officers  of  the  enemy,  who  fell  early  in  the  day,  aided  us  in 
our  final  success  at  this  most  critical  point ; and  the  steady  courage  of 
officers  and  men  in  our  lines  chilled  and  broke  down  the  hordes  of  In- 
dians, cavalry,  and  infantry  that  were  arrayed  against  us.  While  the 
battle  thus  raged  in  the  center  the  right  wing  was  sorely  pressed,  and

pickets  guarded  all  the  other  avenues  to  the  camp.  For  the  purpose  J

Camp  near  Pea  Ridge , Benton  Co.,  Ark.,  March  9,  1862. 
Colonel  : At  2 o’clock  on  the  morning  of.  the  6th  instant  six  com- 
mies of  the  Twenty-fifth  Regiment  of  Illinois  Volunteers  marched  with 
le  main  body  of  the  First  and  Second  Divisions  from  camp  near  Ben- 
mville  to  Sugar  Creek  Hollow.  Scarcely  had  we  reached  the  latter 
lace,  a distance  of  16  miles,  when  he  received  a dispatch  saying  that 
eneral  Sigel,  with  our  rear  guard,  was  surrounded  and  engaged  by  a 
istly  superior  force  of  the  enemy ; that  unless  re-enforced  quickly  he 
ould  certainly  be  cut  off  and  defeated.  Without  waiting  for  orders- 
ordered  an  about  face,  and  retraced  our  steps  on  a double-quick  a dis- 
mce  of  about  5 miles,  where  we  met  the  brave  Sigel,  who  had  most 
illantly  cut  his  way  through  the  enemy’s  lines.  Here  the  four  com- 
mies which  had  been  detached  on  the  day  previous  to  take  possession 
' some  flouring  mills  rejoined  the  regiment.  Night  approaching  and 
ie  enemy  not  appearing  in  any  considerable  force,  I was  ordered  to 
turn  and  take  position  on  the  heights  overlooking  the  valley  of  Sugar 
reek,  put  out  pickets,  rest  upon  our  arms,  and  await  further  orders. 
The  morning  of  the  7th  came,  and  with  it  the  intelligence  that  the 
iemy  in  full  force  had  succeeded  in  gaining  our  rear  and  were  drawn 
> in  line  of  battle.  Soon  was  heard  the  booming  of  cannon,  announc- 
g that  the  batteries  of  both  armies  were  engaged.  Every  officer  and 
an  stood  to  his  place  in  ranks  and  awaited  impatiently,  anxiously 
qiecting  every  moment  to  be  ordered  forward  to  take  part  in  the 
*adly  strife.  Thus  we  stood  until  4 o’clock  p.  m.,  under  the  most  pain- 
i suspense,  all  confident  of  victory,  but  fearful  we  would  not  be 
lowed  to  take  a part  in  achieving  it.  A stern  joy  was  felt  when  Gen- 
al  Sigel  rode  up  in  person  and  ordered  the  regiment,  together  with 
ie  Forty-fourth  Illinois  Volunteers,  to  move  forward  to  the  support  of

of  battle.  The  enemy  soon  left  us  for  the  night.  Four  of  my  men 

were  taken  prisoners  by  the  enemy.

Indian  mercenaries.

Report  of  Capt.  Martin  Welfley , Missouri  Light  Artillery. 

Camp  Pea  Eidge,  March  11,  1862.  1 
General  : Below  I have  the  honor  to  hand  you  a report  of  the  pari 
my  battery  took  in  the  battle  of  Pea  Eidge.  By  order  from  head 
Quarters  I left  Oamp  McKisick  Tuesday,  March  4,  with  two  howitzers,! 
on  an  expedition.  Thursday  night,  the  6th  instant,  I returned  witl 
one  piece  to  Camp  Sugar  Creek,  leaving  the  other  in  charge  ot  Lieu 
tenant  Waizenegger. 

On  Friday  morning,  March  7,  I received  marching  orders,  and  left 
with  the  command,  under  General  Osterhaus,  with  three  howitzers 
leaving  the  two  12-pounder  guns  in  command  of  Lieutenant  Jacoby,  oi 
the  ridge,  looking  south.  Being  ordered  to  advance,  I went  forwarc 
about  half  a mile,  where,  as  I was  advancing  on  a small  road  sur 
rounded  by  a timber,  the  Third  Iowa  Cavalry  rushed  down  upon  men 
a regular  stampede,  running  several  of  my  men  down.  I ordered  mj 
pieces  left  about,  which  movement  was  made  in  good  order,  but  jusi 
as  I was  leaving  the  timber  one  of  the  horses  was  shot  and  broke  thd 
tongue,  and  it  was  impossible  to  take  the  piece  along.  As  soon  as  w< 
had  formed  in  line,  myself  and  Lieutenant  Bencke  went  forward  witl 
two  companies  of  infantry  of  the  Twelfth  Missouri  Volunteers,  and 
after  considerable  labor,  were  able  to  bring  the  piece  from  the  brust 
and  into  action.  We  kept  up  a steady  fire  on  the  enemy  for  about  foui 
hours,  after  which  the  firing  ceased.  About  dark  we  followed  the  maid

with  General  Davis’  division.  A]

No.  15. 

Reports  of  Brig.  Gen.  A.  Asboth , U.  S.  Army,  commanding  Second  Division* 

Headquarters  Second  Division, 

Camp  near  Sugar  Creek , Ark.,  March  8,  1862 — 2 a.  m. 

General  : As  General  Sigel,  under  whose  command  you  have  placed 
me,  with  my  division,  has  not  yet  returned  to  our  camp,  I beg  to  address 
you,  general,  directly,  reporting  that  all  the  troops  of  the  Second  Divis- 
ion were  yesterday,  as  well  as  now,  in  the  night,  entirely  without  for- 
age ; and  as  we  are  cut  off  from  all  supplies  by  the  enemy,  outnumbering 
our  forces  several  times,  and  as  one  more  day  without  forage  will  make 
our  horses  unserviceable,  consequently  the  cavalry  and  artillery  as  well 
as  the  teams  of  no  use  at  all,  I would  respectfully  solicit  a decided 
concentrated  movement,  with  the  view  of  cutting  our  way  through  the 
enemy  where  you  may  deem  it  more  advisable,  and  save  by  this  if  not 
the  w hole  at  least  the  larger  part  of  our  surrounded  army. 

I take  the  opportunity  of  mentioning  the  high  valor  of  the  Second 
Missouri  Volunteers  and  Second  Ohio  Battery,  which,  supported  by  the 
First  Iowa  Battery,  did  save  this  afternoon,  at  a very  critical  time,  our 
camp  from  the  advancing  enemy.  Officers  and  men  all  did  their  duty 
gallantly,  pressing  the  enemy  until  evening,  when  the  last  cartridge 
and  artillery  ammunition  was  exhausted. 

I have  especially  to  mention  the  gallant  conduct  of  Colonel  Schae- 
fer, Lieutenant-Colonel  Laibold,  and  Lieutenant  Chapman,  who  was 
mounded  in  a manner  which  will  deprive  the  army  of  his  services  for 
some  time. 

Finally,  I have  to  communicate  the  gratifying  news  that  the  three 
pieces  of  the  First  Flying  Battery,  detailed  this  morning  from  my  di- 
vision to  General  Osterhaus,  and  supposed  to  have  been  taken  by  the 
memy,  have  been  brought  in  by  Colonel  Pattison,  and  that  the  two 
latteries  will  be  able  to  resume  the  fight  at  daybreak. 

I am,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

ASBOTH, 

Brigadier- General,  Commanding  Second  Division * 

General  Samuel  E.  Curtis, 

Commanding  Southwest  Army. 


Headquarters  Second  Division,

on  ville,  Sugar  Creek,  and  Pea  Eidge.

«nd  Second  Divisions  under  your  command.  I say  happy  union,  be- 
ause  I have  never  witnessed  more  perfect  harmony  either  in  camp  or 
Lpon  the  battle-field.  Native  Americans  and  foreigners  of  varied  na- 
lonalities  have  been  aptly  blended,  and  the  fraternity  of  the  troops 
mds  its  counterpart  in  that  prevailing  between  the  officers  and  com- 
aanders.  No  wonder  the  privations  of  our  arduous  winter  campaign, 
a the  midst  of  a hostile  populace,  were  so  cheerfully  borne,  or  that  the 
nendliness  thus  engendered  should  result  in  so  irresistible  a co-opera-

Regiment  Missouri  Volunteers,  were  designated  as  the  reserve  in  the 
>eginning,  hut  were  soon  drawn  into  the  line  of  battle  and  ordered 
nto  action.  Six  companies  of  the  Second  Missouri  Volunteers,  with 
wo  howitzers  of  the  Ohio  battery,  were  sent  towards  the  enemy’s 
xtreme  right  flank,  southwest  of  Elkliorn  Tavern,  and  forming  our 
xtreme  left.  The  infantry,  deployed  as  skirmishers,  drove  the  enemy 
rom  a thicket  at  the  foot  of  the  hill,  and  there  formed  the  general 
dvance,  the  two  howitzers  of  the  Second  Ohio  Battery  in  the  mean 
diile  dismounting  the  enemy’s  battery  and  driving  their  infantry  from 
he  top  of  a hill  upon  which  it  had  formed. 

I have  to  regret  that  the  efficient  Swiss  regiment,  Fifteenth  Missouri 
TflunteerSj  whose  beautiful  flag  floated  so  picturesquely  throughout 
he  battle-field,  had  not  the  opportunity  they  so  ardently  longed  for  of 
illowing  their  energetic  commander,  Colonel  Joliat,  to  the  heart  of 
he  conflict,  and  of  attesting  by  their  blood  their  devotion  to  the  cause. 
I feel  bound  to  make  honorable  mention  of  the  officers  of  my  staff, 
hey  were  always  at  hand,  regardless  of  danger,  where  duty  called 
aem,  especially  during  our  desperate  attack  on  the  afternoon  of  the 
fch.  Lieutenants  Gillen  and  Haskell,  although  for  the  first  time  in  a 
3vere  engagement,  stood  coolly  at  my  side  under  the  hottest  artillery 
nd  musketry  fire,  while  Lieutenant  Von  Enrich,  a soldier  of  European 
sperience,  carried  my  orders,  dashing  bravely  and  promptly  through 
^ery  danger.  Mr.  Ullfers,  the  accomplished  topographical  engineer 
t my  division  during  the  arduous  campaigns  of  the  .last  six  months, 
though  not  called  by  his  especial  duties  to  the  battle-field,  was 
ferywhere,  regardless  of  danger,  and  while  exhibiting  an  example 
cool  courage,  gathered  from  the  events  of  the  moment  many  iin- 
irtant  features  towards  his  topographical  delineation  of  the  battle 
round. 

Major  Wiegand,  recently  of  the  Garibaldi  Guard,  who  joined  me  the 
ly  before  as  a volunteer  aide,  deserves  my  hearty  commendation, 
ou  ^ ourself,  general,  having  been  everywhere  and  having  seen  every- 
mg,  know  how  well  our  men  and  officers  generally  behaved.  For- 
ard  they  always  moved.  Honor  to  them  all. 

My  report  of  killed,  wounded,  and  missing  is  herewith  submitted, 
shows  comimssioned  officers  killed,  3;  wounded,  3;  enlisted  men 
lied,  17  j wounded,  60;  missing,  36.  One  hundred  and  twenty-six 
isoners  were  delivered  by  Captain  Hesse,  provost-marshal  of  the 
?cond  Division,  to  the  grand  provost-marshal,  Major  Heinrichs. 
ver  ooO  stand  of  arms,  with  a large  amount  of  ammunition  and 
mous  implements  of  war,  were  also  taken  and  delivered  to  Chief 
aartermaster  Carr.  An  artillery  caisson  taken  is  now  with  the  Sec- 
id  Ohio  Battery. 

I submit  topographical  sketches  of  the  extended  Pea  Bidge  battle- 
Rl,  with  our  and  the  enemy’s  position  on  the  7th  and  8th  of  March, 
epared  by  the  topographical  engineer  of  my  division  just  so  honor- 
'll mentioned,  Mr.  Ullfers.  The  sketch  appertaining  to  your  action 
Bentonville  will  follow  in  a few  days.

Report  of  Col.  Joseph  Nemett,  Fifth  Missouri  Cavalry  {Benton  Hussars), 


Sir  : Agreeably  to  your  orders  I hereby  submit  the  following  report 
of  the  part  which  the  Benton  Hussars  took  in  the  battle  of  Sugary 

Creek. 

We  formed  the  rear  guard  of  the  army  on  the  march  from  the  camp 
3 miles  west  of  Bentonville  to  Sugar  Creek,  and  started  about  G a.  m. 
We  arrived  at  Bentonville  about  10.  First  perceived  the  enemy  at  itl 
He  had  then  surrounded  us  on  three  sides,  and  we  were  soon  closely  is 
pressed.  Mv  rear  guard  did  not  exceed  100  men  (Companies  A,  B,  and  F. 
and  9 men  of  Company  D).  Observing  a large  cavalry  force,  about  500 
men,  bearing  a secession  standard,  advancing  rapidly  upon  our  rear,  L 
with  Companies  A and  B,  of  the  Benton  Hussars,  charged  them  and 
put  them  to  flight,  and  by  these  means  kept  them  at  a respectful  dis-| 
tance  for  half  an  hour,  thus  giving  time  to  the  whole  column  to  retreat 
from  the  town  without  molestation.  Following,  we  formed  again  outlie 
hill  east  of  town  in  line  of  battle,  fronting  the  enemy,  who  formed  ii 
town.  On  the  whole  retreat  we  sent  out  flankers  and  skirmishers  tc 
the  rear,  fronting  to  the  enemy  about  every  ten  minutes,  thus  keeping 
them  in  check  and  preventing  their  advance  upon  us.  Although 
delayed  on  the  road  by  the  breaking  down  of  a piece  of  artillery  tor  f 
half  an  hour,  and  separated  by  this  means  over  a mile  from  the  man 
body,  we  kept  the  enemy  from  encroaching  upon  us,  and  succeeded  n 
carrying  off  the  gun.  We  were  continually  fired  upon,  and  only  savet 
ourselves  from  being  cut  off  and  surrounded  by  repeated  charges  to  tin 
rear  and  flanks,  thus  letting  the  enemy  believe  that  our  torce  was 
superior  to  what  it  really  was. 

After  marching  about  3 miles  the  whole  column  halted,  and  we  wer< 
happily  re-enforced  and  supported  by  a battalion  of  the  Second  anc 
Twelfth  Missouri  Infantry  and  two  pieces  of  light  artillery,  our  situa 
tion  haying  then  become  so  critical  that  unless  thus  supported  we  mus 
have  succumbed  to  the  infinitely  superior  numbers.  The  enemy  sooi 
ceased  his  fire,  and  we  marched  5 or  G miles  without  molestation,  lhei 
we  were  again  attacked,  but  ordered  by  General  Sigel  to  proceed  to  oui 

qUMyeforce  was  as  follows : Company  A,  Captain  Pfaff  and  Lieuten 
ant  Apprederis,  28  men ; Company  B,  Captain  Langen  and  30  men 
Company  I),  Lieutenant  Borcherdt  and  9 men ; Company  F,  Lieuten 
ant  Luther  and  26  men ; in  all,  93  men.  Company  E,  45  men,  unde 
command  of  Lieutenant  Galeskowsky,  remained  as  guard  to  the  flymj 
battery,  and  did  its  duty  well.  Company  G.  under  command  oi  Cap 
tain  Lehmann,  had  the  advance  guard,  and,  as  I understand,  at  on* 
time  made  a spirited  charge  and  cleared  the  road  in  front  near  Benton 
ville.  Lieutenant  Kluefer,  of  Company  D,  with  30  men,  had  been  or 
dered  off  two  days  previous,  to  form  part  of  an  expedition  under  Majo 
Conrad : Lieutenant  Hansen,  of  Company  B,  with  30  men,  to  form  par 
of  an  expedition  under  Major  Meszaros ; and  Lieutenant  Schipper,  ot  Coin 
pany  A,  with  20  men,  the  night  before  the  retreat,  as  a scouting  partffl 
Fifteen  men  of  Company  F were  detailed  as  provost  guard  to  Captai 

Hesse,  division  provost-marshal.  _ , _ 

I must  here  observe  that  the  bravery  and  bearing  of  my  men  wer 
exemplary,  but  notwithstanding  this,  had  the  enemy  shown  the  leas 
military  spirit,  we  should  unavoidably  have  been  sacrificed. 

On  tiie  7th,  Companies  A,  B,  E,  and  G,  with  the  First  Missouri  Cav

Iry,  Third  Iowa  Cavalry,  and  three  pieces  of  flying  artillery,  besides 
vo  or  three  regiments  of  infantry  and  Welfley’s  battery,  under  com- 
mand of  General  Osterhaus,  proceeded  to  attack  the  left  flank.  Colo- 
el  Bussey,  of  the  Third  Iowa,  commanded  the  cavalry.  The  order  of 
iarch  was : 1,  First  Missouri ; 2,  Flying  Battery $ 3,  Third  Iowa ; 4,  two 
>mpanies  of  Fremont  Hussars ; 5,  Benton  Hussars.  The  forces  ahead 
? us  had  already  engaged  the  enemy  in  the  timber  (9.30  a.  m.)  Avhen 
e came  upon  the  battle  field.  We  were  about  forming  right  into  line 
hen  suddenly  the  First  Missouri  and  Third  Iowa  rushed  in  mad  flight 
?on  us  and  carried  us  along.  We,  however,  immediately  formed  as 
>on  as  we  reached  the  open  field,  and  were  the  only  cavalry  that  kept 
ie  open  field  the  whole  day.  One  gun  of  Welfley’s  battery,  the  horses 
‘ which  had  been  shot,  was  left  behind  in  the  timber,  but  I imme- 
ately  returned  with  Company  A,  commanded  by  Lieutenant  Schip- 
ir,  rescued  it,  and  brought  it  back  in  safety.  We  after  this  were  all 
ty  posted  on  the  extreme  left  flank  and  as  guard  to  the  battery.  We 
mained  in  the  open  field  exposed  to  the  fire,  which  lasted  until  5.30 
m.  The  rest  of  the  forces  were  then  ordered  off  the  field,  and  the 
snton  Hussars  and  two  companies  Fremont  Hussars  were  alone  left 
maintain  the  battle-field  during  the  night. 

March  8, 1862,  early  in  the  morning,  I was  ordered  back  to  the  Second 
ivision,  posted  on  the  extreme  left  flank  as  guard  to  that  flank,  and 
vanced  until  we  reached  Elkhorn  Tavern.  There  we  were  ordered 
halt,  and  in  the  afternoon  sent  in  pursuit  of  the  enemy,  taking 
prisoners.  In  the  evening  we  reached  the  encampment  and  there 
mained.

In  the  morning  of  the  1st  instant,  in  obedience  to  instructions  from 
^ general,  I broke  up  my  camp  near  Cross  Hollow  and  took  position 
the  heights  of  Pea  Bidge,  on  the  north  side  of  Sugar  Creek,  com- 
ndmg  the  main  road.  On  the  night  of  the  5th  I received  intelli- 
lce  of  the  approach  of  the  enemy  from  the  general  and  of  intention 
concentrate  his  forces  on  my  right  and  left  and  give  battle  at  this 
! . °n  the  morning  of  the  6th  I deployed  the  First  Brigade  of  my 
lsion,  consisting  of  the  Eighth,  Eighteenth,  and  Twenty-second  In- 
na, with  Klauss’  Indiana  battery,  commanded  by  Col.  Thomas  Patti- 
>,  on  the  right  of  the  Fayetteville  road,  so  as  to  command  the  ap- 
•ach  completely.  The  Second  Brigade,  consisting  of  the  Thirty-sev- 
n and  Fifty-ninth  Illinois  (formerly  the  Ninth  Missouri),  with  David-

In  the  mean  time  the  enemy  was  rapidly  approaching  and  advancmi

large  numbers  in  a thick  oak  scrub  extending  to  our  camp.  I mime

his  rear,  who  was  now  exultingly  following  up  bis  temporary  success 
The  Eighteenth  Indiana  soon  executed  the  movement  as  directed 
and  opened  a well-directed  fire  upon  the  enemy’s  rear,  which  had  tn 
effect  of  drawing  his  fire  and  disconcerting  his  pursuit,  so  as  to  enaoi

The  Eighteenth  Indiana  pushed  rapidly  forward  and  drove  the  enemy 
*om  this  part  of  the  field,  and,  advancing  to  the  open  ground,  found 
iree  pieces  in  the  hands  of  the  enemy;  charged  and  routed  him  with 
heavy  loss  from  them.  The  Twenty-second  Indiana  during  this  time 
agaged  a large  portion  of  the  Arkansas  troops  and  Indians,  and  after 
sharp  engagement  put  them  to  flight.  In  the  mean  time  the  Second 
rigade  renewed  the  engagement,  when  the  enemy  fled  from  the  field, 
saving  behind  him  many  of  his  killed  and  wounded.  Among  the 
>rmer  were  Generals  McCulloch  and  McIntosh.  At  this  moment  I 
:dered  the  cavalry  to  charge  the  flying  foe,  but  for  some  unexplained 
iason  it  was  not  done. 

The  enemy  made  an  attempt  to  reform  on  his  former  position  near 
le  Bentonville  road,  but  was  easily  driven  from  it  by  the  action  of 
ir  batteries.  Two  regiments  of  re- enforcements,  with  two  pieces  of 
3avy  artillery  (12-pounders),  arrived  at  this  time  from  General  Sigel’s 
>mmand.  These  I ordered  to  take  position  on  the  right,  so  as  to  be 
lie  to  move  the  more  readily  to  the  support  of  Colonel  Carr’s  division, 
hich  had  been  hotly  engaged  m the  vicinity  of  Elkhorn  Tavern  for 
iveral  hours.  General  Sigel  soon  arrived  himself,  and,  accompanied 
Y Osterhaus’  command,  moved  in  the  direction  of  Carr’s  left.  I at 
te  same  time  threw  forward  the  Second  Brigade  to  the  Bentonville 
id  Elkhorn  Tavern  road.  Finding  the  enemy  gone  and  night  upon 
$, 1 ordered  the  troops  to  bivouac  on  the  field  they  had  so  gloriously 
on. 

After  reporting  to  the  general  the  entire  rout  of  the  enemy  at  Lee- 
>wn,  he  directed  me  to  move  my  division  during  the  night  to  the 
Lpport  of  our  position  of  the  previous  day  at  Elkhorn  Tavern.  The 
repart  of  the  night  was  occupied  by  the  troops  in  collecting  the 
ounded  and  dead.  Daylight,  however,  found  us  in  position  in  front 
‘ the  enemy  at  Elkhorn  Tavern,  where  the  troops  under  Colonel  Carr 
id  so  nobly  fought  the  day  before.  That  gallant  officer,  though  suf- 
ring  much  from  a wound,  was  still  upon  the  ground  to  assist  in  dis- 
cing of  my  troops. 

The  First  Brigade  was  deployed  a few  hundred  yards  to  the  right  of 
e Fayetteville  road  to  support  Klauss’  battery,  which  was  placed  at 
e edge  of  an  open  field  intervening  between  the  range  of  hills  at 
Ikhorn  Tavern  and  the  timber  protecting  our  camp.  Here  the  five 
•mpanies  of  the  Eighth  Indiana,  under  Lieutenant- Colonel  Shunk,

3 o’clock  p.  m.  of  the  first  day’s  fighting  an  order  came  from  Gene:l 
Curtis  to  Colonel  Benton,  commanding  the  Eighth  Indiana  Regime ,

Report  of  the  engagement  of  the  8th  instant . # 

On  the  morning  of  the  8th  instant  I took  position  in  front  of  tl 
enemy,  our  right  resting  on  the  Springfield  road,  three  companies  su 
porting  the  battery  of  the  Peoria  Light  Artillery  on  the  extreme  rigl 
and  the  remainder  of  the  brigade  to  the  left  in  an  open  field,  with  i 
shelter  from  the  enemy’s  batteries  but  a rail  fence.  Our  battery,  1 
direction,  opened  fire  the  first  of  the  day  upon  the  woods  in  fror 
where  a portion  of  the  enemy’s  infantry  were  discovered  in  the  act 
forming  their  line  of  battle.  Our  fire  was  responded  to  by  the  guns 
the  enemy  to  our  right,  where  they  were  masked  by  a dense  growth 
underbrush  and  within  grape  and  canister  distance.  For  about  ha 
an  hour  I sustained  this  position  alone  with  but  four  guns,  our  infant; 
being  entirely  out  of  range  and  therefore  useless,  while  at  the  saD 
time  they  were  greatly  exposed  to  an  enfilading  fire,  which  began

ous  day.  None  faltered;  all  performed  their  duty  nobly.  The 
ioria  Light  Artillery,  however,  on  this  day  had  the  opportunity,  which

ective  fire  of  canister  upon  the  enemy,  who  was  concealed  in  the 
usb,  but  was  immediately  routed  from  his  position  by  this  fire.  The 
ticers  of  this  battery — Capt.  Peter  Davidson  and  Lieutenants  Borris, 
ansel,  and  Fenton — have  exhibited  all  the  qualities  requisite  to  the

aops,  having  always  been  in  order.

Headquarters  First  Brigade,  Fourth  Division, 

Pea  Ridge  Battle-field , Ark.,  March  10,  1862. 
Lieutenant  : I have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  the 
art  taken  by  the  First  Brigade  of  the  Fourth  Division  in  the  battle  on 
ie  7th  and  8th  instant ; also  of  the  killed,  wounded,  and  missing: 

On  the  morning  of  the  7th  I was  ordered  to  take  position  with  my 
rigade  near  Elkhorn  Tavern,  on  the  Springfield  road.  On  my  arrival 
discovered  the  enemy  in  the  timber  about  half  a mile  to  the  right, 
ad  brought  up  one  section  of  the  First  Iowa  Battery,  which  opened 
ie  battle,  doing  considerable  execution.  The  enemy  fled  to  the  hollow, 
hen  I deployed  my  line,  covering  as  much  ground  as  possible,  placing 
ajor  McConnell,  commanding  one  battalion  of  the  Third  Illinois  Cav- 
ry,  on  the  right,  the  Thirty-fifth  Illinois  Infantry  on  the  left,  and  the 
ourth  Iowa  Infantry  and  one  section  of  the  First  Iowa  Battery  in  the 
alter,  on  the  center  sending  forward  a company  of  skirmishers  from 
ie  Fourth  Iowa,  who  soon  became  sharply  engaged,  causing  the  enemy 
► open  on  us  with  shell,  solid  and  grape  shot.  Four  pieces  of  the  First 
>wa  Battery  were  planted  on  the  Springfield  road  near  the  tavern, 
hich  opened  on  the  enemy’s  batteries  to  the  right.  Capt.  J.  A.  Jones 
id  Lieutenant  Gambell  were  wounded  here.  Soon  after  this  the  Thirty- 
?th  Illinois  Infantry  became  engaged  in  the  attack  made  in  the  morn- 
g on  the  left,  and  fought  with  great  bravery.  Colonel  Smith  fell 
ounded  and  the  regiment  lost  severely. 

As  soon  as  the  engagement  had  fairly  begun  I closed  up  my  line  to 
e left  and  awaited  the  attack,  keeping  the  section  of  the  battery  at 
ork  with  my  skirmishers  until  near  2 o’clock,  when  the  enemy  ceased 
ing  and  drew  back.  I soon  discovered  that  the  enemy  were  prepar- 
g for  a general  attack,  and  changed  front  to  the  right,  covering  my 
en  with  a rail  fence,  forcing  the  enemy  to  cross  an  open  field  to  reach 
e.  I formed  my  line  and  opened  fire  with  one  section  of  my  battery, 
e other  four  pieces  having  left  the  field  for  want  of  ammunition, 
le  enemy  answered  with  eight  pieces  of  artillery,  and  advanced  on 
y right,  left,  and  front.  I brought  up  the  skirmishers  and  placed 
em  on  the  left,  and  held  the  position  for  more  than  two  hours  with  at 
ist  6,000  infantry  and  eight  pieces  of  artillery  agtiinst  me,  the  artil- 
L-y  playing  upon  us  at  short  range  with  canister."  My  section  of  the 
Ttery  left  the  field  early,  having  exhausted  all  their  ammunition. 

Near  the  last  of  the  engagement  three  rifled  pieces  of  a German 
dtery  were  sent  to  me  and  took  position  on  my  left,  which,  after 
ing  three  or  four  rounds,  was  compelled  to  retire  from  the  field, 
Ing  flanked  by  a regiment  of  the  enemy.  I then  ceased  firing,  to 
scover  the  position  of  the  enemy’s  forces  on  my  right,  when  they 
i mediately  advanced  to  within  100  feet  of  my  lines,  when  I ordered 
Y men  to  fire,  which  they  did  so  effectually  that  the  enemy  fled  along 
e whole  line  in  confusion.  Fresh  regiments  immediately  filled  their 
aces.  Finding  that  the  enemy  were  outflanking  me  on  the  right  and 
at  my  forces  were  insufficient  to  extend  my  lines,  I sent  for  re-enforce- 
mts,  and  obtained  five  companies  of  the  Eighth  Indiana  Infantry, 
lich  I placed  on  my  right.  The  firing  becoming  more  terrific,  the 
einy  having  placed  a battery  on  my  left  that  enfiladed  my  line,  the 
imunition  of  the  Fourth  Iowa  beginning  to  fail,  the  Thirty-fifth  Illi-

Colonel  : On  the  morning  of  the  4th  instant  I left  Camp  Halleck  aj 
Cross  Hollow  in  command  of  an  expedition  in  the  direction  of  Hunts  j 
ville.  The  forces  consisted  of  350  of  the  Ninth  Iowa  Infantry,  b>< 
from  Colonel  Phelps’  Missouri  regiment,  one  battalion  of  the  Third 
Illinois  Cavalry,  one  section  of  the  Dubuque  Light  Artillery,  and  omj 
section  of  Bowen’s  mountain  howitzers.  We  prosecuted  the  march  am 
arrived  at  Huntsville  at  noon  on  the  5th  without  incident.  A portion 
of  the  enemy’s  stores  were  captured  at  their  camp,  3 miles  beyom 
Huntsville,  and  several  prisoners  taken.  From  the  prisoners  I obtains 
information  that  the  enemy  were  advancing  in  the  direction  of  our  lines 
for  the  purpose  of  attack,  which  information  I immediately  transmittet 
to  headquarters,  and  then  prepared  to  retrace  my  steps.  On  the  same 
evening  I moved  out  of  Huntsville  and  camped  3 miles  distant.  At  : 
o’clock  in  the  morning  1 received  your  order  to  return  and  rejoin  tin 
main  body  at  Sugar  Creek,  and  at  3.30  o’clock  resumed  my  line  of  march 
and  at  dusk  the  same  evening  arrived  in  camp,  having  accomplish^ 
a forced  march  of  40  miles  in  a single  day.  Too  much  praise  cannot  m 
bestowed  upon  officers  and  men  for  energy  and  perseverance  in  siu 
mounting  the  difficulties  of  this  long  and  painful  march. 

On  the  morning  of  the  7th,  being  aroused  by  the  sound  ot  firing  in  tin 
direction  of  Elkhorn  Tavern,  in  obedience  to  your  order  I moved  up  my 
brigade,  consisting  of  the  Ninth  Regiment  of  Iowa  Volunteers,  ( olone 
Phelps’  regiment  of  Missouri  Volunteers,  and  the  Dubuque  Light  Ar 
tillery,  the  Third  Illinois  Cavalry  having  already  been  ordered  to  oh 
serve  the  enemy.  Upon  arriving  at  the  Elkhorn  Tavern  the  artilleiy

immediately  took  position  near  the  main  road  and  opened  a brisk  tire,

Eighth  Indiana,  under  Lieutenant- Colonel  Shunk,  which,  however,  was

nfantry  upon  our  position,  and  to  avoid  the  chance  of  being  flanked 
luring  the  night,  I fell  back  to  a line  of  timber  and  formed  on  the  right

md  we  remained  in  line,  resting  upon  our  arms,  until  near  morning, 
vhen  I again  moved  to  the  left  of  the  road  and  formed  on  the  left  of 
Colonel  Dodge’s  brigade. 

Soon  after  sunrise  the  fire  of  our  artillery  again  opened  upon  the 
meiny  and  he  replied  with  vigor.  At  this  point,  finding  ourselves 
exposed  to  a raking  fire  from  one  of  the  enemy’s  batteries  on  our 
•ight,  we  changed  direction  to  the  east.  About  this  time,  the  First 
Division  coming  into  position  on  our  left,  we  joined  in  the  general  ad- 
vance upon  the  enemy,  the  whole  cavalry  force  participating  and  the 
irtillery  co-operating.  The  enemy  here  broke  into  disorder,  and  the 
fortune  of  the  day  was  decided  in  our  favor. 

I cannot  close  this  account  without  bearing  testimony  to  the  coolness, 
bravery,  and  steadiness  of  all  the  troops  under  my  command.  Colonel 
Phelps  was  especially  active  in  leading  his  command,  and  inspired 
hem  by  his  own  example  to  deeds  of  bravery.  Of  Lieutenant-Colonel 
Eerron,  commanding  the  Ninth  Iowa,  too  much  cannot  be  said.  He 
vas  foremost  in  leading  his  men,  and  with  coolness  and  bravery  never 
excelled  rallied  them  to  repeated  acts  of  daring  and  bravery.  Unfor- 
unately  at  the  close  of  the  day  on  the  7th  his  horse  was  killed  under 
dm,  and  he,  being  disabled  by  the  fall,  was  captured  by  the  enemy. 
Major  Coyl,  also  of  the  Ninth  Iowa,  acted  with  distinguished  bravery 
mtil  disabled  by  a painful  wound,  when  he  was  compelled  reluctantly 
o leave  the  field.

Report 


of  Capt.  Robert  W.  Fyan,  Twenty-fourth  Missouri  Infantry. 


In  Camp  in  the  Field,  March  9,  1862. 

Sir  • I have  the  honor  herewith  to  submit  the  following  report : 

At  about  7 o’clock  a.  m.  of  the  7th  instant  I received  your  order  to 
take  my  company  and  proceed  north  on  the  Cassville  road  as  far  as  1 
was  able,  and  ascertain,  if  possible,  whether  the  enemy  were  advancing 
on  that  road  and  in  what  force.  The  company  were  under  arms  speedy 
ily,  all  of  the  company,  even  the  sick,  turning  out  with  the  utmost 
promptness  and  alacrity.  We  had  not  advanced  inore  than  three^ 
quarters  of  a mile  on  the  road  before  we  came  in  °f  the  enemy s 
cavalry.  In  consequence  of  the  garb  in  which  many  of  them  were 
clothed  I was  in  doubt  whether  they  were  Union  or  rebel  forces.  1 
therefore  threw  out  a squad  of  8 men,  and  deployed  them  in  the  ravines

Report  of  Capt.  Barbour  Lewis , First  Missouri  Cavalry. 

In  Camp  in  the  Field, 

Sunday , March  9,  1862. 

Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  having  received  your 
?der  at  daylight  on  the  morning  of  Friday,  the  7th  instant,  to  fur- 
ish  15  men  immediately  for  scouting  purposes,  I caused  that  number 
► be  mounted  promptly  and  went  with  them  myself.  Five  or  6 
hers  of  my  men  also  asked  leave  to  go,  making  my  force  about  20. 
fe  were  joined  by  about  the  same  number  from  Company  M,  of  the 
hird  Illinois  Cavalry,  but  now  acting  as  provost  guard,  under  your 
ders.  Captain  O’Connor  had  charge  of  his  own  detachment,  and  I 
aced  myself  and  mine  also  under  his  command.  He  discharged  his 
ities  throughout,  I thought,  with  coolness,  ability,  and  judgment. 
e marched  to  the  west  of  your  camp,  near  the  Elkhorn  Tavern,  and 
a half  or  three-quarters  of  a mile  found  some  of  the  scouts  of  the 
icmy  skulking  with  their  horses  in  the  brush.  . Here  we  also  found 
e brave  infantry  boys  of  Company  F,  of  the  Twenty-fourth  Missouri 
olunteers,  under  the  lead  of  their  gallant  captain,  Barris.  The  in- 
ntry  soon  routed  the  enemy  from  the  brush  and  we  all  chased  the 
e some  distance. 

At  about  a mile  from  where  we  first  found  them  they  rallied  to  the 
imber  of  some  150,  but  one  or  two  volleys  fired  by  a portion  of  the  in- 
utry  under  Lieutenant  Hart  soon  scattered  them  in  the  utmost  confu- 
m.  The  lieutenant  gallantly  flanked  them  amid  great  difficulties  and 
Light  them  with  rare  ardor  and  courage.  The  whole  force,  infantry  and 
valry,  pursued  the  enemy  in  a northwestern  direction  nearly  3 miles, 
itil  becoming  certain  that  we  were  near  a camp  where  the  enemy  lay 
heavy  force,  and  having  obtained  valuable  knowledge  of  their  plans 
d purposes,  it  was  deemed  best  to  suspend  the  pursuit  and  to  return 
camp.  I repaired  immediately  to  General  Curtis’  headquarters, 
iere  I found  you,  and  reported  what  I knew.  I then  returned  to 
tnp,  and  sent  out  some  of  my  men  as  scouts  north  and  east.  They 
m_returned’  reporting  the  enemy  to  be  very  near  and  advancing 
!>idly  in  great  force  in  both  directions,  they  having  during  the  night 
me  around  the  whole  camp  on  the  west  side  and  north  with  many 
ousands  of  men  and  several  batteries  of  artillery.  Unfortunately,  a 
age  party  sent  off  from  my  camp  while  I was  absent  in  the  morning 
is  cut  off,  and  Sergeant  Siggins  and  Teamster  Abram  Gallaton,  with 
ine  wagon  and  team,  were  captured  by  the  enemy.  Had  it  not  been 
■ the  bravery,  coolness,  aud  good  conduct  of  Lieut.  George  W.

Camp  Welfley , Arlc.,  March  13,  lcl 

General  : Pursuant  to  your  orders,  dated  Camp  McKisick,  ?l 
3 1862,  I left  camp  on  the  morning  of  the  4th,  my  command  cons  t 
of  two  companies  of  the  Seventeenth,  one  of  the  Twelfth,  one  c 
Third,  one  of  the  Fifteenth  Missouri  Volunteers,  and  one  comp?; 
the  Thirty-sixth  Illinois  Volunteers,  one  section  of  Captain  VVe 
howitzers,  and  30  Fremont  and  30  Benton  Hussars.  Proceediii|i 
southwestern  direction,  I marched  along  Flint  Creek  until  within  6\ 
of  Lindsey’s  Prairie,  where  I camped  the  night  of  the  4th.  Start!. 
7 o’clock  a.  m.  on  the  5th  I still  continued  in  the  same  direction  i 
striking  the  State  line  road,  whence  I turned  north  towards  Mays, 
sending  my  adjutant,  Lademann,  ahead  with  8 Fremont  Hussars 
rest  Mr.  Gunter,  a notorious  secessionist.  He  met  with  i discn  l 
soldiers  of  General  Price’s  army,  and  charging  upon  them,  he  cap 
5 after  a long  chase.  My  guides  not  being  well  acquainted  witfi 
section  of  country,  I marched  some  10  miles  out  of  my  way,  arrivi 
Camp  Walker  towards  evening,  where  I met  Captain  Kielmanseg 
your  staff,  who  had  the  order  that  my  command  should  either  pr 

to  Pineville  or  return  to  camp.  _ A w 

The  infantry  being  very  tired,  we  camped  that  night  m the  Din 
of  the  Vegetarian  Society,  1 mile  east  of  Camp  Walker.  In  the  i 
at  10  o’clock,  Captain  von  Kielmansegge  proceeded  to  Pmeviii 
command  consisting  of  my  cavalry,  one  piece  of  artillery,  and 
of  infantry  hauled  in  a wagon.  At  7 o’clock  in  the  morning  ol

ville  road,  and  at  11  o’clock  a.  m.,  about  12  miles  from  Benton ville  I 
received  your  orders,  dated  Bentonville,  March  6,  10  o’clock  a.  m.  in- 
forming me  to  march  to  Miser’s  farm  and  Waters’  Mill,  and  from  there 
proceed  to  Potson’s  Hill.  I marched  on  about  6 miles  and  turned  to 
the  lett,  the  guide  knowing  a nearer  road  to  Miser’s  farm. 

I had  proceeded  only  about  4 miles  when  I heard  the  report  of  can- 
non m the  direction  ot  Bentonville,  and  afterwards  was  rejoined  by  the 
b Benton  Hussars  who  had  brought  me  your  latest  orders.  It  was  then 
3 o clock  p.  m.  They  had  passed  Waters’  Mill  and  got  to  Sugar  Creek 
Hollow,  when  they  met  2 of  the  enemy  and  disarmed  them.  They  had 
only  proceeded  a short  distance  when  suddenly  they  beheld  2,000  of  the 
enemy’s  cavalry.  They  immediately  turned  round  and  reported  the  cir- 
cumstances to  me,  being  obliged  to  leave  the  prisoners  behind.  I went 
across  the  hills  and  struck  Pineville  road,  endeavoring  to  go  around  the 
enemy  and  join  you  at  Potson’s  Hill,  if  possible.  I followed  that  road 
up  to  McCullough’s  Hollow,  where  I turned  to  the  right  and  marched 
along  the  State  line.  I could  only  proceed  2 miles  in  that  direction 
because  there  was  the  only  water,  and  the  men  were  too  fatigued  to  «o 
any  farther,  haying  marched  some  30  miles  that  day. 

I started  again  at  2 o’clock  on  the  morning  of  the  7th,  gaining  Pea 
Ridge,  and  turning  off  to  the  left  I arrived  at  Shell’s  Mill  at  9 o’clock 
a,  m.  At  12  o’clock  I got  to  a little  creek  4 miles  from  Keetsville,  on 
the  Keetsville  and  Pineville  road,  where  I had  to  halt,  the  exhaustion 
ot  the  men  not  permitting  any  farther  marching.  From  there  I pro- 
ceeded, in  company  with  Lieutenant  Clever,  Dr.  Krumsick,  and  some 
8 cavalry,  to  the  Fayetteville  road  to  reconnoiter.  We  had  proceeded 
as  far  as  the  tan-yard,  where  the  road  to  Bentonville  turns  off  to  the 
right.  There  we  suddenly  came  upon  the  enemy’s  pickets,  taking  them 
prisoners,  when  presently  I beheld  large  numbers  of  the  enemy  comino* 
down  the  Bentonville  road.  I at  once  turned  round  to  retrace  my  way 
to  the  camp,  being  eagerly  pursued  by  the  enemy’s  cavalry.  I now 
knew  that  I was  in  the  rear  of  the  enemy,  and  knowing  also  the  dis- 
tance between  the  tan-yard  and  Potson’s  Hill,  I saw  that  it  was  impos- 
sible for  my  worn-out  men  to  force  a passage.  I therefore  concluded 
to  retreaf  upon  the  nearest  post,  to  give  my  men  rest  and  re-enforce 
the  garrison,  and  at  5 o’clock  p.  m.  I again  moved  forward  to  Keets- 
ville and  from  there  to  Cassville.  In  Keetsville  I halted  an  hour 
waiting  to  escort  a train  of  9 wagons  that  had  endeavored  to  join  Colo- 
nel Davis’  command  and  was  greatly  harassed  by  the  enemy. 

I arrived  in  Cassville  at  11  o’clock  p.  m.  Remaining  there  on  the 
8th,  I received  three  days’  provisions,  only  having  three  days’  rations 
along  when  I started. 

Sunday  the  9th,  I again  moved  forward,  under  command  of  Col. 
C.  Wright,  Sixth  Missouri  Cavalry,  the  whole  force  consisting  of  my 
command,  150  of  Colonel  Wright’s  cavalry,  and  some  300  infantry  that 
got  in  from  Springfield  the  night  previous  with  a train.  That  morning 
I rejoined  your  command  at  Keetsville. 

In  four  days  my  command  marched  a distance  of  125  miles.  The  fol- 
lowing is  my  loss : One  private  of  Twelfth  Missouri,  8 of  Company  A, 
Seventeenth  Missouri,  and  13  of  Company  B,  Fifteenth  Missouri  Vol- 
unteers. These  men,  not  being  able  or  willing  to  stay  with  the  com- 
mand, were  picked  up  by  the  pursuing  enemy. 

I remain,  yours,  respectfully, 


JOSEPH  CONRAD, 

^ _ Major , Commanding  Expedition . 

Brig.  Gen.  Franz  Sigel, 

Commanding  First  and  Second  Divisions .

1 had  directed  General  McCulloch  to  attack  with  his  forces  the  enemy’s  I 
left  and  before  2 o’clock  it  was  evident  that  if  his  division  could  ad- 
vance or  even  maintain  its  ground,  I could  at  once  throw  forward 
Price’s  left,  advance  his  whole  line,  and  end  the  battle.  I sent  him  a 
dispatch  to  this  effect,  but  it  was  never  received  by  him.  Before  it  was 
penned  his  brave  spirit  had  winged  its  flight,  and  one  of  the  most  gal- 
lant leaders  of  the  Confederacy  had  fought  his  last  battle. 

About  3 p.  m.  I received,  by  aides-de-camp,  the  information  that 
Generals  McCulloch  and  McIntosh  and  Colonel  Hebert  were  killed, 
and  that  the  division  was  without  any  head.  I nevertheless  pressed  I 
forward  with  the  attack,  and  at  sunset  the  enemy  was  fleeing  before  our 
victorious  troops  at  every  point  in  our  front,  and  when  night  fell  we 
had  driven  him  entirely  from  the  field  of  battle. 

Our  troops  slept  upon  their  arms  nearly  a mile  beyond  the  point  at 
which  he  made  his  last  stand,  and  my  headquarters  for  the  night  were 
at  the  Elkhorn  Tavern.  We  had  taken  during  the  day  sevdn  cannon 

and  about  200  prisoners.  , x.  I 

In  the  course  of  the  night  1 ascertained  that  the  ammunition  was 
almost  exhausted,  and  that  the  officer  in  charge  of  the  ordnance  sup- 
plies could  not  find  his  wagons,  which,  with  the  subsistence  tram,  had 
been  sent  to  Bentonville.  Most  of  the  troops  had  been  without  any 
food  since  the  morning  of  the  6th  and  the  artillery  horses  were  beaten 
out.  It  was  therefore  with  no  little  anxiety  that  I awaited  the  dawn 
of  day.  When  it  came  it  revealed  to  me  the  enemy  in  a new  and  strong 
position,  offering  battle.  I made  my  dispositions  at  once  to  accept  the

So  far  as  I can  ascertain  our  loss  amounts  to  about  600  killed  and 
wounded  and  200  prisoners,  and  one  cannon,  which,  having  become 
lisabled,  I ordered  to  be  thrown  into  a ravine. 

The  best  information  I can  procure  of  the  enemy’s  loss  places  hi# 
ailed  at  more  than  700,  with  at  least  an  equal  number  of  wounded. 
;iVe  captured  about  300  prisoners,  making  his  total  loss  about  2,000. 
v\re  brought  away  four  cannon  and  ten  baggage  wagons,  and  we 
)urned  upon  the  field  three  cannon  taken  by  McIntosh  in  his  brilliant 
■harge.  The  horses  having  been  killed,  these  guns  could  not  be  brought 
iway. 

The  force  with  which  I went  into  action  was  less  than  14,000  men. 
Chat  of  the  enemy  is  variously  estimated  at  from  17,000  to  24,000. 

During  the  whole  of  this  engagement  I was  with  the  Missouri  di vis- 
on,  under  Price,  and  I have  never  seen  better  fighters  than  these  Mis- 
iouri  troops  and  more  gallant  leaders  than  General  Price  and  his 
>fficers.  From  the  first  to  the  last  shot  they  continually  pushed  on 
md  never  yielded  an  inch  they  had  won,  and  when  at  last  they  re- 
ceived the  order  to  fall  back  they  retired  steadily  and  with  cheers.  Gen- 
Tal  Price  received  a severe  wound  early  in  the  action,  but  would 
leither  retire  from  the  field  nor  cease  to  expose  himself  to  danger. 

No  successes  can  repair  the  loss  of  the  gallant  dead  who  fell  on  this 
rell-fought  field.  McCulloch  was  the  first  to  fall.  I had  found  him,  in 
he  frequent  conferences  I had  with  him,  a sagacious,  prudent  coun- 
selor, and  a bolder  soldier  never  died  for  his  country. 

McIntosh  had  been  very  much  distinguished  all  through  the  opera- 
ions  which  have  taken  place  in  this  region  ; and  during  my  advance 
“rom  Boston  Mountains  I placed  him  in  command  of  the  cavalry  bri- 
gade and  in  charge  of  the  pickets.  ITe  was  alert,  daring,  and  devoted 
o his  duty.  His  kindness  of  disposition,  with  his  reckless  bravery, 
lad  attached  the  troops  strongly  to  him,  so  that  after  McCulloch  fell, 
lad  he  remained  to  lead  them,  all  would  have  been  well  with  my  right 
ving.  But  after  leading  a brilliant  charge  of  cavalry  and  carrying 
he  enemy’s  battery  he  rushed  into  the  thickest  of  the  fight  again  at 
lie  head  of  his  old  regiment  and  was  shot  through  the  heart.  The 
ralue  of  these  two  officers  was  best  proven  by  the  effect  of  their  fall 
ipon  the  troops.  So  long  as  brave  deeds  are  admired  by  our  people 
he  names  of  McCulloch  and  McIntosh  will  be  remembered  and  loved. 

General  Slack,  after  gallantly  maintaining  a long-continued  and  suc- 
cessful attack,  was  shot  through  the  body ; but  I hope  his  distinguished 
cervices  will  be  restored  to  his  country. 

A noble  boy,  [S.]  Churchill  Clark,  commanded  a battery  of  artillery, 
tnd  during  the  fierce  artillery  actions  of  the  7th  and  8th  was  conspic- 
uous for  the  daring  and  skill  which  he  exhibited.  He  fell  at  the  very 
close  of  the  action.  Colonel  Bives  fell  mortally  wounded  about  the 
came  time  and  was  a great  loss  to  us.  On  a field  where  many  gallanl# 
gentlemen  were  I remember  him  as  one  of  the  most  energetic  and 
levoted  of  them  all. 

To  Col.  Henry  Little  my  especial  thanks  are  due  for  the  coolness, 
skill,  and  devotion  with  which  for  two  days  he  and  his  gallant  brigade 
)ore  the  brunt  of  the  battle.  Colonel  Burbridge,  Colonel  Bosser,  Col- 
mel  Gates,  Major  Lawther,  Major  Wade,  Captain  MacDonald,  and  Cap- 
ain  Schaumberg  are  some  gf  those  who  attracted  my  special  attention 
)y  their  distinguished  conduct. 

In  McCulloch’s  division,  the  Louisiana  regiment,  under  Col.  Louis 
debert,  and  the  Arkansas  regiment,  under  Colonel  McBae,  are  espec- 
ally  mentioned  for  their  good  conduct.  Major  Montgomery,  Captain

OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chav.  XVIII. 


Bradfute,  Lieutenants  Loinax,  Kimmel,  Dillon,  and  Frank  Armstrong, 
assistant  adjutant- general,  were  ever  active  and  soldierly.  After  their 
services  were  no  longer  required  with  their  own  division  they  joined 
my  staff,  and  I am  much  indebted  to  them  for  the  efficient  aid  they  gave 
me  during  the  engagement  of  the  8th.  They  are  meritorious  officers, 
whose  value  is  lost  to  the  service  by  their  not  receiving  rank  more 
accordant  with  their  merit  and  experience  than  that  they  now  hold. 

Being  without  my  proper  staff,  I was  much  gratified  by  the  offer  of 
Colonel  Shands  and  Captain  Barrett,  of  the  Missouri  Army,  of  their 
services  as  aides.  They  were  of  great  assistance  to  me  by  the  courage 
and  intelligence  with  which  they  bore  my  orders ; also  Colonel  Lewis, 
of  Missouri. 

None  of  the  gentlemen  of  my  personal  staff,  with  the  exception  of 
Colonel  Maury,  assistant  adjutant-general,  and  Lieut.  C.  Sulivane,  my 
aide-de-camp,  accompanied  me  from  Jacksonport,  the  others  having  left 
on  special  duty.  Colonel  Maury  was  of  invaluable  service  to  me  both 
in  preparing  for  and  during  the  battle.  Here,  as  on  other  battle-fields 
where  I have  served  with  him,  he  proved  to  be  a zealous  patriot  and 
true  soldier;  cool  and  calm  under  all  circumstances,  he  was  always 
ready,  either  with  his  sword  or  his  pen.  His  services  and  Lieutenant 
Sulivane’s  were  distinguished.  The  latter  had  his  horse  killed  under 
him  while  leading  a charge,  the  order  for  which  he  had  delivered. 

You  will  perceive  from  this  report,  general,  that,  although  I did  not, 
as  I hoped,  capture  or  destroy  the  enemy’s  army  in  Western  Arkansas, 
I have  inflicted  upon  it  a heavy  blow  and  compelled  him  to  fall  back 
into  Missouri.  This  he  did  on  the  16th  instant. 

For  further  details  concerning  the  action  and  for  more  particular 
notices  of  the  troops  engaged  I respectfully  refer  you  to  the  reports  of 
the  subordinate  officers,  which  accompany  this  report. 

Yery  respectfully,  sir.  your  obedient  servant, 

EARL  VAN  DORN, 

Major-  General. 

General  Braxton  Bragg,  Commanding , &c.

General  : I regret  to  find  that  in  my  report  of  the  battle  of  Elk- 
horn  no  mention  was  made  of  the  excellent  conduct  of  Lieut.  L.  C. 
Leftwich,  of  General  McCulloch’s  staff.  After  exhibiting  great  cour- 
age and  energy  during  the  engagement  of  that  division  he  joined  my 
staff  and  rendered  me  very  great  assistance  during  the  action  of  the 
8th.  I desire  to  bring  him"  to  your  notice  as  a gallant  and  meritorious 
youngbofficer. 

I am,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

EARL  YAN  DORN, 

Major- General.

Memphis,  Tenn.,  April  29,  18 
General  : I have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  action  of  my 


ip.  xvm.]  pea  ridge,  or  elkhorn  tavern,  ark.  295 

yat  (Fourth  Arkansas)  and  other  troops  under  my  command  in  the 
ttle  of  Sugar  Creek,  or  Elkhorn,  on  March  7 : 

At  about  10.30  a.  m.  my  regiment,  constituting  the  extreme  right  of 
ilonel  Hebert’s  brigade,  composed  of  McIntosh’s,  Hebert’s  (Third 
•uisiana),  Fourth  and  Fourteenth  Arkansas  Regiments,  and  McRae’s 
ttalion,  was  ordered,  with  the  rest  of  the  brigade,  to  take  a battery 
lich  was  directly  in  front,  but  at  some  distance,  and  in  the  rear  of  an 
en  field  and  a strip  of  woods  of  dense  undergrowth  and  filled  with 
len  timber,  intervening  between  us  and  the  field  and  extending 
rand  on  the  left  of  the  field.  Ordering  a charge,  my  men  obeyed 
th  alacrity  and  cheerfulness ; but  after  advancing  some  200  yards 
3y  were,  owing  to  the  nature  of  the  ground  and  obstacles  in  the  way, 
[•own  into  disorder  and  were  halted,  and  reformed  as  well  as  the 
Hind  would  permit.  The  enemy  discovering  us,  immediately  opened 
on  us  a heavy  fire  of  shell  and  grape.  In  a few  moments  the  order 
& given  to  renew  the  charge.  I accordingly  moved  my  regiment  for- 
rd,  obliquing,  however,  to  the  left,  keeping  in  the  skirt  of  woods 
at  extended  around  the  field,  in  order  to  protect  my  men  from  the 
emy’s  fire.  This  I succeeded  in  doing  in  a great  degree. 

While  making  this  movement,  however,  another  portion  of  the  bri- 
de, moving  by  the  flank,  cut  off  two  companies  and  a half  on  the  left 
im  the  main  body  of  my  regiment,  which  did  not  rejoin  it  during  the 
y,  but,  connecting  themselves  with  other  troops  of  the  brigade,  as  I 
credibly  informed,  fought  most  gallantly  through  the  day.  Con- 
uing  to  move  forward,  we  came  upon  a body  of  the  enemy’s  infantry 
ambuscade $ attacked  and  drove  them  back  until  they  were  reformed 
a second  body  in  the  rear.  We  attacked  the  whole  body  and  re- 
Ised  them  again $ but,  rallying  upon  their  reserves,  they  made  a 
nd,  but  were  soon  driven  back  again  by  our  brave  troops.  In  this 
t charge  one  of  the  enemy’s  batteries,  at  a distance  of  200  yards, 
med  upon  us,  but  we  charged  and  took  it  in  a very  short  time.  In 
s charge  the  loss  of  the  enemy  was  very  great. 

Che  enemy,  receiving  heavy  re-enforcements,  made  a simultaneous 
ack  with  cavalry  on  the  left  and  infantry  on  the  right  of  our  brigade 
numbers  far  superior  to  our  own.  After  a fierce  conflict  the  enemy 
re  for  the  fourth  time  repulsed  and  with  heavy  loss.  Generals 
Culloch  and  McIntosh  having  fallen  and  Colonel  Hubert  being  taken 
soner  and  there  being  no  other  field  officers  present,  I assumed  com- 
nd  of  the  brigade,  which  did  not  at  that  time  number  more  than  1,000 
n,  our  ranks  having  been  much  broken  and  thinned  by  casualties  and 
in  being  much  fatigued  and  disordered. 

3erceiving  the  enemy  advancing  heavily  re-enforced,  preparatory  to 
king  an  attack  upon  my  right  wing,  I ordered  Captain  Harris,  who 
s then  in  command  of  the  right  of  the  Third  Louisiana,  to  resist 
m.  He  did  so  with  great  gallantry  and  success,  again  repulsing 
; enemy.  The  enemy’s  cavalry,  at  the  same  time  attacking  my  right, 
s re  defeated  with  actual  slaughter. 

shortly  afterwards  the  enemy  were  seen  advancing  in  several  coi- 
ns towards  us,  numbering  at  least  5,000.  My  command  being  then 
atly  exhausted  and  seeing  no  advantage  likely  to  accrue  from  re- 
iiing  the  position  then  occupied,  after  consulting  with  the  officers 
jler  my  command,  all  agreeing,  I determined  to  fall  back  on  our 
erve,  which  I did  in  good  order  and  without  haste,  the  enemy  not 
oring  to  pursue  us. 

laving  occupied  the  new  position  selected  by  me,  I was  ordered  by 
y general  commanding  to  hold  the  same  until  further  orders.  I did

I would  respectfully  submit  the  following  report  of  my  command  : 
On  the  3d  instant  we  were  ordered  to  take  up  the  line  of  march  early 
e next  morning  towards  the  enemy,  General  McIntosh’s  brigade  to 
ke  the  advance. 

At  7 o’clock  on  the  morning  of  the  4th  we  left  our  encampment  on 
[>ston  Mountains,  my  regiment  going  in  advance. 

That  night  we  encamped  near  Fayetteville.  The  day  had  been  very 
Id,  with  quite  a snow-storm  during  the  morning.  After  leaving  Fay- 
teville  General  McIntosh’s  brigade,  which  was  composed  exclusively 
cavalry,  marched  up  the  Telegraph  or  Springfield  road  for  4 miles, 
lile  General  Price’s  division,  with  the  rest  of  our  army,  was  ordered 
> the  Elm  Springs  road.  Four  miles  from  Fayetteville  Colonel  Stone 
is  ordered  with  his  regiment  to  proceed  a few  miles  farther  up  the 
ilegraph  road,  where  he  would  remain  during  the  night  and  rejoin  our 
rces  the  next  day.  The  rest  of  General  McIntosh’s  brigade  turned  to 
e left,  and  after  carefully  reconnoitering  the  country  and  getting  all 
e information  we  could  of  the  enemy,  joined  the  main  body  of  our 
tny  at  Elm  Springs.  Considerable  snow  fell  again  that  night. 

At  3 a.  m.  on  the  6th  instant  we  left  Elm  Springs,  this  regiment  still 
advance.  When  we  had  gone  2 miles  that  morning  we  were  in- 
med  that  our  pickets  during  the  night  had  fired  upon  the  pickets  of 
3 enemy. 

We  arrived  at  Smith’s  Mill  about  sunrise,  and  here  learned  that  1,000 
deral  infantry  had  left  that  place  at  1 a.  m.,  and  had  gone  in  the 
•ection  of  Bentonville.  On  approaching  Bentonville,  from  the  smoke 
was  evident  that  the  enemy  had  fired  a portion  of  the  town  and 
re  destroying  some  of  their  supplies,  &c.  The  cavalry  were  halted 
the  prairie,  miles  south  of  Bentonville,  in  view  of  the  town,  a 
>rt  time,  for  consultation,  thus  affording  the  rest  of  our  army  time  to 
se  up.  It  was  agreed  that  Colonel  Gates,  with  his  command,  should 
ve  around  to  the  east  of  the  town,  and  that  General  McIntosh,  with 
command,  should  go  to  the  left.  Our  advance  guard  in  the  mean 
ie  had  approached  near  the  town.  When  we  had  got  immediately 
st  of  the  town  several  men  were  sent  up  to  reconnoiter  the  enemy, 
ey  soon  returned,  and  reported  a considerable  force  of  the  enemy 
raed  on  the  public  square.  General  McIntosh,  feeling  confident  that 
enemy  would  take  what  is  known  as  the  Camp  Stephens  road,  de- 
mined to  get  in  rear  ot  them.  Owing  to  the  broken,  rocky,  and 
untamous  character  of  the  country  north  of  the  town  and  the  ab- 
ce  of  a road  leading  from  where  we  were  across  to  the  Camp  Ste- 
als road,  we  found  it  impossible  to  reach  that  road  nearer  than  4 miles 

II  Bentonville,  and  then  only  by  traveling  a very  circuitous  route, 
ten  we  did  reach  it,  it  was  in  a rough,  mountainous  country.  On 
right  there  was  a mountain  the  entire  length  of  the  brigade.  The 
np  Stephens  road  passed  to  the  east  of  this  mountain.  Lieut  J.  S. 
,'gess,  with  20  men,  was  ahead  as  an  advance  picket.  Near  the 
np  Stephens  road  they  came  suddenly  on  a small  picket  of  the 
my,  and  at  once  gave  General  McIntosh  notice  of  it.  About  this 
e tlie  pickets  fired  at  each  other.  General  McIntosh  rode  forward 

ordered  the  advance  to  charge.  This  was  done  as  effectually  as

After  the  command  had  devolved  upon  you,  on  Friday  evening,  and 
when  it  was  supposed  that  the  enemy  would  attempt  to  force  its  way

anxiously  held  that  position  until  near  sunset,  when  the  order  was  given 
to  move  northward  to  a suitable  point  for  camping.  . 

Although  my  men  were  almost  exhausted  by  the  fatigue,  loss  of 
sleep,  and  hunger,  consequent  upon  the  three  days  and  nights  forced 
march  and  the  wearing  and  action  of  the  day,  they  retired  from  the 
field  with  reluctance.  Having  encamped  upon  the  side  of  a mountain 
near  the  enemy’s  line— indeed,  in  plain  view  of  their  camp-fires— we  were 
constantly  in'  hearing  of  the  rumbling  of  the  enemy  s artillery  as  it 
passed  from  the  battle-field  of  the  7th- where  the  brave  Texan  ranger, 
McCulloch,  gave  himself  up  as  a sacrifice  to  his  country  s good  to  join 
the  forces  opposed  to  General  Price,  and  remained  in  sleepless  vigi 
lance  until  1 a,  m.,  at  which  time,  by  your  order,  we  took  up  the  line 
of  march  for  General  Price’s  encampment. 

About  an  hour  before  daylight  Saturday  morning  we  reached  the 
right  of  Price’s  column  on  Sugar  Creek,  and  there,  for  the  first  time  in 
forty-eight  hours,  my  soldiers  were  permitted  to  snatch  a few  moments 
of  troubled  sleep,  only  to  be  aroused  by  the  deep-toned  thunder  of  forty 
cannons  soon  after  sunrise.  . , . \ 

The  soldiers  of  my  command  impatiently  awaited  orders  to  mou

General  : I have  the  honor  of  reporting  to  you  the  action  of  the 
ixth  Eegiment  Texas  cavalry,  under  my  command,  in  the  late  battle 
: Sugar  Creek : 

The  five  mounted  regiments  under  the  command  of  the  late  General 
clntosh  were  formed  in  column  in  the  timber  west  of  the  field  occupied 
y the  enemy,  and  were  thus  marched  into  the  field,  our  gallant  Mcln- 
>sh  at  the  head  and  intrepidly  marching  on  the  foe.  When  about  300 
irds  from  the  enemy’s  lines  a large  force  of  cavalry  was  discovered 
•utheast  of  our  then  marching  position,  bearing  the  colors  of  the  Stars 
id  Stripes.  At  this  moment  from  that  point  three  heavy  guns  opened 
ion  our  columns  a most  destructive  and  galling  fire,  which  mainly 
fected  our  second  battalions.  The  regiment  of  Colonel  Greer  was  on 
ir  extreme  right,  and  next  was  the  regiment  under  my  command.  At 
is  moment  the  order  was  given  to  charge,  and  in  an  instant  our  gal- 
nt  columns  were  pouring  a destructive  fire  in  the  face  of  the  enemy, 
id  at  once  they  abandoned  their  guns,  and  they  were  taken  by  our 
oops  and  secured. 

The  column  under  my  command,  after  the  guns  were  taken,  bore  to 
e left  and  formed  line  immediately  in  front  of  the  infantry  of  the 
lemy,  under  a galling  fire  of  infantry  and  a shower  of  grape  and  shell 
am  their  artillery.  My  regiment  was  then  ordered  to  the  rear,  and 
ecuted  the  command  in  the  most  perfect  order.  I then  reformed 
cm  in  the  open  field,  and  my  regiment  then  stood  in  ranks  unmoved, 
th  the  batteries  playing  full  upon  us.  Having  been  reserved  as  the 
ily  mounted  regiment  in  the  field  I kept  my  position,  receiving  no 
ders  on  account  of  the  fall — the  fated  fall — of  our  illustrious  Generals 
cOulloch  and  McIntosh,  until  late  in  the  evening,  at  which  time  some 
our  columns  were  retreating  and  the  enemy  attempting  to  flank  our 
ft.  I wheeled  my  command  in  position  to  defend  against  the  flanking 
ovement.  After  being  under  march  for  this  purpose  I was  ordered 
f General  Pike  to  protect  the  retreat  and  preserve  our  trains,  which 
mmand  I obeyed  through  many  difficulties,  and  brought  off  the  entire 
vision  train  and  all  of  the  public  property.  I had  no  further  connec- 
m with  the  fight;  a fact  much  regretted  by  the  brave  officers  and 
en  under  my  command.

After  your  advance  movement  was  taken  against  the  enemy  at  Sugar 
>eek  my  immediate  brigadier-general  (McIntosh)  detailed  my  regiment 
o make  a demonstration  against  the  enemy  at  Mud  Town  and  Cross  Hol- 
ow,  while  the  entire  army  moved  by  Elm  Springs  towards  Bentonville. 
This  order  was  delivered  to  me  on  the  5th,  and  was  executed  as  I will 
iow  detail : I moved  my  troops,  unsupported  either  by  artillery  or  in- 
antry,  to  the  batteries  of  the  enemy  at  Mud  Town,  but  their  guns  having 
he  best  range  possible  at  my  column  and  being  heavily  supported  by 
ofantry,  with  overwhelming  odds  against  us,  I determined  to  seek  a 
setter  field.  By  meeting  Colonel  Phelps,  with  his  regiment,  who  was 
q our  rear  on  the  Huntsville  road,  I turned  my  column  in  that  direction 
nd  succeeded  in  capturing  40  prisoners,  10  wagons  with  six-mule  teams, 
ome  loose  mules,  and  a lot  of  horses.  Captain  Jack  Wharton  late  in 
he  evening  had  a spirited  picket  skirmish  and  drove  in  the  enemy’s 
tickets. 

I bivouacked  at  night  in  a strong  natural  position,  looking  for  the 
olumnsof  the  enemy  until  next  morning,  when  we  marched  and  joined 
he  troops  in  the  skirmish  at  Bentonville  on  the  6th. 

On  the  morning  of  the  7th  General  McIntosh  led  our  cavalry  columns 
gainst  the  enemy  at  11.30  o’clock,  and  we  unexpectedly  met  him. 
le  at  once  opened  a galling  and  destructive  fire  upon  our  ranks  from 
is  left.  The  order  to  charge  was  immediately  given,  and  the  heavens 
ssounded  with  the  tramp  of  warriors’  steeds  as  they  swept  the  field 
nd  rushed  impetuously  on  the  enemy’s  battery.  My  regiment  gal- 
mtly  led  in  this  most  brilliant  charge,  which  was  but  momentarily 
ithstood  by  the  enemy,  who  left  his  guns  in  the  most  precipitous 
ight.  The  first  three  companies,  under  Captains  Wharton,  Throck- 
lorton,  and  Bridges,  poured  a most  destructive  fire  upon  the  enemy 
ear  his  guns,  killing  near  80  of  his  number.  Thanks  to  these  gallant 
ffieers  for  their  promptness,  valor,  and  success. 

Passing  the  batteries  with  my  troops,  I drew  up  in  line  of  battle  80 
irds  distant  from  the  enemy’s  line  of  infantry,  supporting  heavy  guns 
q mediately  in  our  front,  which  at  once  began  a destructive  fire  upon 
3.  I waited  for  orders  for  a general  charge,  but  was  directed  to  with- 
i‘aw  to  a greater  distance,  which  I did  in  the  most  perfect  order.  My 
oops  were  the  only  ones  to  be  left  mounted  during  the  day  on  our 
ght,  and  forming  again  in  the  rear  of  our  former  line,  we  stood,  dur- 
g the  balance  of  the  day,  the  continued  fire  of  ball,  shell,  and  shot 
om  the  enemy’s  guns  without  wavering  or  complaint  and  with  the 
ernness  of  veterans  of  a hundred  battles.  All  credit  to  my  brave 
oops. 

About  the  time  of  our  second  formation  of  line  our  distinguished 
ader,  the  gallant,  chivalrous  McCulloch,  fell,  embalming  his  country’s 
use  with  his  own  blood,  and  depriving  his  admiring  soldiery  of  their 
|ilitary  chieftain  and  idol.  But  a short  time  after  this  and  near  the 
me  portion  of  the  field  fell  Brig.  Gen.  James  McIntosh,  in  whose 
airage  the  troops  had  the  most  implicit  confidence.  May  history  do 
eir  characters  justice  and  later  years  appreciate  their  loss  as  we  felt 
on  that  day.  Several  hours  elapsed  before  I knew  certainly  of  their 
d fate,  during  which  time  I dispatched  officers  and  aides  to  every 
:rt  of  the  field  for  orders,  but  who  invariably  returned  without  them, 
wing  me  in  the  most  perplexed  condition  and  mental  anguish.

tion  of  our  end  of  the  field.  During  his  absence  I was  ordered  by

mrchill  Clark ; a child  in  simplicity  and  purity  of  character,  a boy

e age  of  nineteen  years  was  obnoxious  to  no  imputation  of  enemies  or 
volities  which,  alas,  but  too  frequently  characterize  youths  who  have 
t attained  more  than  half  his  years.  His  life  was  useful  to  him  only 
far  as  it  might  be  useful  to  his  country,  and  to  her  liberation  and  the 
fense  of  her  constitutional  rights  were  all  his  energies  consecrated,

iaven  ordained.  He  has  passed  away  before  corruption  had  beguiled 
* heart  or  the  whisperings  of  malice  detracted  from  his  fair  repute, 
ere  it  not  a crime  against  God’s  Providence,  our  hearts  would  envy 
e rest  of  the  silent  but  honored  grave.

Taking  into  consideration  the  great  exposure  of  the  men  in  an  open

et  the  trial,  leaving  14  of  their  number  dead  upon  the  field  and  103 
unded. 

The  officers  who  were  killed  were  gallantly  leading  their  men  to  the

the  battle  of  Elkhorn  Tavern  and  the  operations  leading  thereto  : 
The  troops  under  my  command  consisted  of  Guibor’s  battery,  of  four 
ns,  and  MacDonald’s,  of  three  guns,  and  what  is  known  as  McBride’s 
rision,  comprising  some  500  infantry  and  120  cavalry. 

In  obedience  to  General  Orders,  hTos.  58  and  59,  from  Major-General 
ice,  my  command,  provided  with  three  days’  rations  and  without 
ggage  and  camp  equipage,  proceeded  on  the  march  from  Gove 
eek  on  Tuesday  morning,  the  4th  instant,  in  the  direction  of  Benton 
le. 

On  Thursday  morning,  the  6th  instant,  when  about  6 miles  from  that 
ice,  I received  orders  to  advance  at  double-quick  time,  which  was 
scuted  by  the  command  until  they  arrived  at  the  village,  though 
) late  to  participate  in  the  skirmish  between  our  cavalry  and  Gen- 
ii Sigel’s  retreating  force,  yet  in  advance  of  other  commands  which 
I preceded  them  on  the  march. 

Che  pursuit  continued  without  halt  or  rest  during  the  whole  day, 
I night  found  us  worn  down  with  fatigue  and  our  three  days’  rations 
riausted. 

U 8 o’clock  on  the  same  evening  the  pursuit  was  continued  and 
ted  all  night. 

It  daylight  on  Tuesday  morning  an  hour’s  rest  enabled  the  command 
push  forward  with  some  degree  of  vigor,  although  unremitted  march - 
: and  fasting  had  reduced  its  effective  strength  at  least  one-third  of 
whole  number. 

U about  10  o’clock  on  Friday  morning  I was  ordered  to  form  my  in- 
try  in  line  of  battle  on  a hill  to  the  left  of  the  State  road,  on  Sugar 
>ek.  Subsequently  MacDonald’s,  Wade’s,  Clark’s,  and  Guibor’s  bat 
les  occupied  the  same  position,  which  for  some  hours  exchanged  a 
ivy  fire  with  the  enemy,  during  which  time  my  infantry  and  cavalry 
an  and  during  the  remainder  of  the  action  dismounted)  acted  as  a 
•porting  force. 

he  enemy’s  batteries  being  silenced  or  abandoned,  I received  orders 
nove  my  command  to  the  support  of  Colonel  Little’s  brigade : but 
ng  informed  by  him  that  Burbridge’s  brigade  was  being  heavily 
ssed  on  the  right  of  his  line,  I advanced  my  command  and  relieved 
t regiment,  which  formed  in  my  rear. 

laving  performed  this  duty,  I received  an  order  to  move  my  com-

General  : I have  the  honor  to  submit  a report  of  the  operations  of 
y command  in  the  actions  of  the  7th  and  8th  instant  near  Elkhorn 
tvern : 

In  compliance  with  your  order  all  the  cavalry,  excepting  Captain 
unpbell’s  company,  which  fought  as  infantry,  was  dismounted  before 
iving  camp  in  Boston  Mountains,  and  which  consisted  of  about  80  men, 
e remains  of  Colonel  Frazier’s  and  Colonel  Freeman’s  regiments,  Mis- 
uri  State  Guard,  and  squads  of  Confederates  numbering  105.  These 
-re  attached  to  the  Confederate  Infantry,  together  with  parts  of  two 
mpanies  of  Colonel  Schnable’s  Third  Infantry,  Missouri  State  Guard, 
narched  with  658  men  on  the  4th  instant,  leaving  a strong  camp 
lard  behind. 

On  the  morning  of  the  7th  we  reached  the  enemy’s  rear  near  the  junc- 
>n  of  the  Bentonville  and  Springfield  roads,  the  command  being  some- 
lat  reduced  from  the  severity  of  the  march.  I was  immediately  or- 
red  into  position  by  you  on  the  hill  to  the  left  of  the  road,  where  our 
tteries  were  first  posted.  Here  we  received  the  enemy’s  fire  for  two 
urs,  sustaining  a loss  of  10  in  wounded. 

I was  again  ordered  to  the  right,  to  support  Colonel  Burbridge,  and 
vanced  in  line  several  hundred  yards,  when  I found  myself  in  close 
oximity  to  one  of  the  enemy’s  batteries.  Our  guide  was  missing,  and 
5 had  advanced  a considerable  distance  beyond  Colonel  Burbridge’s 
sition.  The  enemy  opened  on  us  with  canister  and  shell,  but  my  men, 
mg  well  sheltered,  sustained  no  injury.  I held  the  position  for  thirty 
mites,  when  we  were  fired  into  from  one  of  our  own  batteries  and 
re  forced  to  fall  back. 

By  your  order  I now  took  position  on  Colonel  Burbridge’s  left,  and 
vanced  on  the  enemy,  to  the  right  of  Elkhorn  Tavern.  The  timber 
ing  obstructed  by  heavy  undergrowth  at  this  point,  I was  forced  to 
hque  to  the  left,  which  movement  brought  me  to  the  rear  of  the 
rern,  and  here,  by  order,  I took  position  on  Colonel  Hives’  right,  and 
operated  with  that  gallant  and  lamented  officer  during  the  remainder 
the  action.

After  having  marched  the  greater  part  of  the  night  of  the  6th  instant 
rithout  any  other  refreshment  than  a few  hours’  rest,  we  started  at 
laylight  on  the  7th,  and  soon  reached  the  Telegraph  road,  near  which 
te  were  ordered  to  place  our  battery  in  position  while  a reconnaissance 
ras  being  made.  We  soon  advanced  and  took  position  in  the  canon 
rith  the  artillery,  while  the  infantry  crowned  the  crests  of  the  neigh- 
boring hills.  About  10  a.  m.  we  were  ordered  forward  in  double-quick 
ime,  and  ascended  a steep  hill  on  the  left,  up  which  our  artillery  was 
apidly  rolled  by  the  infantry,  who  there  displayed  the  eagerness  with 
duck  they  pushed  forward  to  meet  the  foe.  By  this  movement  we 
eached  the  same  plateau  upon  which  the  enemy  were  posted,  and  our 
attery  was  brought  into  action  under  command  of  Lieutenant  [G.  W.j 
Iiggins,  but  assisted  by  Colonel  [H.  M.]  Bledsoe,  of  the  Sixth  Infantry,

The  major-general  commanding  this  district  desires  to  express  to  the 
'oops  his  admiration  for  their  conduct  during  the  recent  expedition 
gainst  the  enemy.  Since  leaving  camp  in  Boston  Mountains  they 
ave  been  incessantly  exposed  to  the  hardships  of  a winter  campaign 
ad  have  endured  such  privations  as  troops  rarely  encounter. 

In  the  engagements  of  the  6th,  7th,  and  8tli  instant  it  was  the  for- 
me of  the  major-general  commanding  to  be  immediately  with  the 
Missouri  division,  and  he  can  therefore  bear  personal  testimony  to  their 
allant  bearing. 

From  the  noble  veteran  who  has  led  them  so  long  to  the  gallant  S. 
hurchill  Clark,  who  fell  while  meeting  the  enemy’s  last  charge,  the 
fissourians  proved  themselves  devoted  patriots  and  staunch  soldiers, 
ie  met  the  enemy  on  his  chosen  positions  and  took  them  from  him. 
hey  captured  four  of  his  cannon  and  many  prisoners.  They  drove 
im  from  his  field  of  battle  and  slept  upon  it. 

The  victorious  advance  of  McCulloch’s  division  upon  the  strong 
osition  of  the  enemy’s  front  was  inevitably  checked  by  the  misfortunes 
hich  now  sadden  the  hearts  of  our  countrymen  throughout  the  Con-
