Wednesday  at  daylight  we  started  in  pursuit.  Ten  miles  out  we  en- 
)untered  their  pickets,  badly  wounding  one.  Pressing  on,  at  noon  we 
drived  at  their  camp,  to  find  that  during  the  previous  night  it  had  been 
sserted.  Passing  5 miles  beyond,  we  came  to  the  Spring  River  Mill, 
i the  edge  of  Arkansas.  Just  before  arriving  at  the  mill  our  advance 
aard  ran  upon  a squad  of  secesli,  supposed  to  be  Coleman’s  men; 
illed  2 and  wounded  4.  At  the  mill  I had  the  wounds  dressed,  fed 
ir  horses,  released  our  prisoners  as  an  incumbrance,  and  pushed  on 
est,  a part  of  the  time  in  Arkansas  and  part  in  Missouri.  At  9 
clock  we  camped,  having  traveled  40  miles.  At  daylight  started 
> ain  on  the  trail  of  the  rebels,  whom  I had  reason  to  suppose  were  10 
iles  west,  and  had  been  re-enforced  100  men.  Two  miles,  and  we 
?ain  encountered  their  pickets,  but  my  advance  guards  failed  to  cap- 
ire  them.  Ten  miles  brought  us  to  their  camp,  but  again  deserted, 
id  from  all  appearances  in  the  greatest  haste.  Provisions  were  left, 
id  even  breakfast  uneaten.  Being  satisfied  they  were  not  far  in  ad- 
ince,  I cautioned  my  advance  and  flankers  to  be  on  the  alert  to  pro- 
mt surprise,  and  pushed  on  about  5 miles  farther.  I heard  sharp  fir- 
g in  advance,  and  supposing  my  advance  had  encountered  the  re- 
eating rebels,  I galloped  forward  to  find  my  guard  engaged  with  the 
hole  rebel  force,  estimated  at  from  600  to  1,000.  They  had  taken  a 
rong  position  in  one  of  those  pest  holes  of  creation,  an  Arkansas 
vamp,  and  we  within  4 rods  of  them.  Just  then  a ball  struck  Ser- 
vant Rottaken  and  knocked  him  from  his  horse. 

Turning,  I found  my  whole  battalion,  including  the  howitzer,  at  my 
de,  followed  by  Major  Drake  and  the  Iowa  Third.  Our  sudden  ap- 
‘arance  seemed  to  paralyze  the  enemy  for  a moment,  and  knowing 
at  everything  depended  upon  immediate  action,  I ordered  the  how- 
ler into  position  to  shell  the  swamp.  I also  ordered  the  men  of  my 
ittalion  to  dismount,  every  fourth  man  to  take  the  horses  to  the  rear, 
also  ordered  Major  Drake  to  the  right  of  the  swamp.  This  order  was 
>eyed  in  an  instant,  and  the  men  advanced  upon  the  enemy.  Sergeant 
oody  threw  two  shells,  but  I noticed  too  high  for  those  in  our  imme- 
ate  front.  By  this  time  the  enemy  rallied  and  poured  upon  us  a 
‘adly  fire.  My  bugler,  who  was  at  my  side,  fell  from  his  horse.  Young 
att  was  killed  instantly  at  the  cannon.  Pierce,  another  one  at  the 
anon,  was  badly  wounded.  Young  Kendall  fell  mortally  wounded, 
rat  Lieut.  R.  H.  O.  Mack,  of  Company  A,  whilst  leading  his  men 
avely  forward,  fell  mortally  wounded.  Several  others  were  wounded, 
irning,  I rode  to  the  howitzer  and  directed  Sergeant  Moody  to  load 
th  grape  and  lower  his  piece.  Just  then  my  horse  was  pierced  by 
o bullets,  but  Sergeant  Moody  instantly  obeyed  the  order,  when  the 
bels  broke  in  the  greatest  confusion,  my  men  on  foot  advancing  from 
se  to  tree.  The  enemy  at  this  time  attempted  to  retreat,  but  were 
Bt  by  a charge  from  the  Iowa  boys  on  the  north,  which  drove  them 
ick  into  the  swamp  with  a loss  of  20  prisoners  and  a large  number  of 
lied  and  wounded.  Two  prisoners  belonging  to  Major  Bowen’s  bat- 
lion  were  also  released.  Among  the  prisoners  is  a nephew  of  the 
•lebrated  Jim  Lane,  of  Kansas. 

Had  we  been  able  to  pursue  the  enemy  into  the  swamp  our  triumph 
mid  have  been  complete,  but  Major  Drake’s  men  had  no  carbines

ion.  Sergeant  Bottaken,  of  Company  D,  after  being  knocked  from

lut  I could  fill  a page  with  such  acts  of  heroism.  I only  mention

Report  of  Lieut.  Col.  Joseph  W.  McClurg , Missouri  Cavalry , Militia. 

Headquarters  Missouri  State  Militia, 

Linn  Creek , Mo.,  March  26,  1862. 

I have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report,  although  accompanied 
ith  some  regrets :

MARCH  22,  1862. — Skirmish  at  Little  Santa  Fe,  Mo. 

Report  of  Col.  Robert  B.  Mitchell,  Second  Kansas  Cavalry. 

Hdqrs.  Second  Regiment  Kansas  Volunteers, 

Camp  Blair,  March  24,  1862. 1 

Major  : 1 have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  night  of  the  22d,  i 
accordance  with  a request  from  Major  Banzhaf,  commanding  First  Ba 
talion  Missouri  Cavalry,  and  also  in  pursuance  of  a plan  that  I hai 
been  maturing  for  some  time,  I left  camp  with  a detachment  detaile 
from  all  the  companies  in  this  command,  the  detachment  about  300  ii 
number,  with  Majors  Fisk  and  Pomeroy. 

Quantrill,  with  a part  of  his  gang,  had  burned  the  bridge  betwee 
Kansas  City  and  Independence,  and  it  was  contemplated  by  Maj< 
Banzhaf  to ‘march  from  Kansas  City,  and  in  conjunction  with  Colon 
Weer,  Fourth  Kansas,  to  surround  and  entrap  Quantrill. 

I left  camp  about  6.30  p.  m.  of  the  22d  instant,  reached  Little  Sant 
F4  about  10  o’clock  that  night,  and  sent  Major  Pomeroy  about  3 mik 
from  the  town,  with  instructions  to  arrest  one  David  Tate,  whom  I ha 
reason  to  believe  was  connected  with  Quantrill.  Major  Pomeroy  ha 
with  him  a detachment  of  Companies  D and  E,  under  command  < 
Captain  Moore  and  Lieutenant  Stover.  When  Major  Pomeroy  reache 
the  house  he  demanded  entrance,  and  a gun  was  immediately  fire 
through  the  door.  He  then  called  upon  them  to  surrender,  and  to  sen 
out  their  women  and  children  if  they  had  any  in  the  house.  Aft* 
waiting  some  time,  while  shots  were  fired  from  the  house,  he  ordered 
volley  to  be  fired  into  the  house.  The  cries  of  women  were  then  heart 
when  he  ordered  the  men  to  cease  firing.  The  women  and  childre 
then  came  out  and  firing  was  resumed  on  both  sides.  Two  of  the  me 
then  came  out  of  one  of  the  windows  and  surrendered.  They  stated  t 
Major  Pomeroy  that  Quantrill  was  in  the  house  with  26  men.  Majc 
Pomeroy  then  threatened  to  fire  the  house,  and  upon  their  continue 
refusal  to  surrender  he  ordered  the  house  to  be  fired,  and  an  attemi 
was  made  to  fire  it,  but  without  success.  Major  Pomeroy  and  Privat 
Wills,  of  Company  D,  were  at  this  time  shot.  Major  Pomeroy  becomin 
disabled,  Captain  Moore  took  command,  and  sent  back  to  me  requestin 
re-enforcements,  so  as  not  to  let  any  of  the  men  escape.  Captain  Mooi 
having  threatened,  in  case  of  the  enemy  not  surrendering,  to  set  fire  1 
the  house  and  they  still  refusing  so  to  do,  he  ordered  the  house  to  1 
again  set  on  fire,  and  this  time  the  flames  rapidly  enveloped  the  hous'

Here,  to  my  great  chagrin,  I found  that  our  guide  had  remained  al 
Little  River. " Our  troops,  eager  for  the  fray,  pressed  on,  but  found  the

to  repair.  Being  apprehensive  that  in  the  eagerness  of  the  pursuit  we 
might  get  into  an  ambush  I ordered  a portion  of  Captain  Nelson’* 
company  to  dismount  and  proceed  on  foot  in  advance  of  the  column 
They  had  not  proceeded  far  before  they  were  fired  upon  by  person*

our  men — 2 mortally.  I ordered  forward  more  dismounted  men,  ant

which  desperate  charge  was  led  by  Captain  Nelson  to  my  entire  satis 
faction,  and  had  the  desired  effect  to  drive  the  enemy  out  of  gun  range 
At  this  point  we  captured  2 horses. 

The  important  question  was  now'  to  be  decided  whether  to  return  tc 
camp  or  proceed.  It  being  4 o’clock  p.  m.  and  about  21  miles  fron 
camp,  and  4 wounded  men  to  bring  in,  without  ambulances  or  surgeon 
two  of  them,  Matthias  Cockerel,  of  Company  K,  and  Amandus  Tweedy 
of  Company  A,  mortally  wounded,  I called  a council  of  Captains  Nelson 
Hodge,  and  Koehler,  and  Lieutenant  Hunting,  and  it  was  determined 
to  return,  on  account  of  the  lateness  of  the  day  and  the  ground  being 
entirely  impracticable  for  cavalry  to  operate  on.  Whereupon  I dis 
patched  a courier  to  camp  to  have  the  surgeon  and  an  ambulance  senl 
out  to  meet  us.  Our  attention  was  now  given  to  the  wounded  men 
who  were  carried  by  the  men,  using  blankets  and  surcingles  for  tlu 
imrpose.  About  9 p.  m.  the  ambulance  with  the  surgeon  met  us,  and 
decided  at  once  that  the  wounded  men  should  not  be  moved  farther  til 
morning.  The  troops  having  been  under  constant  fatigue  all  day,  Cap 
tains  Graham,  Nelson,  and  myself,  with  some  10  or  12  men,  remained 
The  other  troops  were  sent  to  camp  with  4 prisoners  we  had  taken  anc 
4 horses.  Matthias  Cockerel  died  of  his  wounds  at  11  p.  m.  the  23d 
and  Amandus  Tweedy  at  9 a.  m.  24th. 

The  country  after  passing  Little  River,  14  miles  from  this  point,  n 
impracticable  for  cavalry  troops  to  operate  in  at  this  season  of  tin

or  Grand  Prairie  is  reached,  as  the  only  passage  across  the  swamp  r 
the  aforesaid  plank  road.  It  is  a single  track,  and  the  water  on  either 
side  from  one  to  many  feet  deep,  and  the  rebels  are  represented  to  hav< 
many  light  canoes  (some  of  which  we  saw),  so  that  they  can  glide  alone 
the  flanks  of  a force  on  the  road  (being  masked  by  old  vines  that  hicu 
them  from  Anew),  where  a small  force  may  from  behind  trees  pour  * 
very  destructive  fire  on  persons  traveling  on  the  plank  without  th<

Captain  : I have  the  honor  to  report  for  the  information  of  the  major- 
eneral  commanding  the  result  of  the  expedition  under  Lieutenant-Col  - 
nel  Blood  into  the  upper  part  of  Moniteau  County. 

Lieutenant-Colonel  Blood,  in  obedience  to  orders  from  these  head- 
uarters  of  March  23,  reached  Pisgah,  with  Company  A,  Sixth  Missouri 
Volunteers,  on  the  25th  ; was  joined  at  10  a.  m.  on  the  26th  by  Captain 
idams’  company,  Sixth  Missouri  Volunteers  ; Captains  Bice’s  and 
Sard’s  companies  militia,  and  a section  of  the  Third  Indiana  Battery, 
nder  Lieutenant  Thomas.  The  column  then  moved  cautiously  but 
apidly  forward.  At  2 p.  m.,  having  arrived  at  a point  5 miles  from 
lount  Vernon,  the  location  of  the  rendezvous  was  learned  and  a report 
eard  that  there  were  300  rebels  thereat.  Having  arrived  within  a few 
flies  of  the  school-house  reported  as  the  rendezvous,  and  where  the 
ommand  was  to  separate  to  surround  the  same,  they  suddenly  met  a 
quad  of  9 rebels  coming  directly  towards  them  in  twos  at  shoulder  arms. 
Colonel  Blood  being  in  the  advance,  ordered  the  advance  guard  to  charge, 
t which  the  rebels  ran  for  the  brush,  and  as  our  men  approached,  fired, 
n the  melee  which  ensued  5 were  killed,  2 mortally  wounded  (dying 
he  same  night),  and  2 taken  prisoners,  1 of  whom  was  wounded  in  the 
tip.  The  rebels  were  all  desperate  fellows,  armed  with  double-barreled 
hot-guns,  pistols,  and  knives. 

The  command  was  then  ordered  forward  at  the  double-quick  to  carry 
ut  the  plan  and  surround  the  school-house,  which  was  situated  in 
he  northeast  corner  of  the  point  of  land  at  the  junction  of  the  Little 
Saline  and  Missouri  Bivers.  There  were,  as  our  prisoners  had  protested, 
to  rebels  there.  Watson’s  gang,  they  asserted,  left  there  on  the  20th 
nstant  by  unfrequented  roads  and  by-paths  for  Arkansas.  They  also 
tated  that  Captain  Johnson’s  company  from  Shelby  County  and  Cap 
ain  Spencer’s  company  from  Boone  had  previously  gone  the  same  way, 
aaking  night  marches  and  avoiding  public  roads  and  towns.  The 
louse,  which  was  well  calculated  for  the  purpose  for  which  it  had  been

General  : I have  the  honor  to  report  the  following  movements, 
hich  resulted  in  an  attack  upon  a large  guerrilla  force,  under  the  no  tori  - 
is  Mat.  Houx,  and  the  total  defeat  of  the  same : 

On  the  morning  of  the  25th  [26th]  instant  I received  information  that 
small  party  of  rebels  were  hiding  at  the  house  of  one  Hunter,  3 miles 
>uth  of  this  place.  I immediately  started  with  10  men  belonging  to 
aptain  Houts’  company  to  capture  them.  After  proceeding  about  1 
ile  in  the  direction  above  indicated  a reliable  citizen  informed  me  that 
ere  were  about  25  or  30  rebels  near  Hunter’s  house.  I sent  a messenger 
Captain  Houts  for  re-enforcements,  and  in  a short  time  Lieutenant 
'well  came  up  with  10  men.  I proceeded  cautiously  to  Hunter’s  with- 
it  getting  sight  of  the  enemy  ; however,  when  there,  his  pickets  were 
scovered  about  a mile  north  of  us.  I immediately  moved  toward  them, 
ey  disappearing  over  a hill.  When  I reached  the  hill  where  the 
ckets  were  last  seen  I discovered  half  a mile  ahead  of  us  about  85 
>rsemen  drawn  up  in  line  awaiting  our  approach.  I halted  to  recon- 
>iter  their  position  and  strength.  The  enemy,  being  emboldened  by 
y seeming  hesitancy,  charged  precipitately  down  the  hill  towards  us. 
istantly  I dismounted  the  men  and  prepared  to  receive  them.  They 
me  within  400  yards,  halted,  wavered,  and  breaking  Quickly  to  the 
ght,  disappeared  in  a clump  of  trees  about  300  yards  from  my  left.  I 
counted  my  men  and  disappeared  quickly  over  the  hill  to  the  rear,  and 
iug  concealed  by  the  hill  and  brush  turned  his  right,  and  in  a moment 
is  dismounted  300  yards  from  the  enemy,  and  charging  double-quick 
his  rear  the  rebels  broke  in  confusion.  We  found  here  coats, 
janketSj  &c.  All  this  without  the  firing  of  a gun,  the  enemy  retreat- 
g rapidly  to  the  west.  I followed  him  to  the  crossing  of  the  East  Fork 
Post  Oak  Creek,  2 miles  from  Warrensburg. 

In  the  mean  time,  having  sent  back  to  town  for  re-enforcements  and 
ey  not  coming,  I went  there  immediately,  and  found  Captain  Mel. 
)Ster,  with  20  men,  ready  to  march.  I proceeded  immediately  to  the 
jossing  on  Post  Oak,  and  found  on  examination  that  the  rebels  had 
4 the  road  and  gone  through  the  brush.  Following  his  trail  about  4 
;les,  I came  suddenly  upon  him  on  the  east  bank  of  West  Post  Oak. 
is  pickets,  being  posted  on  a hill  to  my  right,  were  cut  off.  The  enemy 
treated  in  confusion  across  the  ford,  and  hastily  took  his  position  on 
e opposite  bank,  protected  by  log  and  rail  pens  and  almost  entirely

MARCH  26,  1862. — Action  at  Humansville,  Mo. 


Report  of  Lieut,  Col.  Joseph  W.  MeClurg,  Missouri  Cavalry,  Militia. 


Headquarters  Missouri  Si'ate  -Militia,  a,9 
Linn  Creek,  Mo.,  March  31,  1862. 

General  : I have  the  honor  to  submit,  for  your  perusal XVomty 
eration  the  following  report  of  the  fight  at  Humansville,  Polk  County 
I make  it  from  the  official  report  of  Captain  Stockton,  made  out  ontli 
28th  instant.  His  language  is  abbut  as  follows  : 

About  2 o’clock  in  the  afternoon  of  the  26th  instant  a lady  came 
town  and  informed  Captain  Gravely  (Captain  Gravely,  I suppose,  be 
a lady’s  man)  that  a large  force  of  rebels  were  marchin^  upon 
alarm  was  given,  and  the  officers  and  men  of  Compani  ( P 
Stockton),  B (Captain  Cosgrove),  D (Captam  Gravely),  and  E(  at 
Smith)  were  soon  in  line  ready  for  battle.  In  a few  minutes  1 be enem 
were  seen  passing  town  from  west  to  east  on  the  south  of  • 
east  of  town  is  a thicket  of  underbrush,  coming  up  ™thm50imws 
extending  east  and  south  about  a mile.  Believing  it  was  the  intenn 


Chap.  XVin.] 


ACTION  AT  HUMANSVILLE,  MO. 


355 


of  the  rebels  to  attack  us  from  the  east  merely  to  draw  the  attention  of 
our  forces  and  that  the  main  body  would  attack,  us  from  the  west  and 
north,  Company  A marched  to  the  east  of  town,  taking  position  along 
the  fence  running  east  and  south.  Captain  Cosgrove,  of  Company  B, 
and  70  men  of  his  own  and  Captain  Melton’s  company  (both  of  these 
companies  being  at  Warsaw,  and  Captain  Cosgrove  having  gone  to  the 
assistance  of  the  Humansville  companies  by  request,  as  they  were  an- 
ticipating an  attack  or  intended  to  make  one)  were  in  the  rear  of  Cap- 
tain Stockton,  Company  A,  on  the  east  of  town.  Company  D (Captain 
Gravely)  was  paraded  near  the  center  of  town  on  their  horses,  and  or- 
dered to  watch  the  enemy  and  prevent  flanking.  Company  E (Captain 
Smith)  was  on  the  west  of  town. 

By  this  time  the  guard  fired  on  the  right  of  Company  A,  and  the 
enemy  were  seen  in  the  front  and  were  fired  on  by  Company  A.  The 
fire  was  returned,  and  a charge  ordered  by  the  enemy,  who  rushed 
up  through  the  underbrush,  firing  and  taking  shelter  under  fencing 
and  behind  trees.  Company  A fired  several  rounds,  which  told  with 
considerable  effect,  Captain  Cosgrove  marched  his  company  to  the 
assistance  of  Company  A under  a severe  fire,  and  took  position  on  the 
right  of  Company  A and  opened  fire  upon  the  enemy  with  his  whole 
company.  Twenty-five  men  of  Company  A,  under  Lieutenant  Wake- 
field, kept  up  a brisk  fire  from  the  left,  and  the  main  body  of  Company 
A,  with  Captain  Stockton  and  Lieutenant  Akard,  fought  on  from  the 
center.  The  enemy  was  seen  to  begin  to  retreat,  and  Captain  Cosgrove 
gave  them  a galling  fire  from  the  right.  Captain  Stockton’s  leg  was 
broken  when  the  charge  was  ordered  by  the  enemy,  and  Lieutenant 
Akard  remained  and  continued  the  fire  from  the  center  as  long  as  the 
enemy  could  be  seen.  Captain  Cosgrove  was  severely  wounded  in  the 
arm  as  he  moved  to  the  right  of  Company  A,  but  continued  to  command 
his  men  and  superintend  the  battle  (Captain  Stockton  being  disabled 
by  a broken  leg).  When  the  enemy  retreated  Captain  Cosgrove  ordered 
Captain  Gravely  to  follow  them  and  ascertain  if  they  had  men  back, 
thinking  still  that  they  had  a reserve  in  the  brush  and  intended  to 
decoy  us  from  our  position.  He  promptly  obeyed,  fired  upon  their  rear 
guard  several  times  in  the  brush,  until  all  were  known  to  be  retreating 
with  great  rapidity,  but  in  good  order. 

The  enemy’s  force  was  said  to  be  250  men  by  themselves  after  the 
fight  and  before  it  400.  Captain  Gravely,  who  saw  them  in  the  prairie 
4 miles  south  of  town,  estimates  the  number  at  least  400.  We  lost 
none  killed.  Captain  Stockton,  of  Company  A,  was  badly  wounded  in 
the  leg;  Corporal  Smith  dangerously  wounded  in  the  breast;  Privates 
A.  Gordon  and  Wyatt  very  slightly  wounded.  Of  Company  B,  Captain 
Cosgrove  severely  but  not  dangerously  wounded  in  the  arm;  Private 
Divine  severely  wounded,  and  Halbert,  Evans,  Parker,  and  Kidwell 
slightly.  Of  Company  D,  Captain  Gravely,  Private  Boberson  severely 
wounded. 

So  far  as  known  of  the  enemy  Colonel  Frazier  was  killed,  Captain 
Me  Mi  nil  killed,  4 others  dead  on  the  ground,  4 mortally  wounded  and 
left,  6 others  reported  by  their  surgeon,  who  came  in  next  morning,  as 
pertain  to  die,  and  not  less  than  20  others  wounded  in  various  degrees. 
We  took  3 prisoners  and  a number  of  their  horses.  The  officers  and 
men  in  the  fight  behaved  bravely,  did  their  duty,  and  so  well  that  the 
rebels  themselves  acknowledge  they  were  badly  whipped.  Captain 
Smith  kept  his  position,  and  was  not  needed  to  drive  the  enemy  from 
the  brush.  There  was  no  flinching  in  ranks  anywhere. 

The  wagon  of  Captain  Stockton’s  company  was  5 miles  south  of  town, 


356

and  the  rebels  took  it  and  made  their  escape.  Captain  Stockton  has 
very  little  doubt  about  recovering  it.  He  sent  out  150  men  for  that

At  the  fight  we  took  13  horses.  The  men  are  rejoicing,  and  the  ladies  9 
of  the  town  (except  a few  rebel  wives)  are  jubilant.  Drs.  Holbert,  of  9 
Hickory  County,  and  Frazier,  of  Stockton,  Cedar  County,  are  present  1 
and  administering  to  the  wants  and  comforts  of  the  wounded,  and  are  I 
entitled  to  the  thanks  of  the  command.  I 

General,  you  see  that  in  the  command  there  is  some  good  material.  I

may  be  proud,  and  be  assured  I will  use  every  effort  to  add  new  luster,  jj

MARCH  26,  1862. — Skirmish  near  Gouge’s  Mill,  Mo. 

Report  of  Brig.  Gen.  James  Totten , JJ.  S.  Army. 

Headquarters  District  of  Central  Missouri, 

Jefferson  City , Mo.,  March  31,  1862. 

Captain  : I have  the  honor  to  report,  for  the  information  of  the  major- 
general  commanding,  that  on  the  evening  of  the  23d,  in  conjunction 
with  the  expedition  under  Lieutenant-Colonel  Blood,  Sixth  Missouri,  I 
ordered  Lieutenant-Colonel  Eppstein  to  send  out  scouting  parties  to  the 
eastward  and  also  to  keep  himself  well  prepared  for  attack,  which  might 
be  made.  Colonel  Eppstein  sent  out  on  the  25th  Captain  Ostermayer 
with  25  men,  who  had  a skirmish  before  daybreak  on  the  26th,  being 
fired  at  from  woods  15  miles  east  of  Booneville  and  3 miles  east  of 
Gouge’s  Mill.  His  men  returned  the  fire,  but  could  not  pursue  in  the 
night.  Later  they  found  in  the  woods  one  dead  body,  and  followed  a 
bloody  track  for  about  2 miles,  when  this  disappeared.  The  party  were 
to  Booneville,  and  think  the  rebels  numbered  from  40  to  50.  It  is 
thought  they  belonged  to  the  party  which  was  dispersed  by  the  troops 
sent  out  from  this  place  (Jefferson  City  and  Tipton)  under  Lieutenant- 
Colonel  Blood. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

MARCH  29,  1862.— Skirmish  on  the  Blackwater,  near  Warrensburg,  Mo. 

Report  of  Capt.  James  D.  Thompson,  First  Iowa  Cavalry. 

Warrensburg,  Mo.,  March  30,  1862. 
Sir:  Agreeably  to  your  order  of  the  27th  instant  I assumed  com- 
mand of  the  forces  stated  by  you,  consisting  of  parts  of  Company  A, 
under  command  of  Captain  McQueen ; Company  F,  Captain  Elliott  j 


Chap.  XVIII.] 


SKIRMISH  ON  THE  BLACKWATER,  MO. 


357 


Company  G,  Lieutenants  McDermott  and  Poster,  and  two  pieces  of 
First  Missouri  Artillery,  in  all  130  men,  and  marched  from  Sedalia  at  1 
o’clock  of  that  night  and  by  a forced  march  reached  Warrensburg  on 
the  next  morning.  Finding  everything  comparatively  quiet  we  went 
into  camp  during  the  day,  and  sending  out  scouts  from  the  State  Militia 
during  the  night,  received  information  of  a body  of  the  rebels,  supposed 
to  be  some  300  or  400,  at  a camp  some  12  or  15  miles  distant  from  War- 
rensburg, on  the  Blackwater,  at  a place  known  as  Murray’s  Ford.  Major 
Foster,  of  the  State  Militia,  taking  Captain  Elliott’s  company  and  50 
of  his  command,  proceeded  to  the  south  of  the  supposed  camp,  while  I 
took  one  piece  of  artillery  and  a portion  of  State  troops,  under  Lieu- 
tenant Ceathe,  with  the  balance  of  my  command,  and  proceeded  in  a 
more  direct  route  to  the  north  of  the  camp.  We  each  made  a rapid 
march  and  soon  arrived  at  the  supposed  camp,  but  found  no  enemy. 
Again  dividing  our  forces,  I took  my  own  command  and  started  on  my 
return,  being  satisfied  that  no  very  large  body  of  the  enemy  were  in 
that  immediate  vicinity. 

About  4 o’clock  p.  m.  of  the  29th,  as  we  emerged  from  the  timber,  I 
discovered  a body  of  what  I at  first  took  to  be  State  Militia,  but  which 
proved  to  be  Colonel  Parker  and  some  60  or  70  rebels  passing  south 
along  the  edge  of  the  timber,  at  right  angles  to  the  road  on  which  I 
was  moving,  and  the  length  of  his  column  to  my  right,  and  some  80  to 
100  rods  distant.  Their  leader  discovered  my  command  about  the 
same  moment  that  I became  satisfied  of  the  nature  of  his  forces. 

I immediately  ordered  Captain  Elliott,  who  was  in  advance,  to 
charge,  which  he  did,  gallantly  followed  by  Lieutenant  McDermott 
and  his  command.  I then  ordered  Captain  McQueen  to  right-about 
his  command  and  endeavor  to  intercept  the  rebels  at  the  ford.  In  ex- 
ecuting this  order  the  guide  led  him  past  the  point  of  intersection  to 
the  lower  ford,  which  prevented  him  from  efiectually  cutting  them  olf. 
Discovering  that  the  enemy  had  taken  to  the  upper  ford,  he  retraced  his 
steps  and  charged  after  the  fleeing  rebels.  A severe  running  fight  of 
some  4 miles,  through  thick  and  almost  impenetrable  thickets,  told 
fearfully  upon  the  fleeing  enemy.  Our  men  charged  gallantly,  leaving 
from  10  to  15  of  the  enemy  dead  upon  the  field  and  wounding  from  5 
to  10  others. 

We  took  15  prisoners,  besides  1 severely  wounded,  and  some  10  or  15 
horses — the  exact  number  1 am  not  able  to  give,  as  Company  F has 
not  yet  reported  in  reference  to  the  same.  Among  the  prisoners  is  the 
notorious  rebel  leader  Colonel  Parker,  who  has  so  long  been  the  terror 
of  the  more  northern  counties.  We  lost  1 man  killed,  Private  Gerrard, 
of  Company  F,  and  2 wounded,  one  of  whom,  Corporal  Johnson,  of  Com- 
pany F,  is  dangerously  if  not  mortally  wounded. 

Though  perhaps  not  essentially  requisite  in  a report  of  this  kind,  yet 
I cannot  refrain  from  calling  the  attention  of  the  commanding  general 
through  you  to  certain  matters  which  I deem  of  vital  importance  to  the 
well-being  of  that  portion  of  this  State  among  which  is  the  wanton 
destruction  of  life  and  property  of  citizens  of  that  section  by  the  State 
Militia.  A few  nights  before  my  arrival  at  Warrensburg  they  set  fire 
to  Colonel  McCowan’s  residence  in  Warrensburg,  and  entirely  destroyed 
the  house,  furniture,  &c.,  leaving  the  family,  consisting  of  his  wife  and 
some  four  or  five  children,  without  anything  to  support  or  protect  them. 
About  the  same  time  a body  of  them  proceeded,  as  I am  informed  by  the 
Union  men  of  Warrensburg,  to  the  house  of  one  Mr.  Burgess,  and  shot 
aim  and  his  brother  and  burned  the  house  over  the  heads  of  his  family. 
Again  on  Sunday,  the  30th,  Captain  Thomas  W.  Houts,  while  out  with  a 


358  OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chap.  XYIII.  I 

party  of  some  50  men,  killed  one  Mr.  Piper,  and  burned  five  dwellings,  I 
turning  the  families  out  of  doors  and  destroying  everything  m the  I 
houses.  I learn  this  from  Lieutenant  Ceathe,  who  was  with  him,  and  i 
who  positively  refused  to  permit  his  men  to  engage  in  the  nefarious  I 
business.  The  Union  men  of  the  town  are  highly  incensed  at  such  out- 1 
rages,  and  desired  me  to  lay  the  matter  before  the  proper  authorities.  $ 
The  sufferers  in  these  instances  none  of  them  belong  to  the  bushwhack- 1 
ers,  and  were  all,  with  the  exception  of  Colonel  McCowan,  peaceable  I 
citizens,  though  of  Southern  or  secession  principles.  The  Union  men  fl 
are  fearful,  and  truly  so,  that  the  bushwhackers  will  retaliate,  and  be- 1 
tween  the  two  lay  the  whole  country  in  rums. 

I would  suggest  the  policy  of  a united  movement  from  the  north, 
south,  east,  and  west,  driving  the  rebels  towards  Johnson  County,  and 
endeavor  by  concerted  action  to  destroy  their  whole  forces.  As  we 
have  done  heretofore  they  flee  before  us  from  Johnson  to  Henry  and 
back  to  some  other  point,  and  thus  baffle  our  best  endeavors. 

Very  respectfully,  j D THOMPSON, 

Captain  First  Iowa  Cavalry. 

Major  Torrence,  Commanding  Post , Sedalia , Mo. 


MARCH  30,  1862. — Skirmish  near  Clinton,  Mo. 

Report  of  Maj.  Gen.  Henry  W.  Halleck,  U.  8.  Army. 

Saint  Louis,  April  6,  1862. 

Detachment  of  First  Iowa  Cavalry,  sent  out  from  Clinton,  Mo.,  had 
a skirmish  with  rebels  on  the  30th.  Captured  19  prisoners,  8 wagons, 
and  a number  of  horses,  mules,  &c.,  belonging  to  Price’s  army.  One 
rebel  killed  and  7 wounded.  Our  loss  1 man  seriously  wounded. 

H.  W.  HALLECK, 

Major-General . 

Hon.  E.  M.  Stanton,  Secretary  of  War. 


MARCH  31,  1862.— Skirmish  at  Pink  Hill,  Mo. 

Report  of  Maj.  Charles  Banzhaf  First  Missouri  Cavalry. 

Hdors.  First  Battalion,  First  Missouri  Cavalry, 

Kansas  City , Mo .,  April  5,  1862. 

Sir:  I have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  Capt.  Albert  P.  Pea- 
body, commanding  Company  D,  First  Missouri  Cavalry,  hearing  on 
Monday,  March  31,  instant,  of  a collection  of  rebels,  marauders  ot 
Quantrill’s  men,  at  Pink  Hill,  about  19  miles  southeast  of  Independ- 
ence, Mo.,  started  from  Independence  in  pursuit  of  them.  When  near- 
ing Pink  Hill  Captain  Peabody  dispatched  one  party  of  35  men,  under 
Lieutenant  White,  of  Company  C,  to  one  direction,  retaining  with  him 
self  30  men,  and  Second  Lieutenant  Gurnee,  of  Company  D.  The  two 
commands  commenced  to  scour  the  neighborhood  immediately  near 
Pink  Hill.  Captain  Peabody’s  command  in  passing  a double  log-house 
in  an  elevated  position  over  the  road  received  a perfect  volley  of  shots 
fired  from  the  house.  Captain  Peabody  immediately  dismounted  a 
part  of  his  command,  ordering  the  rest  a little  farther  oft  to  take

harge  of  the  horses,  and  then  led  the  command  on  to  the  log-house, 
keeping  up  a constant  firing  through  the  windows  and  doors  for  more 
han  one  hour  and  a half,  but  with  no  more  success  than  to  prevent 
he  marauders,  on  whose  side  all  advantages  were,  from  attacking  his

land  or  camp  he  was  prevented  until  this  day  from  communicating  the

Colonel  : I avail  myself  of  this  opportunity  of  informing  you  of  the 
result  of  the  expedition  sent  by  you  under  my  command. 

I reached  this  point  the  same  day  I left  Lexington.  The  only  thing 
I have  done  of  any  importance  is  the  capture  of  10  kegs  (25  pounds  per 
keg)  of  Parker’s  powder  and  a small  skirmish  with  Quantrill’s  and 
Parker’s  bands  of  jayhawkers.  The  particulars  are  as  follows : 

On  Sunday,  the  30th,  I received  a dispatch  from  Captain  Peabody, 
stating  that  he  had  found  the  enemy  and  wanted  a re-enforcement.  I 
immediately  sent  Captain  Murphy,  with  2 lieutenants,  3 sergeants,  5 
corporals,  and  41  privates,  to  assist  him.  Thef  went  about  9 miles, 
and  found  the  enemy  on  a high  bluff  on  the  waters  of  the  Little  Sni.

panies  of  infantry  and  one  of  cavalry.  By  agreement  they  were  landel

merT  and  agreed  to  form  junction  at  Jackson.  I left  camp  at  8 o’cloca

forts ; proceeded  on  gravel  road  to  within  1 mile  of  J ackson ; halte»

-east  part  of  the  town ; detailed  two  men  to  open  communication  wit

ring  did  not  succeed  in  opening  communication ; waited  till  daybreak 
went  into  the  place,  but  found  nothing  of  importance  ; searched  a 
suspected  houses  with  no  result.

water ; found  everything  quiet  there  also.  Proceeded  same  manue 
to  Dallas,  where  we  arrived  and  surrounded  at  2 p.  m. ; made  no  ai 
rest  of  any  importance;  saw  Mr.  James  Noel,  county  and  circuit  clei 
of  Bollinger  County,  who  reported  to  me  that  he  had  been  taken  pnj 
oner  by  Major  Kitchen  about  four  days  previous,  who  had  a body  c 
about  120  secessionists ; that  they  had  destroyed  the  records  ot  th 
county  and  circuit  court,  and  carried  off  the  records  of  the  swam 
lands  and  other  valuable  papers  ; while  in  Bollinger  and  Cape  Gira 
deau  Counties  they  took  several  prisoners;  also  stole  a number  of. horsei 
Among  the  prisoners  they  took  there  were  two  men  named  Miller  aii 
Mclntee,  who  were  brutally  murdered,  Mclntee  being  killed  by  tli 
hand  of  the  miscreant  Bowles,  and  Miller  by  his  orders.  Mr.  Noel  Wc 
taken  bv  them  below  Bloomfield,  where  he  was  released  by  the  mte 
cession  of  some  of  his  friends.  He  reports  that  Jeff.  Thompson  s tore 
is  somewhere  about  1,000  men ; also  he  reports  the  current  beliel 
that  their  destination  is  Pocahontas. 

Left  Dallas  on  the  morning  of  the  4th  instant  and  returned  by  tt 
way  of  Jackson  to  camp,  where  we  arrived  on  the  evening  of  the  sam 
day.  Colonel  Toler’s  command  arrived  next  day  and  proceeded  t 
Oairo  on  steamer  J.  D.  Perry.

Report  of  Col . Clark  Wright , Sixth  Missouri  Cavalry. 

Headquarters  Sixth  Missouri  Cavalry, 

Cassville , Mo .,  April  9,  1862. 

Sir  : I arrived  here  late  this  evening  with  my  command,  with  Cap- 
n Banning,  and  train  loaded  with  subsistence,  and  some  65  head  of 
ttle.  I passed  out  by  the  way  of  Gadfly,  Newtonia,  Granby,  Neosho 
cl  down  the  valley  of  Indian  Creek,  dispersing  all  the  rebel  and  iay- 
wkmg  bands  in  the  country  through  which  we  passed.  We  had 
ne  three  skirmishes,  killing  Neut.  Cole,  Dr.  Adams,  Dr.  Cummons, 
d severely  it  not  mortally  wounding  Yancy  Richardson,  Dr.  Wills 
lison,  and  slightly  wounding  several  others,  and  capturing  some  125 
isoners,  all  of  whom  except  25  I turned  loose  after  a critical  exarni- 
tion  and  administering  the  oath  of  allegiance  to  them.  I only  re- 
ned  the  leaders  and  desperadoes,  the  remainder  expressing  a desire 
lay  down  their  arms  and  go  to  work.  I endeavored  to  discriminate 
sely,  and  among  all  the  better  class  of  secessionists  I think  I left  a 
ry  favorable  impression.  We  drove  all  the  gangs  down  to  Stand 
atie,  a point  on  the  line  of  the  Indian  Territory  some  15  miles  be- 
y Neosho.  They  are  embodied  there,  600  in  number,  between  Cow- 
n and  Buffalo  Creek  and  some  10  miles  below.  Pike  has  some  1,500 
bans.  I did  not  think  it  prudent  to  attack  these  combined  forces 
rP  “y  f”rce  and  expose  the  train.  I learned  to-day,  however,  that 
kir  bands  followed  us  as  we  retired  up  the  country  some  distance, 
nmittmg  depredations.  There  is  a horrible  state  of  affairs  in  that 
ner  of  the  State.  Our  trip  was  quite  a success  in  the  way  of  sub- 
tence.  I shall  remain  here  to-morrow  to  shoe  our  horses.  The  com- 
ssary,  Captain  Banning,  will  turn  over  all  our  subsistence,  to  be  for- 
med to  the  army,  and  we  will  reload  the  train  and  join  the  com- 
nd  by  a circuitous  route  at  Forsyth  in  a few  days,  unless  otherwise 

rpce  passed  through  Clarksville,  on  Arkansas  River,  yesterday,  one 
ek  ago  (Sunday  morning),  on  his  way  to  Little  Rock.  I learned 
m a very  intelligent  man  just  from  Price’s  army  that  he  (Price) 
aid  move  to  a point  where  he  could  re-enforce  the  rebels  on  the  Mis- 
sippi  at  any  point  most  needed. 

Ye  captured  horses  enough  to  mount  the  remainder  of  our  men  this 

I am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

CLARK  WRIGHT, 

Colonel  Sixth  Missouri  Cavalry.

night,  but  it  did  not  take  effect.  The  Home  Guard  garrisoned  tl

Saint  Louis,  Mo.,  October  29,  1861. 
General  Meigs,  Washington , D.  C. : 

Dear  Sir  : I am  sorry  to  have  caused  you  so  much  annoyance  by 
ly  frequent  importunity  for  money  and  complaints  at  existing  state  of 
Wngs,  but  really  our  difficulties  have  been  legion,  and  it  is  now  almost 
doubtful  struggle  in  coming  out  right  in  the  quotient ; that  is,  of  hav- 
lg  gun  and  mortar  boats  in  efficient  condition  for  going  down  the  river 
l December. 

I am  urging  on  the  gunboats  proper,  but  amid  difficulties  almost  in- 
iperable.  Still  I hope  to  succeed.  I have  appointed  Mr.  S.  Hen- 
ques  paymaster-in-chief,  who,  independently  of  doing  a single  paymas- 
pr’s  duty  for  a gunboat,  not  only  acts  as  my  clerk  and  secretary,  but 
Iso  performs  the  duties  of  supervising  contracts;  in  fact,  is  a think- 
ig  as  well  as  working  man.  I appointed  him  to  do  the  work  intended 
>r  Mr.  Wise  while  he  acted  in  that  capacity  before  being  appointed 
ssistant  paymaster.  I give  him  in  all  $200  per  year  less  than  Mr. 
^ise  received.  I trust  that  this  is  all  right ; in  fact,  I cannot  get  on 
ithout  him,  and  he  only  could  be  secured  at  his  present  pay. 

Excuse  my  hurry. 

Respectfully  and  truly,  yours, 

A.  H.  FOOTE.

dew  of  the  great  desolation  of  the  country  and  suffering  of  thousands  of

for  your  consideration : 

Whereas  there  is  now  and  has  been  a large  force  of  the  rebel  troops 
n Southwestern  Missouri,  laying  waste  the  whole  country  and  subject- 
ng  women  and  children  to  destitution  and  starvation ; and  whereas 
hat  portion  of  the  State  has  remained  loyal  to  the  Government  under 
ill  the  trials  and  reverses  through  which  she  has  been  compelled  to 
3assj  and  whereas  that  part  of  the  State,  in  an  agricultural  point  of 
dew,  will  compare  favorably  with  any  other  of  the  Western  States 
md  contains  more  mineral  wealth  than  any  other  State  of  the  Union- 
md  whereas  that  portion  of  the  State  lying  between  Springfield  and 
Seosho  is  the  key  to  Southern  and  Western  Missouri,  as  also  to  Kansas 
md  the  Indian  Territories,  from  an  invasion  from  the  South;  and 
vhereas,  if  that  portion  of  the  State  was  held  by  Federal  forces  it 
vould  enable  the  Federal  and  State  authorities  to  raise  several  thou- 
sand troops  for  the  service: 

Resolved , therefore , 1st,  That  the  Government  of  the  United  States 
s under  obligations  to  the  people  of  that  part  of  the  State  to  protect 
hem  in  their  rights  as  American  citizens. 

Resolved , 2d,  That  the  recent  retrograde  movement  of  our  army  from 
Springfield  has  been  the  cause  of  from  3,000  to  5,000  men,  women  and 
hildren  leaving  their  homes,  without  money  and  many  in  a suffering: 
iondition.  s 

Resolved , 3d,  That  the  people  of  the  Southwest  entertain  the  highest 
»pmion  of  the  military  skill  of  Brig.  Gen.  Franz  Sigel,  and  that  we 
espectfully  petition  you  to  send  to  the  Southwest  sufficient  force  to 
fold  that  part  of  the  State. 

Resolved , 4th,  That  we  believe  that  15,000  men,  under  a competent 
general,  will  be  sufficient  to  drive  the  rebels  from  our  land  and  restore 
>eace  to  the  country.

Saint  Louis,  Mo.,  November  22,  1861. 
Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

Commander  of  the  Western  Department : 

Dear  Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  represent  to  you  that  the  force  now 
under  my  command  at  Jefferson  City  is  very  small  (numbering  only 
about  1,000  effective  men),  which  is  to  garrison  the  post,  furnish  the 
police  of  the  city,  and  guard  the  Osage  and  Moreau  Bridges  on  the 
Pacific  Railroad  and  five  bridges  over  Gray’s  Greek  on  the  same  rail- 
road. Jefferson  City  being  the  seat  of  government  of  Missouri,  the 
only  political  point  in  the  State,  the  home  of  Gov.  C.  F.  Jackson,  in- 
creases the  anxiety  of  the  rebel  army  under  General  Price  to  recapture 
Jefferson  City  over  any  other  point  in  Missouri.  The  prestige  given 
the  secessionists  in  Missouri  would  be  very  powerful  in  the  occupation 
of  the  capital  of  the  State;  therefore  the  enemy  will  make  a greater 
effort  to  retake  that  point  than  all  others  in  Missouri. 

I would  respectfully  submit  for  your  consideration  the  propriety  of 
placing  a good  force  at  Jefferson  City  and  at  as  early  a period  as 
possible.  If  we  had,  say,  one  good  regiment  of  cavalry  and  two  or 
three  regiments  of  infantry,  in  addition  to  what  we  have,  with  some 
artillery,  which  we  greatly  need,  we  would  be  able,  with  the  completion 
of  our  fortifications,  which  can  be  finished  in  a few  weeks,  to  hold  Jeffer- 
son City  against  a very  large  force. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

TIIOS.  L.  PRICE, 

Brigadier -General,  U.  S.  Army , Comdg.  Post , Jefferson  City. 


Rolla,  Mo.,  November  22,  1861. 

Assistant  Adjutant-General  : 

The  rebel  forces  between  Springfield  and  Lebanon  are  large.  Their 
pickets  extend  10  miles  this  side  of  Lebanon.  Their  forces  are  scat- 
tered over  a large  part  of  the  country  for  subsistence.  They  pick  up 
many  stragglers  and  rob  the  fugitives.

Capt.  J.  C.  Kelton,  Saint  Louis , Mo. : 

I have  frequently  reported  to  the  Western  Department  that  the  line 
of  steamers  plying  between  Saint  Louis  and  Cairo,  by  landing  at  points 
on  the  Missouri  shore,  were  enabled  to  afford  aid  and  comfort  to  the 


374 


OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chap.  xvin. 


enemy.  I have  been  reliably  informed  that  some  of  the  officers,  par- 
ticularly the  clerks  of  these  boats,  were  regularly  m the  employ  of  the 
Southern  Confederacy,  so  called.  The  case  of  the  Platte  Yalley,  a few 
days  since,  confirmed  me  in  this  belief.  I have  heretofore  recommended 
that  all  the  carrying  trade  between  here  aud  Saint  Louis  be  performed  » 
by  Government,  charging  uniform  rates.  I would  respectfully  renew 
the  suggestion,  and  in  consideration  of  the  special  disloyalty  of  South- 1 
eastern  Missouri  I would  further  recommend  that  all  commerce  be  cut 
off  from  all  points  south  of  Cape  Girardeau.  There  is  not  a sufficiency 
of  Union  sentiment  left  in  this  portion  of  the  State  to  save  Sodom. 
This  is  shown  from  the  fact  that  Jeff.  Thompson  or  any  of  the  rebels 
can  go  into  Charleston  and  spend  hours  or  encamp  for  the  mgffit  on 
their  way  north  to  depredate  upon  Union  men,  and  not  one  loyalist  is 
found  to  report  the  fact  to  our  pickets,  stationed  but  l^iniles  on.

Sedalia,  November  24,  1861. 

Col.  Ered.  Steele, 

Commanding  Post , Sedalia  : 

Sir  • I have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  my  proceedings  as  command-  i 
ant  of  the  post  at  Warsaw,  Mo.  In  obedience  to  orders  from  General 
Sturgis  on  the  14th  instant,  I was  ordered  to  remain  at  Warsaw  with  S 
my  own  company  (H,  First  Regiment  Nebraska  Volunteers),  m con- 
nection with  one  company  of  Merrill’s  Horse,  Capt.  H.  Wilson,  to 
occupy  the  place,  protect  the  Government  stores,  and  remain  until 
all  the  commissary  and  quartermaster’s  stores  were  removed  to  some 
other  point.  On  the  night  of  the  18th,  learning  from  undoubted  au- 
thority that  the  enemy  were  concentrating  in  small  bodies  at  various 
points  within  from  8 to  15  miles  of  us  on  this  side  of  the  Osage  and 
were  contemplating  an  attack  on  us,  I deemed  it  proper  to  telegraph 
you  for  a small  re-enforcement.  On  the  night  of  the  20th  re-enforce- 
ments came  to  the  number  of  about  150  men,  viz : Captain  Baird,  of 
Merrill’s  Horse,  60  men,  and  Captain  Williams,  of  Seventh  Missouri 
Volunteers  (two  detachments),  about  90  men,  together  with  24  wagons. 
On  the  morning  of  the  21st  the  wagons  were  all  loaded.  During  the 
morning  of  the  21st  a telegraphic  dispatch  was  received  by  the  com- 
missary of  the  post,  Captain  Schenck,  at  Sedalia,  from  Captain  Swain, 
quartermaster,  stating  that  52  teams  were  sent.  The  balance  are  only 
ten  hours  behind  those  already  there.  These  teams  did  not  arrive. 

On  the  evening  of  the  21st  a fire  broke  out  in  some  old  buildings 
on  the  southwest  corner  of  the  public  square,  and  diagonally  from  the 
quarters  occupied  by  myself,  my  company,  and  the  hospital  depart- 
ment, on  the  opposite  side  of  the  street.  This  occurred  at  dusk  in  the 
evening  and  as  the  guard  were  being  posted.  I immediately  sent  a 
soldier  to  ascertain  what  the  light  originated  from.  He  quickly  re- 
turned, and  reported  to  me  that  a fire  was  burning  between  two  old 
deserted  houses  about  2 feet  apart,  and  that  a man  in  citizen’s  dress 
ran  away  from  the  place  and  disappeared  in  the  darkness  on  his 
approach.  I immediately  ordered  a portion  of  the  guard  to  the  spot 
with  axes  and  a few  buckets  of  water,  and  endeavored  to  arrest  the 
fire,  but  in  vain,  as  a heavy  wind  was  blowing  from  the  southeast.  The 
whole  corner  of  the  block  was  in  a very  few  moments  in  flames,  with 
the  wind  blowing  very  hard  towards  my  quarters  and  the  hospitals  in 
the  same  building.  It  required  our  utmost  exertions  to  prevent  the 
whole  from  being  in  flames.  At  this  juncture  the  wind  veered  to  the 
southwest,  and  in  a very  short  time  all  of  the  block  of  brick  buildings 
in  which  the  Government  property  was  stored  was  in  flames,  borne  ol 
the  Government  stores  were  got  out  of  the  buildings,  but  the  heat 
became  so  intense  that  it  was  impossible  for  men  to  work  and  it  was 
nearly  all  consumed.  . 

I had  previously  ordered  Captain  Schenck,  commissary  of  the  post, 
that  if  the  balance  of  our  teams  did  not  arrive  soon  and  there  was  no 
prospect  of  getting  away  what  remaining  property  was  not  loaded  into 
the  wagons  already,  to  burn  it,  in  order  to  save  it  from  falling  into  the 
hands  of  the  enemy.  But  very  little  of  the  stores  were  burned  at  our

hands,  as  the  flames  spread  so  rapidly  that  it  was  impossible  to  remove 
them  from  the  buildings. 

We  left  the  place  at  10  o’clock  that  night  (21st)  and  bivouacked  4 
miles  from  town  until  morning;  reached  here  on  the  23d,  in  the  after- 
noon ; met  the  balance  of  the  train  of  wagons  sent  to  us  15  miles  from 
this  place  on  the  23d  at  night. 

My  own  conclusion  is,  in  reference  to  the  origin  of  the  fire,  that  it 
was  done  and  deliberately  planned  by  the  enemy.

* * # # * # # 

III.  Numerous  cases  have  been  brought  to  the  attention  of  the  com- 
' landing  general  of  alleged  seizure  and  destruction  of  private  property 
i this  department,  showing  an  outrageous  abuse  of  power  and  a viola- 
on  of  the  laws  of  war.  To  avoid  a recurrence  of  these  evils  the  follow- 
lg  rules  will  hereafter  be  observed : 

1st.  No  private  property  will  be  taken,  except  where  necessary  for 
ie  subsistence  or  transportation  of  the  troops  or  in  cases  of  persons 
1 arms  against  the  United  States  or  affording  aid  and  assistance  to 
he  enemy. 

2d.  Where  it  becomes  necessary  to  take  private  property  for  the 
>rmer  purpose,  intelligent  and  responsible  officers  will  be  detailed  for 
ikt  purpose,  who  will  take  an  accurate  account  of  the  property  so 
iken,  and  give  receipts  therefor.  All  such  property  must  be  duly  re- 
lrned  and  accounted  for,  and  the  authority  for  the  seizure  must  be 
bated  in  the  receipts  and  returns.  Any  unauthorized  and  unnecessary 
Ifizure  or  destruction  of  private  property  will  be  punished  with  the  ex- 
reme  penalty  imposed  by  the  laws  of  war,  which  is  death. 

3d.  The  seizure  and  conversion  of  the  private  property  of  an  enemy 
.vhere  not  required  for  immediate  supplies,  as  provided  in  the  forego  - 
i g paragraph)  is  justifiable  only  in  particular  cases,  provided  for  by 
ie  laws  of  the  United  States  and  the  general  laws  of  war,  and  should 
ever  be  made  except  by  the  orders  of  the  officer  highest  in  command, 

110  will  be  held  accountable  for  the  exercise  of  this  power.  Great 
aution  should  be  used  in  this  matter,  as  much  injustice  has  been  done 
) individuals  who  are  not  enemies,  and  much  discredit  cast  upon  our 
atriotic  army  by  excesses  committed  by  unauthorized  persons  pre- 
siding to  act  in  the  name  of  the  United  States.  All  property  taken 
'om  alleged  enemies  must  be  inventoried  and  duly  accounted  for. 

Any  person  violating  these  rules  will  be  immediately  arrested  and 
iported  to  headquarters. 

IV.  In  all  cases  where  prisoners  taken  at  other  posts  or  in  the  field 
re  sent  to  Saint  Louis,  they  will  be  accompanied  with  a written  state- 
ment of  the  charges  against  them  and  the  evidence  upon  which  the 
rrest  was  based.  Otherwise  prisoners  so  sent  will  be  released  on  their 

rrival  here. 

V.  No  person  will  be  hereafter  arrested  without  good  and  substantial 
lasons,  and  officers  making  arrests  without  sufficient  cause  or  without 
iithority  will  be  held  to  account  and  punished.  And  officers  sending 
nsoners  to  Saint  Louis  without  charges,  proofs,  or  proper  explanations, 

111  be  charged  with  the  expenses  of  their  transportation.

Sir  : I have  received  your  letter  of  the  15th  [21st]  instant,  and  am

Ejecting  particularly  to  the  grade  or  name  of  paymaster. 

Allow  me  in  regard  to  this  subject  to  state  that  Commodore  Rodgers, 
believe  with  your  concurrence,  appointed  three  captains’  clerks  and 
"ting  paymasters  for  the  three  gunboats  under  his  command.  These 
ipointments  were,  in  accordance  with  the  usage  in  the  gunboat  and 
•ansport  service,  at  a salary  of  $1,200  per  annum,  and  a responsible 
3rd  given  by  each  of  these  men  so  appointed,  with  two  good  bonds- 
en,  in  the  sum  of  $5,000,  certified  to  by  the  United  States  district 
torney.  This  plan  prevailed  under  Commodore  Rodgers,  and  I 
lopted  a similar  one,  and  appointed  good  men  for  these  positions, 
ith  responsible  bondsmen,  to  act  under  the  authority  and  direction  of 
leir  respective  commanders  and  myself  in  their  various  disburse- 
ents. 

You  are  aware  that  you  gave  me  the  authority  by  which  I appointed 
r.  Wise  as  a kind  of  an  assistant  to  me  at  a salary  of  $200  per  month. 
On  my  arrival  at  Saint  Louis  and  after  consulting  with  Commodore 
odgers  we  both  saw  the  necessity  of  finding  a person  with  attain- 
ts and  business  capacity,  not  only  to  assist  me  personally  in  my 
irious  duties,  but  a man  with  naval  experience  in  all  needed  matters 
the  difficult  task  of  organizing  a navy  in  the  West. 

Commodore  Rodgers  and  myself  immediately  secured  the  services  of 
r.  S.  Henriques  for  this  purpose,  who  we  both  have  sailed  with  in  the 
avy,  and  in  whom  we  both  knew,  from  personal  experience,  that  we 
ould  find  the  needed  and  requisite  qualities.  He  has  been  in  the 
rvice  of  the  Government  for  upwards  of  twenty  years,  and  his  serv- 
es have  been  and  are  indispensable  to  me. 

Not  knowing  what  to  do  with  Mr.  Wise,  who  was  not  fully  qualified 
r my  purposes  in  this  respect,  and  finding,  according  to  your  letters  to 
e,  that  you  intended  to  send  me  the  money  for  disbursement,  I applied 
you  for  a quartermaster,  and  thus  relieve  myself  from  any  direct 
oney  disbursement,  as  my  time  would  necessarily  have  been  occupied 
’ many  detail  matters  of  less  importance.  I also  informed  Mr.  Wise  to 
'Ply  for  the  position,  not  imagining  for  an  instant  that  the  appoint- 
ed; ot  Mr.  Wise  would  debar  me  of  the  more  useful  services  of  Mr. 
enriques,  the  former  of  which  could  not  efficientlv  take  charge  of  all 
e disbursing  agents  on  board  the  gunboats. 

In  view  of  these  circumstances,  and  to  get  up  a system  and  supervis- 
1 all  matters  in  the  flotilla  connected  with  my  arduous  duties,  and

The  practice  of  going  outside  the  legal  agents  of  the  Quartermaster  s - 
Department— the  officers  selected  and  appointed  by  the  President,  by 
and  with  the  advice  and  consent  of  the  Senate — to  make  contracts  and 
disbursements  is  liable  to  great  abuse,  and  should  be  resorted  to  only,

1 also  inclose  a telegram  received  from  James  M.  Beebe  & Co.,  boston, 
bv  which  it  appears  that  they  are  informed  that  General  Fremont  has

its  funds  thus  under  the  control  of  a committee  responsible  only  to  pub- 
lie  opinion.  Certainly  as  Quartermaster-General  and  legal  head  of  this 
department  I cannot  hold  myself  responsible  for  the  acts  of  this  com- 
mittee or  of  Inspector  Beeside,  with  whose  appointment,  so  far  as  at 
present  informed,  no  officer  of  this  department  has  had  anything  to  do, 
and  whose  functions  and  powers  I learn  only  from  themselves  or  from 
those  with  whom  they  attempt  to  deal. 

I am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

M.  C.  Mhlub,

Taj.  Gen.  Georoe  B.  McClellan, 

Commanding  the  Army , Washington  City: 

General:  1 reached  this  city  on  the  18tli,  where  I met  General 
lunter,  who  had  just  arrived.  On  the  19th  I assumed  the  command, 
nd  have  since  used  every  endeavor  to  ascertain  the  true  condition  of 
ffairs  here,  but  for  the  want  of  proper  staff  officers  and  in  the  absence 
f returns  my  progress  in  this  matter  has  not  been  as  rapid  as  I could 
rish.  One  week’s  experience,  however,  is  sufficient  to  prove  that 
very  thing  here  is  in  complete  chaos.  The  most  astonishing  orders  and 
ontracts  for  supplies  of  all  kinds  have  been  made  and  large  amounts 
airport  to  have  been  received,  but  there  is  nothing  to  show  that  they 
ave  ever  been  properly  issued,  and  they  cannot  now  be  found,  if 
ver  really  received,  they  have  either  been  stolen  or  diverted  from 
heir  legitimate  purposes.  Many  of  these  diversions  are  represented 
o have  been  made  by  order  of  Capt.  1.  C.  Woods,  of  the  Commissary 
department,  who  acted  as  a colonel  of  General  Fremont’s  staff  and  chief* 
f transportation.  Captain  Woods  was  ordered  to  report  to  me  in  per 
on  and  to  turn  over  all  property  in  his  possession.  He  has  reported, 
ut  says  he  has  no  property  belonging  to  the  United  States,  and  that 
e has  never  been  responsible  for  any.  It  is  officially  reported  to  me 
hat  such  diversions  were  frequently  made  by  Captain  Woods  and  no 
sceipts  whatever  given  to  the  officers  who  were  accountable  for  the 
roperty  diverted.  Property  invoiced  and  sent  from  this  place  to  offi 
ers  at  other  places  never  reached  its  destination  and  was  never  re- 
e ip  ted  for  either  by  the  officer  to  whom  it  was  directed  or  by  the  per- 
i)n  who  arrested  it  on  the  way  and  diverted  it  to  some  other  purposes, 
ametimes  probably  very  proper,  and  sometimes  very  improper.  It 
» exceedingly  difficult  to  obtain  reliable  information  on  this  matter, 
is  this  business  seems  to  have  been  carried  on  in  such  a manner  as  to 
‘ave  the  least  possible  trace  behind.  Captain  Woods  has  reported  to 
apt.  T.  J.  Haines,  chief  commissary,  but  from  the  reputed  bad  char- 
ter of  Captain  Woods  Captain  Haines  is  unwilling  to  assign  him  to 
ny  duty. 

Many  of  the  troops  at  different  points  are  reported  to  be  without  arms 
nd  suffering  tor  the  want  of  clothing  and  blankets.  It  being  impos- 
ble  to  ascertain  whether  or  not  sufficient  supplies  had  already  been 
sued  in  such  cases,  I detailed  Brigadier-General  Sturgis  to  examine 
ito  the  condition  of  those  in  this  vicinity  and  sent  Brigadier- General 
herman  to  examine  the  three  divisions  near  Sedalia  and  the  detach - 
icnts  along  the  road.  General  Sturgis  has  already  remedied  some  of 
iese  evils  here  and  I hope  soon  to  hear  the  result  of  General  Sherman’s 
ission.  I have  no  officers  to  send  to  other  points  in  the  department.

There  was  a general  movement  of  the  Missouri  troops  northward, 
nd  their  line  was  formed  on  Tuesday  last,  November  26,  from  Stock 
>n  on  the  right  to  a point  near  Nevada  City  on  the  left— the  right 
ing,  about  6,000,  under  command  of  General  McBride  $ the  left,  under 
eneral  Bains.  General  Price,  commanding  the  center,  was  then  prob- 
bly  near  Montevallo.  Colonel  Clarkson,  bringing  up  the  rear,  left 
reen  field  last  Sunday,  November  24.  The  whole  fighting  force  was 
bout  14,000  men,  as  per  statement  of  the  quartermaster.  The  men  are 
oorly  clad  and  very  short  in  food  and  forage,  and  express  manifest 
ireats  against  Kansas.  They  think  that  their  present  move  is  directed 
gainst  that  State.  Some  entertained  the  hope  that  they  would  remain 
l their  present  position  several  weeks.  They  say  they  have  nearly  sixty 
ieces  of  cannon  and  some  batteries,  lately  received  from  the  Confed- 
•ate  States.  My  scout  further  says  that  an  order  from  General  Price  to 
eneral  McCulloch  to  follow  up  with  his  command  was  disregarded  by 
le  latter,  and  that  he  and  McCulloch  were  performing  retreat  into 
rkansas.  General  McCulloch  was  at  or  near  Springfield  on  the  23d  of 
ovember.  There  are  no  troops,  except  a few  scattering  marauding 
inads,  in  all  the  country  east  of  Stockton.  My  authority  passed  near 
uffalo  on  the  26tli.  The  next  day  he  came  through  Lebanon,  and 
aid  last  night  on  the  road  about  30  miles  from  Rolla,  and  he  met  no 
oops,  but  heard  of  an  occasional  scout.

My  opinions  about  Price’s  forces  are  confirmed  by  intelligence  from 
l quarters.  His  army  is  scattered  all  over  the  country  for  a hundred 
iles  in  every  direction  in  squads  more  or  less  large,  it  is  more  than 
mbtful  whether  they  will  again  unite.  I think  it  certain  they  will  not 
is  winter.  1 1 is  known  that  the  term  of  enlistment  of  nearly  ail  of  them 
pires  this  month.  They  are  anxious  to  get  home  to  the  river  counties 
td  North  Missouri.  It  is  probable  that  Price  himself  has  not  crossed 
e Osage,  and  has  a small,  if  any,  force  with  him.  Pursuit  will  only 
atter  them  more,  without  other  result  than  breaking  down  our  own 
oops.  Our  forces  are  suffering  much  for  want  of  shelter,  which  can 
>t  be  found  in  this  section.

This  Major  Marvin  is  a loyal  citizen,  and  in  my  opinion  perfect 
reliable.  From  the  information  1 have  obtained  from  different  sourc 
1 am  satisfied  that  there  will  be  no  movement  of  the  enemy  upon  tli  t 
point  so  long  as  our  troops  occupy  their  present  position,  nor  do 
believe  that  they  will  move  north  of  us  except  in  small  parties. 

We  frequently  hear  of  marauding  parties  making  their  way  to  wan 
Warrensburg  and  Lexington,  who  are  represented  as  soldiers  on  ft! 
lough  from  Price’s  army.  Major  Marvin  told  me  that  Price’s  army  d 
not  number  as  many  now  by  5,000  as  it  did  two  weeks  ago.  It  is  sa 
that  the  rebel  army  is  almost  destitute  of  clothing  and  their  numbe 
have  been  considerably  diminished  by  desertions.  The  hoof  disease 
among  their  animals  and  has  rendered  a large  proportion  of  the 
totally  unfit  for  service. 

If  it  should  be  ascertained  that  the  principal  part  of  Price’s  am 
had  crossed  the  Osage,  I should  be  in  favor  of  endeavoring  to  enga. 
them  with  a well-organized  force  from  this  command  by  rapid  man 
at  night.  I am  satisfied  that  they  will  not,  with  their  present  fort 
give  us  battle  as  long  as  they  can  run. 

If  it  is  the  intention  for  this  command  to  winter  here,  we  can  get  a go< 
camping  ground  about  3 miles  from  the  depot,  sheltered  from  the  win 
and  with  facilities  for  obtaining  fuel,  good  water,  and  forage.  The 
is  a saw  mill  near  this  place  belonging  to  the  Government,  where  p 
on  el  Bissell’s  battalion  of  mechanics  are  now  stationed.  Colonel  Bite 
informs  me  that  he  has  considerable  timber  out  now,  and  could  m 
short  time  furnish  enough  to  hut  the  whole  command. 

I shall  probably  move  the  division  to  this  locality  to-morrow,  and  wn 
to  be  advised  as  to  whether  I shall  commence  building  huts.  The  t roo 
have  already  suffered  from  the  inclemency  of  the  weather;  the  sickly 
is  constantly  increasing,  and  if  we  have  not  soon  some  protection  fro 
the  weather  besides  tents  the  consequences  may  be  still  more  senoi 
I continue  to  throw  out  scouting  and  reconnoitering  parties,  wlii« 
besides  the  information  which  they  bring  me,  has  the  effect  of  intin 
dating  the  enemy.

My  letter  of  the  25th*  explains  in  relation  to  martial  law,  the  authority

Headquarters  Department  of  the  Missouri, 

Saint  Louis , November  30,  1861. 
Maj.  Gen.  George  B.  McClellan, 

Commander -in- Chief,  Washington , I).  C. : 

General  : There  can  be  no  doubt  that  the  enemy  is  moving  north 
with  a large  force,  and  that  a considerable  part  of  Northern  Missouri  is. 
in  a state  of  insurrection.  The  rebels  have  organized  in  many  counties., 
taken  Union  men  prisoners,  and  are  robbing  them  of  horses,  wagonsl 
provisions,  clothing,  &c.  There  is  as  yet  no  large  gathering  in  any  one 
place  so  that  we  can  strike  them.  To  punish  these  outrages  and  to 
arrest  the  traitors  who  are  organizing  these  forces  and  furnishing  sup- 
plies, it  is  necessary  to  use  the  military  power  and  enforce  martial  law, 
I cannot  arrest  such  men  and  seize  their  papers  without  exercising- 
! martial  law,  for  there  is  no  civil  law  or  civil  authority  to  reach  them. 
The  safety  of  Missouri  requires  the  prompt  and  immediate  exercise  of 
this  power,  and  if  the  President  is  not  willing  to  intrust  me  with  it  he 
should  relieve  me  from  the  command.  It  is  and  has  been  for  months 
exercised  here  by  my  predecessors,  but  I cannot  find  any  written  au- 
thority of  the  President  for  doing  so.  I mean  to  act  strictly  under 
authority  and  according  to  instructions,  and  where  authority  will  not 
be  granted  the  Government  must  not  hold  me  responsible  for  the  result. 
Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLECK, 

Major-  General . 


Roll  A,  Mo.,  November  30,  1861. 

Major-General  Halleck  : 

Another  of  my  scouts  in  from  the  southwest.  Left  Osceola  Tuesday 
light.  Price  was  there  with  4,000  men,  McBride  at  Stockton  with

0 will  receive  his  instructions  direct  from  these  headquarters. 

{I.  It  is  represented  that  there  are  numerous  rebels  and  spies  within 
f camps  and  in  the  territory  occupied  by  our  troops,  who  give  infor- 
tion,  aid,  and  assistance  to  the  enemy;  that  rebels  scattered  through 
:5  country  threaten  and  drive  out  loyal  citizens  and  rob  them  of  their 
|>perty;  that  they  furnish  the  enemy  with  arms,  provisions,  clothing, 
rses,  and  means  of  transportation ; and  that  insurgents  are  banding 
^ether  in  several  of  the  interior  counties  for  the  purpose  of  assisting 
|>  enemy  to  rob,  to  maraud,  and  to  lay  waste  the  country.  All  such 
"sons  are  by  the  laws  of  war,  in  every  civilized  country,  liable  to 
pital  punishment.  The  mild  and  indulgent  course  heretofore  pursued 
rard  this  class  of  men  has  utterly  failed  to  restrain  them  from  such 
lawful  conduct.  The  safety  of  the  country  and  the  protection  of  the 
es  and  property  of  loyal  citizens  justify  and  require  the  enforcement 
a more  severe  policy.  Peace  and  war  cannot  exist  together.  We 
mot  at  the  same  time  extend  to  rebels  the  rights  of  peace  and  enforce 
linst  them  the  penalties  of  war.  They  have  forfeited  their  civil  rights 
citizens  by  making  war  against  the  Government,  and  upon  their  own 
ids  must  fall  the  consequences. 

II.  Commanding  officers  of  districts,  posts,  and  corps  will  arrest  and 
ee  in  confinement  all  persons  in  arms  against  the  lawful  authorities 
the  United  States,  or  who  give  aid,  assistance,  or  encouragement  to 
! enemy.  The  evidence  against  persons  so  arrested  will  be  reduced 
writing  and  verified  on  oath,  and  the  originals  or  certified  copies  of 
•h  affidavits  will  be  immediately  furnished  to  the  provost-marsh  al- 
lieral  in  this  city.  All  arms,  ammunition,  and  other  personal  prop- 
y required  for  the  use  of  the  Army,  such  as  horses,  wagons,  provis- 
s,  &c.,  belonging  to  persons  so  in  arms  or  so  assisting  and  encour- 
ng  the  enemy,  will  be  taken  possession  of,  and  turned  over  and  ac- 
uited  for.  Such  property,  not  of  a proper  character  for  issue,  will 
examined  by  a board  of  officers,  and  sold  as  directed  by  the  Army 
io-ulations.

persons  charged  with  aiding  and  assisting  the  enemy,  the  destruc- 

1 of  bridges,  roads,  and  buildings,  and  the  taking  of  public  or  pri- 
e property  for  hostile  purposes,  and  also  for  the  condemnation  of

Army.

iation  for  like  acts  of  the  enemy,  it  permits  any  retaliatory  measimi 
within  the  prescribed  limits  of  military  usage.  If  the  enemy  murclel

we  may  enforce  on  them  the  severest  penalties  justified  by  the  laws 
war  for  the  crimes  of  their  fellow  rebels.  The  rebel  forces  in  the  sout 
western  counties  of  this  State  have  robbed  and  plundered  the  peace 
ful  non-combatant  inhabitants,  taking  from  them  their  clothing  arl 
means  of  subsistence.  Men,  women,  and  children  have  alike  bee

wav  to  this  city  barefooted,  half  clad,  and  in  a destitute  and  star\  ill 
condition.  Humanity  and  justice  require  that  these  sufferings  shou 
be  relieved  and  that  the  outrages  committed  upon  them  should  be  r, 
taliated  upon  the  enemy.  The  individuals  who  have  directly  cans* 
these  sufferings  are  at  present  mostly  beyond  our  reach.  Put  the 
are  in  this  city  and  in  other  places  within  our  lines  numerous  wealth 
secessionists  who  render  aid,  assistance,  and  encouragement  to  tlio; 
who  commit  these  outrages.  They  do  not  themselves  rob  and  plundej 
but  they  abet  and  countenance  these  acts  in  others.  Although  le 
bold,  they  are  equally  guilty.  It  is  therefore  ordered  and  directed  tli 
the  provost-marshals  immediately  inquire  into  the  condition  of  the  pe 
sons  so  driven  from  their  homes,  and  that  measures  be  taken  to  quart

avowed  secessionists  and  of  those  who  are  found  guilty  of  giving  ai 
assistance,  and  encouragement  to  the  enemy.  _ _

master  in  a slave  used  for  insurrectionary  purposes.  Should  Congre

assistance,  and  encouragement  to  the  enemy,  such  provisions  will 
strictly  enforced.  Military  officers  do  not  make  laws,  but  they  snou 
obey  and  enforce  them  when  made.

will  be  strictly  guarded,  and  kept  as  far  as  possible  from  communiCc 
ing  with  the  command  where  employed.

scidedly  mutinous  and  it  may  be  necessary  to  forcibly  disarm  them, 
he  garrison  at  Boonevilleis  in  a similar  condition.  A force  was  sent 
om  Sedalia  two  days  ago  to  Marshall,  Waverly,  and  Arrow  Eock,  to 
sperse  the  rebels,  and  to  destroy  the  stores  and  boats  collected  at 
lose  places.  Eesult  not  yet  known.  Major  Bowen,  with  500  cavalry, 
in  pursuit  of  rebels,  under  Colonel  Turner,  south  of  Salem. 

Scouting  parties  from  Eolla  and  Sedalia  represent  Price  as  only  7 
iles  north  of  Osceola.  Spies  and  others  say  his  force  is  larger  than 
had  supposed.  Our  forces  at  Sedalia  and  Eolla  are  held  in  readiness 
» move,  but  their  efficiency  is  greatly  reduced  by  disorganization  and 
ckness.  Many  have  never  regularly  been  mustered  into  service,  and 
is  doubtful  if  they  can  be  persuaded  to  come  in.  The  camp  measles 
re  prevailing,  and  daily  increase  our  sick  list. 

We  have  already  done  much  to  relieve  the  pressing  wants  of  the 
oops,  and  now  are  engaged  night  and  day  in  attempting  to  organize 
tern  according  to  law  and  regulations.  This,  however,  is  a very  diffi- 
dt  task,  for  want  of  returns  and  muster  rolls.  Many  of  them  are 
egally  mustered,  and  refuse  to  be  mustered  over  again  for  future  or 
» cover  past  services.  Some  were  merely  sworn  in  without  any  mus- 
r rolls  at  all,  and  yet  they  have  been  paid  and  supplied  as  regular 
oops.  The  officers  in  many  cases  oppose  being  mustered,  hoping  in 
iis  way  to  avoid  accountability  for  public  property  wasted  and  stolen 
id  for  offenses  committed.  Moreover,  many  of  the  organizations  on 
iper  are  mere  shams — companies  and  regiments  not  having  half  the 
imbers  returned  and  paid  for,  the  officers  in  such  cases  having  appro- 
bated to  their  own  use  the  surplus  clothing  and  provisions  issued 
i these  false  returns.  The  most  outrageous  frauds  are  daily  being 
iveloped,  especially  in  the  quartermaster’s  department.  Many  of  the 
gimental  quartermasters  are  unworthy  of  trust  or  confidence.  It  will 
ke  time,  General,  to  ferret  out  these  abuses  and  to  properly  organize 
id  discipline  our  forces  here,  but  I will  do  it  if  you  will  give  me  time 
id  assistance.  The  material,  so  far  as  the  men  are  concerned,  is 
m er ally  excellent,  but  that  of  the  officers  very  poor.  It  is  impossible 
it  to  form  any  correct  idea  of  their  numbers.  In  many  cases  no 
turns  have  been  made  and  many  of  those  sent  in  are  entirely  unre- 
ible.  There  is  probably  not  one-half  the  effective  force  shown  on 
iper. 

This,  General,  is  no  army,  but  rather  a military  rabble.  A high 
freer,  who  was  at  Washington  at  the  time  of  the  battle  of  Bull  Eun, 
ys  the  army  here  is  more  disorganized  than  that  of  the  Potomac 
ter  its  defeat.  Every  one  appreciates  the  change  which  you  have 
tected  in  that  army  in  five  months.  I hope,  with  your  assistance,  to 
> the  same  here.  You  are  aware  that  I am  almost  destitute  of  reg- 
ar  officers,  and  those  of  the  volunteers  are,  with  some  exceptions, 
itirely  ignorant  of  their  duties.  It  is  said,  General,  that  you  have 
iarly  as  many  regular  officers  on  your  personal  staff  as  I have  in  this 
kole  department.  I was  very  sorry  to  receive  your  orders  to-day 
king  away  four  or  five  of  the  very  few  I now  have.  I will,  however, 

) the  best  I can  without  them. 

Your  telegram  of  last  evening  indicates  your  intention  to  withdra  w 
so  a portion  of  the  troops  from  Missouri.  I assure  you,  General,  this 
nnot  be  done  with  safety  at  present.  Some  weeks  hence  I hope  to

hat  there  are  no  forces  of  the  enemy,  except  small  scouting  and  steal- 
Qg  bands,  which  are  in  all  the  counties  around  this  post.  The  news 
rom  Lebanon  is  the  same.  Mr.  Scott,  one  of  my  scouts  who  left  Leb- 
non  yesterday  morning,  says  there  were  no  forces  there,  except  a band 
f State  Guards  under  Captains  Sweeney  and  McNey.  All  the  little

Osawatomie,  Kans.,  December  8,  1861. 

len.  James  H.  Lane  : 

Sir  : Everything  is  going  wrong  here.  What  you  and  I feared  at 
Ipringfield  is  coining  to  pass.  The  enemy  is  advancing.  He  disbanded 
is  three-months’  men  about  the  20th  of  November,  and  moved  north 
rith  his  regulars,*  some  10,000  strong.  He  marched  by  way  of  Sar- 
oxie,  Greenfield,  Stockton,  and  Bolivar,  striking  the  Osage  at  Warsaw 
nd  Osceola.  The  disbanded  men  have  carried  their  arms  home  with 
hem  and  engaged  in  guerrilla  operations.  The  country  swarms  with 
uerrillas,  and  this  makes  it  difficult  to  procure  information.  Our  faith- 
til  scouts  (Breedin  and  Nelson)  brought  me  accurate  information  of 
he  enemy’s  movements,  though  they  obtained  it  with  great  difficulty, 
•eing  shot  at  not  less  than  one  hundred  times.

General  : Yours  of  the  6th  has  this  moment  reached  me.  I am 
bliged  to  you  for  the  spirit  of  frankness  in  which  it  is  written.  Let 
Le  begin  by  replying  to  the  last  part  of  your  letter. 

You  will  probably  remember  that  soon  after  General  Hunter  assumed 
mmand  of  the  department  he  ordered  two  divisions  from  Western 
[issouri  to  Saint  Louis,  regarding  them  as  available  for  other  service. 
Y dispatch  was  predicated  on  that,  and  if  you  had  informed  me  that 
m had  any  available  troops  I intended  to  propose  to  you  a movement 
i concert  with  Buell.  His  project,  though  very  important,  must 
ther  be  deferred  or  be  carried  ®ut  in  some  other  way.  I have  no 
tention  of  stripping  you  of  troops  when  you  cannot  spare  them.  I 
>-day  directed  General  Thomas  to  telegraph  to  you  that  Major  Ketch um 
ight  remain  with  you  and  that  I would  recommend  him  as  a brigadier- 
3neral.  I had  already  determined  to  try  to  secure  his  appointment, 
do  not  understand  your  statement  that  four  or  five  of  the  regular 
ficers  you  now  have  are  ordered  away,  but  will  look  into  it  in  the 
orning.  There  is  some  mistake  about  it,  unless  you  allude  to  the 
iroled  officers,  who  cannot  under  their  parole  be  of  any  service  to  you. 
ou  are  also  misinformed  as  to  the  number  of  regular  officers  on  my 
qrsonal  staff.  I have  two  regular  aides,  instead  of  the  authorized, 
imber  of  three,  and  one  chief  of  staff ; the  others  apparently  are  my 
irsonal  staff,  and  are  really  doing  their  appropriate  duties  in  the  line 
id  their  respective  corps.  Even  my  personal  aides  are  on  duty  con- 
antly  as  inspectors. 

I am  sorry  to  learn  the  very  disorganized  condition  of  the  troops, 
appreciate  the  difficulty  of  the  task  before  you,  and  you  may  rest 
sured  that  I will  support  you  to  the  full  extent  of  my  ability.  Da* 
>t  hesitate  to  use  force  with  the  refractory.  Can  you  yet  form  any 
ea  of  the  time  necessary  to  prepare  an  expedition  against  Columbus; 
j 0I*e  up  the  Cumberland  and  Tennessee  rivers,  in  connection  with 
lelPs  movements'?  I shall  send  troops  to  Hunter,  to  enable  him  to 
• 3ve  into  the  Indian  Territory  west  of  Arkansas  and  upon  Northern 
ixas.  That  movement  should  relieve  you  very  materially.  It  will 
j quire  some  little  time  to  prepare  Hunter,  but  when  he  moves  you 
ight  act  in  concert  with  him. 

In  haste,  very  truly,  yours, 

geo.  b.  McClellan,

ag  a trusty  man,  sent  some  ten  days  ago  into  the  counties  of  Henry

1 the  counties  of  Henry  and  Cass  and  in  Price’s  army,  corroborating
