Price’s  forces  are  greatly  in  need  of  clothing  and  are  suffering  very 
mch.  In  a speech  he  made  them  on  Sunday  Price  stated  to  them 
lat  Missouri  had  been  annexed  to  the  Southern  Confederacy ; that  his 
rmy  would  be  reorganized  and  incorporated  with  the  Southern  Army, 
lad  that  money  and  clothing  would  be  immediately  furnished  to  all 
ho  remained  in  service.  Price  was  daily  expecting  his  commission 
3 major-general  from  Kichmond,  though  it  was  already  whispered  in 
imp  that  Jackson  had  succeeded  in  having  him  superseded.  The 
reatest  dissatisfaction  prevailed  in  the  army  in  consequence  of  this 
;port,  one-half  of  the  men  declaring  openly  that  they  would  serve 
ader  no  one  else;  that  they  were  fighting  for  Missouri,  and  not  for 
te  Southern  Confederacy. 

It  is  very  sure  that  no  graver  mistake  could  possibly  be  made  in 
ichmond  than  to  displace  Price  from  the  command  of  this  Missouri 
’my.  He  is  greatly  beloved  by  his  whole  force,  and  it  is  his  popu- 
rity  and  his  influence  which  keep  so  large  a body  of  men  in  arms  in 
lis  State  without  pay,  without  clothing,  and  with  very  scanty  rations, 
any  of  Price’s  men,  even  as  it  is,  are  very  anxious  to  return  home, 
id  will  take  almost  any  oath  if  they  can  thus  be  exempted  from 
rest.  Those  whose  time  has  expired  are  also  afraid  to  return  home 
st  they  be  arrested  and  taken  to  Saint  Louis.  If  there  were  any 
ethod  of  holding  such  men  to  their  engagements  I have  little  doubt 
at  an  assurance  of  exemption  from  arrest  on  taking  the  proper  oath 
auld  bring  many  hundreds  to  their  homes. 

Price  is  not  recruiting  nearly  so  fast  as  he  is  losing  men.  My  scout  es- 
nates  his  whole  force  at  12,000  or  13,000,  which  I am  sure  is  too  large  an 
lowance.  They  have,  for  the  present,  plenty  of  corn  meal,  flour,  and 
ef,  but  the  region  in  which  they  are  encamped  will  soon  be  exhausted, 
ley  have  almost  destroyed  the  country  in  their  rear.  Price  notified

(1  clothing  from  their  homes  as  soon  as  possible,  as  he  did  not  mean

lieve  that  there  are  7,000  or  8,000  Federal  troops  west  of  Jefferson 
ty.  I will  send  you  a paper  published  in  his  camp.  His  advanced 
Mkets  are  near  Calhoun,  as  are  ours,  though  they  have  not  yet  met.

a large  steam  mill,  4 miles  south  of  Calhoun.

December  11,  1861. 

dajor-General  Halleck, 

Commanding  Department  of  the  Missouri  : 

General  : The  constantly-increasing  disturbances  in  all  this  region,, 
occasioned  by  the  efforts  of  Price’s  scouting  officers  and  straggling 
>arties  of  guerrillas,  exhibited  in  the  general  alarm,  the  robbing  of 
>eaceful  inhabitants,  the  outrages  of  every  description  perpetrated  in 
very  village,  hamlet,  and  farm-house,  are  caused  directly  by  the  en- 
ouragement  and  countenance  given  to  such  acts  by  the  presence  of 
he  enemy  in  such  force  on  the  Osage.  Once  driven  from  that  position 
nd  forced  back  into  the  region  of  country  which  he  has  so  recently 
aid  waste,  and  all  encouragements  would  be  withdrawn  from  his  ad- 
herents and  sympathizers  now  disposed  to  enlist  in  his  army. 

We  can  march  from  the  railroad  in  this  vicinity  with  a full  and  well- 
ppointed  army  of  15,000  men  and  forty  pieces  of  artillery  and  still 
save  force  enough  along  the  railroad  to  guard  all  the  public  stores  and 
>rotect  the  road  itself  from  any  damage.  I would  respectfully  suggest,, 
herefore,  that  to  quiet  all  the  disturbances  and  uneasiness  engendered 
y the  presence  of  so  large  a hostile  force  in  this  region  an  advance  in 
orce  against  Price  be  made  as  soon  as  possible.  For  this  army  of 
5,000  men  there  is  abundance  of  transportation  and  of  supplies,  and 
hey  constitute  a force  large  enough,  considering  the  difference  of  or- 
ganization, discipline,  and  arms,  to  deal  with  Price  easily,  even  had  he 
he  50,000  men  he  calls  for  in  his  proclamation.  Most  of  his  men  are 
nly  armed  with  shot-guns,  and  have  scarcely  the  pretense  of  an  organ- 
nation.  He  has  perhaps  4,000  or  5,000  tolerable  troops,  armed  with 
mskets,  and  about  thirty  pieces  of  artillery,  few  of  which  can  be  prop- 
rly  served,  and  some  of  which  are  rough  iron  pieces,  made  in  Missouri. 

Our  forces  here  are  in  such  condition  that  they  can  march  with  two 
ours’  notice.  Each  regiment  has  its  own  transportation,  and  there  is 
othing  necessary  except  to  throw  into  the  wagons  camp  equipage  and 
at  ions. 

Should  such  a movement  be  intrusted  to  me  I would  respectfully 
uggest  the  following  plan : The  first  object  to  be  kept  in  view  is  that 
be  enemy  to  some  extent  must  be  surprised,  in  order  that  he  may  be 
rought  to  an  engagement.  For  this  purpose  I would  propose  that  for 
sveral  days  before  the  real  movement  was  made  strong  bodies  of  cav- 
lry,  with  some  artillery,  be  sent  forward  on  the  Warsaw  and  Clinton 
aads,  to  force  in  their  pickets,  reconnoiter  in  force,  and  then  return  j 
bat  this  operation  be  repeated  several  times,  and  that  finally,  under 
°ver  of  such  a movement,  the  whole  force  be  rapidly  thrown  forward 
) the  Osage  at  Warsaw.  I believe  by  proper  management  and  vigor 
be  advanced  division  of  this  army  could  cross  the  Osage  before  the 
ews  of  the  movement  could  reach  the  enemy.  If  he  then  crossed  the 
ver  and  attempted  to  retreat  to  the  southwest  he  must  at  least  lose 
is  baggage  train  and  supplies.  Whilst  his  line  of  retreat  would  be 


426 


OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T. 


[Chap.  XVIIT. 


threatened,  if  not  intercepted,  by  such  a movement,  ours  would  be 
open  to  the  railroad  at  almost  any  point  east  of  Otterville.  1,  however, 
do  not  suppose  for  a moment  that  he  will  stand  unless  retreat  is  cut  off 
and  in  either  event  the  disturbances  in  this  section  will  be  ended.  Such 
a campaign  would  not  last  more  than  twenty  days,  if  so  long,  and  £he 
forces  here  would  enter  upon  it  with  a feeling  very  different  from  that 
of  going  into  winter  quarters  on  the  La  Mine.  ^ , 

I submit  these  views  to  you  with  much  diffidence,  and  should  prob 
ably  not  do  so  at  all,  but  that  I am  impressed  with  the  belief  that 
neither  secession  in  Missouri  nor  Price’s  army  can  survive  another  re 
treat  toward  Arkansas. 

I am,  general,  your  obedient  servant,  jNO  p0pB

Syracuse,  December  11, 1861. 


Major-General  Halleck: 

I transmit  a number  of  letters  captured  with  the  mail-carrier. 
There  is  a large  number  of  them,  but  in  substance  they  convey  the 
same  information,  viz,  that  Price’s  force  is  disintegrating;  that  he  has 
short  of  10,000  men  now  with  him ; that  recruiting  is  very  slow ; that 
unless  he  can  raise  five  regiments  to  enter  the  Confederate  service  he 
cannot  get  a commission  in  their  army,  &c. 

I am  satisfied  that  a rapid  movement  would  utterly  destroy  his  army, 
either  as  the  result  of  an  action  or  of  a retreat.  His  army  cannot  pos 
siblv  survive  another  retreat  south.  His  men  are  only  kept  togethe 
noW  by  the  speedy  termination  of  their  terms  of  service  and  the  pros- 
pect of  getting  home  by  New  Year’s  Day.  They  will  not  be  led  soutt 
again  in  any  large  number.  With  the  delightful  weather  we  have  hat 
and  which  promises  to  continue  for  some  time  and  the  good  roads, 
such  a movement  would  consume  but  a few  days,  and  would  destroy  u 
a moment  all  hope  of  recruiting  for  Price  in  this  whole  region. 

I am,  general,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,  p0pE 

Brigadier-General,  Commanding.

Headquarters  Department  of  Kansas, 
Fort  Leavenworth , Kans .,  December  11,  1861. 


[Brig.  Gen.  Lorenzo  Thomas:] 

General  : Your  letter  of  the  26th  ultimo,  in  consequence  ot  the 
destruction  by  the  enemy  of  railroad  bridges,  was  delayed  a number  of 
days.  In  reply  I have  the  honor  to  report  that  I think  the  expedition 
proposed  by  the  General-in-Chief  altogether  impracticable.  We  have! 
a hostile  Indian  force,  estimated  at  10,000,  on  the  south,  and  Price’sji 
command,  some  20,000,  on  our  east  and  north.  To  cope  with  this  force 
we  have  only  about  3,000  effective  men,  scattered  over  an  extended 
frontier.  So  far  from  being  able  to  make  successful  expeditions  into 
the  enemy’s  country  with  our  present  force,  I think  we  shall  be  very 
fortunate  if  we  prevent  his  having  possession  of  the  whole  of  Kansas.! 
The  guns  necessary  for  the  defense  of  this  post  were  taken  away  by 
order  of  General  Fr6mont,  and  have  not  been  replaced.  The  posses- 
sion of  Leavenworth  would  be  a great  feather  in  the  enemy’s  cap,  and 
really  there  is  nothing  to  prevent  his  having  it  any  day  he  may  see  fit. 
We  will  give  him  a hard  fight,  but  he  will  have  ten  to  our  one. 

In  my  humble  opinion  the  division  of  the  Western  Department  was 
not  for  the  good  of  the  service, 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  serv- 


ant, 


D.  HUNTER, 
Major-  General , Commanding. 


Unofficial.]  Headquarters  of  the  Army, 

Washington , December  11,  1861. 

Maj.  Gen.  D.  Hunter, 

Commanding  Department  of  Kansas  : 

General  : Your  telegram  to  General  Thomas*  surprised  me  exceed- 
ingly. Realizing  as  I do  the  very  trying  nature  of  the  circumstances 
in  which  you  are  placed,  I have  attributed  it  to  momentary  irritation, 
which  your  cooler  judgment  will  at  least  lead  you  to  regard  as  unnec- 
essary. 

In  regard  to  placing  General  Halleck  in  command  of  the  Department 
of  Missouri,  that  step  was  taken  from  the  evident  necessity  of  placing 
some  one  there  who  was  in  no  manner  connected,  for  or  against,  with 
the  unfortunate  state  of  affairs  previously  existing  in  that  department. 
Immediately  after  you  were  assigned  to  your  present  department  1 
requested  the  Adjutant-General  to  inform  you  that  it  was  deemed 
expedient  to  organize  an  expedition  under  your  command  to  secure 
the  Indian  territory  west  of  Arkansas,  as  well  as  to  make  a descent 
upon  Northern  Texas,  in  connection  with  one  to  strike  at  Y estem 
Texas  from  the  Gulf.  The  general  was  to  invite  your  prompt  attention

I.  The  suffering  families  driven  by  rebels  from  Southwestern  Mis- 
souri which  have  already  arrived  here  have  been  supplied  by  volun- 
ary  contributions  made  by  Union  men.  Others  are  on  the  way  to 
jrive  in  a few  days.  These  must  be  supplied  by  the  charity  of  men 
mown  to  be  hostile  to  the  Union.  A list  will  be  prepared  of  the 
lames  of  all  persons  of  this  class  who  do  not  voluntarily  furnish  their 
luota,  and  a contribution  will  be  levied  on  them  of  $10,000,  in  cloth- 
Qg,  provisions,  and  quarters,  or  money  in  lieu  thereof.  This  levy  will 
>e  made  upon  the  following  classes  of  persons,  in  proportion  to  the 
-uilt  and  property  of  each  individual : 1st,  Those  in  arms  with  the  en- 
my  who  have  property  in  this  city;  2d,  Those  who  have  furnished 
•ecuniary  or  other  aid  to  the  enemy  or  to  persons  in  the  enemy’s  serv- 
3e;  3d,  Those  who  have  verbally,  in  writing,  or  by  publication  given 
ncouragement  to  insurgents  and  rebels. 

II.  Brig.  Gen.  S.  B.  Curtis,  U.  S.  Volunteers ; Lieut.  Col.  B.  G.  Far- 
ar,  provost-marshal-general,  and  Charles  Borg,  esq.,  assessor  of  the 
ounty  of  Saint  Louis,  will  constitute  a board  of  assessors  for  levying 
tie  aforementioned  contribution.  In  determining  the  amount  of  prop- 
rty  of  the  individuals  assessed  the  board  will  take  into  consideration 
tie  official  assessment  lists  for  municipal  taxes. 

III.  As  soon  as  any  part  of  this  contribution  has  been  assessed  by 
ae  board  the  provost-marshal-general  will  notify  the  parties  assessed 
leir  agents  or  representatives,  stating  the  amount  of  provisions,  cloth- 
lg,  or  quarters,  and  the  money  value  thereof  required  of  each  ; and  if 
ot  furnished  within  the  time  specified  in  such  notice  he  will  issue  an 
xecution,  and  sufficient  property  will  be  taken  and  sold  at  public  auc- 
on  to  satisfy  the  assessment,  with  costs,  and  a penalty  of  25  per  cent 

i addition.  Where  buildings  or  parts  of  buildings  are  to  be  used! 
nd  where  any  of  the  sufferers  are  to  be  quartered  on  families,  care 
lould  be  taken  to  produce  as  little  inconvenience  to  the  owners  or 
unities  as  possible,  this  not  being  considered  a military  contribution 
■vied  upon  the  enemy,  but  merely  a collection  to  be  made  from  friends 
c the  enemy  for  charitable  purposes.

The  other  ten  companies,  under  various  names,  I propose  to  unite  into 
i battalion,  and  to  muster  them  in  as  infantry  on  the  saihe  terms  as 
BisselPs  regiment ; that  is,  to  have  the  extra  allowance  when  acting  as 
ingineer  troops.  To  effect  this  it  will  probably  be  necessary  to  break 
ip  the  present  organizations,  so  as  to  dispense  in  the  new  with  the 
>xtra  officers.  The  two  companies  of  telegraph  men  and  telegraph 
guards,  9 officers  and  225  men,  have  already  been  mustered  out,  but 
nany  of  them  are  ready  to  reorganize  as  infantry  in  the  manner  pro- 
>osed.  1 

The  Engineer  Corps  proper,  as  it  is  called,  has  no  troops,  but  proba- 
cy about  50  officers.  The  names  of  43  have  already  been  ascertained 
>ut  some  one  turns  up  every  few  days  holding  a commission  or  appoint- 
ment from  General  Fremont.  Some  of  these  are  already  discharged* 
•ut  it  is  impossible  to  discharge  them  all  at  present,  their  services  being 
bsolutely  indispensable  in  the  construction  of  the  works  which  are  now 
emg  built  at  Paducah,  Cairo,  Fort  Holt,  Girardeau,  Eolla,  Jefferson 
'ity,  ba  Mine  Cantonment  near  Sedalia,  &c.  The  commanding  officers 
t these  places  report  that  it  is  impossible  to  proceed  with  these  de- 
mises, now  partially  constructed,  without  the  aid  of  one  or  more  en- 
ineer  officer  at  each  place.  I coincide  in  their  opinion,  and  shall  be 
bilged  to  retain  in  service  some  10  or  12  of  the  most  competent  of  these 
fficers,  with  the  pay  of  captains  and  lieutenants  of  Engineers,  until 
)me  arrangement  can  be  made  to  replace  them  by  regular  officers. 

I would  remark  that  the  pontonier  company  has  a large  and  costly 
ridge  train  nearly  complete,  and  that  the  signal  company  has  in  its 
ossession  signal  instruments,  not,  perhaps,  of  much  value  for  military 
aerations,  but  which  have  cost  a large  sum  of  money. 

The  changes  proposed  will  obviate  the  present  irregularities  and 
lomalies  of  organization $ greatly  reduce  the  expenses,  and  give  effi- 
ency  to  this  branch  of  the  service,  which  now  seems  to  be  without 
rm  and  almost  without  use.  I consider  myself  authorized  by  the  in- 
ructions  of  the  2d  instant  to  make  them,  and  shall  do  so  as  rapidly  as 
issible,  unless  otherwise  directed.  The  reorganization  of  the  frag- 
entary  bodies  of  artillery,  cavalry,  and  infantry  will  be  pushed  forward 
i th  all  possible  dispatch. 

I inclose  herewith  a communication  of  this  date  from  General  Cul- 
m*  It  is  of  vital  importance  that  this  request  be  granted.  I have 
it  one  regular  engineer  and  one  topographical  officer  for  duty  in  this 
• partment,  and  these  have  also  to  perform  the  duties  of  aides-de-camp, 
lportant  defenses  are  being  constructed  without  any  competent  person 
direct  them. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLEOK, 

Major-General.

Saint  Louis,  December  16,  1861. 

ol.  J.  W.  Birge, 

Commanding  Sharpshooters , Centralia , Mo. : 

Colonel  : As  soon  as  you  have  cleaned  out  Centralia,  Sturgeon,  and 
tenick,  and  the  roads  leading  to  Columbia  and  Fayette,  I wish  you  to 
irn  your  attention  to  the  rebels  about  Huntsville,  Randolph  County, 
ad  Mexico,  Anderson  County.  You  will  arrest  not  only  enemies  in 
rms,  but  all  who  aid  and  assist  them,  and  you  will  have  it  distinctly 
nderstood  everywhere  that  rebels  will  be  punished  and  Union  men 
rotected  ; but  the  latter,  in  order  to  deserve  protection,  must  do  some- 
ling  for  themselves.  Induce  them  to  unite  under  the  protection  of 
our  forces  in  that  part  of  the  country  and  form  companies  of  State 
lilitia.  Heretofore  probably  many  have  been  deterred  from  acting 
l self-defense  against  rebels  from  a fear  that  the  Union  troops  might 
nally  abandon  this  State.  This  will  never  be  done.  Missouri  is  and 
lust  remain  in  the  Union  and  all  rebels  must  be  driven  out  or  punished, 
'here  must  be  no  more  half-way  measures,  and  there  can  be  no  middle 
ourse  of  individual  neutrality.  All  citizens  who  are  not  rebels  must 
>yally  support  the  Government.  If  they  aid  rebels,  they  are  traitors ; 

‘ they  refuse  aid  to  the  cause  of  the  Union,  they  are  disloyal,  and  by 
ais  disloyalty  give  countenance  to  those  who  are  openly  enemies. 
>otk  classes  will  be  treated  as  their  conduct  deserves.  Those  who  are 
ot  for  us  will  be  regarded  as  against  us.  We  must  know  who  are 
iends  and  who  are  enemies ; the  line  will  be  distinctly  drawn.  There 
an  be  no  individual  neutrality  in  the  rear  in  Missouri.  Let  the  people 
here  you  go  distinctly  understand  this. 

It  is  said  that  parties  of  men  are  cutting  down  telegraph  posts  and 
ttempting  to  destroy  the  railroad.  Shoot  down  every  one  engaged  in 
uch  attempts  and  put  in  close  confinement  every  one  who  lias  done 
a ; also  seize  every  one  making  signal-fires  or  who  conveys  informa- 
ion  to  the  enemy. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLECK, 

Major-General.

Carrollton,  December  17,  1861. 

Major-General  Halleck  : 

I leave  here  to-day  for  Utica,  having  accomplished  object  of  trip. 
Some  500  have  crossed  from  this  county  to  join  Price.  They  have 
gone  without  outfit,  and  have  destroyed  all  ferries  that  I could  find. 
The  counties  through  which  we  have  passed  have  furnished  large  quan- 
tities of  clothing  for  Price,  most  of  which  crosses  at  Lexington,  which 
place,  in  my  opinion,  should  be  held  by  our  troops. 

B.  M.  PBENTISS. 


Saint  Louis,  Mo.,  December  17,  1861. 

P.  B.  Ewino,  Esq.,  Cincinnati , Ohio: 

Dear  Sir:  Your  note  of  the  13th,  with  inclosure,  is  received.  I am 
not  surprised  that  General  Sherman  should  be  abused  by  the  newspa- 
pers, for  it  seems  to  have  become  the  fashion  all  over  the  United  States 
for  editors  and  scribblers  to  criticise,  abuse,  and  even  blackguard  any 
officer  who  devotes  his  time  and  health  and  life  to  the  service  of  his 
country.  I have  had  a pretty  good  share  of  it  myself  within  the  last 
few  weeks,  but  I have  not  and  shall  not  notice  anything  they  say  of 
me.  I hope  General  Sherman  will  not  let  these  squibs  trouble  him  in 
the  least.  They  can  do  him  no  serious  injury.  When  General  Sher- 
man came  here  his  health  was  much  broken  by  long  and  severe  labor 
and  his  nervous  system  somewhat  shaken  by  continuous  excitement 
and  responsibility.  Those  who  saw  him  here  may  have  drawn  wrong 
inferences  from  his  broken-down  appearance  and  rather  imprudent  re- 
marks; but  no  one  who  was  personally  acquainted  with  him  thought 
that  anything  was  the  matter  with  him  except  a want  of  rest.  I have 
no  doubt  that  the  quiet  of  home  will  enable  him  in  a short  time  to  re-

The  whole  account  of  the  enemy  being  in  such  force  at  Lexing 
and  having  passed  west  in  large  todies  from  the  Osage  is  a most  gros

xaggeration.  I have  been  very  reluctant  from  my  previous  experience 
ii  this  State  to  credit  such  reports,  but  they  were  brought  from  Lexing- 
j on  and  communicated  to  me  by  persons  of  undoubted  respectability, 
Lnd  asserted  with  such  positive  certainty  that,  although  not  fully  con- 
vinced of  their  truth,  I could  not  without  obstinacy  refuse  to  credit 
i liem  to  some  extent. 

The  plain  facts  are  these  : A few  men  detailed  from  each  of  the  five 
>r  six  divisions  of  Price’s  army  made  their  way  in  squads  of  from  10 
o 150  to  the  neighborhood  of  Lexington.  They  were  never  in  the  town 
bt  all,  and  did  not  number  altogether  more  than  800  or  1,000  men.  The 
ecruits  they  were  sent  up  to  bring  down  are  largely  estimated  at  1,200, 
n rags,  without  arms,  and  without  supplies.  In  their  march  to  the 
outh  they  picked  up  in  all  about  70  two-horse  wagons.  They  fled  pre- 
cipitately as  soon  as  they  heard  of  our  approach,  and  when  the  pursuit 
erminated,  near  Johnstown,  it  is  to  be  doubted  if  there  were  500  men 
md  10  wagons  left  together.  Only  15  wagons  crossed  Grand  River. 
The  rebel  force  scattered  as  they  ran ; the  wagons  were  driven  into 
arm-yards,  and  the  men,  going  in  small  parties,  sought  refuge  in  paths 
tnd  by-ways.  The  cavalry  reconnaissance  through  Clinton,  designed 
o cover  our  pursuit,  drove  in  and  captured  the  pickets  of  Rains’  di vis- 
on,  which  is  encamped  this  side  the  Osage,  pursuing  and  capturing 
hem  inside  the  lines. 

All  information,  both  from  the  prisoners  and  from  the  people  of  the 
country,  concurs  that  Price  has  not  over  8,000  or  10,000  men,  and  that 
le  is  losing  many  more  men  than  he  can  recruit.  I have  no  doubt  that 
f it  were  known  that  those  willing  to  return  home  could  do  so  without 
nolestation,  by  taking  the  oath  not  again  to  take  up  arms  or  to  aid  or 
jibet  the  rebels,  a very  large  number  of  his  men  would  leave  him  at 
mce.  I say  this  after  examination  of  the  prisoners  and  full  commu- 
nication with  people  of  this  section  entirely  acquainted  with  the  con- 
dition of  affairs  in  Price’s  command. 

I do  not,  of  course,  know  what  are  your  views  in  relation  to  Price, 
jut  it  is  certain  that  as  long  as  he  remains  in  this  part  of  the  country 
here  will  be  excitement  and  more  or  less  recruiting  for  him.  Compel 
lim  to  fly,  and  the  inducement  is  at  an  end.  I have  no  idea  that,  with 
my  possible  means  of  surrounding  him,  his  forces  could  be  captured. 
They  would  disperse  in  all  directions  at  the  approach  of  danger,  hiding 
cheir  artillery  in  the  woods  and  distributing  their  wagons  among  the 
farm-houses,  where  it  would  be  impossible  to  identify  them.  Opera- 
tions against  him  as  if  he  commanded  an  organized  army  must  be 
futile.  I have  abundant  force  to  drive  his  from  the  country,  and  should 
be  glad  to  be  allowed  to  do  so. 

My  command  will  return  slowly  to  Sedalia,  and  if  you  think  it  best 
will  resume  their  positions  at  Otterville.  I shall  proceed  there,  and 
will  probably  be  in  Sedalia  day  after  to-morrow.  The  whole  region  as 
far  south  as  the  Osage  is  in  a just  state  of  alarm  from  this  expedition, 
and  I think  their  rest  north  will  not  soon  be  troubled  again  by  Price’s 
peojfle.  The  cavalry  force  I sent  in  advance  encamped  in  Johnstown 
last  night,  and  scouted  the  country  south  of  Grand  River  on  their 
return  to  within  a few  miles  of  Clinton.  I should  not  be  at  all  sur- 
prised to  learn  that  the  movement  had  caused  Price  to  break  up  his 
camp  and  retreat  south. 

I am,  general,  your  obedient  servant, 

JRO.  POPE, 

Brigadier-  General , Commanding .

Headquarters  Department  of  the  Missouri, 

Saint  Louis , December  19,  1861. 

Maj.  Gen.  Georoe  B.  McClellan, 

General-in-Chief  of  the  Army , Washington  City: 

General  : The  expeditions  of  Generals  Prentiss  and  McKean  through 
the  counties  north  of  the  Missouri  River  have  been  entirely  successful. 
Every  insurgent  organization  there  has  now  been  broken  up,  and  I 
think  it  will  be  safe  in  a short  time  to  withdraw  a portion  of  the  troops 
from  that  district.  At  Glasgow  our  troops  yesterday  captured  about 
two  tons  of  powder,  which  it  is  said  was  purchased,  in  Chicago  and 
brought  in  on  the  Saint  Joseph  and  Hannibal  Railroad  among  dry 
goods  and  in  demijohns  marked  “brandy.”  It  was  carried  through  in 
small  quantities  by  rebel  country  merchants  and  farmers  and  collected 
at  Glasgow,  to  be  thence  forwarded  to  General  Price.  Colonel  Mar- 
shall’s expedition  to  Arrow  Rock  and  Waverly  prevented  its  crossing 
the  river,  and  it  consequently  fell  into  the  hands  of  our  troops  on  the 

north  side.  , . 

General  Pope’s  party  intercepted  a portion  of  the  insurgents  who 
crossed  at  Lexington.  He  attacked  their  camps  of  2,200  near  Shawnee 
Mound,  between  Warrensburg  and  Clinton,  and  completely  scattered 
them,  capturing  their  tents,  wagons,  horses,  baggage,  &c.,  and  taking 
150  prisoners.  If  General  Prentiss  had  kept  me  advised  of  his  move- 
ments, as  I had  directed,  I would  have  taken  the  whole  party.  Our 
forces  at  Sedalia  were  for  several  days  ready  to  move  at  a moment  s 
warning,  and  only  waiting  to  hear  where  Prentiss  was.  On  the  whole, 
however,  the  result  is  satisfactory.  We  have  within  the  last  two  weeks 
taken  about  500  prisoners,  one  piece  of  artillery,  a number  of  arms, 
wagons,  horses,  and  a considerable  amount  of  ammunition  and  cloth- 
ing": and,  what  is  of  most  importance,  we  have  pretty  effectually  crushed 
out  the  insurrection  along  the  Missouri  River,  upon  which  Price  placed 
his  main  reliance  for  recruits  and  clothing.  His  army  is  pretty  welM 
supplied  with  provisions  and  arms,  but  is  greatly  in  want  of  clothing 
and  shoes.  He  has  a large  park  of  artillery,  and  from  all  I can  learnl 
will  make  a good  fight.  He  and  many  of  his  men  are  virtually  outj 
laws,  and,  it  is  said,  are  determined  to  win  a victory  or  die.  Another 
retreat  would  effectually  ruin  his  cause  in  this  State.  I had  hoped  to 
draw  him  north  to  the  Missouri  River,  so  that  I could  effectually  cutofl 
his  retreat,  but  his  main  force  has  not  yet  crossed  the  Osage,  and  the 
columns  which  he  advanced  on  Clinton  and  Warsaw  have  been  with- 
drawn. In  that  position  I cannot  cut  him  off  by  moving  from  Rolla, 
as  our  troops  would  be  compelled  to  cross  the  Osage  Mountains  oven 
narrow  and  difficult  roads,  which  would  make  our  movements  necesj 
sarily  slow,  affording  him  plenty  of  time  to  fall  back.  It  is  therefore 
possible  that  I may  be  compelled  to  attack  him  in  front.  The  ravaged 
committed  by  his  troops  may  make  it  advisable  to  move  against  hinfl 
soon,  notwithstanding  the  great  inconveniences  of  a winter  campaign 
in  this  climate,  which  is  very  much  more  unfavorable  than  that  ol 
Washington.  The  roads,  too,  will  probably  be  almost  impassable,  4 
hope,  however,  to  be  able  to  overcome  these  obstacles.  At  any  rate,  I 
shall  not  hesitate  to  act  as  soon  as  I can  get  the  troops  in  anything  like 
organization  and  discipline. 

The  conduct  of  the  columns  sent  through  the  river  counties  forms  aj 
striking  contrast  to  that  of  previous  expeditions.  Citizens  from  thes€| 
counties  assure  me  that  they  have  all  acted  with  perfect  propriety,  com 
mitting  no  depredations,  and  producing  a most  favorable  impression. 
This  certainly  indicates  a vast  improvement  in  discipline.  By  a le\*

>vere  punishments  for  marauding  and  pillaging  I hope  to  put  an  end

I am  progressing  slowly  with  the  reorganization  of  the  forces  here.  It 
a most  difficult  task,  increased  by  the  injudicious  orders  of  the  War 
epartment  and  the  jealousies  of  the  Governors  of  States.  The  ad- 
inistration  and  machinery  for  the  supply  of  the  army  is  rapidly  get- 
ig  into  working  order.  This  was  a matter  of  the  greatest  necessity 
consequently  has  absorbed  most  of  my  attention.  An  army  is 
on  disorganized  unless  properly  supplied  and  its  wants  provided  for. 
am  discharging  most  of  the  steamers  formerly  in  the  Government  em 
oyment,  and  mustering  out  of  service  what  is  called  “ Marine  Corps,” 
aich  are  nothing  more  than  hired  men  on  these  boats.  This  will  be 
great  saving  of  expense.  The  Home  Guards  are  also  being  dis- 
rnded  as  rapidly  as  I can  supply  their  places.  The  U.  S.  Reserve 
)rps,  as  they  are  called,  are  generally  regularly-organized  Missouri 
flunteers,  mustered  in  for  three  years  or  the  war,  without  limitation 
to  place  of  service.  The  Pay  Department  has  objected  to  pay  these 
x>ps,  on  the  ground  that  there  was  some  outside  verbal  or  tacit  under  - 
rnding  that  they  would  not  be  ordered  out  of  the  State.  I cannot 
cognize  any  such  unrecorded  verbal  understanding,  and  must  be 
jiided  alone  by  the  muster  rolls,  which  are  perfectly  regular.  More- 
|er  General  Curtis  informs  me  that  he  refused  to  permit  them  to  be 
nstered  in  with  any  reservation  whatever.  I have  therefore  ordered 
|em,  or  rather  all  of  them  in  actual  service,  to  be  paid  on  their  nius- 
l rolls.  They  are  not  generally  very  efficient  troops,  and  I purpose 
« disband  a part  of  them  as  soon  as  I can  do  so  with  safety.  1 shall 
1 50  disband  most  of  the  fragmentary  and  irregular  organizations.  This 
. *mld  not  do  all  at  once.  The  condition  of  the  country  and  the  state 
< public  feeling  here,  resulting  from  General  Fremont’s  removal,  ex- 
led  by  designing  party  politicians,  rendered  it  prudent  to  move  in 
hs  matter  slowly  and  cautiously.  The  task  imposed  on  me  here  in 
ns  chaos  of  incendiary  elements  is  not  an  easy  one,  and  those  at  a dis- 
Juce,  who  cannot  understand  the  real  condition  of  affairs,  should  not 
hasty  m judging  of  my  conduct,  and,  above  all,  they  should  not  em- 
iTTass  me  by  unnecessary  interference.  This  I know  very  well  you 
not  do>  for  you  will  readily  appreciate  the  difficulties  of  my  posi- 
1 n.  I shall  obey  all  orders  sent  to  me,  but  I hope  the  War  Depart- 
jbnt  will  allow  me  a hearing  before  it  acts  hereafter  on  mere  ex-part  e 
* dements.  My  efforts  to  introduce  a system  of  order  and  economy" 
ju  to  ferret  out  frauds  will  very  naturally  create  opposition,  and  I 
| all  not  be  surprised  to  find  myself  an  object  of  very  bitter  abuse  in 
3 newspapers  and  on  the  floor  of  Congress.  This,  however,  will  not 
mbie  me  much,  so  long  as  I am  sustained  by  my  superiors  and  feel 
' it  I am  pursuing  the  right  course  of  conduct. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLECK,

In  order  that  the  Treasury  of  the  United  States  may  not  be  burdened

iven  by  said  act  of  Congress  to  officers  in  the  United  States  service 
►erforming  the  same  duties. 

The  field  officers  of  a regiment  in  the  State  Militia  are  1 colonel,  1 
ieutenant-colonel,  and  1 major,  and  the  company  officers  are  a captain, 
first  lieutenant,  and  a second  lieutenant.

General-in-Chief  of  the  Army,  Washington,  D.  C.  : 

General:  My  telegrams  will  have  informed  you  of  the  success 
General  Pope’s  expedition  to  cut  off  the  forces  moving  from  Lexiu 
ton,  Waverly,  &c.,  to  join  Price.  It  is  now  pretty  well  ascertain 


at.  XVIII.] 


CORRESPONDENCE,  ETC. UNION. 


463 


(at  these  forces  numbered  about  5,000.  Had  the  expedition  moved 
reive  hours  sooner  it  would  probably  have  caught  the  whole.  Gen- 
al  Pope  was  held  in  readiness  some  forty-eight  hours,  but  the  gen- 
al  commanding  north  of  the  river  failed  to  keep  me  informed  of  his 
ovements.  The  result,  however,  is  satisfactory,  as  the  enemy  was 
•mpletely  broken  up  and  deprived  of  most  of  his  supplies. 

Recent  events  have  proved  that  the  information  received  soon  after 
assumed  the  command,  that  an  insurrection  of  some  12,000  or  15,000 
med  men  had  been  organized  north  of  the  Missouri  River,  was  cor- 
ct.  The  two  expeditions  sent  from  Saint  Joseph  and  Jefferson  City 
rough  the  river  counties  broke  up  a part  of  this  organization  and 
reed  those  who  had  already  taken  arms  to  move  south,  where  they 
ere  captured  and  scattered  by  Pope’s  forces.  The  insurrection  in 
ncoln,  Pike,  Ralls,  Monroe,  and  Adrian  Counties  broke  out  before 
ey  heard  of  the  capture  of  the  rebels  at  Shawnee  Mound  and  Mil- 
l'd. The  burning  of  the  railroad  bridges  and  destruction  of  the  tele- 
aph  lines  formed  a part  of  the  plan.  I had  anticipated  this,  and 
rected  General  Prentiss  to  have  the  railroad  bridges  well  guarded 
‘fore  he  went  to  Saint  Joseph.  These  orders  were  probably  very  im- 
■rfectly  executed.  Had  I moved  General  Pope’s  command  at  Sedalia 
rainst  Price  before  partially  breaking  up  these  insurrectionary  organ i- 
tions  1 should  have  had  some  15,000  insurgents  in  his  rear,  without 
e means  of  re-enforcing  him,  on  account  of  the  destruction  of  the 
ilroads  and  telegraphs.  As  it  is,  the  insurrection  is  pretty  well 
ushed  out ; the  injuries  to  the  roads  will  not  materially  affect  our 
ilitary  operations,  and  Price’s  army  is  completely  cut  off  from  all 
>pes  of  re-enforcements  or  supplies. *”  He  is  believed  to  be  still  in  the 
cinity  of  Osceola,  in  such  a position  that  I cannot  well  reach  him  or 
>t  in  his  rear,  as  he  is  nearer  to  the  Arkansas  line  than  I am,  and  even 
an  I am  to  him.  I am  satisfied  that  he  will  retreat  the  moment  I 
ake  a move,  and  as  a majority  of  the  people  are  secessionists,  he  is 
Pt  fully  advised  of  everything  I do.  It  is  barely  possible  that  I 
| ay  throw  a large  cavalry  force  in  his  rear  and  flank  so  as  to  greatly 
ibarrass  his  retreat,  but  unfortunately  our  cavalry  is  but  half  armed, 
jim  waiting  most  impatiently  for  the  11,000  arms  you  promised,  hoping 
at  they  may  partly  supply  the  wants  of  the  cavalry  arm.  The  forces 
Rolla  are  ready,  and  will  move  the  moment  that  arms  are  received, 
ice’s  army  will  certainly  be  driven  out  of  the  State,  and  possibly, 
ough  not  very  probably,  a portion  of  it  may  be  captured. 

These  bridge  burnings  are  the  most  annoying  features  of  the  war. 
iey  are  effected  by  small  parties  of  mounted  men,  disguised  as  farm- 
s' but  well  armed.  They  overpower  or  overawe  the  guards,  set  fire 
the  bridges,  and  escape  before  a force  can  be  collected  against  them, 
samples  of  severe  punishment  are  the  only  remedies.  I shall  carry 
t in  this  respect  my  General  Orders,  NTo.  32,  inclosed  herewith. 

It  I receive  arms  in  time  to  carry  out  my  present  plans  in  Missouri 
Jiink  I shall  be  able  to  strongly  re-enforce  Cairo  and  Paducah  for 
terior  operations  by  the  early  part  of  February. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLECK, 

Major-General.

meral  Asboth,  Bolla , Mo. : 

General  : It  would  seem,  from  the  report  of  Major  Waring  to  you 
iferred  to  these  headquarters),  that  he  had,  in  compliance  with  your 
fractions.  delivered  to  a Captain  Holland  a fugitive  in  his  camp, 
timed  by  Captain  Holland  as  the  property  of  his  father-in-law.  This 
contrary  to  the  intent  of  General  Orders,  No.  3.  The  object  of  these 
lers  is  to  prevent  any  person  in  the  Army  from  acting  in  the  capacity 
negro-catcher  or  negro -stealer.  The  relation  between  the  slave  and 
> master  or  pretended  master  is  not  a matter  to  be  determined  by 
litary  officers,  except  in  the  single  case  provided  for  by  Congress, 
is  matter  in  all  other  cases  must  be  decided  by  the  civil  authorities, 
le  object  in  keeping  fugitive  slaves  out  of  our  camp  is  to  keep  clear 
all  such  questions.  Masters  or  pretended  masters  must  establish 
i rights  of  property  to  the  negroes  as  best  they  may  without  our 
^stance  or  interference,  except  where  the  law  authorizes  such  inter  - 
ence.  Orders,  No.  3,  do  not  apply  to  the  authorized  private  servants 
officers  nor  the  negroes  employed  by  proper  authority  in  the  camps, 
ipplies  only  to  fugitive  slaves.  The  prohibition  to  admit  them  within 
r lines  does  not  prevent  the  exercise  of  all  proper  offices  of  humanity 
giving  them  food  and  clothing  outside  where  such  offices  are  neces- 
7 to  prevent  suffering. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

I In  carrying  on  war  in  a portion  of  country  occupied  or  threatend 
to  bo  attacked  by  an  enemy,  whether  within  or  without  the  territor 
of  the  United  States,  crimes  and  military  oitenses  are  frequently  con 
mitted  which  are  not  triable  or  punishable  by  courts-martial  and  whic 
are  not  within  the  jurisdiction  of  any  existing  civil  court.  Such  case 
however,  must  be  investigated  and  the  guilty  parties  punished.  T1 
good  of  society  and  the  safety  of  the  army  imperiously  demand  thil 
They  must  therefore  be  taken  cognizance  of  by  the  military  powei 
but,  except  in  cases  of  extreme  urgency,  a military  commander  shoul, 
not  himself  attempt  to  decide  upon  the  guilt  or  innocence  of  mdivitj 
uals.  On  the  contrary,  it  is  the  usage  and  custom  of  war  among  » 
civilized  nations  to  refer  such  cases  to  a duly-constituted  military  t 
bunal  composed  of  reliable  officers,  who,  acting  under  the  solemnity 
an  oath  ami  the  responsibility  always  attached  to  a court  of  recor. 
will  examine  witnesses,  determine  the  guilt  or  innocence  of  the  parti 
accused  and  fix  the  punishment.  This  is  usually  done  by  courts-ma 
tial ; but  in  our  country  these  courts  have  a very  limited  junsdictio 
both  in  regard  to  persons  and  offenses.  Many  classes  of  persons  ca. 
not  be  arraigned  before  such  courts  for  any  offense  wliatsoei  er,  ar 
many  crimes  committed,  even  by  military  officers,  enlisted  men,  ' 
camp  retainers,  cannot  be  tried  under  the  Rules  and  Articles  of  TV  a 
Military  commissions  must  be  resorted  to  for  such  cases,  and  these  coi 
missions  should  be  ordered  by  the  same  authority,  be  constituted  in 
similar  manner,  and  their  proceedings  be  conducted  according  to  t 
same  general  rules  as  courts-martial,  in  order  to  prevent  abuses  wln< 

miSIhtAshmuch  misapprehension  has  arisen  in  this

a court-martial.  In  other  cases  we  must  be  governed  by  the  general

6th.  Treason,  as  a distinct  offense,  is  defined  by  the  Constitution,  and 
list  be  tried  by  courts  duly  constituted  by  law;  but  certain  acts  of  a 
Dasonable  character,  such  as  conveying  information  to  the  enemy,  act- 
as  spies,  &c.,  are  military  offenses,  triable  by  military  tribunals,  and 
] nishable  by  military  authority. 

7th.  The  fact  that  those  persons  who  are  now  carrying  on  hostilities 
J ainst  the  lawful  authorities  of  the  United  States  are  rebels  and  trai- 
ls to  the  Government  does  not  deprive  them  of  any  of  the  rights  of 
nr,  so  far  as  the  military  authorities  are  concerned.  In  our  inter- 
<urse  with  the  duly- authorized  forces  of  the  so-called  Confederate 
S ates  and  in  the  treatment  of  prisoners  of  war  taken  from  such  forces 
n must  be  governed  by  the  usages  and  customs  of  war  in  like  cases. 

1 it  the  rights  so  given  to  such  prisoners  by  the  laws  of  war  do  not, 
i cording  to  the  same  code,  exempt  them  from  trial  and  punishment  by 
1 3 proper  courts  for  treason  or  other  offenses  against  the  Government. 

- te  rights  which  they  may  very  properly  claim  as  belligerents  under 
1 3 general  rules  of  belligerent  intercourse — commercia  belli — cannot 
t empt  them  from  the  punishment  to  which  they  may  have  subjected 
t cmselves  as  citizens  under  the  general  laws  of  the  land. 

3th.  Again,  a soldier  duly  enrolled  and  authorized  to  act  in  a mili- 
tpy  capacity  in  the  enemy’s  service  is  not,  according  to  the  code 
ilitary,  individually  responsible  for  the  taking  of  human  life  in  bat- 
t , siege,  &c.,  while  at  the  same  time  he  is  held  individually  responsi- 
J } for  any  act  which  he  may  commit  in  violation  of  the  laws  of  war. 
r us  he  cannot  be  punished  by  a military  tribunal  for  committing  acts 
( hostility  which  are  authorized  by  the  laws  of  war,  but  if  he  has 
unmitted  murder,  robbery,  theft,  arson,  &c.,  the  fact  of  his  being  a 
1 isoner  of  war  does  not  exempt  him  from  trial  by  a military  tribunal. 
1th.  And,  again,  while  the  code  of  war  gives  certain  exemptions  to  a 
idier  regularly  in  the  military  service  of  an  enemy,  it  is  a well-

feelings  you  express,  and  do  not  doubt  for  a moment  that  we  can  co-o 
erate  harmoniously  in  the  important  work  in  which  we  are  engaged.

to  the  affairs  of  this  district,  and  hope  that  ere  long  I may  have  tl 
pleasure  of  forming  a personal  acquaintance  and  lasting  friendship 
a general  whom  I have  already  learned  to  esteem  so  highly. 

I have  left  General  Henderson  with  his  command  ot  State  troops 
Mexico,  with  instructions  to  operate  in  the  country  north  and  east 
that  point.  I presume  the  force  between  Mexico  and  Hudson  is  si 
ficient  for  the  protection  of  the  road ; if  not,  please  inform  me,  and

points  along  the  road  frtrai  Mexico  to  Saint  Charles,  and  organizing 
regular  system  of  scouting,  by  which  I hope  to  capture  the  small  ban 
of  rebels  that  are  now  scattered  over  this  part  of  the  State.  1 clo

ilized  human  beings  in  their  stead.  If  this  be  done,  as  I doubt jncfl

Headquarters  Cavalry  Expedition, 

Camp  Buggies,  on  Gasconade,  Laclede  County,  Mo.,  Jan.  3,  1862. 

'o  the  Assistant  Adjutant-General, 

Hdqrs.  Southwestern  List.,  Dept,  of  Missouri,  Bolla,  Mo.  : 

Sir  : I sent  off  this  morning  a report  by  the  expressman  returning 
iving  an  account  of  my  operations  up  to  last  night.  The  party  which 
sent  out  under  Colonel  Lewis  ran  60  of  the  enemy  about  10  miles, 
hey  ate  the  enemy’s  breakfast,  and  took  about  100  cattle,  30  sheep,  and 
) fat  hogs.  Some  of  the  cattle  escaped.  Being  in  a brushy  country 
ad  driving  in  the  night,  the  hogs  could  not  travel.  I shall  have  such 
3 are  fit  for  food  killed  for  this  command,  and  such  as  are  stock  cattle 
shall  send  in,  if  practicable. 

The  expedition  to  Lebanon  failed  on  account  of  a message  having 
sen  sent  from  Cook’s  Mill,  where  we  crossed  the  Boubideaux.  There 
as  no  enemy  found  in  town,  but  2 men  ran  and  were  caught.  The 
lemy  has  a hospital  in  town,  where  there  were  1 wounded  and  1 sick 
an — perhaps  more. 

The  weather  turned  very  bad  yesterday  evening,  with  rain  and 
eet— such  weather  as  none  but  a soldier  would  be  out  in.  I had  a party 
;ady  to  send  toward  Hartville  this  morning,  but  it  was  so  very  cold 
id  bad  and  the  rains  had  made  the  roads  so  bad  that  I did  not  send, 
ine  of  my  parties  was  at  the  house  of  Bowman,  a noted  secession  cap- 
yesterday,  towards  Hartville,  but  he  was  not  at  home,  and  very 
w men  were  at  home,  but  there  were  many  tracks  of  horses,  mostlv 
hshod,  going  west. 

About  3 o’clock  this  afternoon  some  of  my  men,  who  were  out  getting 
rage,  thought  they  heard  cannon-firing  in  the  direction  of  Lebanon, 
j seems  very  improbable,  but  the  men  stick  to  their  story,  and  say  that 
|e  woman  of  the  house  told  them  that  she  had  heard  that  Price  was 
;>ing  to  attack  us  before  12  o’clock  to-morrow.  I have  sent  a party  of 
: towards  Lebanon  to  gain  information  and  shall  send  out  other  scout- 
|g  parties  in  the  morning. 

My  greatest  trouble  is  with  this  train,  which,  now  that  the  roads  are 
d,  can  only  move  very  slowly.  The  mules  are  weak  and  the  drivers 
id.  Two  scouts  towards  Springfield,  who  should  have  been  here 
Is  ter  day,  have  not  returned,  which  looks  bad,  and  I have  received  no 
pssage  from  you  except  the  one  started  New  Year’s  Eve.  The  dupli- 
te  arrived  here  to-day,  having  been  nearly  to  Lebanon.  He  does 
\t  satisfy  me  that  he  is  all  right. 

|I  hope  you  will  tell  the  quartermaster  to  send  good  men,  and  also  to 
Mid  our  mail  whenever  a safe  opportunity  offers, 
it  have  an  escort  of  20  men  left  back  to  escort  up  the  doctor.  They 
jp  under  the  charge  of  Lieutenant  Black,  of  my  regiment,  a member 
3 the  court-martial  in  Asboth’s  division.  If  the  doctor  is  not  coming 
pant  my  men. 

1 find  that  instead  of  being  in  Wright  County,  as  my  guide  led  me  to 
Jheve,  I am  in  Laclede,  2£  miles  from  the  line  between  it  and  Pulaski, 
r the  Gasconade.

tinue  so  for  any  length  of  time  shall  he  sent  to  this  city.  There  are

The  source  of  most  of  the  sickness  in  this  division  can  be  traced  to 
the  crowded  condition  of  some  of  the  tents  and  barracks,  especially  the 
Wedge  tent,  which  averages  five  and  a half  persons  to  a tent  of  8 by  if 
Bad  as  this  tent  is,  the  close  and  crowded  barracks  are  even  worse. 
Two  companies  are  crowded  into  a barracks  30  by  60  feet,  11  feet  high. 
The  air  is  most  foul  and  breeds  disease  and  death. 

At  Camp  Benton  the  commander  of  the  post  has  most  promptly  com- 
plied with  the  recommendation  of  Dr.  Warriner,  the  inspector  of  camps 
for  Mie'United  States  Sanitary  Commission,  in  improving  the  ventila- 
tion, but  with  the  number  of  inmates  no  amount  of  ventilation  will 
suffice.  The  regulations  allow  225  square  feet  for  6 men.  At  these 
barracks  there  is  but  60  feet  for  6 men,  which  is  entirely  inadequate. 

The  small-pox  has  made  its  appearance  at  several  posts  and  in  one 
ff  our  hospitals ; every  precaution  has  been  taken  to  prevent  its  spread- 
ing? but?  in  order  to  arrest  and  mitigate  the  horrors  of  this  dreaded  dis- 
ease it  is  necessary  that  some  obligatory  order  be  issued  to  colonels  of 
’egiments,  holding  them  responsible  for  the  .prompt  execution  of  the 
same. 

Among  the  other  duties  which  devolved  upon  the  Sanitary  Comrnis- 
lon  was  the  obtaining  from  the  community  at  large  such  additional 
neans  of  increasing  the  comfort  and  promoting  the  moral  and  social 
welfare  of  the  men  in  camp  and  hospital  as  may  be  needed  and  cannot 
)e  furnished  by  Government  regulations.  To  carry  out  this  object  ap- 
>eals  have  been  made  to  the  community  through  the  press  and  have 
)een  most  generously  responded  to.  The  various  Ladies’  Aid  Societies, 
is  well  as  individuals,  have  showered  their  offerings  upon  us.  From 
Massachusetts  alone  we  have  received  over  150  boxes  of  supplies.  We 
lave  already  distributed  over  18,759  articles,  consisting  of  shirts,  drawers, 
ocks,  comforts,  and  a variety  of  other  articles  of  comfort  and  useful- 
ness, besides  over  1,000  books. 

The  Commission  feel  the  necessity  of  having  another  medical  gentle- 
Lian  on  our  Commission,  and  would  respectfully  recommend  the  appoint- 
nent  of  Dr.  S.  Pollok,  a gentleman  of  acknowledged  ability  and  experi- 
nce  as  a sanitarian.

Benton,  to  enter  them  upon  the  books  of  that  gunboat,  and  we  pay  ai 
ration  them  as  we  do  the  crew  of  the  Benton.  .

Your  suggestions  about  officers  in  arrest  are  approved.  You  are 
ithorized  to  suspend  their  arrest  and  order  them  into  the  field.  The 
rart-martial  will  close  its  proceedings  and  adjourn  sine  die.  Fletcher’s 
attery  will  leave  here  for  Eolla  Wednesday  morning.  You  now  have 
?enty-four  pieces.  This  will  give  you  thirty.  When  the  Ninth  Iowa

olla  as  soon  as  General  Schofield  can  spare  the  section  now  with  him. 
hie  Forty-third  Illinois  will  be  sent  to  you  as  soon  as  they  are  better 
•med;  also  the  Second  Iowa  the  moment  I can  relieve  them.  Perhaps 
may  be  able  to  spare  two  other  regiments  in  course  of  the  week.  At 
ly  rate,  your  forces  will  be  superior  to  any  reliable  estimate  I have 
reived  of  Price’s  army.  As  your  advance  will  necessarily  be  slow,  the 
lditional  force  will  reach  you  this  side  of  Springfield  and  will  serve 
} a reserve. 

With  regard  to  routes  three  have  been  proposed — that  by  Lebanon, 
iat  by  Hartville,  and  a middle  road.  Colonel  Phelps  thinks  the  mid- 
e road  the  best;  others  say  not.  You  will  act  from  the  best  informa- 
m you  have  there,  which  is  better  than  I can  get  here. 

Accounts  are  so  contradictory  that  I am  unable  to  advise  you.  Leba- 
)n  is  certainly  the  best  military  line  if  the  road  is  equally  good. 
Distribute  transportation  as  directed  in  my  letter  of  yesterday,  ex- 
pt,  if  you  deem  advisable,  give  a limited  number  of  provision  wagons 
each  brigade  or  division.  This  is  generally  preferable  to  making  the 
'0 vision  train  entirely  separate  from  the  troops.  Ten  days’  provisions 
ill  in  that  case  go  with  each  command. 

Care  should  be  taken  about  having  provisions  cooked  in  the  morning 
r the  day’s  march,  and  also,  when  in  the  vicinity  of  the  enemy,  to 
tve  at  least  two  days’  cooked  provisions  in  the  haversacks.  If  officers 
sglect  this,  the  men  suffer.  Make  marches  at  first  short,  so  that  the 
en  may  be  kept  in  order  and  not  overfatigued.

Several  other  skirmishes  have  taken  place  and  some  200  prisoners

' Mexico.  The  enemy  has  scattered  in  every  direction,  but  as  our

lrners  will  eventually  be  caught.  Most  of  them  are  from  Price’s  army,

ipressed  into  Price’s  service.  No  reliance  whatever  can  be  placed 
oon  these  pretended  refugees  from  military  impressment. 

A body  of  some  1,800  cavalry  was  sent  some  days  ago  to  make  a

only  organized  in  a manner  entirely  contrary  to  law,  but  are  by  no  means 
reliable.  On  the  contrary,  being  mostly  foreigners,  officered  m many 
cases  by  foreign  adventurers  or  perhaps  refugees  from  justice  and  hav- 
ing been  tampered  with  by  political  partisans  for  political  purposes, 
they  constitute  a very  dangerous  element  in  society  as  well  as  in  the 
armv  I have  endeavored  to  remove  the  causes  of  complaint  for  want 
of  pay  and  clothing  as  much  as  possible  by  mustering  them  for  pay 
even  in  their  present  illegal  organizations,  and  I am  supplying  their 
places  as  fast  as  possible  by  other  troops.  The  Body  Guards  Marine 
Corps,  Telegraph  Corps,  Bailroad  Guards,  and  Benton  Cadets  have 
already  been  mustered  out  of  service.  The  Home  Guards  at  Boone- 
ville  and  Jefferson  City  have  been  forcibly  disarmed,  and  a number 
of  other  bodies  of  these  irregular  troops  will  be  discharged  m a few 
days.  Some  of  these  foreign  troops  are  most  excellent  men,  while 
others  are  without  discipline  or  subordination,  and  m the  field  are  little 
better  than  armed  barbarians.  Wherever  they  go  they  convert  all 
Union  men  into  bitter  enemies.  The  accompanying  letter  of  General 
Schofield  is  a fair  specimen  of  what  is  reported  of  them  m other  places. 
Indeed,  strong  Union  men  in  Southwestern  Missouri  (and  among  them 
Colonel  Phelps,  a Member  of  Congress)  have  begged  me  not  to  permit 
General  Sigel’s  command  to  return  to  that  part  of  the  country,  as  they 
robbed  and  plundered  wherever  they  went  friends  and  enemies  alike. 
I shall,  however,  be  obliged  to  employ  his  division,  as  I have  no  other 
forces  to  send  against  Price.  If  I could  withdraw  them  entirely  from 
this  State  and  send  them  to  Cairo  to  operate  in  the  enemy  s country  m 
more  compact  masses,  perhaps  I might  reduce  them  to  better  discipline. 

I nurpose  doing  so  as  soon  as  possible.  _ 

As  a specimen  of  the  kind  of  reliance  which  can  be  placed  upon  some 
of  the  foreign  adventurers  who  have  been  p Laced  m high  positions  m 
our  volunteer  service  I will  mention  the  fact,  which  has  been  reported

Wellsville,  Mo.,  January  2,  1862. 

Col.  J.  0.  Kelton, 

Asst.  Adjt.  Gen.,  Dept,  of  the  Missouri , Saint  Louis , Mo. : 

Colonel:  I have  the  honor  to  urgently  request  the  immediate  action 
ff  the  commanding  general  upon  a matter  which  I regard  of  vital  im- 
portance. 

Upon  my  arrival  at  Warrenton  I found  a battalion  of  Reserve  Corps 
Cavalry,  under  command  of  Major  Hollan,  the  only  cavalry  at  my 
iisposal.  These  men  had  preceded  me  only  a few  days,  but  they  had 
already  murdered  one  of  the  few  Union  men  in  that  vicinity  and  com- 
mitted numerous  depredations  upon  the  property  of  peaceful  citizens. 
Since  that  time  their  conduct  has  been  absolutely  barbarous — a burn- 
ing disgrace  to  the  army  and  to  the  Union  cause.  In  spite  of  all  my 
efforts  to  the  contrary  they  have  plundered  and  destroyed  the  property 
af  citizens  (many  of  them  the  best  Unibn  men  in  the  State)  to  the 
amount  of  many  thousands  of  dollars.  Their  officers  either  connive  at 
t or  else  have  no  power  to  restrain  their  men.  I cannot  trust  them  out 
af  my  sight  for  a moment,  and  of  course  they  are  of  no  use  to  me  as 
aavalry  so  long  as  this  is  the  case.  I have  succeeded  in  detecting  five 
jf  the  robbers  and  have  them  in  irons  and  have  arrested  the  major 
and  one  of  the  captains  and  placed  them  in  close  confinement. 

I have  placed  Lieutenant  Sheldon,  of  my  staff,  in  command  of  the 
two  companies  in  this  place,  but  I cannot  long  spare  him  from  his 
proper  duties,  and  there  are  still  three  companies  at  other  posts,  and  it 
is  beyond  my  power  to  prevent  their  acts  of  robbery  if  I make  any  use 
ff  them.  No  doubt  there  are  some  good  men  in  this  battalion,  but  as 
i class  they  are  well-mounted  and  well-armed  barbarians. 

I am  told  there  is  at  Benton  Barracks  a considerable  force  of  good 
mounted  men  without  arms.  I therefore  urgently  request  that  a bat- 
talion of  them  be  sent  to  me  without  arms  or  horses,  and  that  I be 
authorized  to  dismount  and  disarm  Major  Hollands  battalion  and  send 
t to  Saint  Louis.  If  something  of  the  kind  is  not  done  soon  there  will 
i)e  very  few  Union  men  in  this  part  of  the  State. 

I will  as  soon  as  possible  forward  charges  against  Major  Hollan, 
Dap  tain  Winkel,  and  the  men  I have  arrested. 

I am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  M.  SCHOFIELD, 
Brigadier- General,  U.  S.  Volunteers.

and  also  in  turning  and  maneuvering  in  action,  and  I regret  to  inform 
you  that  her  speed  did  not,  in  the  judgment  of  Commanders  Pennock 
and  Stembel,  who  I appointed  to  make  this  trial,  exceed  2£  knots  per

that  these  gentlemen  came  to  the  conclusion  that  she  is  altogether  too 
deficient  in  steam  power  to  be  considered  at  all  available  as  a gunboat 
without  a heavier  engine.  Under  these  circumstances  I do  not  feel 
authorized  to  accept  the  Benton  without  having  further  direction  from 
you,  as  the  vessel,  with  her  present  engine,  could  not  be  handled  near 
the  rebel  batteries  at  all  effectively. 

The  Benton  is  so  strong  a boat,  well  plated,  and  with  so  large  a bat- 
tery, that  I concur  most  heartily  with  those  two  gentlemen  in  strongly 
recommending  that  a new  engine  and  boilers  be  placed  in  her  imme- 
diately. 

The  seven  gunboats  built  by  contract  I have  accepted,  after  an  ex- 
amination of  the  vessels  and  contract  by  Commanders  Pennock  and 
Stembel,  and  will  commission  them  to-morrow,  although  some  work  yet 
requires  to  be  done  before  they  are  fully  completed. 

I respectfully  call  your  attention  to  a former  letter,  in  which  I re- 
quested instructions  about  the  mortar  boats,  all  of  which  are  here ; but 
their  magazines  leak  badly,  and  I learn  from  Colonel  Symington  that 
but  one  mortar  and  no  beds  are  now  prepared  in  Pittsburg,  the  mor- 
tars and  beds  which  were  originally  designed  for  these  mortar  boats 
having  been  transferred  to  New  York. 

The  report  of  Commanders  Pennock  and  Stembel  will  be  forwarded 
to-morrow.

Washington , January  17,  1862. 

Maj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halleck, 

Commanding  Department  of  Missouri , Saint  Louis , Mo. : 

General  : I am  instructed  by  the  Commanding  General  to  acknowl- 
edge the  receipt  of  the  report  of  the  Board  of  Army  and  Navy  Officers 
ordered  by  you  to  examine  into  the  condition  of  the  gun,  tug,  and 
mortar  boats  destined  for  service  in  the  Western  waters. 

From  the  information  received  from  the  Navy  Department  it  appears 
that  the  efficiency  of  a large  portion  of  the  flotilla  is  destroyed  by  the 
want  of  crews  (gunners).  Efforts  have  been  made  for  some  time  past 
to  ship  the  men  required,  but  these  efforts  have  entirely  failed,  and  at,

this  late  hour  it  becomes  necessary  to  resort  to  other  means  to  utilize 
the  great  expense  that  has  been  already  incurred.  The  flotilla,  together 
with  the  naval  offlcers  on  duty  with  it,  is  completely  under  your  orders, 
and  it  is  expected  that  you  will  devise  the  means  of  overcoming  the  i 
obstacles  that  have  presented  themselves.  It  will  be  more  economical, ; 
and  it  seems  quite  proper,  to  use  volunteer  troops  to  supply  the  defi- 
ciencies in  the  gunners,  and  it  is  suggested  that  if  there  is  any  difficulty 
from  a surplus  of  officers  one  remedy  would  be  to  detail  a portion  of , 
the  volunteer  officers  on  other  duty,  while  a portion  of  the  uninstructed 
officers  hired  by  the  Navy  might  also  be  discharged.  . 

Your  early  attention  is  called  to  this  subject,  and  it  is  expected  thati 
some  means  will  be  devised  to  render  the  flotilla  efficient  at  a very 
earlv  day.  The  matter  is  placed  in  your  hands,  and  it  is  thought  that 
a full  interchange  of  views  between  Commodore  Foote  and  yourself 

will  result  in  a solution  of  the  difficulty.  . 

Your  views  as  to  the  best  employment  of  the  flotilla  are  invited.

Headquarters  Department  of  the  Missouri, 

Saint  Louis , January  18,  1862. 

Brig.  Gen.  Lorenzo  Thomas, 

Adjutant- General  of  the  Army , Washington : 

General  : I inclose  herewith  a copy  of  a letter  from  Colonel  Steele, 
3ommanding  at  Sedalia,  in  relation  to  depredations  committed  by 
Jennison’s  men  in  Western  Missouri.  Similar  accounts  are  received  of 
:he  conduct  of  the  First  Kansas  Kegiment  along  the  Missouri  Kiver,  in 
;he  counties  of  La  Fayette  and  Jackson. 

These  men  do  not  belong  to  this  department,  and  have  no  business 
o come  within  the  State.  I have  directed  General  Pope  to  drive  them 
rat,  or,  if  they  resist,  to  disarm  them  and  hold  them  prisoners.  They 
ire  no  better  than  a band  of  robbers  ; they  cross  the  line,  rob,  steal, 
)lunder,  and  burn  whatever  they  can  lay  their  hands  upon.  They  dis- 
grace the  name  and  uniform  of  American  soldiers  and  are  driving  good 
Jnion  men  into  the  ranks  of  the  secession  army.  Their  conduct  within 
he  last  six  months  has  caused  a change  of  20,000  votes  in  this  State, 
f the  Government  countenances  such  acts  by  screening  the  perpe- 
rators  from  justice  and  by  rewarding  with  office  their  leaders  and 
tbettors  it  may  resign  all  hopes  of  a pacification  of  Missouri.  If  Kan- 
as  troops  are  again  permitted  to  come  into  this  State  to  commit  depu- 
tations, the  State  can  be  held  only  by  the  strong  arm  of  military  power, 
ffie  bitter  animosity  created  against  these  troops  is  naturally  trans- 
erred  to  the  Government  which  supports  them  and  in  whose  name 
hey  pretend  to  act. 

I hope  this  matter  will  be  brought  to  the  attention  of  the  Secretary 
f War  and  the  Commanding  General  of  the  Army. 

Yery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLECK, 

Major-General.

I have  received  no  information  in  respect  to  the  general  plan  of  cam- 
>aign,  and  I therefore  feel  much  hesitation  in  recommending  any  line  of 
derations  for  these  and  other  troops  which  I may  be  able  to  withdraw 
rom  Missouri.  Of  course  this  line  must  be  subordinate  to  some  general 
)lan.  I take  it  for  granted,  general,  that  what  has  heretofore  been  done 
las  been  the  result  of  political  policy  rather  than  military  strategy,  and 
hat  the  want  of  success  on  our  part  is  attributable  to  the  politicians 
•ather  than  to  the  generals. 

So  far  it  seems  to  me  the  war  has  been  conducted  upon  what  may  be 
-ailed  pepper-box  strategy — scattering  our  troops  so  as  to  render  them 
nferior  in  numbers  in  any  place  where  they  can  meet  the  enemy.  Oc- 
upying  the  circumference  of  a great  circle,  with  the  enemy  within  that 
ircumference  and  near  the  center,  we  cannot  expect  to  strike  any 
treat  blow,  for  he  can  concentrate  his  forces  on  any  one  point  sooner 
han  we  can  ours.  The  division  of  our  force  upon  so  many  lines  and 
>oints  seems  to  me  a fatal  policy.  I am  aware  that  you,  general,  are 
n no  way  responsible  for  this,  these  movements  having  been  governed 
>y  political  expediency  and  in  many  cases  directed  by  politicians  in 
rder  to  subserve  particular  interests ; but  is  it  not  possible  with  the 
tew  Secretary  of  War  to  introduce  a different  policy  and  to  make  our 
uture  movements  in  accordance  with  military  principles'?  On  this  sup- 
>osition  I venture  to  make  a few  suggestions  in  regard  to  operations  in 
he  West. 

The  idea  of  moving  down  the  Mississippi  by  steam  is,  in  my  opinion, 
mpracticable,  or  at  least  premature.  It  is  not  a proper  line  of  opera- 
ions,  at  least  now.  A much  more  feasible  plan  is  to  move  up  the 
Cumberland  and  Tennessee,  making  Nashville  the  first  objective  point. 
Ckis  would  turn  Columbus  and  force  the  abandonment  of  Bowling 
Ireen.  Columbus  cannot  be  taken  without  an  immense  siege  train 
11  d a terrible  loss  of  life.  I have  thoroughly  studied  its  defenses; 
hey  are  very  strong.  But  it  can  be  turned,  paralyzed,  and  forced  to 
urrender.  This  line  of  the  Cumberland  or  Tennessee  is  the  great 
entral  line  of  the  Western  theater  of  war,  with  the  Ohio  below  the 
aouth  of  Green  Biver  as  the  base  and  two  good  navigable  rivers 
xtending  far  into  the  interior  of  the  theater  of  operations.  But  the 
>lan  should  not  be  attempted  without  a large  force,  not  less  than 
0,000  effective  men.

These  suggestions  are  hastily  written  out,  but  they  are  the  result  of 
much  anxious  inquiry  and  mature  deliberation.  I am  confident  that 
the  plan,  if  properly  carried  out,  would  produce  important  results.  I 
also  believe  it  to  be  feasible. 

I have  not  designated  any  particular  line  or  lines  of  movement. 
That  must  be  a matter  of  further  study  if  the  general  idea  should  be 
approved.  Perhaps  the  main  column  should  move  from  Smithland. 
between  the  rivers,  by  Dover,  &c.  Perhaps  the  line  east  of  the  Cum- 
berland or  that  west  of  the  Tennessee  would  be  preferable.  These* 
questions,  however,  are  matters  easily  determinable. 

I have  been  sick  for  more  than  a week  with  the  measles,  and  several 
members  of  my  staff  are  unable  to  attend  to  any  duty.  Under  these 
aircumstances  some  delay  must  occur  in  answering  the  communications, 
from  the  Adjutant-General  of  the  Army. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLECK, 

Major-  General.

I must  call  your  attention  to  certain  irregularities.  Your  dissolution

composing  the  court  are  ordered  into  the  field  the  court  ceases  to  act  as 
ucli,  but  it  cannot  be  dissolved  or  the  prisoners  released  except  by 
he  authority  ordering  it. 

Again,  your  Special  Orders,  No.  41,  ordering  men  from  General  Sher- 
.nan’s  command,  is  entirely  irregular.  You  cannot  give  any  orders  to 
roops  at  Benton  Barracks.  You  should  have  made  a requisition  on 
ne  for  the  corporal  and  men  wanted.  These  may  appear  small  mat- 
ers, but  they  create  difficulties  and  annoyances  which  it  takes  much 
>i  my  time  to  arrange.  It  is  just  as  easy  to  follow  the  law  and  regula- 
10ns  as  it  is  to  violate  them. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLECK,

>en  warfare,  or,  if  we  capture  them,  we  shall  treat  them  as  prisoners 
f war. 

But  it  is  well  understood  that  you  have  sent  numbers  of  your  adher- 
its,  in  the  garb  of  peaceful  citizens  and  under  false  pretenses,  through 
ir  lines  into  Northern  Missouri,  to  rob  and  destroy  the  property  of 
nion  men  and  to  burn  and  destroy  railroad  bridges,  thus  endangering 
le  lives  of  thousands,  and  this,  too,  without  any  military  necessity  or 
)ssible  military  advantage.  Moreover,  peaceful  citizens  of  Missouri, 
lietly  working  on  their  farms,  have  been  instigated  by  your  emis- 
iries  to  take  up  arms  as  insurgents,  and  to  rob  and  plunder  and  to 
>mmit  arson  and  murder.  They  do  not  even  act  under  the  garb  of 
•ldiers,  but  under  false  pretenses  and  in  the  guise  of  peaceful  citizens, 
ou  certainly  will  not  pretend  that  men  guilty  of  such  crimes,  although 
specially  appointed  and  instructed  by  you,”  are  entitled  to  the  rights 
id  immunities  of  ordinary  prisoners  of  war.  If  you  do,  will  you  refer 
e to  a single  authority  on  the  laws  of  war  which  recognizes  such  a 
aim  ? 

You  may  rest  assured,  general,  that  all  prisoners  of  war  not  guilty 
‘ crime  will  be  treated  with  all  proper  consideration  and  kindness, 
ith  the  exception  of  being  properly  confined,  they  will  be  lodged 
id  fed,  and  where  necessary  clothed,  the  same  as  our  own  troops.  1 
a sorry  to  say  that  our  prisoners  who  have  come  from  your  camps 
> not  report  such  treatment  on  your  part.  They  say  that  you  gave 
em  no  rations,  no  clothing,  no  blankets,  but  left  them  to  perish  with 
ant  and  cold.  Moreover,  it  is  believed  that  you  subsist  your  troops 
t robbing  and  plundering  the  non-combatant  Union  inhabitants  of 
e southwestern  counties  of  this  State.  Thousands  of  poor  families 
ive  fled  to  us  for  protection  and  support.  They  say  that  your  troops 
bbed  them  of  their  provisions  and  clothing,  carrying  away  their  shoes 
id  bedding,  and  even  cutting  cloth  from  their  looms,  and  that  you 
ive  driven  women  and  children  from  their  homes  to  starve  and  perish 
the  cold.  I have  not  retaliated  such  conduct  upon  your  adherents 
kre,  as  I have  no  intention  of  waging  such  a barbarous  warfare ; but 
shall,  whenever  I can,  punish  such  crimes,  by  whomsoever  they  may 
J committed. 

I am  daily  expecting  instructions  respecting  an  exchange  of  prison- 
's of  war.  I will  communicate  with  you  on  that  subject  as  soon  as 
ey  are  received.

Headquarters  District  Central  Missouri, 

Otterville , January  23,  1862. 

aj.  Gen.  H.  W.  Halle ck, 

Commanding  Department  of  the  Missouri , Saint  Louis , Mo. : 
General  : I have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your 
tter  of  the  22d  instant.*  The  Second  Division  marches  to-morrow 
orning  for  Linn  Creek.  I fear  there  is  a mistake  about  fords  near  that 
ace  which  can  be  crossed  at  any  season.  Any  ford  over  3 feet  in 
pth  will  render  the  passage  of  wagons  loaded  with  baggage  or  sup- 
ies  impracticable  without  great  difficulty.  No  doubt  Colonel  Davis 
II  find  means  to  cross,  but  it  will  require  time. 

Before  receiving  your  letter  I had  directed  a scout  to  be  made  in  the 
rection  of  Lexington  and  Waverly.  I have  sent  nine  companies  of 
valry  and  a section  of  artillery  to  go  to  the  neighborhood  of  Lexing- 
n,  thence  to  Waverly,  thence  to  Arrow  Eock,  and  from  the  latter  place 
return  direct  to  Sedalia.  The  expedition  will  be  absent  about  eight 
ys. 

I receive  frequent  letters  from  Glasgow  in  relation  to  posting  troops 
that  place.  Unless  the  system  of  occupying  every  considerable  or 
I considerable  towrn  in  the  State  is  to  be  adopted  I do  not  see  that 
'asgow  has  any  claims  not  advanced  by  Lexington,  Booneville,  &c. 
jlasgow  is  important  in  some  respects  as  a military  position,  but  1 
ink  not  as  much  so  as  Brunswick.  As  neither  place,  however,  is 
thin  the  limits  of  my  command,  I can  only  refer  the  matter  for  your 
nsideration. 

Posting  troops  in  the  towns  has  very  much  the  same  effect  as  issuing 
; gar  and  coffee  to  Dutch  and  Irish  soldiers : what  they  never  felt  the 
int  of  before  immediately  becomes  a necessity,  and  cannot  possibly 
dispensed  with.  Once  station  troops  in  these  towns  and  it  becomes 
arly  impossible  to  get  them  away  for  any  service  without  great  clamor 
>m  the  inhabitants,  who  profit  in  more  ways  than  protection  from  their 
i-esence. 

I am,  general,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JNO.  POPE, 

Brigadier- General , Commanding.

County,  of  which  the  inclosed  is  a copy.*  J 

You  will  immediately  proceed  to  Sidney,  in  said  county,  and  fully  n 
vestigate  the  matters  therein  set  forth.  Consult  Judge  Sears  and  Co 
onel  Hedges,  and  if  you  shall  be  satisfied  the  preservation  of  the  publi 
peace  so  requires,  call  into  the  service  such  ot  the  volunteer  companic 
of  the  county  as  may  be  necessary  to  that  end  and  keep  them  in  sen 
ice  as  long  as  their  services  may  be  required.  If,  in  your  judgment, 
shall  be  necessary  to  call  out  any  military  force,  make  them  call  1m 
upon  the  company  at  Sidney.  = 

Call  for  no  more  troops  than  in  your  best  judgment  will  be  nece 
sary  and  keep  them  in  service  only  so  long  as  may  be  necessary.  1 
this  matter  1 must  trust  to  your  discretion,  and  I will  hold  you  respoi 
sible  for  its  sound  exercise.  Procure  proper  quarters  for  such  troaf 
as  vou  may  call  out  and  make  the  best  arrangements  you  can  lor  the 
subsistence.  You  must  make  all  your  arrangements  as  economical]

s possible.  No  extravagant  charges  for  quarters  or  subsistence  will 
e allowed. 

You  will  preserve  the  public  peace  and  protect  the  prisoners  at  all 
azards. 

I desire  full  information  on  the  following  points : 

I.  Have  rebels  or  rebel  sympathizers  from  Missouri  come  into  Fremont 
bounty,  bringing  with  them  their  property,  or  have  such  persons  sent 
heir  property  from  Missouri  into  the  county  ? If  so,  give  the  names  of 
uch  persons,  a description  of  the  property  brought  or  sent,  and  the 
ames  of  the  persons,  if  any,  of  our  own  citizens  who  have  such  prop- 
rty  in  possession. 

II.  Does  the  bringing  or  sending  of  the  property  of  such  persons  into 
he  county  tend  to  endanger  the  public  peace 

III.  I desire  a full  detail  of  all  the  facts  connected  with  the  attack 
n Mr.  Fugitt  and  of  the  capture  of  those  under  arrest  with  the  causes 
f all  the  acts  done,  so  far  as  you  can  ascertain  them. 

IY.  It  has  been  stated  to  me  that  one  or  two  persons,  supposed  to 
.e  of  the  party  that  attacked  Mr.  Fugitt,  were  shot  by  some  of  our  citi- 
ens  near  Hamburg  upon  refusal  to  surrender.  You  will  investigate 
he  facts  of  this  transaction  and  report  to  me  fully  thereon.  I am 
etermined  to  preserve  the  peace  of  our  State  and  to  protect  the  prop- 
rty  of  our  citizens,  but  I am  also  determined  that  our  State  shall  not 
>e  made  an  asylum  for  rebels  who  have  been  compelled  to  flee  from 
heir  own  State  in  consequence  of  their  outrages  on  Union  men  there, 
f affording  such  asylum  is  to  peril  the  peace  of  our  own  people.  I 
m also  determined  that  those  of  our  own  citizens  who  sympathize 
vith  and  protect  these  fleeing  rebels  shall  not  make  the  consequences 
*f  their  own  acts  the  pretext  for  a breach  of  the  public  peace. 

The  peace  must  be  preserved,  and  those  persons  afforded  full  pro- 
motion and  a fair  and  impartial  trial. 

You  will  report  to  me  in  writing  as  soon  as  possible,  and  keep  me 
id  vised  at  intervals  of  the  situation  of  affairs. 

Yery  respectfully, 

SAMUEL  J.  KIRKWOOD.

Ion.  Samuel  J.  Kirkwood, 

Governor  of  Iowa , Des  Moines : 

Sir:  I received  your  letter,  dated  January  8,  1862,  inclosing  a com- 
nunication  from  citizens  of  Fremont  County,  and  in  accordance  with 
rour  instructions  I proceeded  on  to  Sidney  on  the  morning  of  the  13th 
nstant,  for  the  purpose  of  carrying  out  said  instructions,  and  have  to 
•eport  my  action  as  follows : 

I found  the  statements  contained  in  the  communication  above  referred 
o to  be  true  in  all  material  points.  I will  answer  the  four  interroga- 
ions  propounded  in  your  letter  in  order : 

1st.  Yes.  Rebels  to  the  number  of  thirty  families,  at  least,  with  a 
arge  amount  of  horses,  mules,  cattle,  hogs,  &c.,  have  left  Missouri, 
;ame  into  Fremont  County,  and  many  of  the  same  class  have  sent  their 
property  who  have  not  come  into  this  State  themselves.  These  per- 
sons have  come  themselves  or  sent  their  property  to  save  the  same 
rom  seizure  by  the  Government  that  they  have  outraged  for  the  past 
rear.  1 was  able  to  find  the  whereabouts  and  names  of  but  a portion 
if  these  persons,  but  such  as  I have  found  I append  below,  and  will
