give  you  further  information  upon  this  point  at  an  early  day.  The 
parties  named  below  are  all  either  rank  secessionists  or  rebel  sympa- 
thizers, and  I will  make  no  distinction  between  them.  It  is  enough  to 
know  that  they  are  “ not  with  us”— are  not  Union  men. 

Mr.  John  Pugh  has  5 horses,  owned  in  Missouri  5 owner’s  name  un- 
known. Mr.  Preeman  has  2 horses;  owner  unknown.  Mr.  Baldwin 
has  2 horses;  owner  unknown.  H.  G.  Bowen  has  15  horses  and  mules, 
owned  by  Nichols  and  Schouler.  Nichols  lives  at  Saint  Stevens,  Nebr.,. 
and  has  furnished  the  rebels  in  North  Missouri  with  arms,  and  is  a 
prominent  rebel.  Milton  McOartners  has  8 or  10  horses  and  mules ; 
owner  unknown.  Mr.  Welty  has  8 or  10  horses  and  mules,  owned  by 
Mr.  Holland,  who  lives  near  Bockport.  The  Heatt  brothers  have  0 
horses,  60  hogs,  and  25  or  30  cattle;  owners’  names  unknown.  They 
had  consulted  Mr.  Cornish  as  to  whether  they  could  lawfully  keep 
stock  which  belonged  to  secessionists  in  Missouri,  for  if  they  could  they 
could  make  d large  amount  of  money  by  so  doing,  as  the  secesh  were 
willing  to  pay  high  prices.  These  men  (Heatt)  have  6 horses,  ownedi 
by  one  Hall,  who  left  Missouri  in  the  night  to  save  his  property.  Mr.  1 
Hollaway  brought  25  horses  and  mules  into  this  State,  and  has  theml 
scattered  around  at  several  places.  Mr.  Davis  has  8 horses,  belonging!! 
to  a man  in  Bockport,  name  unknown;  can  be  found  and  identified,  as 
he  is  well  known  in  Iowa.  Mr.  English  (senator),  some  three  weeks  j 
ago,  went  to  Missouri  and  brought  the  personal  property  of  one  Poin-  < 
dexter,  either  the  officer  in  Price’s  army  or  a brother ; at  all  events  a 
rabid  rebel,  and  it  is  reported  and  believed  in  Sidney  that  Poindexter! 
himself  is  about  McKinsock’s  Grove.  Mr.  English  has  a horse  belong- 1 
ing  to  Poindexter  now  in  his  possession,  but  has  sent  him  away  from 
his  own  farm  to  a brother-in-law’s  for  fear  of  jayhawking. 

The  above  property  has  all  of  it  been  sent  from  Missouri  to  avoid 
seizure  and  confiscation  by  the  Government.  There  have  also  been, 
horses  sent  from  Missouri  lately  by  rebels  who  dared  not  leave  their  > 
goods  in  Fremont  County,  and  one  lot  of  40  went  on,  the  man  saying  he 
was  too  near  home  in  Fremont.  I think  that  there  are  at  the  present 
time  100  to  125  horses  in  Fremont  County,  brought  there  by  rebels  to 
save  them.  Many  place  the  number  much  higher,  but  from  all  my 
information  I place  the  number  asabove. 

In  reply  to  your  second  question,  I will  say  that  by  these  acts  I 
think  the*  public  peace  is  endangered,  and  I find  all  the  Union  men  in 
Fremont  are  very  certain  it  does,  and  say  that  unless  it  is  stopped 
bloodshed  will  be  the  result.  My  reasons  for  thinking  that  it  does  en- 
danger the  public  peace  are  that  there  is  great  danger  of  this  property 
being  pursued  by  jayhawkers  and  others,  which  would  be  almost  cer- , 
tain  to  bring  on  a collision  and  bloodshed.  Second,  the  accession  of 
these  rebels  to  the  number  of  the  same  kind  and  their  sympathizers  in 
Fremont  County  increases  the  bitter  feelings  between  the  two  parties, 
and  which  now  requires  but  a word  to  bring  on  a civil  strife  in  that 
county.  As  a sample,  one  John  Cooper,  of  McKinsock’s  Grove,  has, 
he  says,  25  Missouri  friends  with  him,  and  he  will  keep  them  there  as 
long  as  they  will  stay;  that  they  are  well  armed,  and  will  shoot  the  first 
man  who  tries  to  arrest  any  of  their  number  or  seize  a horse. 

Questions  3 and  4 1 will  answer  together.  On  the  night  of  December 
30  a body  of  armed  men  from  Missouri  and  Nebraska,  under  Capt.’ 
Warren  Price,  who  is  said  to  be  the  leader  of  a band  of  jayhawkers,

pose, as  they  avowed  on  their  way,  of  seizing  some  horses  which  had 
been  taken  from  Missouri  and  owned  by  rebels  in  Missouri.  Several  of

The  Union  men  of  Missouri  say  that  all  the  party  who  went  into 
Missouri  were  secessionists,  and  that  Iowa  allows  rebels  to  flee  into  her 
State  to  avoid  punishment,  and  then  allows  secessionists  to  come  to 
Missouri  and  arrest  Union  men  without  a shadow  of  law  or  right.  1 
was  able  to  disabuse  them  of  this  idea,  or  at  least  all  I had  a chance  to 


talk  with.  _ . . 

This  feeling  is  particularly  bitter  between  Union  men  m Missouri 
and  the  secesh  sympathizers  in  McKinsock’s  Grove,  who  are  nearly  all 
that  kind,  and  being  so  near  the  line  increases  the  danger  ot  collision. 
An  armed  guard  is  kept  out  now  in  many  neighborhoods  to  warn  them 
of  approach  of  enemies.  I find,  further,  that  many  men  who  have  been 
avowed  rebels  and  hooted  at  all  soldiers  as  Lincoln  thieves  are  now 
very  clamorous  for  armed  protection,  and  now  there  is  organized  a com- 
pany which  has  memorialized  you  for  commissions  and  arms  that  are 

not  safe  to  arm.  , , , . 

The  board  of  supervisors  of  Fremont  are  secesh,  and  they,  at  then 
last  meeting,  passed  a resolution  instructing  their  chairmen,  Mr.  Sipple 
and  Mr.  Cornish,  to  transmit  to  you  what  they  wanted.  They  got  Mr. 
Cornish  in  to  have  some  Union  influence.  The  chairman  of  supervisors 
proposed  a paper  which  did  not  suit  Cornish,  and  he  refused  to  sign  it. 
Sipple  then  proposed  another,  which  he  would  not  show  Cornish,  and 
sent  the  same  to  you.  It  is  supposed  to  be  a request  to  commission, 
arm,  and  call  in  service  their  men  at  McKinsock’s  Grove.  They  are 
not  the  men  to  have  State  arms.  I also  telegraphed  you  not  to  com- 
mission Fremont  militia.  I found  the  infantry  were  all  good  men,  witn 
sound  Union  officers,  but  the  mounted  company  was  formed  by  Judge 
Rector,  and  is  not  sound.  e _ 

One  officer,  Mr.  Bovine,  has  since  his  election  said  that  he  was  a 
secessionist,  and  he  did  not  care  who  knew  it.  We  want  no  such  men 
with  either  arms  or  authority.  I told  Colonel  Hedges  that  it  should 
be  disbanded  and  an  infantry  company  put  in  its  place,  and  told  him 
that  it  was  not  legally  organized,  and  it  is  not,  as  there  has  been  n 
special  authority  granted,  as  is  necessary,  to  organize  any  but  mtantry. 
I presume  you  will  get  the  organization  of  another  infantry  company 
which  will  make  Colonel  Hedges’  regiment  to  a maximum,  when  it 
should  be  commissioned  at  once.  , A

force  of  State  troops  in  Fremont  County  unless  for  immediate  use. 
They  should  be  commissioned  and  armed  and  ready  to  go  at  an  hour’s 
notice,  but  I think  should  be  called  into  camp  only  as  a last  resort. 

The  best  way  to  preserve  the  peace  and  remove  the  danger  of  collis- 
ion I believe  to  be  in  sending  a small  force  of  Federal  troops,  say  one 
or  two  companies  of  cavalry,  from  Saint  Joe  or  Leavenworth,  under 
some  prudent,  reliable  Union  officer,  and  clothe  him  with  power  to 
arrest  armed  secessionists  either  in  Missouri  or  Iowa  and  seize  their 
effects,  to  be  sent  at  once  to  headquarters  for  adjudication.  This  will 
avoid  increasing  the  personal  hatred  among  the  two  classes  of  our  own 
citizens,  which  would  be  increased  by  arming  and  calling  out  any  State 
troops  either  from  Iowa  or  Missouri,  and  lessen  the  danger  of  blood- 
shed if  any  arrests  are  to  be  made,  and  the  State  troops  would  have 
no  place  to  send  prisoners  even  if  they  have  authority  to  make  arrests. 
I feel  certain  that  calling  out  any  State  troops  would  bring  on  a collis- 
ion, and  the  aim  is  to  preserve  the  peace  more  than  to  conquer  rebels, 
as  I understand  it. 

I am  sustained  in  this  view  by  all  the  Union  men  in  Fremont  except 
Colonel  Hedges,  who  is  very  anxious  to  drill  his  regiment,  but  I would 
prefer  sending  an  armed  force  in  command  of  some  Federal  officer  who* 
would  have  no  personal  enemies  to  deal  with,  and  I think  the  arrest  of 
a very  few  men,  and  the  seizure  of  the  property  belonging  to  rebels,  who 
have  sent  the  same  to  Iowa  for  safety,  will  not  only  quiet  the  present 
troubles,  but  remove  the  danger  of  a recurrence  in  future. 

If  I have  been  lengthy  in  this,  it  is  because  there  was  a good  deal  of 
ground  to  go  over.  I find  that  in  all  facts  I have  stated  the  Union 
men  from  whom  I receive  my  information  are  supported  by  the  state- 
ments of  the  other  side,  so  far  as  1 had  an  opportunity  to  inquire, 
in  all  material  points.  Many  of  the  facts  in  regard  to  Fugitt’s  case 
and  the  prisoners  arrested  were  received  from  one  who  was  with  the 
sheriff,  and  is  called  a secessionist  by  Union  men.  I refer  to  W.  C. 
Sipple.  He  claims  to  be  a good  Union  man  now.  The  Union  men  from 
whom  I received  most  information  were  Judge  Sears,  Colonel  Hedges* 
Mr.  Cornish,  Mr.  Linkinfitter,  Mr.  Warren,  formerly  sheriff,  and  Squire 
Fanner,  who  lives  at  McKinsock’s  Grove,  all  of  whom  agree  upon  the 
case  as  I have  presented  it. 

Since  my  return  I have  received  your  letter  of  14th  instant.  I will 
proceed  at  once  to  Rockport,  and  on  my  return  report  such  other  facts 
as  I may  come  in  possession  of.  In  the  mean  time  I hope  to  receive  fur- 
ther instructions  in  regard  to  an  armed  force  in  Fremont  County. 

I remain,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

H.  C.  NUTT.

Captain  : Advance  of  cavalry  under  Lieutenant- Colonel  Wright  reoc- 
cupied Lebanon  on  22d.  Some  20  rebels  fled.  Lieutenant  Pratt,  First 
Missouri  Cavalry,  in  pursuit ; killed  Capt.  Tom  Craig  in  running  fight

Washington , January  24,  1862. 

Major-General  Hunter,  U.  S.  A., 

Commanding  Department  Kansas , Fort  Leavenworth: 

General  : By  direction  of  the  General-in-Chief  I have  respectfully 
to  inform  you  that  Brig.  Gen.  J.  H.  Lane,  U.  S.  Volunteers,  has  urged 
upon  the  President  and  Secretary  of  War  an  expedition  to  be  conducted 
by  him  from  Fort  Leavenworth  against  the  region  west  of  Missouri  and 
Kansas  [Arkansas].  The  outlines  of  his  plan  were  stated  by  him  to  be 
in  accordance  with  your  own  views.  The  following  force,  with  supplies 
therefor,  has  been  ordered  to  Kansas  to  operate  under  General  Lane: 
Seven  regiments  cavalry,  three  batteries  artillery,  four  regiments  in- 
fantry, and  he  has  been  authorized  also  to  raise  about  8,000  to  10,000 
Kansas  troops  and  to  organize  4,000  Indians. 

The  General-in-Chief,  in  conveying  to  you  this  information,  desires  it 
to  be  understood  that  a command  independent  of  you  is  not  given  to 
General  Lane,  but  he  is  to  operate  to  all  proper  extent  under  your  super- 
vision and  control,  and  if  you  deem  proper  you  may  yourself  command 
the  expedition  which  may'be  undertaken.  Under  these  circumstances 
the  General  will  not  give  you  a formal  leave  according  to  your  applica-

tion,  but  he  authorizes  you  to  absent  yourself  from  your  commaud  for 
twenty  days,  at  your  own  discretion. 

I am,  sir,  &c., 

’ ’ ’ L.  THOMAS,

Hdqrs.  Southwestern  District  of  Missouri, 

Eolla , January  25,  1862. 

Brig*.  Gen.  Franz  Sigel: 

General:  General  Halleck  has  intelligence  which  makes  him  be- 
lieve Price  will  escape  us,  which  of  course  we  have  great  reason  to  fear. 

I cannot,  however,  see  how  he  can  have  later  intelligence  than  mine, 
since  I see  men  every  day  direct  from  Springfield,  and  have  supposed 
by  mv  backward  movement  of  cavalry  I have  quieted  the  nerves  of  the  i 
-enemy  as  to  an  attack. 

We  must  not,  however,  delay  a moment,  and  I leave  to-morrow  tor 
Lebanon,  with  a view  of  procuring  all  I possibly  can  in  the  way  of  sup- 
plies,  watching  the  movements  of  the  enemy,  and  being  ready  for  a final  ii 

^ General  Halleck  thinks  we  best  not  wait  for  Colonel  Davis,  but  allow 
him  to  wait  at  Osage.  We  can  tell  better  when  we  get  in  the  immediate 
presence  of  the  enemy  as  to  the  need  of  that  force,  but  if  occasion  arises 
I wish  you  would  give  the  general  the  benefit  of  your  experience  in  re- 
gard to  the  force  of  Price.  It  always  will  be  underrated  by  our  friends, 
who  are  over-anxious  for  us  to  come  to  their  relief,  and  by  our  enemies, 
who  are  anxious  we  should  not  come  too  strong.  Besides,  his  force  is 
never  in  camp  except  when  a battle  is  anticipated,  when  they  come  m 
from  all  the  hills  and  hollows  of  the  surrounding  country. 

My  object  is  to  have  you  come  on  at  your  earliest  convenience,  and 
move  the  remainder  of  your  forces  at  least  as  far  as  we  can  feed  them 
with  regimental  trains. 

I hope  as  little  as  possible  will  be  made  public  of  our  movement,  as 
the  starting  of  generals  is  more  likely  to  give  the  alarm  to  the  enemy, 
who  I hope  to  keep  ignorant  of  our  purpose  as  long  as  possible  previous 
to  our  concentration  at  Lebanon. 

I hope  Davis  will  not  move  one  way  and  look  the  other.  As  at  pres- 
ent advised  he  should  keep  his  eye  on  a union  with  us  at  Lebanon. 

I am,  general,  very  truly,  your  obedient  servant, 

’ 8 ’ SAML.  R.  CURTIS, 

Brigadier-  General.

Hdqrs.  Southwestern  List.,  en  route  from  Rolla  to  Lebanon , Jfo.  : 

Sir  : I received  the  general’s  letter  of  the  25th  this  evening.  I am 
:ery  glad  he  is  coming  for  many  reasons. 

I inclose  letter  from  Lieutenant- Colonel  Wright,  giving  his  views.* 
Che  lieutenant-colonel  is  evidently  anxious  for  an  advance  to  Spring- 
ield.  As  I previously  have  remarked,  I do  not  believe  in  taking  that 
)lace  (even  if  we  can)  for  the  purpose  of  giving  it  up  again,  and  if  the 
inemy  has  30,000  in  Arkansas  he  will  send  them  to  keep  the  war  out  of 
hat  State,  without  inquiring  whether  Price’s  appointment  is  confirmed 
>r  not.  Meantime,  with  12,000,  all  that  I can  yet  hear  from  at  the  dis- 
posal of  the  general  (perhaps  less),  and  they  far  behind  and  we  far 
way  from  our  supports,  how  can  we  sustain  ourselves,  even  if  we  can 
ake  Springfield. 

In  case  there  are  forces  from  the  north  or  other  supports,  of  which  I 
m not  informed,  it  will  be  different.  I have  ordered  out  a battalion  of 
avalry  to  take  post  at  Bennett’s  Mill,  12  miles  a little  north  of  west  from 
lere,  and  one  on  or  near  the  Osage  Fork,  11  miles  southeast.  This  will 
ontrol  the  sources  of  supply  and  form  a front  of  23  miles,  by  which  I 
iope  we  can  conceal  our  movements  and  make  the  country  tributary. 

I had  already  sent  a company  to  Bennett’s  Mill,  and  have  reports 
hat  it  can  furnish  15,000  pounds  per  day  and  do  the  custom-work.  I 
m afraid  I have  overestimated  the  capacity  of  the  two  mills,  but  hope, 
dtli  the  aid  of  what  we  can  get  from  the  Osage,  to  fill  out  what  I said. 

send  Colonel  Phelps  to  Osage  Fork  with  a few  of  his  men,  mounted. 
Ie  will  talk  with  the  people  and  start  the  system  of  collecting  sup- 
lies,  and  be  able  to  report  to  the  general  on  Tuesday. 

Colonel  Osterhaus  had  a fine  brigade  drill  to-day,"  but  discipline  is 
till  very  bad.  As  relates  to  plundering,  it  will  be  very  disagreeable 
o the  general  to  use  the  necessary  means  to  stop  it,  but  I hope  he  will 

0 so,  as  I feel  it  a disgrace  to  myself  to  be  connected  with  people  who 
ommit  such  crimes  as  some  of  these. 

1 will  make  the  best  arrangements  I can  to  find  quarters  for  the  gen- 
ral  and  his  staff,  but  they  must  not  expect  the  luxuries  of  Rolla. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  A.  CARR,

Saint  Louis,  January  27,  1862.  ■ 

Brigadier- General  Pope, 

Commanding , Otterville , Mo. : 

General:  Yours  of  the  24th  is  received.  I approve  all  your  dispo- 
sitions, except  that  I do  not  see  that  any  garrison  is  provided  tor  Lex- 
ington. I think  that  should  be  occupied,  at  least  for  the  present.  1 
had  hoped  that  the  detachment  of  our  troops  in  Kansas  would  arrives 
there  by  the  time  the  Kansas  regiment  left.  General  Denver  assured 
me  that  they  had  been  ordered  back  while  he  was  at  Leavenworth,  but 
I can  hear  nothing  of  them. 

If  General  Curtis  can  dispense  with  Davis’  division  it  will  marcn  to 
Jefferson  City,  and  be  sent  south  if  the  condition  of  the  country  should 
then  admit  of  their  withdrawal.  In  regard  to  yourself,  general,  per- 
haps it  will  be  best  for  you  to  remain  in  charge  of  the  district  till  it  is 
fully  organized,  as  you  can  readily  rejoin  the  division  brought  here  or 
when  it  reaches  its  destination.  You  will  certainly  have  a suitable 
command  if  I can  give  it  to  you. 

Accounts  from  Washington  indicate  that  the  new  furore,  “On  to 
Richmond!”  is  abating.  If  so,  we  will  get  time  to  concentrate  and 
organize  our  forces  for  the  new  campaign.

iring  private  houses,  barns,  mills,  &c.”  I presume  you  refer  to  a 
nd  of  outlaws  on  the  Kansas  frontier.  They  do  not  belong  to  my 
mmand,  and  they  entered  this  department  without  ray  authority. 
) soon  as  I heard  of  their  depredations  I ordered  General  Pope  to 
her  drive  them  out  of  the  State  or  to  disarm  and  confine  them.  Be 
sured,  general,  that  no  acts  of  wanton  spoliation,  such  as  “firing 
ivate  houses,  barns,  mills,  &c.,”  and  “burning  and  destroying  rail- 
id  bridges,  &c.,w  will  be  countenanced  by  me.  On  the  contrary,  I 
opose  to  punish  with  the  utmost  severity  every  act  of  wanton  destruc- 
m of  property,  public  or  private,  and  every  act  of  pillage,  marauding, 
ibery,  and  theft  committed  in  this  department,  no  matter  under  whose 
thority  or  orders  the  guilty  parties  may  have  acted.

Fort  Leavenworth,  January  28,  1862. 


To  our  Great  Father , the  President  of  the  United  States: 


Father  : We  are  told  by  our  friends  that  there  is  some  doubt  as  t 
whether  the  great  war  chief,  General  Lane,  will  command  the  expedi 

tion  to  our  country.  . x , , . , ~ 

Our  object  in  having  this  letter  sent  to  you  is  to  beg  that  Genera 
Lane  be  placed  in  command  of  that  expedition,  as  we  believe  no  war  - 
rior can  place  us  in  possession  of  our  country  again  as  effectually  as  hi 
can.  Our  people  have  heard  of  General  Lane  many  seasons  ago.  ihe 
have  heard  how  with  but  a handful  of  warriors  he  beat  back  the  enem 
when  they  were  as  numerous  as  the  leaves  of  the  forest  and  restorer 

peace  and  quiet  to  Kansas.  I 

Our  people  have  been  told  that  he  would  come  with  an  army  to  ro 
store  them  to  their  homes  and  to  avenge  the  great  wrongs  they  hav 
suffered. 

It  has  made  their  hearts  glad  to  hear  it. 

Our  people  have  suffered  a great  deal.  They  have  been  driven  froi 
their  homes  in  the  dead  of  winter  when  the  earth  was  clothed  wit 
white.  Many  of  them  have  frozen  to  death.  All  of  them  have  los 

all  they  possessed.  . _ ^ J 

There  are  now  6,000  women  and  children  m Southern  Kansas  withon 
tents,  but  scantily  clothed,  and  exposed  to  all  the  horrors  of  a sever 

Our  agents  have  done  and  are  now  doing  all  they  can  to  relieve  u: 
but  we  leave  comfortable  homes  in  our  own  country  and  we  wish  t 

be  restored  to  them.  , , _ . , T i • d 

General  Lane  is  our  friend.  His  heart  is  big  for  the  Indian.  11 
will  do  more  for  us  than  any  one  else.  The  hearts  of  our  people  wi 
be  sad  if  he  does  not  come.  They  will  follow  him  wherever  he  direct; 
They  will  sweep  the  rebels  before  them  like  a terrible  fire  on  the  dr 

HT/HTlP  I 

We  beg  our  Great  Father  and  our  great  war  chief,  General  M< 
Clellan.  that  they  will  listen  to  the  prayers  of  their  children.

Head  Chief  of  the  Creek  Nation.

Cairo,  January  28,  1862. 
iiartermaster-General  M.  C.  Meigs,  U.  S.  A. : 

General  : Since  forwarding  my  report  to  you  that  I had  accepted 
e seven  gunboats  built  by  contract  by  Mr.  Eads,  in  which  was  con- 
ined  a report  of  Commanders  Pennock  and  Stembel  that  the  engines 
the  Benton  were  so  much  wanting  in  power  that  I did  not  feel  au- 
orized  to  accept  her— in  fact  I concurred  in  their  report  and  sugges- 
)ns  to  place  a new  engine  in  her — I have,  however,  since  then,  on  con- 
Ration  with  several  practical  men  and  in  view  of  our  pressing  want 
the  Benton,  come  to  the  conclusion  that  by  raising  the  wheel  of  that 
;ssel  18  inches,  widening  her  buckets,  and  giving  12  inches  more  to  her 
dder  at  the  water’s  surface,  she  will  handle  sufficiently  well  to  answer 
Lr  purpose.  All  this  can  be  done  in  less  than  three  weeks  after  I get 
ithority  to  do  it  and  for  less  than  $2,000,  including  a new  donkey 
igine. 

I have  telegraphed  twice  for  permission  to  accept  the  Benton,  but  as 
e wires  have  been  out  of  order  or  for  some  other  cause  I have  had  no 
iswer. 

Will  you  please  answer  by  telegram  immediately  on  receiving  this, 
we  are  waiting  to  make  a demonstration.

Capt.  J.  0.  Kelton,  Assistant  Adjutant- General : 

Captain  : My  forward  pickets  are  now  located  37  miles  from  Spring 
field,  and  my  scouts  will  continually  approach  much  nearer.  Om 
arrived  during  last  night,  giving  news  direct  from  Springfield.  AL 
was  quiet  there : Price  still  occupying  Mr.  Graves’  house,  and  no  signs^ 
of  running  away.  This  was  Thursday  last,  day  before  yesterday.  1 
I am  in  receipt  of  the  general’s  letter  of  the  27  th,  expressing  the  belie 
that  Price  will  not  fight,  but  retreat,  and  urging  the  return  of  Davis 
division  before  his  crossing  the  Osage  at  Linn  Creek. 

I cannot  go  on  the  presumption  that  an  enemy  that  has  heretoion 
so  successfully  fought  and  held  Springfield  will  not  fight  for  it  now 
although  I think  also,  in  the  fear  of  a superior  force,  he  may  retreat.  I 
I have  now  in  this  vicinity  about  6,000  men,  and  I am  sorry  to  heai 
that  my  orders  to  move  all  forward  from  Bolla  has  not  started  th< 
remainder  of  General  Asboth’s  and  Sigel’s  divisions  before  yesterday 
Other  forces  which  the  general  had  ordered  had  not  yet  arrived  a 
that  point.  At  present,  therefore,  the  Davis  division  is  nearer,  and  i 
he  crosses  the  Osage  he  may  arrive  before  the  Bolla  force.  He  thinks 
it  will  take  two  days  to  cross  it  now ; I think  at  least  three,  it,  then 
he  stays  on  the  north  side,  he  is  less  accessible  than  at  Bolla.  As  noT 
situated,  I cannot  decide  that  his  force  is  not  “absolutely  necessary o 
but  on  the  contrary  I think  it  is.  As  fast  as  my  force  and  supplier 
will  permit  I shall  press  closer  on  the  enemy ; but  I cannot  draw  my^ 
self  into  a general  battle  till  I get  more  force,  and  for  active  recon 
naissance  and  supply  gathering  I am  overworking  the  1,366  cavalry 

which  is  all  I have  in  my  command.  , „ ^ I 

The  supply  trains  that  started  about  the  24th  from  Bolla  are  not 
beginning  to  arrive,  and  as  fast  as  unloaded  many  will  return  to  kei] 
forward  other  troops.  They  are  getting  on  quite  as  well  as  I expectet 
during  the  worst  of  weather.  I wish  the  Bolla  troops  had  started,  a 
ordered,  about  the  6th;  they  would  have  got  to  this  point  by  this  turn 
I find  the  men’s  shoes  so  miserable,  they  have  worn  them  entirei, 
out  in  six  days’  marching.  Some  of  my  force,  too,  are  so  improviden 
I have  to  constantly  order  and  watch  these  items  of  necessity  to  kee] 
them  fit  to  move,  it  is  peculiar  to  our  service  that  officers  seem  to  D 
satisfied  when  they  publish  without  enforcing  the  execution  ot  orders. 

These  little  things  had  been  especially  and  carefully  itemized  by  m 
in  a printed  order,  and  yet  shoes,  cartridges,  haversacks,  and  litti 
necessaries  are  every  day  found  wanting.  . 

But  in  the  main  my  force  is  in  good  health  and  spirits,  and  1 trus 
the  general  will  find  them  giving  a good  account  of  themselves,  t ue. 
contend  with  mud,  water,  and  snow  and  ice  manfully,  and  1 trust  tnej 
will  not  falter  in  the  face  of  a more  active  foe. 

I am,  general,  very  respectfully,  r 

Briaadier- General,  Commanding.

C.  Kelton,  Assistant  Adjutant- G ener al : 

Captain  : Although  I get  very  accurate  reports  of  the  location  of 
e enemy,  it  is  not  easy  to  estimate  his  force.  Colonel  Wright,  whose 
3n  were  in  and  out,  according  to  his  account,  estimates  the  force 
)in  10,000  to  15,000.  Colonel  Phelps,  who  reported  to  me  yesterday, 
timates  it  at  from  20,000  to  25,000,  and  both  these  men  have  similar 
portunities  of  judging.  His  available  force,  in  my  judgment,  is 
,000. 

Of  course  I interrogate  scouts,  deserters,  and  all  kinds  of  witnesses. 
Price  has  called  for  fifteen-day  volunteers.  A large  train,  80  or  90 
igons,  reached  him  with  supplies  from  the  south  last  week.  A large 
t of  mules,  which  were  a few  miles  out,  have  been  drawn  in ; yet 
?ice  and  all  are  quiet  in  Springfield.  This  is  a summary  of  my  latest 
ws  from  the  front.  My  trains  and  troops  are  coming  forward  slowly. 
The  stormy  weather  continues  and  waters  have  been  high.  Some 
isitation  and  delay  in  starting  from  Rolla  has  occurred,  but  at  last

Hdqrs.  Fourth  Division,  Southwestern  Dist.  Mo., 

Camp  Vernon,  February  6,  1862. 

General  Samuel  R.  Curtis, 

Commanding  S.  W.  Dist.,  Department  of  the  Mo. : 

General  : In  connection  with  my  report  of  yesterday,  numbered 
397,*  I have  the  honor  to  state  that  I have  arrived  with  my  whole 
command,  and  am  now  encamped  at  the  eastern  end  of  the  town  of 
Lebanon,  on  the  hills  north  of  the  Waynesville  road. 

Despite  the  overladen  wagons  and  hardly  practicable  roads  and  the 
many  river  crossings,  I occupied  but  six  days  from  the  time  of  my 
departure  from  Rolla  to  that  of  my  arrival  here.  At  the  Little  Piney 
uud  Roubidoux  Rivers  I was  obliged  to  construct  bridges  for  the  in- 
fantry. At  the  Big  Piney  I had  to  unload  the  commissary  train  and 
bring  the  infantry  over  by  wagons.  At  the  Gasconade  they  were 
transported  in  a ferry-boat  of  your  providing. 

The  cavalry,  artillery,  and  trains  everywhere  forded  the  rivers,  with 
the  exception  of  the  Big  Piney,  where  I considered  it  proper  to  transfer 
the  ammunition  to  regulation  wagons. 

My  force  consists  of  the  remainder  of  the  Fourth  Division,  which  I 
had  the  honor  of  commanding  for  the  last  five  months,  viz : The  First 
Brigade  of  Acting  Brigadier-General  Albert,  now  temporarily  com- 
manded by  Colonel  Joliat,  comprising  the  Fifteenth  Missouri  Infantry, 
the  First  Flying  Battery,  and  Company  A of  the  Fourth  Missouri  Cav- 
alry, and  the  Second  Brigade  of  Acting  Brigadier-General  Carr,  tem- 
porarily commanded  by  Colonel  Schaefer,  comprising  the  Second  Mis- 
souri Yolunteers,  Second  Ohio  Battery,  and  a company  of  the  Third 
Illinois  Cavalry.

The  balance  of  the  two  cavalry  regiments  preceded  the  division  upon 
a cavalry  expedition  under  Acting  Brigadier-General  Carr. 

The  First  and  Second  U.  S.  Reserve  Corps  were  left  behind  by  your 
orders  to  guard  the  railroad  beyond  Rolla,  and  two  pioneer  companies, 
under  Captains  Gerster  and  Krausnick,  are  building,  under  directions- 
of  Lieutenant  Hoeppner,  the  bridge  across  the  Gasconade  at  the  mouth 
of  the  Little  Piney  River.  . 

To  restore  the  division  if  not  to  its  original  strength,  as  promised  by 
Generals  Fremont  and  Hunter,  at  least  to  that  numerical  force  with 
which  I conducted  it  from  Springfield  to  Rolla,  I would  respectfully  ask 
that  the  cavalry  here  and  near  Lebanon  be  returned  to  it  and  the  two 
Reserve  Corps  infantry  regiments  replaced  by  others,  and  that  Captain 
Gerster’s  pioneer  company  be  restored  to  the  division,  to  repair  roads 
and  construct  bridges  when  required. 

I left  Rolla  with  85  regulation  teams,  7 two-horse  teams,  5 ambulances,, 
and  2 apothecary  wagons.  Twenty-seven  regulation  teams  wTere  loaded 
with  commissary  supplies.  The  balance  of  the  teams  are  apportioned 
to  the  respective  commands  in  accordance  with  their  numerical  strength. 

As  Captain  McKay,  late  quartermaster  of  the  Fourth  Division,  was 
ordered  to  transfer  more  than  70  six-mule  and  four-horse  Government 
teams  to  the  post  quartermaster  at  Rolla  at  the  beginning  of  January,. 
25  of  the  teams  used  on  the  march  were  ordered  by  the  post  quarter- 
master at  Rolla  from  General  Sigel’s  Third  Division,  and  10  were  given, 
in  accordance  with  your  orders,  by  Colonel  Wyman  from  his  regiment, 
under  my  obligation  to  return  them,  and  in  this  relation  I would  beg 
also  your  orders. 

For  the  troops  with  me  I am  still  provided  with  five  days  rations, 
but  have  no  forage,  and  my  acting  quartermaster,  Captain  Bensberg, 
was  directed  by  the  post  commissary,  Captain  Winslow,  to  collect  forage 
for  himself. 

The  health  of  the  troops  is  remarkably  good  and  they  are  ready  to- 
march  to-morrow,  but  I have  lost  several  horses  and  mules  by  over- 
exertion  and  cold,  and  shall  have  to  replace  them. 

In  closing,  I beg  to  mention  the  zeal,  activity,  and  indefatigable  ex- 
ertions of  both  commanders  of  my  batteries,  Captain  Elbert,  of  the 
First  Flying  Battery,  and  First  Lieutenant  Chapman,  in  command  of 
the  Second  Ohio  Battery.  They  worked  day  and  night,  and  it  is  to- 
heir  merit  that  the  batteries  are  here. 

I am,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

ASBOTH, 

Brigadier- General,  Commanding  Fourth  Division.

Ee  Forty-third  Illinois,  promised  in  the  general's  letter,  and  the  Curtis

ent  the  steamboat  from  Linn  Creek  down  to  Jefferson  City  with  a 
equest  that  General  McKean  would  send  a boat  load  of  commissary 
tores  back  to  Linn  Creek. 


There  are  Home  Guards  enough  to  hold  that  place,  and  supplies 
'ould  be  much  more  accessible  to  this  place  or  Springfield  if  located 
here;  meantime  the  supplies  of  the  country  are  coming  in,  so  that 
ivers  and  bad  roads  are  not  going  to  starve  us  back.  Although  each 
i vision  has  a terrible  narrative  of  trying  events  of  “ flood  and  field" 
n their  way,  our  stock  have  not  broken  down  and  we  have  lost 
othing. 

Some  dysentery  has  broken  out.  I was  right  sick  yesterday  myself, 
ut  I am  well  to-day,  and  the  general  health  and  spirits  of  the  troops 
3ntinue  good.  I am  busy  overhauling  matters— shoeing  horses  and 
lules— expecting  to  resume  the  forward  march  as  early  as  Monday, 
fc  has  again  turned  cold  and  the  roads  are  frozen  quite  solid. 

The  enemy  was  quiet  at  Springfield  at  last  accounts;  probably  re- 
viving some  re-enforcements  from  their  call  for  volunteers  for  twenty 
ays,  but  not  many.

Special  Orders,  ) Hdqrs.  Southwestern  Dist.  of  Mo., 

No.  75.  j Lebanon , Mo.,  February  7,  1862. 

The  commanding  general  tenders  to  the  troops  in  this  command  his 
learty  commendation  for  the  energy  and  endurance  manifested  on  the 
aarch  to  this  place. 

You  have  moved  during  the  coldest  and  most  stormy  period  of  a 
old  winter,  and  so  far  brought  your  trains  and  equipments  through 
now,  mud,  floods,  and  frost  without  his  hearing  of  a murmur  and  with- 
ut  the  loss  of  property  or  men. 

But  the  success  of  this  winter  campaign  now  requires  a further  draught 
n the  patience  and  fortitude  of  this  army.  We  must  strip  for  a forced 
larch  and  final  conflict. 

Six  days’  light  rations  and  necessary  covering  must  be  condensed  in 
special  train,  to  be  ready  for  the  occasion.  This  ration  must  be  hard 
read,  flour,  hominy,  rice,  desiccated  potatoes,  and  mixed  vegetables, 
ugar,  coffee,  and  salt.  Pinole  (ground  parched  corn  and  sugar)  ought 
o be  procured. 

The  commissary  will  provide  on  the  way  whatever  extra  rations  of 
'•esh  pork  and  beef  the  soldiers  may  need,  so  as  to  save  these  trans- 
iorted  rations. 

The  rations  can  only  be  cooked  of  nights,  and  some  beef  should  be 
irked  (dried  over  a slow  fire)  to  carry  in  the  haversack,  to  be  eaten 
dth  pinole.  If  officers  and  men  will  carry  out  this  order  in  good  faith 
hey  will  avoid  danger  of  suffering  and  greatly  enhance  the  efficiency 
f our  force. 

The  camp  equipment,  most  of  the  cooking  utensils,  change  of  cloth- 
i g,  and  most  of  the  tents,  trunks,  and  boxes  must  all  be  left  with  the 
imainder  of  the  regimental  wagons,  which,  with  full  supplies  of  pro- 
isions,  will  be  pressed  forward  by  the  quartermaster  as  fast  as  circum- 
kances  will  allow. 

On  the  forced  march  the  commanding  general  will  limit  himself  to 
lese  restrictions  of  food  and  clothing. 

The  teams  for  this  train  for  the  forced  march  should  be  selected  and 
ich  wagon  not  loaded  over  2,000. 

Thus  arranged,  the  trains  will  be  separated  and  inspected  by  regi- 
tental  officers,  and  the  number  for  each  properly  reported  through  com- 
landers  of  divisions  to  these  headquarters  as  soon  as  completed. 

By  order  of  Brig.  Gen.  S.  B.  Curtis : 

T.  I.  McKENNY, 

Acting  Assistant  Adjutant- General.

Secretary  of  War: 

Sir  : I would  respectfully  submit  to  you  the  following  extracts  taker 
from  the  report  of  Maj.  A.  Baird,  assistant  inspector-general,  TJ.  S 
Army,  on  the  inspection  of  the  Kansas  troops,  viz : 

If  the  practice  of  seizing  and  confiscating  the  private  property  of  rebels,  which  i- 
now  extensively  carried  on  by  the  troops  known  as  Lane’s  brigade,  is  to  be  continued: 
how  may  it  be  managed  so  as  to  prevent  the  troops  being  demoralized  and  the  Lov 

erament  defrauded?  . , , 

The  practice  has  become  so  fixed  and  general  that  I am  convinced  that  orders  arrest- 
ing  it  would  not  be  obeyed,  and  that  the  only  way  of  putting  a stop  to  it  would  be  tc 


remove  the  Kansas  troops  to  some  other  field  of  action. 


The  fact  that  the  property  of  citizens  seized  and  confiscated  by  the 
troops  engaged  in  the  service  of  the  United  States  is  substantiated  bj 
both  official  and  reliable  private  evidence,  and  from  the  frequent  repe 
tition  of  these  acts  the  commanding  officers  in  Kansas  appear  to  hav( 
assumed  its  legality.  The  authority  under  which  it  is  done  is  unknowx 
to  me,  further  than  such  destruction  of  private  property  as  is  unavoid 
able  from  a state  of  war,  conducted  according  to  the  established  usage* 


hap.  XYin.J  CORRESPONDENCE,  ETC. UNION.  55& 

f civilized  nations.  I would  therefore  request  the  policy  of  the  Gov- 
rnment  for  my  guidance  in  dealing  with  questions  of  this  nature. 

To  what  extent  can  the  right  of  confiscation  legally  be  carried,  and 
>y  what  tribunal,  civil  or  military,  are  the  questions  that  will  naturally 
rise  to  be  decided,  that  the  innocent  will  not  suffer  while  punishing 
he  guilty,  and  that  the  dignity  and  justice  of  the  Government  may 
iot  be  atthe  mercy  of  individuals  governed  by  cupidity  or  revenge  t 
?his  question  has  assumed  such  proportions  that  it  will  require  vigor- 
ous means  and  well-defined  authority  to  suppress  or  direct  its  applica- 
ion.

I must  write  you  a very  hasty  answer  to-day.  You  are  entirely  mis 
taken  about  my  having  received  any  information,  official  or  unofficial 
from  Washington  about  the  “great  jayhawking  expedition.”  Fot  a 
word  or  hint  has  been  communicated  to  me.  Orders  were  sent  by  Gen 
•era!  Thomas  direct  to  various  regiments  in  this  department  to  inline

iately  repair  to  Fort  Leavenworth  and  report  to  General  Hunter  as  a 
art  of  General  Lane’s  expedition,  ^o  notice  of  such  orders  was  given 
3 me.  To  put  a stop  to  these  irregularities  I issued  General  Orders, 
To.  8,  and  protested  both  to  General  Thomas  and  General  McClellan 
gainst  such  an  irregular  and  unmilitary  proceeding.  No  reply.  I 
topped  some  of  the  troops  on  their  way,  and  reported  that  they  could 
ot  move  till  some  order  was  sent  to  me.  No  reply. 

I am  satisfied  that  there  have  been  many  of  such  orders  issued 
irectly  by  the  President  and  Secretary  Cameron  without  consulting 
ieneral  McClellan,  and  for  that  reason  no  reply  could  be  given  without 
xposing  the  plans  of  the  great  jayhawker  and  the  imposition  of  him- 
elf  and  Cameron  on  the  President.  Perhaps  this  is  the  key  to  the 
ilence  of  the  authorities  at  Washington.  I know  nothing  on  the  sub- 
let except  what  I see  in  the  newspapers. 

In  regard  to  my  own  plans,  they  are  very  simple.  I have  sent  some 
6,000  or  17,000  men,  under  General  Curtis,  against  Price  at  Spring- 
eld.  He  has  been  re-enforced  by  McIntosh,  and  it  is  said  that  Yan 
)orn  and  Frost  are  also  marching  to  his  relief.  If  it  would  be  possi- 
le  for  you  to  move  a cavalry  force  rapidly  by  Fort  Scott  to  threaten 
‘rice’s  right  flank  it  would  have  a most  excellent  effect.  This  possibly 
as  the  original  intention  of  Lane’s  expedition,  but  I protested  to 
Washington  against  any  of  his  jayhawkers  coming  into  this  depart- 
lent,  and  saying  positively  that  I would  arrest  and  disarm  every  one 
could  catch. 

The  remainder  of  all  my  available  force  will  be  sent  to  the  lines  of 
he  Cumberland  and  Tennessee.  Who  will  take  the  immediate  com- 
land  there  is  not  yet  determined. 

Yours,  in  haste, 

H.  W.  HALLECK.

General  Orders,  ) Hdqrs.  Department  of  the  Missouri, 

No.  39.  ) . Saint  Louis , February  14,  1862.  I 

I.  Information  having  been  received  that  certain  judicial  officers  in 
trusted  with  the  administration  of  the  criminal  laws  and  ordinances  ii 
this  department  have  misunderstood  the  objects  and  purposes  of  th< 
establishment  of  martial  law  in  this  city  of  Saint  Louis,  and  in  conse 
quence  of  such  misunderstanding  have  failed  to  enforce  all  those  lawi 
and  ordinances ; and  as  crimes  and  misdemeanors  should  at  all  times  tx 
strictly  suppressed,  it  is  hereby  enjoined  upon  all  such  civil  officers 
whether  as  judges,  attorneys,  sheriffs,  marshals,  coroners,  clerks,  jus 
tices  of  the  peace,  presiding  officers  of  police  courts,  constables,  o] 
members  of  the  police,  to  strictly  enforce  all  criminal  laws  and  ordi 
nances,  to  have  arrested,  tried,  and  punished  in  the  courts  establishec 
in  the  State,  and  in  the  manner  prescribed  by  the  laws  of  the  State 
all  persons  guilty  of  any  violation  of  such  laws  and  ordinances,  in  tht 
same  manner  as  if  martial  law  had  not  been  declared  to  exist. 

II.  And  it  is  especially  enjoined  upon  the  judge  of  the  Saint  Louif 
criminal  court  to  have  a full  complement  of  grand  jurors  at  every  sk 
ting  of  the  court,  to  strictly  charge  said  grand  jurors  to  diligently  in 
quire  into  ail  crimes  and  misdemeanors  under  the  laws  of  the  Staff 
that  may  come  to  their  knowledge,  and  present  for  trial  such  offender* 
known  to  them.  And  the  assistant  circuit  attorney  for  this  county  k 
particularly  required  to  faithfully  aid  and  assist  the  said  grand  jurors 
and  officers  of  said  court  in  the  discharge  of  their  duties,  and  to  strictly 
perform  all  charges  devolving  upon  him  by  the  laws  of  the  State. 

III.  By  the  establishment  of  martial  law  in  the  city  of  Saint  Louis 
it  is  not  designed  to  interfere  with  or  suspend  the  operation  of  the  laws 
and  ordinances  of  the  State  or  city  with  reference  to  crimes  and  misde 
meanors  nor  the  remedies  and  process  of  the  civil  courts,  except  sc 
far  as  the  interests  of  the  Government  imperatively  require.  The  civil 
authorities  who  attempt  to  interfere  with  the  execution  of  military 
orders  emanating  from  these  headquarters  will  be  punished  for  military 
offense,  but  in  all  other  cases  it  is  their  duty  to  enforce  the  laws  and 
punish  crimes  and  misdemeanors. 

By  order  of  Major-General  Halleck  : 

N.  H.  McLEAN,

nunicipal,  county,  or  town  officers,  every  voter  will  be  required  to  take 
he  oath  of  allegiance  prescribed  in  article  six  of  the  ordinance  of  the 
Convention  dated  October  16,  1861.  Officers  of  the  polls  will  see  to 
he  execution  of  this  order.  If  they  receive  votes  of  persons  not  taking 
he  oath,  they  will  be  arrested  and  tried  for  military  offense  and  the 
•lection  will  be  declared  null  and  void.

ifficers  named  therein,  but  simply  to  point  out  their  duties  during  the

ating Mud  Town,  Ark.,  poisoned  the  provisions  which  they  were  obliged

We  cannot  retaliate  by  adopting  the  same  barbarous  mode  of  war 
fare,  nor  can  we  retaliate  by  punishing  the  innocent  for  the  acts  oi  the 
guilty.  The  laws  of  war  forbid  this.  But  the  same  code  authorizes  us 
to  retaliate  upon  the  guilty  parties.  Any  person  guilty  oi  such  acts, 
when  captured,  will  not  be  treated  as  ordinary  prisoners  ot  war:  tne\ 
will  not  be  shot,  but  will  suffer  the  ignominious  punishment  oi  being 
hung  as  felons.  Moreover,  all  officers  are  in  a measure  responsible  tor 
the  acts  of  the  troops  under  their  command.  Officers  oi  troops  guiltj 
of  such  acts,  although  not  themselves  the  advisers  or  abettors  of  crime, 
will  therefore,  when  captured,  be  put  in  irons,  and  conveyed  as  cnmi

his  army  in  person. 

The  Second  Division,  under  Brig.  Gen.  J.  M.  Palmer,  will  march  on 
Saturday  morning,  the  1st  instant,  and  encamp  5 or  6 miles  north  of 
hkeston,  where  further  instructions  will  be  received. 

Under  no  consideration  will  any  ambulances  or  wagons  be  permitted 
o move  in  the  columns,  except  such  as  are  needed  to  carry  the  neces- 
ary  ammunition. 

Division  trains  of  the  several  divisions  will  move  in  the  rear  of  their 
espective  divisions  in  the  order  in  which  the  brigades  are  posted  in 
he  column.  A sufficient  rear  guard  will  march  in  front  of  the  trains, 
pith  orders  to  prohibit  any  officer  or  soldier  from  passing  to  the  rear 
f the  column,  and  regimental  quartermasters  will  be  held  responsible 
hat  no  one  be  permitted  to  ride  in  the  wagons  except  with  a written 
ertificate  of  the  surgeon  that  he  should  do  so. 

Bear  guards  of  not  less  than  three  companies  of  infantry  will  be 
laced  in  the  rear  of  the  division  trains,  and  mounted  patrols  will  be 
:ept  out  upon  the  flanks  to  prevent  any  straggling  from  the  ranks, 
vith  positive  instructions  to  shoot  down  any  person  belonging  to  the 
rmy  engaged  in  depredation  or  outrages  upon  the  people  of  the 
ountry. 

It  is  enjoined  upon  division,  brigade,  and  regimental  commanders  to 
jive  their  personal  attention  to  the  march  of  their  respective  com- 
aands,  to  see  that  they  are  kept  well  closed,  and  no  straggling  what- 
ver  from  the  ranks  be  permitted. 

The  utmost  attention  to  the  posting  of  all  necessary  guards  will  be 
•iven  by  the  commanders  above  designated  and  the  utmost  vigilance 
>e  observed. 

It  is  enjoined  upon  division  and  brigade  commanders  to  be  careful 
o move  at  the  hours  and  to  the  places  designated ; without  such  exact- 
less  it  is  impossible  to  move  so  large  a force  without  confusion  and 
lifficulty.  The  headquarters  of  the  army  will  be  in  Sikeston  on  Sat- 
urday night,  the  1st  instant,  and  will  habitually  accompany  the  leading 
livision. 

The  artillery  not  attached  for  temporary  service  with  divisions  will 
)e  massed  under  the  command  of  Capt.  Henry  Hescock,  First  Mis- 
souri Light  Artillery,  and  will  habitually  march  between  the  First  and 
Second  Divisions.  The  officer  commanding  it  will  report  for  orders  to 
:hc  general  commanding  as  soon  every  day  as  his  command  arrives  at 
sts  place  of  encampment.  The  parole  and  countersign  will  be  furnished

to  division  commanders  for  ten  days  from  these  headquarters,  and

to  be  prompt  and  attentive  to  their  duties  and  careful  to  comply  exactly

is  very  fearful  that  the  mills  will  be  burned. 

The  Texans  camped  not  far  from  the  mills,  both  going  and  returning 
They  report  about  the  same  that  our  own  people  do,  viz,  that  the 
burned  4 wagons  and  got  about  40  horses.  They  sent  word  to  Colon*

come  and  hang  every  d— d Yankee  there.  Dodge,  however,  was  nc 
quite  ready  to  leave  and  the  Texans  thought  better  of  it.

Headquarters  Army  of  the  Southwest, 

Camp  Halleck , Ark.,  March  1,  1862. 

1 have  received  a private  communication  from  an  intelligent  writer, 
iitizen  of  Arkansas,  who  says : 

Ve,  as  citizens,  have  left  our  homes  and  firesides  for  the  purpose,  as  we  supposed,  of 
/iug  to  defend  ourselves  against  a brutal  soldiery,  that  would  lay  waste  our  humble 
nes  and  outrage  the  chastity  of  our  wives  and  daughters  and  place  our  own  lives 
; eopardy.  We  have  organized  what  is  called  Home  Guard  companies,  partly  of  Union 
n and  partly  of  Southern  men,  all  of  whom  are  anxious  to  return  to  their  homes, 
are  happy  to  find  you  and  your  men  are  not  composed  of  that  class  of  persons  com- 
ply called  jayhawkers,  who  do  not  regard  the  rights  of  citizens  and  property,  but 
line  the  war  to  its  “legitimate  object.” 

The  falsehoods  circulated  concerning  us  have  driven  thousands  from 
hr  homes,  and  I take  the  liberty  of  responding  publicly  to  the  senti- 
nts  expressed  by  the  writer,  because  these  falsehoods  have  involved 
s whole  community  in  the  troubles  which  he  seeks  to  mitigate. 

The  only  legitimate  object  of  the  war  is  peace,  and  the  writer  only 
3s  me  justice  when  he  says  I adhere  to  this  legitimate  object.  Peace- 
e citizens  shall  be  protected  as  far  as  possible.  I act  under  strict 
lers  of  Major-General  Halleck.  The  flight  of  our  foes  from  their 
nps,  and  the  imitation  of  their  conduct  by  the  citizens,  in  fleeing  from 
;ir  homes,  leaving  their  effects  abandoned  as  it  were  for  their  victors, 
i much  embarrassed  me  in  my  efforts  to  preserve  discipline  in  my  com 
nd,  as  these  circumstances  offered  extraordinary  temptations, 
the  burning  of  farms  and  fields  of  grain  in  Missouri  and  extensive 
Tacks  and  valuable  mills  in  Arkansas  by  the  enemy  has  induced 
no  resentments  on  the  part  of  my  troops,  which  I have  severely  pun- 
ed.  Necessary  supplies  for  my  command  could  not  keep  up  with  my 
>id  movements,  and  peaceable  citizens  not  being  at  home  to  sell  them 
my  quartermasters,  I am  compelled  to  take  them  without  purchase4, 
'king  settlement  difficult  and  doubtful,  occasioning  irregularities 
1 ich  I have  labored  to  counteract.  If  peaceably-disposed  citizens  will 
y at  home  or  return  home  and  check  the  clandestine,  stealthy  war- 
'C  that  is  carried  on  under  the  cover  and  cloak  of  peaceable  citizens, 

1 ch  of  the  havoc  of  war  will  be  avoided  and  many  poor  families  can

Gentlemen  : The  city  policemen  are  in  the  habit  of  arresting  negro(j 
a as  runaways,”  and  frequently  arrest,  or  attempt  to  arrest,  the  serj 
ants  of  the  army  officers,  who  are  put  to  the  trouble  of  obtaining  ordel 
to  prevent  their  servants  from  being  taken  from  them  on  the  very  ej 
of  their  leaving  the  city.  This  is  exceedingly  annoying  to  officers  undj 
marching  orders.  They  do  not  desire  to  be  considered  as  resisting  an 
civil  process.  It  is  not  their  intention  nor  the  intention  of  the  militai 
authorities  to  interfere  with  or  prevent  the  owner  of  a slave  from  pd 
suing  his  legal  remedies  to  recover  his  slave,  but  I have  to  request  tk, 
hereafter  the  city  police  be  confined  in  their  arrests  of  negroes  as  ru» 
awavs  ” strictly  to  such  negroes  as  may  be  m a legal  manner  claim® 
by  liis  or  her  owner.  Negroes  must  be  arrested  as  runaways  J 
fugitives  from  labor  by  a writ  issued  from  a court  having  junsdictic 
of  the  case.  This  is  necessary  in  order  that  the  slave  may  have  tli 
opportunity  to  plead  the  act  of  Congress  of  July,  loo-i. 

I am,  very  respectfully,  gentlei^^^r  obed.erd  ^vaut,

Cairo,  March  4,  1862. 


Have  just  received  copy  of  Pope’s  dispatch  to  you  of  yesterday.  He 
itimates  enemy’s  force  at  New  Madrid  at  5,000.  Gave'orders  late  last 
ght  to  have  strong  re-enforcements  sent  here  to  General  Pope.  Five 
giments  of  infantry  and  one  of  cavalry  have  left  to-day.  More  going, 
eneral  Paine,  who  I sent  out  to-day  to  hurry  forward  troops  and  push 
ilroad  to  Sikeston,  brings  rumor  of  New  Madrid  being  evacuated  and 
oops  going  to  Point  Pleasant  and  Island  No.  10. 

Is  it  your  wish  to  evacuate  Columbus  ? It  is  too  large  to  be  held  by 
smaller  force  than  present  garrison.  You  have  presented  me  with  an 
ephant  by  way  of  aides,  who  have  no  military  information.  I am  quite 
lwell.  Will  it  be  possible  to  let  Sherman  take  my  place  for  a week 
id  allow  me  to  visit  Saint  Louis  to  wind  up  my  affairs  ? 

G.  W.  CULLUM, 
Brigadier-  Gen  eral .

Upon  examination  of  ground  north  of  the  bayou  where  I had  intended

an  the  ground  south  of  the  bayou  and  is  now  untenable.  I send  to-

dch  case  I will  carry  the  intrenchments.  I find  on  close  reconnais-

> receiving  large  re-enforcements.  A little  would  help  me.  They

eneral  Cullum: 

Colonel  Plummer,  who  was  sent  with  3,000  men  to  occupy  Point 
leasant  last  night,  has  not  yet  been  able  to  effect  a lodgment  on  the 
inks  for  his  rifle  pits  and  batteries  on  account  of  finding  two  gun- 
>ats  at  that  place.  A third  has  joined  them  since  from  below.  Plum- 
er’s  sharpshooters  occupy  the  town,  and  were  attempting,  when  I 
st  heard,  to  drive  the  artillerymen  of  the  gunboats  from  their  pieces, 
ow  they  will  succeed  I cannot  yet  tell.  I made  a strong  demonstra- 
on  upon  the  works  here  this  afternoon,  driving  in  the  enemy’s  skir- 
ishers  and  his  whole  force  below  the  bank  and  down  upon  the  water, 
le  enemy’s  loss  was  about  25  killed ; ours  1 killed  and  4 wounded, 
lere  are  now  here  and  at  Point  Pleasant  eight  gunboats,  which  we 
nnot  take  of  course,  and  which  render  the  town  here  untenable, 

I en  if  in  eur  possession.  I hope  to  see  our  gunboats  in  a day  or  two, 
i which  case  everything  here  will  fall  into  our  hands.  I hope  Plum- 
tar  by  to-morrow  morniug  will  effect  his  lodgment.  Meantime  the 
! actice  here  is  excellent  for  the  troops.  I give  them  a smart  skirmish 
ery  day.  The  importance  of  making  a lodgment  at  Point  Pleasant 
btead  of  this  place  will  be  apparent  to  you  when  you  examine  the 
culiar  bend  of  the  river  and  the  position  of  Island  Ko.  10.  It  is  only 
miles  across  by  land  from  the  island  to  a point  on  the  river  below 
d nearly  opposite  to  Point  Pleasant,  to  which  boats  can  come  up  and 
ike  off  the  garrison  without  being  molested  by  us  at  New  Madrid.  I 
! all  use  all  possible  exertions.  Will  you  communicate  the  substance 
i this  letter  to  General  Halleck  $

;3cretary  Scott  is  here,  who  fully  understands  the  peculiarities  and 
abarrassments  of  our  condition,  I asked  him  if  he  would  explain  it, 
id  have  given  him  your  letter  for  that  purpose. 

Situated  as  we  are  here,  and  having  at  times  received  men  from 
lint  Louis  who  were  discharged  from  the  Army  after  shipping  in  the 
itilla,  I naturally,  even  if  not  properly,  applied  the  same  rule  or  rate 
pay  as  to  them.  It  would  be  difficult,  indeed,  to  go  on  with  the 
itilla,  or  even  to  keep  the  men,  if  we  made  a difference  in  persons 
jrforming  the  same  duty  now.  It  would  lead  to  a stampede  among 
em  if  we  attempt  to  reduce  their  pay ; and  if  it  is  to  be  charged 
gainst  me  by  the  Government,  I must  see  the  flotilla  is  not  ren- 
ted ineffective,  or  keep  up  the  rate  of  pay  which  I have  instituted, 
ill  the  loss  of  half  or  all  my  pay  would  in  itself  be  a slight  consid- 
ation  to  the  mental  agony  and  physical  exhaustion  which  I have  suf- 
red  for  the  last  six  months.  No  results,  however  successful,  would 
all  compensate  me  for  what  I have  suffered  in  the  progress  of  our 
)rk.  Although  results  which  can  tend  to  vindicate  our  right  to  re- 
in all  the  States  m the  Union  would  be  cheaply  purchased  at  my  sac- 
ice,  and  that  of  dozens  like  me,  with  a wounded  foot  keeping  me  on 
latches,  in  great  pain,  leads  me  to  say  that  whenever  the  Department 
| disposed  to  send  any  officer  in  my  place  I will  willingly  surrender 
If  position  to  him. 

The  changing  of  crews,  for  want  of  men,  from  disabled  to  sound 
sips,  with  other  difficulties,  have  rendered  it  impossible  to  keep  the 
tancial  as  well  as  all  other  departments  of  the  flotilla  in  that  strict 
d correct  form  that  in  a regular  service,  belonging  exclusively  to 
ker  War  or  Navy  Departments,  would  do $ still,  I write  rather  to  ex- 
am why  I consult  Secretary  Scott,  and  trust  that  you  will  appre- 
ite  my  motives. 

We  move  on  Island  No.  10  and  New  Madrid’  on  Wednesday,  and  ex- 
ct  a fight  at  both  places.  I have  sent  Captain  Wise  to  stop  repairs 
the  Essex  till  the  estimates  are  sent  to  you  for  approval. 

I am  required  to  send  Lieutenant  Wise  a telegram  daily,  which  is 
id  to  the  President,  all  of  which  I presume  you  understand,  which, 

► th  my  absence  and  great  pressure  of  business,  has  prevented  my 
iting  to  you  much  of  late.

d of  the  gunboats  from  Cairo.  The  enemy,  finding  he  could  make 
) impression  on  the  force  at  Point  Pleasant,  has  withdrawn  his  bat- 
ries  from  the  opposite  shore  and  ceased  to  pass  up  and  down  the 
iver. 

Transports  are  only  able  to  pass  when  masked  closely  by  at  least 
yo  gunboats  for  each  steamer,  and  then  only  by  passing  close  to  the 
;>posite  shore.  He  is  landing  troops  4 miles  below  Point  Pleasant, 
i the  opposite  shore,  and  marching  them  across  the  neck  of  land  and 
ten  recrossing  to  Island  No.  10.  In  this  way  considerable  re-enforce- 
ients  have  been  thrown  on  to  the  island  within  a day  or  two.  From 
.e  island  this  place  has  also  been  considerably  re-enforced,  until  the 
lemy’s  force  here  cannot  be  much  short  of  11,000  men.  As  soon  as 
can  drive  off  the  gunboats  all  the  forces  there  will  be  taken. 

I am  very  anxious  (for  service  on  the  river)  to  have  larger  field  guns, 
le  20-pounder  Parrotts  are  exactly  the  gun  we  want,  and  by  ha  ving 
veral  batteries  of  them  our  efficiency  would  be  a thousand  times 
creased.  Our  smaller  guns  have  not  range  enough  to  cover  the 
hole  breadth  of  the  river  with  certainty.  With  enough  of  the  20- 
rnnder  Parrotts  we  can  pass  below  and  mask  every  work  the  enemy 
n erect  or  has  erected  on  the  river.  I am  sure  you  will  aid  me  in 
e matter.  I send  an  open  order  for  the  disposition  of  troops  within 
is  district.  General  Paine,  for  some  singular  reason,  has  sent  frag- 
pnts  of  regiments  here,  detailing  two  companies  from  one,  four  from 
nther,  &c.,  where  one  single  regiment  taken  together  would  have 
en  sufficient,  and  have  given  us  full  regiments  here.  I have  endeav- 
ed,  in  the  order  inclosed,  to  correct  this,  but  before  having  it  executed 
bmit  it  to  you,  that  I may  not  interfere  with  arrangements  of  yours, 
wish  the  whole  affair  at  Commerce  broken  up.  The  sick  ought  to  be 
mt  somewhere  to  be  taken  care  of.  I need  staff  officers,  especially 
1 idical  officers,  more  than  I can  tell.

Captain  : An  order  has  been  sent  you  through  Colonel  Morsey  to 
oceed  with  two  companies  to  Troy,  in  Lincoln  County,  and  occupy 
at  place. 

I want  you  to  use  your  utmost  exertions  to  ferret  out  and  bring  to 
stice  the  insurgents  and  jayhawkers  in  that  region. 

The  general  order,  a copy  of  which  is  inclosed,*  will  be  your  general 
ide  m the  discharge  of  your  duty.  You  will  observe  that  a certain 
id  of  property  only  is  to  be  seized  and  that  only  from  a particular 
bss  of  persons.  Even  this  to  be  restored  if  the  owner  voluntarily 
^es  himself  up  and  is  found  to  be  such  a one  as  should  be  released 
bond  and  oath. 

[t  is  of  the  greatest  importance  that  you  prevent  your  men  frmn  com- 
i ttmg  depredations  upon  private  property.  The  object  is  not  so  much 
punish  the  rebels  for  what  they  have  done  as  to  prevent  them  from 
ng  injury  in  the  future. 

Chis  is  to  be  done  by  putting  the  incorrigible  out  of  the  way,  either 
death  or  imprisonment,  and  by  securing  the  good  conduct  of  others 
ough  the  obligation  of  a bond  and  oath,  while  many  may  be  reclaimed 
justice  mingled  with  kindness. 

t is  reported  that  there  is  an  extensive  organization  in  Lincoln  and 
oimng  counties  of  men  who  are  determined  to  continue  their  insur- 
it  operations,  apparently  for  the  purpose  of  plunder  and  revenge, 
none  of  these  escape  you,  and  be  careful  not  to  release  improper 
sons  on  any  conditions. 

hope  to  hear  the  best  reports  from  your  command. 

Yours,  very  truly,

[ established  last  night  the  heavy  guns  in  position  and  opened  at

k on,  though  several  of  them  are  injured.  Our  loss  has  been  1 officer 
led  and  6 men  wounded.  The  heavy  guns  are  established  within 
p yards  of  the  enemy’s  lower  redoubt,  and  I shall,  under  the  cir- 
tnstances,  be  obliged  to  work  on  towards  the  river  by  trenches,  so 
to  establish  the  heavy  battery  directly  on  the  bank.  This  will  re- 
ire  a day  or  two.  The  enemy  will  not  be  able  to  dislodge  us  from 
r present  position  nor  from  any  other,  as  they  depend  and  must 
I pend  altogether  on  the  gunboats.  There  are  now  nine  gunboats 
ire,  and  it  is  apparent  that  the  enemy  means  to  make  a stand  here 
long  as  possible.  I will  commence  to-night  to  push  approaches  to- 
rds  the  river  and  move  forward  the  battery  as  soon  as  I can.  The 
?my  continues  to  re-enforce  from  above,  but  I think  not  heavily.  If 
> gun  and  mortar  boats  were  here  to  drive  off  the  gunboats  of  the 
uny,  we  could  easily  deal  with  his  land  forces.  The  20-pounder  Par- 
ts will  help  us  greatly.  We  must  also  have  more  24-pounder  and 
ich  howitzer  ammunition  as  soon  as  possible.  Also  two  or  three 
re  heavy  guns,  if  possible.  The  troops  are  in  fine  spirits  and  ex- 
it wonderful  gallantry.

Toads  and  telegraph  lines ; and  even  m these  localities  military  oflicei 
are  specially  directed  not  to  interfere  with  the  lawful  process  of  an 
loyal  civil  court.  It  is  believed  that  the  time  will  soon  come  when  th 
rebellion  in  Missouri  may  be  considered  as  terminated,  and  when  eve 
the  partial  and  temporary  military  restraint  which  has  been  exercise 
in  particular  places  may  be  entirely  withdrawn.  By  none  is  this  moi 
desired  than  by  the  general  commanding.  . j 

II  ii  must,  however,  be  borne  in  mind  that  m all  places  subject  1 
the  incursions  of  the  enemy  or  to  the  depredations  of  insurgents  an 
guerrilla  bands,  the  military  are  authorized,  without  any  formal  dedal 
ation  of  martial  law,  to  adopt  such  measures  as  may  be  necessary  i 
restore  the  authority  of  the  Government  and  to  punish  all  violatioi 
of  the  laws  of  war.  This  power  will  be  exercised  only  where  the  pea<j 
of  the  country  and  the  success  of  the  Union  cause  absolutely  reqvure  ij 

III  Evidence  has  been  received  at  these  headquarters  that  Mai 
Gen.  Sterling  Price  has  issued  commissions  or  licenses,  to  certain  bad 
dits  in  this  State,  authorizing  them  to  raise  “guerrilla  forces,”  for  tt 
purpose  of  plunder  and  marauding.  General  Price  ought  to  know  th, 
such  a course  is  contrary  to  the  rules  of  civilized  warfare,  and  th, 
every  man  who  enlists  in  such  an  organization  forfeits  his  life  and  b 
comes  an  outlaw.  All  persons  are  hereby  warned  that  if  they  join  an 
guerrilla,  band  they  will  not,  if  captured,  be  treated  as  ordinary  pn 
oners  of  war,  but  will  be  hung  as  robbers  and  murderers.  Their  liyl 
shall  atone  for  the  barbarity  of  their  general.

le  rebellion  in  Missouri  and  proved  yourselves  worthy  members  of  the 
rave  Army  of  the  West. 

H.  W.  HALLECK, 

Major-  General. 


New  Madrid,  March  14,  1862. 

[ajor-General  Halleck: 

New  Madrid  is  in  our  possession.  Our  lines  were  drawn  closely 
round  the  works  all  day  yesterday  under  furious  cannonading  from 
ine  gunboats  and  from  heavy  batteries  on  land.  Last  night  the  place 
as  hurriedly  evacuated  under  cover  of  the  furious  storm  which  raged 
1 night.  All  of  their  artillery  (field  batteries  and  siege  guns),  an 
nmense  quantity  of  military  stores,  all  their  tents,  wagons,  mules,  &c., 
ave  fallen  into  our  hands.  The  enemy  carried  off  nothing  except  his 
en,  who  were  landed  immediately  opposite  on  the  wide  bottom  and 
ispersed.  Hamilton’s  division  is  now  entering  this  place. 

JNO.  POPE, 

Brigadier- General,  Commanding. 


Headquarters  Mississippi  District, 

New  Madrid,  March  14,  1862. 


ajor-General  Halleck  : 


Our  success  has  been  even  greater  than  I reported.  Twenty-five  pieces 
’heavy  artillery,  24-pounders  and  rifled  32s,  two  batteries  of  field  ar- 
llery,  an  immense  quantity  of  mixed  ammunition,  several  thousand 
and  of  small-anns,  with  hundreds  of  boxes  of  musket  cartridges,  300 
ules  and  horses,  tents  for  an  army  of  12,000  men,  and  an  immense 
nantity  of  other  valuable  property  of  not  less  value  than  a million  of 
idlars,  have  fallen  into  our  hands.  The  men  only  escaped,  but  the 
lemy’s  whole  force  is  demoralized  and  dispersed  in  the  swamp  on  the 
i>posite  side  of  the  river.  The  enemy  abandoned  the  works  so  hur- 
edly  as  to  leave  all  the  baggage  of  officers  and  knapsacks  of  men,  their 
sad  unburied,  their  suppers  on  the  tables,  and  the  candles  burning  in

Hon.  E.  M.  Stanton, 

Secretary  of  War , Washington: 

After  several  days’  skirmishing  and  a number  of  attempts  by  th( 
enemy’s  gunboats  to  dislodge  General  Pope’s  batteries  at  Point  Pleasanl 
the  enemy  has  evacuated  his  fort  and  intrenchments  at  New  Madrid 
leaving  all  his  artillery,  field  batteries,  tents,  wagons,  mules,  &c.,  am 
an  immense  quantity  of  military  stores.  Brig.  Gen.  Schuyler  Hamiltor 
has  occupied  the  place.  This  was  the  last  stronghold  of  the  enemy  u 
this  State.  There  is  no  rebel  flag  now  flying  in  Missouri. 

H.  W.  HALLEOK, 

Major-  General .

Believing  that,  owing  to  various  causes,  the  condition  and  resources 
‘ this  department  have  been  misrepresented  and  grossly  exaggerated 
yT  the  press  and  in  public  speeches,  I would  most  respectfully  submit 
ie  following  statement  as  to  the  condition  of  the  other  Kansas  troops  : 
Nothing  could  exceed  the  demoralized  condition  in  which  General 
unter  found  the  Third  and  Fourth  Kansas  Infantry  and  Fifth  and 
sixth  Kansas  Cavalry,  formerly  known  as  “ Lane’s  brigade,”  on  liis 
rival  in  this  department.  The  regimental  and  company  commanders 
lew  nothing  of  their  duties  and  apparently  had  never  made  returns 
reports  of  any  kind.  The  regiments  appeared  in  worse  condition 
lan  they  could  possibly  have  been  in  during  the  first  week  of  their 
llistment,  their  camps  being  little  better  than  vast  pig-pens,  officers 
id  men  sleeping  and  messing  together;  furloughs  in  immense  num- 
3rs  being  granted,  or,  where  not  granted,  taken ; drill  having  been 
)andoned  almost  wholly,  and  the  men  constituting  a mere  ragged, 
ilf-armed,  diseased,  and  mutinous  rabble,  taking  votes  as  to  whether 
iy  troublesome  or  distasteful  order  should  be  obeyed  or  defied. 

Vast  amounts  of  public  property  had  been  taken  from  the  depots  at 
ort  Scott  and  Fort  Lincoln  without  requisition  or  any  form  of  respon- 
bility,  and  horses  in  great  quantities  and  at  extravagant  prices  had

geable  to  come  within  a shorter  range  without  endangering  their  being 
arried  under  the  enemy’s  guns.  We  opened  upon  the  upper  fort  on 
he  Tennessee  shore  at  meridian,  and  continued  quite  a brisk  fire  until 
larkness  obscured  the  forts  from  view.  The  ten  mortars  in  the  mean 
ime  shelled  the  troops  out  of  range,  excepting  those  in  the  forts  man- 
ling  the  batteries.  The  upper  fort  was  badly  cut  up  by  the  Benton 
md  the  other  boats  with  her.  and  the  men  at  times  ran  from  their  guns. 
Colonel  Buford  has  been  busy  and,  I trust,  profitably  engaged  in  mak- 
ng  reconnaissances,  and  is  preparing  to  mount  his  siege  guns. 

In  the  attack  of  to-day  this  vessel  received  five  shots,  while  a rifled

ve  can  plant  the  mortars  in  a position  where  we  expect  to  be  able  to 
ihell  the  rebels  out  of  their  batteries. 

This  place  is  stronger  and  even  better  adapted  for  defense  than 
jolumbus  ever  was.  Each  fortification  commands  the  one  above  it. 
vVe  can  count  forty-nine  guns  in  the  different  batteries,  where  there 
ire  probably  double  the  number,  with  10,000  troops.  Exhaustion,  aris- 
ng  from  continuous  service  and  want  of  sleep,  will  excuse  this  inco- 
lerent,  discursive  report.

unboat  was  sunk  and  several  badly  damaged.  Many  of  the  gunners 
ere  shot  down  from  our  rifle  pits.  We  lost  a single  man.  Our  lower 
attery  is  so  placed  that  it  commands  the  upper  end  of  the  overflowed 
mds  on  east  side  of  river,  and  no  communication  from  below  with  the 
uemy  is  now  possible.  They  are  shut  up  in  the  bend  of  the  river,  with 

0 egress  whatever  except  by  a road  from  Tiptonville  to  Union  City,

at-boat.  If  I had  the  means  to  cross  the  river  with  my  command  1 
ould  bag  the  whole  of  them.

rENERAL : Your  telegram  in  relation  to  canal  (without  date*)  is  just 
Oived.  I heartily  approve  of  your  plan.  Impress  all  the  negroes 
r can  find  to  assist  in  the  work.  If  you  can  in  this  way  turn  and 
ture  the  enemy,  it  will  be  one  of  the  most  brilliant  feats  of  the  war. 
V'hen  occasion  requires  you  will  assume  command  of  all  the  forces 
ler  Colonel  Buford  on  the  other  side  of  the  river,  and  also  those  at 
umbus.  Colonel  Buford  has  a number  (five,  I think)  of  large  siege 
3es.  Use  them  wherever  you  think  they  will  be  of  the  most  advan- 
e.  I will  not  attempt  to  hamper  you  with  any  minute  instructions. 
5 great  object,  you  know,  is  to  cut  the  enemy  off  from  any  chance 
etreat  by  water.  I leave  you  to  accomplish  this  according  to  your 
1 judgment,  having  full  confidence  in  your  ultimate  success.  Buell 
effect  a junction  with  Grant  and  Smith  by  Monday.  We  shall 
1 have  70,000  men  at  a single  point  on  the  Tennessee  with  which  to 
the  enemy’s  center,  destroy  their  railroad  connections,  and  thus 
ofl  the  retreat  by  land  of  Polk,  McCown,  &c.  Unless  the  enemy  is 
h stronger  at  Corinth  than  reported,  I can  see  no  chance  of  failure, 
re  will  probably  be  a big  battle  somewhere  in  that  vicinity, 
nfortunately,  just  as  I am  preparing  additional  re-enforcements  for 
Army  of  the  Tennessee,  to  make  everything  still  more  certain,  I 
e received  official  dispatches  of  new  troubles  in  New  Mexico  and 
condition  of  Colonel  Canby’s  forces.  This  compels  me  to  immedi- 
y fit  out  a column  of  5,000  men  for  Canby’s  assistance.  I do  it 
t willingly,  for  the  Government  has  shamefully  neglected  him,  but 
jae  same  time  it  seriously  interferes  with  my  plans. 

Yours,  truly, 

H.  W.  HALLECK,

Iir  : I have  just  received  your  report  (without  date)*  of  your  opera- 
ins  against  the  enemy’s  batteries  in  the  vicinity  of  Island  No.  10. 
file  I am  certain  that  you  have  done  everything  that  could  be  done 
icessfully  to  reduce  these  works,  I am  very  glad  that  you  have  not

aid  have  been  a most  serious  loss  to  us  in  the  future  operations  of 
I campaign,  whereas  the  reduction  of  these  batteries  this  week  or 
:t  is  a matter  of  very  little  importance.  Indeed,  I think  it  will  turn 
in  the  end  that  it  is  much  better  for  us  that  they  are  not  reduced 
we  can  fully  cut  oh*  the  retreat  of  their  troops. 

Everything  is  progressing  well  on  the  Tennessee  Eiver  towards 
sning  your  way  down  the  Mississippi.  The  reduction  of  these  works 
mly  a question  of  time,  and  we  are  in  no  hurry  on  that  point, 
thing  is  lost  by  a little  delay  there.  I am  directing  all  my  attention 
v to  another  object,  and  when  that  is  accomplished  the  enemy  must 
cuate  or  surrender.

Assistant  Adjutant- General : 

Captain  : I have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  a commu- 
cation,  dated  Saint  Louis,  Mo.,  March  21,  1862,  from  Major-General 
alleck,  commanding  the  department,  touching  certain  reports  of  dis- 
irbances  in  La  Fayette,  Jackson,  and  Johnson  Counties,  in  this  State, 
is  instructions  shall  be  attended  to  carefully  and  at  the  earliest  pos- 
ble  day. 

In  connection  with  this,  I would  also  mention,  for  the  information  of 
ie  major-general  commanding,  that  I have  just  heard  rumors  from 
her  sources  of  a disorderly  state  of  things  in  Bates  County,  where  a 
xtain  scoundrel,  Jackman,  heads  a band  of  robbers  and  desperadoes, 
imbering,  it  is  reported  by  Colonel  Warren,  as  high  as  500.  Before 
y arrival  here  my  predecessor,  General  McKean,  had  given  orders 
liich,  when  carried  out,  places  eight  companies  of  the  First  Iowa  Cav- 
ry  and  one  section  First  Missouri  Light  Artillery  at  Clinton,  Henry 
aunty.  The  obj  ect  of  this  was  undoubtedly  to  watch  J ackman  in  Bates 
aunty,  and  also  to  keep  an  eye  to  the  quiet  of  the  other  counties  ad- 
cent  to  Henry.  The  order  of  General  McKean  directs  two  companies 
irst  Iowa  Cavalry,  stationed  at  Lexington,  to  proceed  to  Sedalia  when 
lieved  by  Companies  A and  C,  Missouri  State  Militia,  from  Booneville. 
The  two  companies  First  Iowa  Cavalry  from  Lexington  are  repre- 
nted  as  being  broken  down  in  horses  and  as  requiring  rest.  When 
ese  two  companies  reach  Sedalia,  and  General  McKean’s  orders  are 
•mplied  with,  there  will  be  four  companies  of  cavalry  at  Sedalia. 

I am,  captain,  your  obedient  servant,

to  me  to  muster  out  of  service  I have,  in  a few  cases,  resorted  to  tt

Pretended  Union  man  from  New  Orleans  just  arrived  within  our  hr

place,  clad  in  railroad  iron,  like  the  Merrimac.  Such  a river  boat  cm 
pass  any  of  our  batteries,  destroy  Commodore  Foote’s  flotilla,  and  bi 
the  steamboats  in  the  Western  waters.  This  is  a very  serious  matt 
which  requires  immediate  attention. 

If  there  are  any  very  heavy  guns  at  Pittsburgh  they  should  be  s* 
immediately  down  the"  Ohio,  to  be  mounted  at  Cairo  or  Columbus.

can  be  more  heavily  iron-clad,  so  as  to  meet  the  apprehended  dang

The  matter  seems  to  me  to  admit  of  no  delay.

Secretary  of  War , Washington : 

Sir  : I have  directed  that  Jefferson  Barracks  be  evacuated,  the  nub- 
property  to  be  removed,  and  the  buildings  to  be  turned  over  to  the 
hdical  department  for  a hospital.  General  Buell  reports  the  number 
■ k and  absent  of  his  army  (of  101,000  men)  to  be  30,000,  or  nearly 
c in  every  three.  This  is  certainly  an  enormous  sick  list  for  an  army 
it  has  been  engaged  in  no  serious  battle.  Of  the  regiments  which  I 
:lye  recently  sent  up  the  Tennessee  Kiver,  now  numbering  in  all  about 
000  men,  all  the  sick  were  left  behind  in  hospital,  and  yet,  after 
! n g less  than  two  weeks  in  the  field,  it  is  reported  that  5,000  men  are 
eady  on  the  sick  list.  This,  at  a healthy  season  of  the  year,  is  cer- 
nly  an  unprecedented  condition  of  things,  and  would  seem  to  indi- 
te a radical  deficiency  somewhere.  I am  confident  it  does  not  result 
im  a want  of  proper  provisions  and  hospital  stores,  for  no  army  was 
‘ ‘i  better  supplied.  I have  given  the  subject  as  much  attention  as 
i time  would  permit,  and  I think  one  great  source  of  the  evil  is  in 
r ^competency  of  the  brigade  and  regimental  surgeons  of  volun- 
rs.  It  is  alleged  that  men  are  placed  on  the  sick  list  and  given  cer- 
j cates  of  inability  as  a mere  matter  of  favoritism,  in  order  that  they 
y visit  their  homes  or  avoid  disagreeable  service  in  the  field.  On 
jeral  occasions  I have  ordered  medical  boards  to  re-examine  men 
jt  from  the  field  to  the  hospitals  in  this  city,  and  a large  portion  of 
»se  so  re-examined  have  been  reported  fit  for  duty  in  the  field.  This 
t serious  evil,  but  very  difficult  to  remove.  To  order  men  into  the 
d who  are  reported  by  their  surgeons  as  sick  would  seem  a cruel 
►I  ced are  on  the  part  of  a commander. 

In  detailing  General  Denver  for  the  command  in  Kansas  I followed 
advice  of  the  officers  of  General  Hunter’s  staff.  They  gave  it  as 
j ir  opinion  that  he  was  best  suited  for  the  place,  and  as  l had  very 
V?  Personal  acquaintance  with  him  I felt  bound  to  follow  the  best 
vice  I could  obtain.  Subsequent  information  convinces  me  that  it 
V good,  and  that  a better  selection  could  not  have  been  made.  There 
||  if  any,  enemies  in  Kansas,  and  the  qualities  most  required  there 
administrative.  I think  General  Denver  would  preserve  peace  on
