AP.  XVIII.] 

Lall  probably  do  the  work  yrith  the  army  alone.  Our  canal  has  been 
gigantic  work  5 it  has  been  infinitely  more  difficult  than  at  first  sup- 
>sed.  Six  miles,  through  a great  forest  of  immense  trees,  which  had 
be  sawed  off  4 feet  under  water,  and  then  through  cypress  swamp 
ickly  studded  with  cypress  knees,  have  furnished  us  with  an  amount 
1 labor  surpassing  any  one’s  belief  who  has  not  seen  it.  We  have  now 
i canal  50  feet  wide,  4 feet  deep,  and  6 miles  long,  through  which 
irge  steamers  can  pass  and  all  our  supplies  be  delivered  to  us. 

I am,  general,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JNO.  POPE, 

Major- General , Commanding. 


New  Madrid,  April  2,  1862. 

' ijor-General  Halleck  : 

Our  boats  are  in  the  main  bayou  and  ready  to  move  into  the  river 
i a moment’s  notice.  1 keep  them  up  the  bayou,  concealed  from  the 
>3iny.  I am  only  waiting  to  finish  the  floating  battery,  which  carries 
p 8-inch  columbiad  and  three  32s.  It  will  be  finished  by  to-mor- 
W night,  and  I think  will  be  impregnable  to  any  batteries  the  ene- 
r can  establish  in  any  reasonable  time.  I have  no  hope  of  Com- 
idore  Foote.  He  has  postponed  trying  to  run  any  of  his  gunboats 
pt  Island  No.  10  until  some  foggy  or  rainy  night.  The  moon  is  begin- 
ug  to  make  the  nights  light,  and  there  is  no  prospect  of  fogs  during 
s sort  of  weather.  We  must  do  without  him.  I will  give  you  details 
the  manner  I intend  to  cross  by  mail. 

JNO.  PQPE, 

Major- General , Commanding.

E.  M.  Stanton, 

Secretary  of  War  : 

The  commodore  opened  fire  at  11  o’clock  yesterday  with  cannon  and 
ortars.  Struck  their  large  floating  battery  a number  of  times.  Our 
outs  report  it  completely  disabled.  Also  burned  a steamer  the  enemy 
id  sunk  in  Missouri  channel.  Will  report  from  New  Madrid  to-night 
"eat.her  delightful. 


THOMAS  A.  SCOTT,

April  4,  1862. 

ipt.  N.  H.  McLean, 

Assistant  Adjutant- General,  Saint  Louis,  Mo.  : 

Captain  : Men  direct  report  Price,  with  infantry  and  artillery,  went 
st,  with  intent  to  reach  Pocahontas  very  soon  by  rail  and  water. 

Six  regiments  of  cavalry  were  moving  east  or  north  through  Jasper 
d Sunday.  The  cavalry  at  Salem,  Ark.,  were  also  gaining  recruits. 
Have  sent  to  Forsyth  and  Yellville  to  ascertain  the  further  move- 
mts  of  the  enemy. 

No  signs  of  force  at  Huntsville  and  Fayetteville.  If  line  gets  open 
Saint  Louis  I desire  to  confer  with  the  general  as  to  a counter  move.

SAML.  R.  CURTIS,

Headquarters  District  of  Central  Missouri, 

Jefferson  City,  Mo.,  April  5,  1862. 

:ig.  Gen.  John  M.  Schofield, 

Commanding  Missouri  State  Militia: 

General:  Numerous  irregularities  and  outrages,  such  as  indicated 
i Special  Orders,  No.  27,  of  this  date,  from  these  headquarters  (a  copy 
which  has  been  inclosed  to  your  assistant  adjutant- general),  have 
Sen  brought  to  the  notice  of  the  undersigned;  and  I now  have  the 
luor  to  call  your  attention  to  the  same,  and  propose  a remedy,  in  some 
i?asure,  by  which,  possibly,  they  may  be  hereafter  prevented. 

The  disturbances  throughout  this  district,  wherever  the  Missouri 
: ate  Militia  have  been  implicated  in  improper  conduct,  have  princi- 
lly  arisen  from  a desire  for  personal  revenge  to  satisfy  past  difficul- 
I ;s,  having  no  bearing  whatever  upon  the  cause  for  which  we  are  now 
I boring. 

Private  quarrels  of  long  standing,  originating  out  of  matters  con- 
i cted  with  property,  county  politics,  and  neighborhood  disagreement, 
e too  often  the  cause  of  persecution  of  those  in  military  power,  and 
jl  is  made  to  appear  as  connected  with  the  rebellion. 

This  state  of  things  should  be  put  a stop  to,  and  officers  and  enlisted 
i?n  should  be  made  to  feel  that  they  are  watched,  and  will  be  punished 
r any  such  conduct  not  warranted  by  the  necessities  of  the  case. 

At  present  I can  contrive  no  better  method  than  having  a constant 
•stem  of  inspections  made  by  impartial  officers  unprejudiced  on  either 
•le. 

I therefore  have  to  propose  that  some  officer  of  sufficient  rank  may 
! appointed  and  authorized  as  inspector- general  by  the  State  auth on- 
es to  inspect  and  investigate  all  such  matters,  as  well  as  to  attend  to 
le  military  functions  of  his  office  in  connection  with  the  Missouri  State 
lilitia.  My  staff  is  too  small  and  the  business  of  this  office  too  exten- 
; reto  admit  of  my  detailing  one  from  these  headquarters.  If,  there- 
I’e,  you  could  detail  such  an  officer  as  indicated  and  direct  him  to 
i port  to  me  for  such  orders  as  I might  give  I think  great  good  might 
1 tbe  result. 

Ool.  W.  D.  Wood,  aide-de-camp  to  the  Governor,  I am  inclined  to 
tink  would  impartially,  intelligently,  and  justly  fill  the  position,  and 
auld  he  be  detailed,  if  only  temporarily,  I should  hope  to  accomplish 
■ tnething  beneficial  in  preventing  such  troubles  and  outrages  as  men- 

t*ned. 

1 beg  that  you  will  give  your  early  attention  to  this  and  inform  me 
your  conclusions  and  actions  in  the  case. 

I am,  general,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

JAS.  TOTTEN, 

Brigadier -General,  Commanding  District.

Island  Ho.  10,  April  8,  1862. 

Major-General  Halleck  : 

Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  inform  the  department  that  since  I sent  th< 
telegraph  last  night  announcing  the  surrender  of  Island  10  to  uu 
possession  has  been  taken  of  both  the  island  and  the  works  upon  tin 
Tennessee  shore  by  the  gunboats  and  the  troops  under  commando: 
General  Buford.  Seventeen  officers  and  368  privates,  besides  100  o 
their  sick  and  100  men  employed  on  board  transports,  are  in  our  handy 
unconditional  prisoners  of  war. 

I have  caused  a hasty  examination  to  be  made  of  the  forts,  batteries 
and  munitions  of  war  captured.  There  are  eleven  earthworks,  witt 
seventy  heavy  cannon,  varying  in  caliber  from  32s  to  100  pounders 
rifled.  The  magazines  are  well  supplied  with  powder,  and  there  ar< 
large  quantities  of  shot  and  shell  and  other  munitions  of  war,  and  als< 
great  quantities  of  provisions.  Four  steamers  afloat  have  fallen  in  om 
hands,  and  two  others,  with  the  rebel  gunboat  Grampus,  are  sunk,  bui 
will  be  easily  raised.  The  floating  battery  of  sixteen  heavy  guns  turner 
adrift  by  the  rebels  is  said  to  be  lying  on  the  Missouri  shore  beloi\| 
New  Madrid. 

The  enemy  upon  the  main  land  appear  to  have  fled  with  great  precip 
Ration  after  dark  last  night,  leaving  in  many  cases  half-prepared  meal! 
in  their  quarters,  and  there  seems  to  have  been  no  concert  of  action  be! 
tween  the  rebels  upon  the  island  and  those  occupying  the  shore,  but  the 
latter  fled,  leaving  the  former  to  their  fate. 

These  works,  erected  with  the  highest  engineering  skill,  are  of  grea: 
strength,  and  .with  their  natural  advantages  would  have  been  impregf 
liable  if  defended  by  men  fighting  in  a better  cause.  A combined  at 
tack  of  the  naval  and  land  forces  would  have  taken  place  this  afternoon 
or  to-morrow  morning  had  not  the  rebels  so  hastily  abandoned  this 
stronghold.  To  mature  these  plans  of  attack  have  absolutely  re 
quired  the  past  twenty-three  days’  of  preparation.  General  Pope  h 
momentarily  expected  to  arrive  with  his  army  at  this  point,  he  having 
successfully  crossed  the  river  yesterday  under  a heavy  fire,  which  n( 
doubt  led  to  the  hasty  abandonment  of  the  works  last  night.  I 

I am  unofficially  informed  that  the  two  gunboats  which  so  gallantly 
run  the  fire  of  the  rebel  batteries  a few  nights  since,  yesterday  attacked 
and  reduced  a work  of  the  enemy  opposite  New  Madrid  mounting  eight 
heavy  guns.  I regret  that  the  painful  condition  of  my  foot,  still  requir 
ing  me  to  use  crutches,  prevented  me  from  making  a personal  examina 
tion  of  the  works.  I was  therefore  compelled  to  delegate  that  duty  t(

i Assistant  Adjutant- General,  Saint  Louis  : 

High  water  detained  me  so  I have  only  arrived  to-day  at  2 p.  in. 
kirmishing  with  a rear  guard  of  enemy’s  cavalry,  and  some  prisoners 
iken. 

My  cavalry  is  scouring  the  country  down  in  Arkansas.  No  force  of 
msequence  near.  Main  force  was  cavalry,  and  left  some  days  since, 
he  country  is  very  rough.  Roads  pass  down  deep  valleys  or  run  on 
arrow  divides.  My  main  force  m ust  remove  back  to  more  open  ground, 
erhaps  near  Ozark,  for  forage  and  convenience  of  movement  east  or 
est.  One  division,  with  cavalry,  could  hold  this  point  against  the 
orld,  and  keep  the  enemy  pressed  down.  I shall  try  to  alarm  the  en- 
ny  in  front,  but  cannot  extend  far  enough  to  do  much.  The  taking 
Island  No.  10  may  soon  give  you  the  mouth  of  the  river,  which  is  the 
By  to  Arkansas.  I am  arranging  a rope-ferry  for  convenience.  White 
iver  is  not  fordable,  and  rebels  come  and  fire  across.  Will  soon  stop 
lat. 

I will  try  to  get  into  telegraphic  communication  as  soon  as  I com- 
lete  arrangements  here. 

This  is  a dilapidated  town.  It  is  only  important  when  steamboats 
e running  and  commerce  is  safe  on  the  White  River.  The  surround - 
ig  country  is  not  cultivated.

| Proclamation  to  the  People  of  Central  and  North  Missouri. 

Marshall,  Mo.,  November  26,  1861. 
Fellow-Citizens:  In  the  month  of  June  last  I was  called  to  the 
nmand  of  a handful  of  Missourians,  who  nobly  gave  up  home  and 
nfort  to  espouse,  in  that  gloomy  hour,  the  cause  of  your  bleeding  . 
mtry,  struggling  with  the  most  causeless  and  cruel  despotism  known 
ong  civilized  men.  When  peace  and  protection  could  no  longer  be 
ioyed  but  at  the  price  of  honor  and  liberty  your  chief  magistrate 
| led  for  50,000  men  to  drive  the  ruthless  invader  from  a soil  made 
fitful  by  your  labors  and  consecrated  by  your  homes. 

Co  that  call  less  than  5,000  responded;  out  of  a male  population  ex- 
Ming  200,000  men,  one  in  forty  only  stepped  forward  to  defend  with 
pir  persons  and  their  lives  the  cause  of  constitutional  liberty  and 
man  rights. 

|Mme  allowances  are  to  be  made  on  the  score  of  a want  of  military 
'anization,  a supposed  want  of  arms,  the  necessary  retreat  of  the  army 
ithward,  the  blockade  of  the  river,  and  the  presence  of  an  armed 
jl  organized  foe.  But  nearly  six  months  have  now  elapsed;  your 
ps  have  been  tilled;  your  harvests  have  been  reaped;  your  prepa- 
jions  for  winter  have  been  made;  the  Army  of  Missouri,  organized 
1 equipped,  fought  its  way  to  the  river;  the  foe  is  still  in  the  field ; 

V country  bleeds,  and  our  people  groan  under  the  inflictions  of  a foe 
i rked  with  all  the  characteristics  of  barbarian  warfare ; and  where 
v are  the  50,000  to  avenge  our  wrongs  and  free  our  country?  Had 
000  men  Hocked  to  our  standard  with  their  shot-guns  in  their  hands 
re  would  not  now  be  a Federal  hireling  in  the  State  to  pollute  our 
l.  Instead  of  ruined  communities,  starving  families,  and  desolated 
tricts,  we  should  have  had  a people  blessed  with  protection  and  with 
res  to  supply  the  wants  and  necessities  and  comforts  of  life.  Where 
those  50,000  men  ? Are  Missourians  no  longer  true  to  themselves? 
e they  a timid,  time-serving,  craven  race,  fit  only  for  subjection  to  a 
spot?  Awake,  my  countrymen,  to  a sense  of  what  constitutes  the 
J'nity  and  true  greatness  of  a free  people.  A few  men  have  fought 
ir  battles;  a few  men  have  dared  the  dangers  of  the  battle-field;  a 
: have  borne  the  hardships  of  the  camp,  the  scorching  suns  of  sum- 
Jr,  the  frosts  of  winter,  the  malaria  of  the  swamps,  the  privations 
ndent  to  our  circumstances,  fatigue,  and  hunger,  and  thirst,  often 
jhout  blankets,  without  shoes,  with  insufficient  clothing,  with  the 
a,  wet  earth  for  a bed,  the  sky  for  a covering,  and  a stone  for  a pil- 
j > glad  only  to  meet  the  enemy  on  the  field,  where  some  paid  the

noblest  devotion  known  among  men  on  earth  to  the  cause  of  yoi

But  where  one  has  been  lost  on  the  field  three  have  been  lost  by  d] 
eases  induced  by  privation  and  toil.  During  all  these  trials  we  hajj

rally  to  our  standard ! I must  have  50,000  men.  I call  upon  you  i 
the  name  of  your  country  for  50,000  men.  Do  you  stay  at  home  to  tall

countrymen.  ^ . J 

But  where  are  our  Southern-rights  friends?  We  must  drive  tl

Citizens  of  Missouri,  I call  upon  you  by  every  consideration  of  mtj

Strike  till  each  armed  foe  expires! 

Strike  for  your  altars  and  your  fires! 

For  the  green  graves  of  your  sires, 

God  and  your  native  land ! 

The  burning  fires  of  patriotism  must  inspire  and  lead  you  or  alt 
lost ; lost,  too,  just  at  the  moment  when  all  might  be  forever  savj

Let  the  farmer  leave  his  fields.  Let  the  mechanic  leave  his  shop.  I

the  aspirants  for  office  and  place  know  they  will  be  weighed  in  the  D

crouching  spirits,  who  have  not  the  greatness  of  soul  to  respond  to  t 
country’s  call  for  help,  let  them  stay  at  home,  and  let .only  the  brt 
and  true  come  out  to  join  their  brethren  on  the  tented  field.

Y Dear  Sir:  Language  was  said  by  Talleyrand  to  be  useful  fbr 
lioncealment  of  one’s  thoughts ; but  in  our  day  it  fails  to  commu- 
te any  thought.  If  it  had  been  otherwise,  the  complaint  in  relation 
leneral  Price  of  which  you  speak  could  not  have  been  made.  The 
missioners  of  Missouri  were  informed  that  when  that  State  offered 
)S  they  would  be  organized  according  to  our  military  laws  and 
rals  would  be  appointed  for  brigades  and  divisions.  Until  then  I 
no  power  to  appoint  generals  for  those  troops.  The  same  state- 
substantially,  was  made  to  the  members  of  Congress  from  Mis- 
who  called  on  me  yesterday.  They  were  also  informed  that, 
conversation  with  informed  persons  and  from  correspondence 
on  file  in  the  War  Department,  I was  convinced  that  it  was  need- 
) the  public  interest  that  a general  should  be  sent  to  the  Arkansas 
Missouri  Division  who  had  not  been  connected  with  any  of  the 
>s  on  that  line  of  operations ; and  to  the  statement  that  the  Mis- 
| troops  would  not  fully  enlist  under  any  one  except  General 
k I asked  if  they  required  their  general  to  be  put  in  command  of 
troops  of  Arkansas,  of  Texas,  and  of  other  Southern  States.  To 
If  these  different  forces  into  harmonious  co-operation  is  a necessity. 
re  sought  to  effect  it  by  selecting  General  Heth  to  command  them 
intonation.  If  it  is  designed,  by  calling  Heth  a West  Point  Cadet, 
Ly  to  object  to  his  education  in  the  science  of  war,  it  may  pass  for 
it  is  worth;  but  if  it  be  intended  to  assert  that  he  is  without 
■ience,  his  years  of  active  and  distinguished  service  on  the  frontier 
issouri  and  the  territory  west  of  it  will,  to  those  who  examine 
e they  censure,  be  a sufficient  answer.  The  Federal  forces  are  not 
i>fter,  as  heretofore,  to  be  commanded  by  path  finders  and  holiday 
3rs,  but  by  men  of  military  education  and  experience  in  war.  The 
st  is  therefore  to  be  on  a scale  of  very  different  proportions  than 
3f  the  partisan  warfare  witnessed  during  the  past  summer  and 
I have  long  since  learned  to  bear  hasty  censure,  in  the  hope  that 
;e,  if  tardy,  is  sure ; and  in  any  event  to  find  consolation  in  the 
ance  that  all  my  ends  have  been  my  country’s. 

With  high  respect,

The  President  op  the  Confederate  States  : 

Sir  : The  Hon.  William  A.  Harris  will  present  this  letter  to  y 
and  will  also  make  known  to  Your  Excellency  the  present  condition 
affairs  in  this  State.  I have  particularly  instructed  him  to  endeavoi 
impress  upon  you  the  importance  of  the  instant  and  active  co-opo 
tion  of  the  Confederate  forces  in  Northwestern  Arkansas  with  tl 
army.  I have  repeatedly  assured  your  Government  that  such  coj 
eration  would  enable  me  to  take  and  maintain  possession  ot  tin? 
fourths  of  the  State  and  to  gather  around  me  at  least  50,000  recru! 
These  cannot  come  to  me  in  the  present  condition  of  the  State.  M| 
of  them  are  compelled  to  stay  at  home  to  give  whatever  protect! 
they  can  to  their  families  against  the  armies  and  marauding  gail 
which  are  laying  waste  and  desolating  the  State;  and  thousands  \1 
would  gladly  join  the  army,  if  they  could  get  to  it,  are  prevented  li 
doing  so  by  the  extension  of  the  enemy’s  fines  across  the  State  j| 
their  occupation  of  every  approach  to  the  army.  All  that  I can 
under  the  circumstances  is  to  occupy  the  most  threatening  positi 
which  I can  dare  to  assume,  so  as  to  hold  in  check  the  greatest  ] 
sible  number  of  the  enemy  and  so  prevent  them  from  being  employ 
against  us  elsewhere.  It  is  this  consideration  which  leads  me  to  a 
my  present  position,  which  is  one  of  the  greatest  peril. 

I hope  that  Your  Excellency  will  be  pleased  to  order  the  Contedei 
forces  in  Northwestern  Arkansas  to  co-operate  with  me,  and  to  d 
immediately.  I fear  that  our  cause  in  Missouri  may  otherwise  becc 
desperate.  The  enemy  are  not  only  laying  waste  those  parts  ot 
State  which  are  liable  to  fall  into  our  possession  or  which  are  occui 
by  our  friends,  but  they  openly  declare  that  no  crops  shall  be  s 
which  can  possibly  fall  into  our  hands.  It  is  altogether  important  t 
this  work  of  ruin  and  devastation  should  be  speedily  arrested, 
present  winter  is  the  most  favorable  season  for  operations,  and  I ass 
you  that  nothing  stands  in  the  way  of  complete  success  but  the  w 
of  co-operation  between  the  Confederate  and  State  forces.

> tendered  to  the  Confederate  Government,  in  order  that  they  may  be 
ganized  into  brigades  and  divisions  and  general  officers  appointed 
r them,  or,  if  preferable  to  them,  received  as  independent  companies 
battalions,  for  such  further  organization  as  the  interest  of  the  service 
d the  character  of  the  troops  may  indicate.  By  this  it  is  thought 
at  their  efficiency  will  be  increased;  and  that  they  will  be  relieved 
)m  the  anomalous  position  they  now  occupy  as  militia  of  the  Con- 
| derate  States  without  being  a part  of  their  organized  Army. 

This  arrangement  seems  very  desirable  to  me,  both  for  the  sake  of 
ie  Missouri  troops  and  the  advancement  of  our  cause,  and  I hope  it 
11  meet  with  your  concurrence.

Fort  Thompson,  Mo.,  December  21,  1861. 

ajor-General  Polk  : 

Dear  Sir  : Regarding  this  place  as  of  too  much  importance  in  the 
fense  of  the  Mississippi  Valley  to  be  lost  or  jeopardized  (and 
lowing  that  you  so  regard  it),  I cannot  refrain,  at  the  expense,  pos- 
dy,  of  being  thought  obtrusive,  from  giving  a short  statement  of 
ings  as  they  exist  here. 

Our  force  consists  of  two  artillery  companies  (one  of  them  well  drilled), 
i d the  Twelfth  Arkansas  Regiment,  armed  and  equipped.  Of  General 
iLompsoffis  immediate  command  600  or  700  only  are  left.  They  are  a 
’ etched,  ragged,  dispirited  looking  set  of  men;  half  armed,  undis- 
i dined,  careless,  and  inattentive.  There  is  no  Confederate  cavalry, 
ie  garrison  in  the  fort  is  at  the  mercy  of  the  Missouri  pickets.  Of 
lese,  one  entire  company,  while  on  picket  duty  several  days  ago,  left 
1 eir  posts,  disbanded,  and  went  home.  I have  no  sort  of  confidence  in 
lo  vigilance  and  fidelity  of  the  others.  You  can’t  induce  them,  and, 
’iat  is  worse,  the  officers  who  take  charge  of  them,  to  apprehend  any 
( nger.  A feeling  of  too  great  security  has  resulted  in  a consequent 
’nit  of  vigilance  and  attention,  and  these  men  will  soon  disband. 
These  things  are  not  written  to  annoy  or  give  you  trouble  or  uneasi- 


718  OPERATIONS  IN  MO.,  ARK.,  KANS.,  AND  IND.  T.  [Chap.  XVIH 

ness,  but  from  a sense  of  duty.  Based  upon  them  I desire  to  make  the 
following  suggestions,  not  matured,  but  just  such  as  occur  to  me  at  the 
moment : That  Colonel  Smith’s  regiment  be  sent  here  from  Island  No. 
10  and  that  from  200  to  400  horses,  with  cavalry  arms  and  equipage, 
be  sent  from  Memphis  (I  understand  they  can  be  procured  there)  as 
soon  as  possible.  These  to  be  used  by  detachments  from  the  infantry  as 
pickets.  The  soldiers  would  be  delighted  and  benefited  by  the  change. 
This  is  proposed  merely  to  meet  the  present  emergency ; is  suggested 
by  the  scarcity  of  cavalry  in  reach  and  the  poverty  of  means  at  hand 
just  now.  The  horses  and  arms  could  be  used  in  a few  weeks  as  a per 
manant  basis  for  that  number  of  cavalry. 

The  result  proposed  is  to  have  the  pickets  so  arranged  that  we  car 
be  advised  of  the  enemy’s  advance  at  least  twenty-four  hours  before 
the  attack,  and  so  be  able,  even  with  our  small  force  and  imperfecl 
preparations,  to  hold  out  until  we  can  get  re- enforcements  from  above 
As  it  is,  we  may  be  attacked  at  any  moment,  for  I have  no  earthly 
confidence  in  this  mutinous  and  insubordinate  remnant  of  Missour: 

Militia  around  us.  _ A ,, 

It  is  due  to  General  Thompson,  who  is  a brave,  gallant,  and  worthj 
officer,  to  state  that  this  condition  of  things  is  attributable  to  circumi 
stances  over  which  he  has  no  control,  and  could  not  have  been  pre 
vented  by  any  one.  It  is  proper  to  add  that  it  is  by  no  means  impos 
sible  that  my  apprehensions  may  be  groundless,  and  that  I may  err  ii 
my  opinion  in  reference  to  the  fidelity,  &c.,  of  these  men,  and  tha'1 
your  means  of  information  may  be  such  as  to  satisfy  you  of  my  error: 
I hope  this  may  be  so.  Nevertheless,  believing  what  I state  to  b< 
true  and  entertaining  the  apprehensions  that  I do,  I think  it  best  ou 
of  abundance  of  caution  to  advise  you  of  it. 

There  are  reasons  of  smaller  importance  why  these  or  some  troopi 
should  be  sent  here.  General  Thompson  can  furnish  no  detail  fo: 
work  on  the  fort.  The  teams  and  men  of  my  regiment  are  constant^ 
required.  All  the  timber  and  materials  must  be  hauled  by  them.  Thu 
forces  me  to  neglect  the  barracks,  which  a few  days  would  finish 
Winter  is  upon  us  and  we  ought  to  be  housed. 

Can’t  I get  the  powder  and  buckshot  I sent  for  ? Don’t  you  thml 
them  better  in  a close  fight  from  the  fort  ? Can  I get  a few  wagonil 
and  teams  ? 

One  of  my  sentinels  arrested  a Lincolnite.  He  was  two  days  ou 
from  Cape  Girardeau.  Says  they  intend  taking  possession  of  tin 
place  when  Thompson’s  men  disband.  A lady  from  Charleston  oi 
Wednesday  reported  1,000  troops  there;  that  they  were  conversan 
with  matters  here,  and  expressed  the  same  intention.  Latest  account 
are,  all  the  Federal  pickets  drawn  in  from  near  Charleston. 

I hope  in  the  hurried  statement  of  the  facts  above  I shall  not  w 
understood  as  censuring  or  reflecting  upon  any  one;  It  is  quite  foreigi 
to  my  nature  or  purpose. 

In  haste,  your  obedient  servant,

His  Excellency  the  President  oe  the  Confederate  States  : 

Sir  • Tour  letter  of  the  21st  instant,  forwarded  by  Colonel  Garni 
has  been  received.  With  respect  to  the  matter  of  transferring  t 
Missouri  troops  to  the  Confederate  Government,  I have  to  say  that  t 
measure  has  not  only  my  concurrence  but  my  hearty  approval.

“for  the  war”  if  possible.  What  success  has  attended  the  genera 
efforts  I have  no  means  of  knowing,  not  having  heard  iyom i him  sine

New  Madrid,  Mo.,  January  1,  1862. 
j.  Gen.  Sterling  Price,  Mo.  S.  G.,  in  Gamp : 

Dear  General  : The  instructions  from  your  headquarters  and  your 
cular*  were  received,  and  I have  endeavored  as  far  as  possible  to  com- 
' with  your  orders.  I have,  however,  been  very  much  discouraged  by 
i action  of  my  command  and  from  newspaper  rumors.  I am  fearful 
i have  suffered  in  the  same  way.  I endeavored  to  get  all  to  dis- 
id  and  reorganize  on  the  same  day,  each  company  of  men  selecting 
mce  their  new  officers,  and  without  any  cessation  to  go  on  with  our 
)d  work,  but  I could  not  get  a corporal’s  guard  to  agree  to  re-enlist 
hout  first  returning  home  or  taking  the  Christmas  holidays  or  some 
ler  excuse,  and  I had  to  adopt  a plan  to  suit  the  condition  of  things ; 
vas  to  march  each  regiment  to  the  nearest  safe  point  to  the  majority 
their  homes,  and,  setting  different  days  for  them  to  disband,  to  en- 
ivor  to  induce  them  to  re-enlist.  Of  those  disbanded  at  this  place 
i)  few  have  volunteered  up  to  this  time.  The  Stoddard  County  regi- 
nt  disbands  this  day  at  Camp  Blanton,  in  Stoddard  County.  The 
nklin  County  regiment  disbands  on  the  4th  at  Clarkton,  and  the  Rip- 
County  regiment  disbands  on  the  8th  at  Pitman’s  Ferry.  How 
ny  of  these  will  volunteer  it  is  impossible  to  tell,  but  I am  sure  I 
1 have  but  a skeleton  force  until  February  or  March.  The  men  are 
sounder  than  the  officers,  and  if  I could  but  stop  their  croaking  all 
aid  be  well.  I do  not  censure  all,  for  many  of  them  are  patriotic 
ltlemen,  who  are  willing  to  serve  anywhere  or  work  in  any  kind  of 
ness,  but  many  also  who  cannot  be  re-elected,  from  incompeteucy 
ither  causes,  for  the  purpose  of  covering  their  own  defeat,  hunt  a 
usand  excuses,  and  delay  others  who  would  immediately  join, 
am  now  without  an  army,  but  still  have  hope,  and  if  left  single- 
lded  and  alone,  I will  keep  the  enemy  in  my  neighborhood  uneasy 
l on  guard.

His  Excellency  Jefferson  Davis: 

Being  desirous  to  know  the  exact  state  of  things  in  Missouri  so  f 
as  the  forces  in  the  interest  of  the  Confederacy  were  concerned,  as  a) 
to  know  the  views  and  plans  of  Generals  McCulloch  and  Price,  I se 
a trustworthy  messenger  from  this  post  to  both  of  their  camps  for  tb 
purpose.  That  messenger  has  just  returned,  and  I have  thought  it  be 
to  send  him  without  delay  to  you,  which  I do  on  to-morrow. 

I gave  General  Price  to  understand  that  I regarded  energetic  acti< 
on  his  part  in  keeping  the  enemy  employed  in  Missouri  of  the  highe 
importance  to  the  defense  of  my  present  position,  and  that  I hoped 
would  leave  no  effort  unmade  to  keep  himself  in  the  field  during  tl 
winter.  In  my  letter  to  him  I expressed  the  opinion  that  if  the  Go 
federate  Government  could  help  Missouri  from  the  east  it  must 
through  Columbus,  and  I was  not  without  hope  of  yet  aiding  in  t 
emancipation  of  Saint  Louis  through  this  route.  In  reply  he  has  wntb

at  length,  and  the  letter  is  of  sncli  a character  as  to  induce  me  to

his  associate,  General  McCulloch,  and  I am  constrained  to  say  that 
the  information  1 receive  from  that  quarter  (and  I am  hearing  con-

jrENERAL : 1 acknowledge  with  very  great  pleasure  the  receipt  of  your 
er  of  the  4th  instant.  It  was  handed  to  me  yesterday  by  Mr.  Bur- 
1,  who  also  gave  me  the  information  which  you  desired  him  to  com- 
plicate to  me.  I fully  agree  with  you  that  it  is  all-important  that 
! should  be  kept  advised  (so  far  as  it  may  be  safe  or  expedient)  of 
ih  other’s  position,  strength,  and  plans,  and  shall  be  glad  to  aid  you 
(he  accomplishment  of  that  object.  Your  plans  as  made  known  to 
ij  by  Mr.  Burton  meet  my  full  concurrence,  and  I promise  you  my 
pest  co-operation  in  the  execution  of  them. 

> here  are  two  main  obstacles  in  the  way  of  the  successful  prosecu- 
u of  the  war  in  this  State,  one  of  which  ought  to  have  been  long 
be  overcome  and  the  other  of  which  ought  never  to  have  existed,  and 
) present  existence  of  both  of  which  is  due  mainly,  if  not  altogether, 

) the  conduct  of  General  McCulloch : 1st,  the  fact  that  the  great 
Jority  of  those  who  desire  to  take  up  arms  on  the  part  of  the  South 
prevented  from  doing  so  by  the  enemy’s  occupation  of  the  State, 
ch  closes  to  them  every  avenue  of  approach  to  my  army ; and,  2d, 
i dissatisfaction  which  General  McCulloch’s  constant  refusal  to  co- 
[ rate  with  us  has  engendered  in  the  minds  of  the  people  of  Missouri, 
i which  leads  them  to  doubt  whether  the  Confederate  Government 
I ly  sympathizes  with  and  desires  to  aid  them, 
he  most  populous  and  truest  counties  of  the  State  lie  upon  or  north 
he  , Missouri  River.  Had  General  McCulloch,  in  response  to  my

ties  of  a Missouri  winter,  but  to  the  fury  of  an  enemy  whose  barbam 

cannot  be  described.  * 

I could  not  refuse  their  reasonable  request,  and  my  army  became

the  Osage,  threatened  as  I was  from  Kansas,  from  Sedalia,  and  fro 
Rolla.  Knowing,  however,  that  thousands  of  the  people  on  the  noPi 
side  of  the  Missouri  would  come  to  me  even  at  this  season  if  I cou

getlier  about  2,500  recruits,  and  escorted  them  in  safety  to  me  at  C 
ceola.  Could  the  detachment  have  remained  on  the  river  only  a Id

°*  I,hav?  been  Preparing  my  troops  to  give  you  assistance,  and  in- 
ended  to  leave  here  to-morrow  with  some  of  my  cavalry  to  pay  you  a 
apid  visit.  At  the  same  time  I would  have  advanced  some  troops  on 
be  way,  but,  general,  at  8 a.  m.  to-day  we  have  here  eight  inches  of 
now  and  a heavy  fall  still  going  on.  It  is  of  course  impossible  for  me 
a move  my  command. 

As,  general,  I intend  to  do  all  things  practicable  to  assist  you,  I still 
equest  that  you  do  me  the  kindness  of  keeping  me  informed.

I.  The  undersigned,  by  order  of  the  President,  assumes  command  of 
le  Trans-Mississippi  District,  which  comprises  the  States  of  Missouri 
ad  Arkansas,  except  that  portion  of  them  lying  between  the  Saint 
rancis  and  Mississippi  Rivers,  as  far  north  as  Scott  County,  Missouri: 
ie  State  of  Louisiana,  as  far  south  as  Red  River  and  the  Indian  Ter- 
tory  west  of  Arkansas.  Headquarters,  until  otherwise  directed,  at 
ocahontas,  Ark. 

Commanders  of  troops  in  the  service  of  the  Confederate  States- 
ithin  this  district  will  at  once  make  a report  of  the  strength  and  con- 
fa011  of  their  commands,  accompanied  with  a written  report  in  full 
everything  relating  to  the  supplying  of  the  troops,  their  wants,  their 
ms  and  equipments,  their  clothing,  ammunition,  and,  in  a word,  of 
erything  that  might  be  considered  useful  to  be  known  at  liead- 
larters. 

II.  All  officers,  non-commissioned  officers,  and  soldiers  belonging  to 
>e  troops  of  this  district,  now  on  furlough,  are  hereby  ordered  to  re- 
rn  immediately  to  their  regiments.  The  sick  alone  are  excepted. 

| ^ hoped  that  this  order  will  be  considered  a sufficient  guarantee 
at  there  is  a necessity  for  the  immediate  services  of  every  soldier  in 
e district,  and  that  those  to  whom  it  relates  will  respond  with  cheer- 
mess  and  alacrity  to  it.

larters :

This  seems  to  me  the  movement  best  calculated  to  win  us  Missouri 
id  relieve  General  Johnston,  who  is  heavily  threatened  in  Kentucky, 
nee  in  the  city  of  Saint  Louis,  the  railroads  leading  to  it  from  the 
tst  should  be  at  once  destroyed  by  our  cavalry  as  far  as  practicable j 
so  the  road  to  Cairo.  We  should  fortify  opposite,  on  the  Illinois  side, 
he  city  once  ours  the  State  is  ours,  and  the  armies  of  the  enemy  on 
3r  soil  and  in  Kansas  would  supply  us  with  arms  for  her  people,  who 
ould  gather  to  our  standard  from  the  west  and  north. 

Flour,  salt,  and  a little  bacon  in  our  wagons,  and  beef  cattle  driven 
ith  us,  should  be  our  commissariat.  Grain-bags,  to  contain  two  days7 
tions  of  corn,  to  be  carried  on  our  troopers’  saddles,  and  money 
ir  paymaster’s  department,  and  sufficient  ammunition  our  ordnance 
apartment. 

Being  between  Ironton  and  Kolia,  if  we  are  immediately  threatened 
i either  hand  we  can  strike  with  our  whole  force  to  the  right  or  to  the 
ft,  as  might  seem  most  advisable,  taking  the  two  armies  in  detail, 
we  were  repulsed  from  Saint  Louis,  or  if  we  found  it  not  advisable 
practicable  to  attempt  it,  we  could  attack  the  enemy  in  the  field 
wards  Kolia  and  Sedalia,  passing  up  the  river,  and  gathering  together 
ir  friends  in  that  section  of  country  to  re-enforce  us. 

This  is  as  much,  general,  as  I can  now  write,  as  I desire  to  send  off 
airiers  early  in  the  morning  to  Generals  McCulloch  and  Pike  and 
Lionel  Hubert ; but  I hope  to  see  you  before  the  1st  of  April,  when  1 
ill  confer  fully  with  you  upon  the  subject. 

Now,  with  this  plan  in  view,  I do  not  think  it  advisable  to  disturb 
ie  enemy  or  alarm  him  any  more  than  is  necessary  until  we  are  ready 
march.  But  if  in  the  mean  time,  with  the  force  at  your  disposal,  you 
ink  it  perfectly  practicable  to  strike  him  a blow  at  Kolia,  secure  his 
ms,  and  check  his  intention  of  advancing  for  a while,  it  is  well  to  do 
|.  Having  done  this,  pause  where  you  are,  and  call  in  recruits  from 
at  section  of  country  and  north,  and  watch  closely  the  enemy  to  the 
irthwest,  and  maneuver  your  column  over  the  country  between  Kolia 
id  Springfield  until  I am  in  readiness  with  my  column  to  join  you  at 
near  Potosi.  Pike  can  aid  you  in  this,  but  he  should  not  go  too  far, 
he  would  leave  Western  Arkansas,  the  Indian  Territory,  and  the 
unties  west  of  you  exposed  too  much  to  the  half-savage  enemy  in 
ansas. 

if  I could  enter  more  fully  into  this  subject  and  set  forth  the  ad- 
mtages  which  it  presents  to  my  mind,  1 think,  general,  that  I would 
tve  your  hearty  co-operation  in  the  campaign  in  Missouri.  I am  truly 
‘voted  to  the  interest  of  the  whole  Confederacy,  and  look  to  the  whole 
Id  of  operations  from  the  Potomac  to  the  plains  of  New  Mexico  for 
y study,  and  pray  God  to  guide  me  in  the  true  paths  to  victory  and 
y country’s  independence. 

I sincerely  hope  that  if  you  attempt  this  move  you  may  add  new 
urels  to  the  wreath  already  encircling  your  brow,  and  that  Missouri 
ay  again  boast  of  having  struck  another  gallant  blow  for  her  liberty 
i(l  the  vindication  of  her  rights.

His  Excellency  C.  F.  Jackson, 

Governor  of  Missouri : 

Sir  : I have  the  honor  to  lay  before  you  an  account  ot  the  circuj 
stances  surrounding  my  command  within  the  last  two  weeks,  comp* 
ling  me  to  evacuate  Springfield  and  retreat  beyond  the  State  line  iu'j 
the  territory  of  Arkansas,  the  intelligence  of  which  has  no  dou| 
reached  you. 

About  the  latter  part  of  December  I left  my  camp  on  Sac  River,  Sai 
Clair  County,  fell  back,  and  took  up  my  quarters  at  Springfield,  for  t 
purpose  of  being  within  reach  of  supplies,  protecting  that  portion! 
our  State  from  both  Home  Guard  depredations  and  Federal  invasid 
as  well  as  to  secure  a most  valuable  point  for  military  movement.  J 
Springfield  I received  from  Grand  Glaze  considerable  supplies  of  clot] 
ing,  camp  and  garrison  equipage,  and  having  built  huts,  our  soldie 
pwere  as  comfortable  as  circumstances  would  permit.  I am  pleased  i 
say  few  complaints  were  either  made  or  heard.  Missouri  having  be 
admitted  as  an  equal  member  of  the  Confederate  States,  and  having  ij 
command  much  augmented  by  recruits,  I was  enabled  to  raise  at 
equip  about  4,000  men  for  the  Confederate  service.  A brigade  of  the 
consisting  of  two  regiments  of  infantry,  one  regiment  of  cavalry, 
two  light  batteries  of  artillery,  have  been  tendered  the  Confedera 
Government. 

About  the  latter  part  of  January  my  scouts  reported  that  the  enei 
were  concentrating  in  force  at  Rolla,  and  shortly  thereafter  they  occ 
pied  Lebanon.  Believing  that  this  movement  could  be  for  no  otb 
purpose  than  to  attack  me,  and  knowing  that  my  command  was  mac 
quate  for  such  successful  resistance  as  the  interest  of  my  arm;y  andt 
cause  demanded,  I appealed  to  the  commanders  of  the  Confedera 


P.  XVllI.j  CORRESPONDENCE,  ETC. CONFEDERATE.  757 

ops  in  Arkansas  to  come  to  my  assistance.  This,  from  correspond - 
je,  I was  led  confidently  to  expect,  and,  relying  upon  it,  I held  my 
fition  to  the  very  last  moment,  and,  as  the  sequel  proved,  almost  too 
g,  for  on  Wednesday,  the  12th  February,  my  pickets  were  driven  in, 
1 reported  the  enemy  advancing  upon  me  in  force.  No  resource  was 
w left  me  except  retreat,  without  hazarding  all  with  greatly  unequal 
mbers  upon  the  result  of  one  engagement.  This  I deemed  it  unwise 
do.  I commenced  retreating  at  once.  I reached  Cassville  with  loss 
worthy  of  mention  in  any  respect.  Here  the  enemy  in  my  rear 
nmenced  a series  of  attacks  running  through  four  days.  Eetreating 
I fighting  all  the  way  to  the  Cross  Hollow,  in  this  State,  I am  re- 
3ed  to  say  my  command,  under  the  most  exhausting  fatigue  all  that 
Le,  with  but  little  rest  for  either  man  or  horse  and  no  sleep,  sus- 
ned  themselves  and  came  through,  repulsing  the  enemy  upon  every 
lasion  with  great  determination  and  gallantry.  My  loss  does  not 
;eed  4 to  6 killed  and  some  15  or  18  wounded.  That  of  the  enemy 
know  to  be  ten  times  as  great. 

Jol.  Henry  Little,  commanding  the  First  Brigade,  with  Cols.  B.  A. 
res  and  J.  Q.  Burbridge  of  the  infantry,  and  Col.  E.  Gates  of  the 
/■airy,  covered  this  retreat  from  beyond  Cassville  and  acted  as  the 
iT  guard.  The  colonel  commanding  deserves  the  highest  praise  for  un- 
iting watchfulness  and  the  good  management  of  his  entire  command, 
eartily  commend  him  to  your  attention.  All  these  officers  merit 
I should  receive  the  thanks  of  both  Government  and  people.  To  all 
i officers  and  men  of  my  army  I am  under  obligations.  No  men  or  offi- 
s were  ever  more  ready  and  prompt  to  meet  and  repel  an  enemy, 
lovernor,  we  are  confident  of  the  future. 

STEELING  PEICE, 
Major-General , Commanding  Mo.  S.  G.

Major- General  Polk,  Commanding : 

Houses  burned  and  torn  down,  as  occasion  required.  Captain  Hallum, 
Fifth  Regiment,  wounded  yesterday ; also  3 men  on  the  Polk  and  1 
jcout.  A lively  skirmish  yesterday  evening. 

A heavy  demonstration  this  afternoon  on  New  Madrid.  Were  driven 
lack  by  Captain  Bankhead’s  guns  and  the  gunboats. 

The  enemy  has  established  a battery  at  Point  Pleasant  of  small  rifled 
pins.  The  river  would  be  closed  if  New  Madrid  was  abandoned.  A 
arge  force  would  be  required  to  hold  Island  10  if  New  Madrid  was  in 
he  hands  of  the  enemy.  It  is  necessary  to  hold  the  place  until  forces 
tre  thrown  here  to  defeat  the  enemy.  The  quicker  the  better.  I see 
10  other  course  to  pursue.  If  I had  20,000  more  men  such  would  be 
ny  course. 

McCOWN.

lace  the  navigation  from  below  will  virtually  be  cut  off*.  The  gunboats 
an  drive  them  from  the  bank  while  they  are  firing,  but  they  fall  back 
ut  of  reach  and  advance  again  as  soon  as  the  gunboats  leave.  The 
tiemy  are  said  to  have  moved  a large  force  to  that  place.  I should  say 
hat  unless  large  re-enforcements  are  sent  to  you  to  meet  the  enemy 
ow  in  our  front  we  shall  either  be  compelled  to  leave  this  place  or 
ive  up  our  communication  in  transports  from  Tipton ville  to  this  place. 

I would  suggest  planting  a good  heavy  battery  on  the  Tennessee 
ide  to  shell  them  in  conjunction  with  the  river  battery  in  the  gunboats; 
lis  may  obviate  the  difficulty  until  your  re-enforcements  arrive,  and  if 
on  have  a mortar,  it  could  be  used  to  great  advantage,

lol.  Thomas  Jordan, 

Adjutant- General,  Jackson , Tenn.: 

Colonel:  I received  yours  of  March  10.  As  soon  as  I can  deter- 
line  the  guns  required  here  I shall  forward  the  remainder  to  Fort 
*illow.  As  soon  as  a gunboat  opens  fire  upon  the  enemy  they  di  sap  - 
ear,  but  return  as  soon  as  the  boat  leaves.  They  are  fortifying  Point 
Peasant.  I have  placed  two  24-pounder  siege  guns  and  a company 
f cavalry  opposite  that  point. 

The  river  is  now  falling.  I am  making  every  effort  to  save  battery 
To.  1.  1 have  not  constructed  any  works  in  front  of  my  works  at  New 

ladrid  as  yet.  The  reasons  that  have  influenced  me  in  not  advancing 
ly  works  are  that  a gunboat  in  the  mouth  of  the  bayou  and  one  below 
tie  work  covers  all  the  ground — cross-fire  in  front  of  the  work.  The 
alien t proposed  to  be  erected  in  advance  of  the  two  works  would  inter- 
ire  with  this  fire.  Also,  the  position  the  work  would  occupy  is  also 
nder  the  fire  of  the  boats.  Another  reason,  it  would  require  more 
roops  to  occupy  it.  I now  have  five  regiments  at  the  two  works  in 
trew  Madrid.  I must  not  be  too  weak  on  this  side  of  the  river.  I keep 
Iransports  there  all  the  time.  If  they  assault  the  works,  I believe  they 
ill  be  repulsed  with  loss  with  the  co-operation  of  Commodore  Hollins, 
lere  I desire  to  say  that  Commodore  Hollins,  as  well  as  all  his  eom- 
land,  have  given  me  the  most  hearty  support  in  everything.  I feel 
onfident  of  defeating  the  enemy’s  gunboats  if  they  stop  to  fight $ if 
key  run  past,  I shall  endeavor  to  pass  them  in  a crippled  state  to 
5 ;>m m odore  Hollins. 

Tbe  enemy  are  still  receiving  re-enforcements,  and  will  be  able  to 
ring  24-pounders  from  Sikeston. 

Assure  the  general  that  I shall  do  all  in  my  power  to  hold  the  enemy 
i check,  but  shall  risk  nothing  on  rash  enterprises. 

Yours,  sincerely, 

J.  P.  McCOWN, 
Brigadier-  General , Commanding .

Headquarters, 

Madrid  Bend , March  13,  1862 — 9.10  a.  m. 

General  : Brigadier-General  McCown  left  this  place  for  New  Madri 
at  12  m.  last  night.  This  morning  at  daylight  the  fight  commenced  i| 
earnest.  A courier  has  just  arrived  by  land  from  opposite  Madrid,  whl 
confirms  that  the  enemy  are  attacking  our  works  with  infantry  anl 
artillery.  The  firing  is  very  rapid  and  distinct,  and  is  plainly  hear 
from  this  point.  There  has  been  two  distinct  attacks,  lasting  abou 
an  hour  each,  with  half  hour  cessation  intervening.  A third  attac 
is  now  being  made,  as  the  roar  of  artillery  plainly  indicates.  Of  cours 
I may  be  mistaken  as  to  the  amount  of  infantry  engaged,  but  the  ba. 
has  opened  and  General  McCown  will  give  them  a splendid  fight. 

I have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  most  respectfully, 

H.  S.  BRADFORD, 
Assistant  Adjutant- General.  I

ol.  Thomas  Jordan: 

Dear  Colonel:  Nearly  ever  since  my  arrival  here,  over  two  weeks, 
have  had  the  enemy  in  my  front  and  flank. 

I am  satisfied  that  the  force  at  New  Madrid  is  not  less  than  30,000 
en,  or  maybe  thirty  regiments,  with  artillery  and  cavalry. 

General  Sherman  (“Cump”),  I believe,  commands  the  force  with  the 
set.  Over  600  shot  and  shell  were  thrown  at  us  yesterday.  They 
ill  soon  have  heavy  guns  in  New  Madrid.  They  are  building  a rail- 
ad  to  that  place  from  Sikeston.  The  gunboats  of  Commodore  Hol- 
is  have  done  all  they  could.  I abandoned  New  Madrid  because  it 
volved  a constant  loss  of  life  to  hold  it.  It  was  of  no  use,  with  Point

[ need  not  remind  you  that  all  of  these  gentlemen  have  been  for 
my  years  in  the  military  profession.  But  I desire  most  earnestly  to 
press  upon  you  the  necessity  for  my  having  out  here  experienced 
d educated  officers  of  rank  sufficient  to  enable  me  to  use  their  infor- 
ition  and  attainments  to  good  effect. 

[n  the  recent  operations  against  the  enemy  on  Sugar  Creek  I found 
3 want  of  military  knowledge  and  discipline  among  the  higher  officers 
be  so  great  as  to  countervail  their  gallantry  and  the  fine  courage  of 
fir  troops.  I have  no  hesitation  in  saying  that  could  I have  substi- 
,ed  some  of  the  officers  above  named  (who  exerted  themselves  most 
bly  to  insure  the  success  of  our  arms  on  the  bloody  field  of  Elkhorn) 
some  of  the  highest  commanders,  my  orders  would  have  been 
>mptly  and  intelligently  carried  out  and  the  enemy’s  army  put  to 
er  rout. 

These  gentlemen  have  been  most  faithfully  serving  our  cause  since 
jy  left  the  Army  of  the  old  United  States,  but  they  are  in  false  posi- 
ns,  without  a degree  of  rank  commensurate  with  their  value  and 
vices,  and  it  is  utterly  impossible  to  endeavor  to  use  their  experience 
the  best  advantage  unless  this  is  remedied. 

' cannot  convey  to  you  a correct  idea  of  the  crudeness  of  the  material 
:h  which  I have  to  deal  in  organizing  an  army  out  here.  There  is  an 
solute  want  of  any  degree  of  sound  military  information,  and  even  an 
Lorance  of  the  value  of  such  information.  Nowhere  in  the  Confeder- 
r is  it  more  important  that  educated  officers  should  be  placed  in  high 
fitions  than  in  the  district  I have  the  honor  to  command. 

Che  greatest  need  I have  is  for  good  brigadiers,  and  I therefore  hope 
i will  urge  immediate  action  upon  the  recommendation  1 made  by 
sgraph  for  promotions  to  this  grade.  I inclose  a copy  of  those  nomi- 
ions,  and  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

EARL  VAN  DORN, 

Major- General.

I have  debated  this  movement  in  my  own  mmd  and  think  that  it  i 
the  best  I can  make.  I attempted  first  to  beat  the  enemy  at  Elklion 
but  a series  of  accidents,  entirely  unforeseen  and  not  under  my  contrc 
and  a badly-disciplined  army,  defeated  my  intentions  The  death  | 
McCulloch  and  McIntosh  and  the  capture  of  Hebert  left  me  withoi 
an  officer  to  command  the  right  wing  (which  was  thrown  into  utto 
confusion),  and  the  strong  position  of  the  enemy  the  second  day  le 
me  no  alternative  but  to  retire  from  the  contest.  A heavy  blow  m 
struck  them,  however,  and  they  are  somewhat  paralyzed,  1 ska 
march  to  another  field  before  they  recover,  and  before  their  re-enforc; 
ments  arrive,  which  they  are  daily  expecting.  If  I give  battle  to  ttj 
troops  near  Kew  Madrid,  I relieve  Beauregard.  If  I find  this  not  a< 
visable  or  practicable,  I shall  march  boldly  and  rapidly  toward  San 
Louis,  between  Ironton  and  the  enemy’s  grand  depot  at  Rolla.  I thin 
I shall  accomplish  something  in  that  direction.  I shall  at  all  oven] 
task  my  bumble  abilities  to  their  utmost  to  achieve  some  success  ■ 
our  cause,  and  I earnestly  hope  that  I may  be  successful. 

I shall  not  be  able  to  make  my  report  of  the  battle  of  Elkhorn  n 
some  time,  on  account  of  the  difficulty  I have  of  getting  subordma 
reports.  Our  loss  was  not  as  heavy,  however,  as  I had aE 
as  was  reported  to  me,  not  being  more  than  800  or  1,000  killed  ai 
wounded  and  between  200  and  300  prisoners.  The  enemy’s  loss  w; 
about  800  killed  and  1,000  or  1,200  wounded  and  about  300  prisoner 
We  also  took  two  batteries  of  artillery,  one  of  which  was  destroyed  t 
fire  (burnt  up).  The  enemy’s  position  was  a strong  one,  but  we  dro\ 
him  from  it  and  slept  on  our  arms  on  the  field  of  battle.  The  secor] 
day  we  found  him  at  daylight  in  a new  and  stronger  position,  to  t 
rear  of  his  first,  about  2 miles  off.  From  all  the  circumstances  wki( 
surrounded  me  I determined  to  withdraw.  I therefore  made  a demo 
stration  in  front  to  cover  the  movement  and  put  the  army  on  the  roa 
Huntsville,  toward  the  east,  and  retired  with  a heavy  heart,  but  wi 
a determination  to  recover  as  soon  as  possible  and  fight  again,  l v. 
not  defeated,  but  only  failed  in  my  intentions.  I am  yet  sanguine 
success,  and  will  not  cease  to  repeat  my  blows  whenever  the  opport 

nity  is  offered.  , _ .

troops)  whether  past  or  proposed.  AH  telegraphic  operators  are  c,

of  newspapers  are  earnestly  and  respectfully  requested  to  exercise  ca

liich  can  convey  aid  or  comfort  to  our  enemies,  or  suggest  to  them  the 
bsition,  condition,  or  designs  of  our  armies. 

III.  The  burning  of  mills,  workshops,  barracks,  store-houses,  stables, 
' any  other  buildings  in  regions  of  country  which  it  may  become  neces- 
,try  for  our  troops  to  retire  from  temporarily  is  forbidden. 

The  attention  of  all  commanders  is  called  to  the  orders  prohibiting 
te  troops  from  depredating  in  any  manner  upon  the  property  of  the 
tizens  in  whose  vicinity  they  march  or  encamp.  Any  officer  or  sol- 
er  who  may  injure  or  take  fencing,  stock,  poultry,  forage,  or  any  other 
.’operty,  without  proper  authority  and  right,  will  be  at  once  taken  in 
targe  by  the  provost-marshal  and  dealt  with  according  to  his  offense, 
uartermasters  and  commissaries  will  be  careful  to  pay  fair  prices  or 
give  exact  and  proper  receipts  for  forage  and  other  supplies  which 
may  become  necessary  to  procure  for  the  use  of  the  army,  and  the 
•oper  disbursing  officer  will  pay  the  money  on  these  acknowledg- 
ents  when  presented  for  payment  with  as  little  delay  and  inconven- 
nce  to  the  holder  as  possible. 

IV.  The  general  commanding  finds  it  necessary  to  remind  the  troops 
the  Articles  of  War  respecting  safeguards,  which  provides  that  any 

■freer  or  soldier  who  disregards  and  violates  a safeguard  given  by  the 
oper  authority  for  the  protection  of  persons  or  property  shall  be  tried 
Y a court-martial,  and  if  convicted  shall  suffer  death. 

V . Commanding  officers  will  have  read  to  the  troops  of  their  command 
e Rules  and  Articles  of  War  at  least  once  a month.

spiked  by  the  enemy,  are  being  unspiked.  The  rat-tail  files  have  be«

leither  is  a sufficient  arrangement  made  for  j>re venting  tlie  moisture  in 
lie  ground  from  leaking  through  the  walls. 

Service  magazines  near  to  the  batteries  are  entirely  missing,  neither 
s the  ordnance  department  provided  with  a laboratory  or  a suitable 
dace  for  the  protection  of  ordnance  stores. 

Island  No.  10  has  no  magazine  at  all.  The  undersigned  found  five 
segs  of  powder  protected  by  tarpaulins.  The  order  for  the  immediate 
jonstruction  of  a magazine  has  been  given  at  once. 

The  place  has  no  bomb-proof  and  the  men  are  entirely  unprotected 
igainst  the  shells  of  the  enemy.  They  imagine  themselves  safe  in  some 
imall  rooms  that  have  been  built  in  the  traverses  of  Batteries  B,  Nos. 

5 and  3,  and  which  originally  were  intended  for  service  magazines. 

The  ordnance  department  is  well  supplied  with  solid  round  shot, 
'rape,  and  cannister,  but  there  is  not  the  fifth  part  of  ammunition  on 
land  that  would  be  required  by  the  columbiads  and  rifled  pieces  during 
n engagement  lasting  over  two  days.  Powder  for  cartridges  and  the 
harges  of  shells,  shell  and  fuse  plugs  and  Reed  balls  are  very  much 
ranted. 

The  right  flank  of  the  position  is  partially  protected  by  a line  en 
remaillere  extending  from  the  Mississippi  River  to  Black  Bayou.  It 
3 1,200  yards  long,  not  finished  yet,  and  at  the  present  moment  sub- 
aerged.  The  high  stage  of  the  water  and  Reelfoot  Lake  form,  there- 
ore,  the  only  protection  to  the  right  for  the  present  moment;  a protec- 
ion  that  will  be  weakened  considerably  by  the  falling  of  the  water. 
The  water  batteries  on  the  main  shore  and  the  island  will  be  able  to 
eat  the  enemy’s  boats  back  by  daylight.  Whether  they  will  be  able 
r not  to  prevent  them  from  passing  by  during  a dark  and  boisterous 
ight  the  future  alone  can  disclose. 

The  left  flank  has  some  protection  by  the  batteries  from  Nos.  6 to  12, 
ut  mainly  by  the  strong  current  of  the  Mississippi  River. 

The  road  from  this  point  to  Tiptonville  is  practicable,  but  to  any 
oint  on  the  shore  below  Tiptonville  entirely  impassable,  on  account  of 
le  high  water. 

A glimpse  at  the  map  being  sufficient  to  give  a correct  idea  of  the 
atteries,  their  ranges,  &c.,  the  undersigned  has  the  honor  to  give  here 
is  views  with  reference  to  what  he  considers  the  only  chance  for  hold- 
lg  the  position  against  an  attack  by  land  either  from  the  direction  of 
[ickman  and  Union  City,  which  may  be  expected  as  soon  as  the  water 
ill  have  fallen  enough  to  render  approaches  from  that  side  practicable, 
r against  an  enemy  that  have  landed  from  the  Missouri  shore. 

This  morning’s  report  shows  the  strength  of  the  command  to  be,  infan- 
cy, 2,273  men,  of  whom  about  400  [are]  without  arms;  heavy  artillery, 
fty-one  guns,  1,166  men;  light  artillery,  Captain  Stewart’s  battery; 
ivalry,  two  companies;  sappers  and  miners,  one  company;  seven 
ansports,  of  which  two  are  used  as  hospitals ; one  floating  battery, 
mtaining  eight  8-inch  columbiads  and  one  32-pounder,  rifled. 

The  enemy’s  force,  according  to  the  best  information  received,  con- 
sts  of  seven  gunboats,  four  mortar  boats,  five  transports,  two  tugs, 
ine  batteries,  erected  between  New  Madrid  and  Andy  Riddle’s,  con- 
fining about  twenty-five  guns,  varying  in  caliber  from  32s  to  rifled  12s, 
id  from  20,000  to  25,000  men,  encamped  along  the  river  in  rear  of  these 
atteries. 

The  whole  line  from  Battery  No.  1 around  the  peninsula  to  Tipton- 
Ile  is  24  miles  long,  13  of  which  afford  good  landings  to  the  enemy ; 
asides,  a line  4 miles  long  has  to  be  guarded  to  the  right. 

The  floating  battery  placed  just  below  the  island  could  render  the

General  Orders,  ) Hdqrs.  Missouri  State  Guard, 

No.  79.  J Des  Arc , Ark.,  April  8,  1862.  1 

Soldiers  of  the  State  Guard: 

I command  you  no  longer.  I have  this  day  resigned  the  commissio]| 
which  yonr  patient  endurance,  your  devoted  patriotism,  and  you - 
dauntless  bravery  have  made  so  honorable.  I have  done  this  that  I 
may  the  better  serve  you,  our  State,  and  our  country — that  I may  till 
sooner  lead  you  back  to  the  fertile  prairies,  the  rich  woodlands,  an<  j 
majestic  streams  of  our  beloved  Missouri — that  I may  the  more  ceil 
taiiily  restore  you  to  your  once  happy  homes  and  to  the  loved  one  j 
there. 

Five  thousand  of  those  who  have  fought  side  by  side  with  us  undel 
the  Grizzly  Bears  of  Missouri  have  followed  me  into  the  Confederatl 
camp.  They  appeal  to  you,  as  I do,  by  all  the  tender  memories  of  thl 
past,  not  to  leave  us  now,  but  to  go  with  us  wherever  the  path  of  dutl 
may  lead,  till  we  shall  have  conquered  a peace  and  won  our  independ] 
ence  by  brilliant  deeds  upon  new  fields  of  battle. 

Soldiers  of  the  State  Guard ! Veterans  of  six  pitched  battles  ami 
nearly  twenty  skirmishes!  Conquerors  in  them  all!  Your  country! 
with  its  “ ruined  hearths  and  shrines,”  calls  upon  you  to  rally  onc<] 
more  in  her  defense,  and  rescue  her  forever  from  the  terrible  thraldom 
which  threatens  her.  I know  that  she  will  not  call  in  vain.  The  insoj 
lent  and  barbarous  hordes  which  have  dared  to  invade  our  soil  and  t<| 
desecrate  our  homes  have  just  met  with  a signal  overthrow  beyond  th<j 
Mississippi.  Now  is  the  time  to  end  this  unhappy  war.  If  every  man 
will  but  do  his  duty,  his  own  roof  will  shelter  him  in  peace  from  tin 
storms  of  the  coming  winter. 

Let  not  history  record  that  the  men  who  bore  with  patience  the  pri 
vations  of  Cowskin  Prairie,  who  endured  uncomplainingly  the  burning 
heat  of  a Missouri  summer,  and  the  frosts  and  snows  of  a Missouri 
winter;  that  the  men  who  met  the  enemy  at  Carthage,  at  Oak  Hills 
at  Fort  Scott,  at  Lexington,  and  in  numberless  lesser  battle-fields  ii 
Missouri,  and  met  them  but  to  conquer  them ; that  the  men  who  foughil 
so  bravely  and  so  well  at  Elkhorn  ; that  the  unpaid  soldierly  of  Misj 
souri  were,  after  so  many  victories  and  after  so  much  suffering,  une 
qual  to  the  great  task  of  achieving  the  independence  of  their  magnifi 
cent  State. 

Soldiers ! I go  but  to  mark  a pathway  to  our  homes.  Follow  me ! 

STEELING  PEICE.

Maj.  Gen.  George  B.  McClellan, 

General-in-Chief  of  the  Army , Washington , D.  C.  : 

General:  Since  my  last  (Ho.  4*)  I have  very  little  to  report.  By 
latest  advices  Major  Bowen,  with  re-enforcements?  had  driven  Turner 
as  far  south  as  Texas  County.  I sent  particular  directions  not  to  ven- 
ture too  far,  lest  he  might  be  cut  off.  A number  of  prisoners  of  war, 
among  them  several  of  Price’s  officers,  have  been  taken  in  the  vicinity 
of  Sedalia.  It  is  rumored  that  the  expedition  to  Marshall  and  Waverly 
has  been  successful,  but  I can  get  no  official  information,  although  i| 
have  repeatedly  asked  for  it  by  telegraph.  Persons  here  from  Saint 
Joseph  say  that  General  Prentiss’  column,  in  Clinton,  Platte,  Clay, 
and  Ray  Counties,  is  scattering  the  insurgents,  but  I can  get  no  infor- 
mation whatever  from  him,  either  as  to  the  strength  or  disposition  ol 

his  forces.  , ....  , Pij- 

It  was  my  intention,  on  learning  that  the  expedition  sent  north  lrom 
Sedalia  was  successful,  to  co-operate  with  General  Prentiss  by  pushing 
forward  a force  to  Lexington  about  the  time  he  reached  the  other  side 
of  the  river,  and  thus  scatter  or  capture  the  large  band  of  insurgent^ 
in  that  place.  But  as  these  commanders  seem  determined  to  keep  me 
in  ignorance  of  all  their  movements  I can  form  no  effective  plan  oi 
co-operation.  Everything  here  is  in  such  total  disorganization  anu 
there  is  such  a general  lack  of  discipline  that  officers  systematically 
neglect  to  answer  either  telegrams  or  letters  of  instruction. 

for  this  reason  I am  unable  to  get  reports  from  many  parts  ot  the 
department,  although  repeated  orders  to  that  effect  have  been  sent.  I 
hope  in  time  to  establish  a more  stringent  system  of  discipline  and 
accountability. 

We  have  many  regiments  here  ready  to  take  the  field,  but  they  nave 
no  arms,  and  the  arms  of  some  of  those  sent  out  are  totally  worthless. 
It  is  roughly  estimated  that  30,000  troops  in  this  department  are  with- 
out efficient  arms.  I learn  indirectly  that  several  thousand  have  within 
the  last  few  days  been  sent  to  Cairo.  Why  this  should  be  done  without 
giving  me  any  notice  is  certainly  very  unaccountable.  Moreover,  m

Saint  Louis,  December  31, 1861. ! 
Brigadier-General  Pope,  Otterville  : 

General  : I send  herewith  the  proceedings  of  a military  commissicji 
ordered  by  Colonel  Deitzler,  First  Kansas  Begiment,  for  the  trial  < 
certain  prisoners  at  Tipton,  Mo.,  within  the  limits  of  your  command.! 

In  the  first  place,  a military  commission  can  be  ordered  only  by  tl 
General-in-Chief  of  the  Army  or  by  a general  commanding  a deparl 
ment,  consequently  all  the  proceedings  of  the  commission  ordered  1 
Colonel  Deitzler  are  null  and  void.  The  prisoners  are  therefore  in  prj 
cisely  the  same  position  as  if  no  trial  had  taken  place. 

In  the  second  place,  military  commissions  should,  as  a general  rul 
be  resorted  to  only  for  cases  which  cannot  be  tried  by  a court-marti 
or  by  a proper  civil  tribunal.  They  are,  in  other  words,  tribunals  < 
necessity,  organized  for  the  investigation  and  punishment  of  offense 
which  would" otherwise  go  unpunished.  Their  proceedings  should  1| 
regulated  by  the  rules  governing  courts-martial,  so  far  as  they  may  1; 
applicable,  and  the  evidence  should  in  all  cases  be  fully  recorded. 

^Prisoners  of  war,  properly  so  called — that  is,  men  duly  enrolled  ar 
commissioned  in  the  service  of  an  acknowledged  enemy — are,  so  far  s| 
the  military  authorities  are  concerned,  to  be  treated  in  the  manner  pr 
scribed  by  the  usages  and  customs  of  war.  They  are  entitled  to  tl 
rights  of  war ; but  this  fact  does  not  exempt  them  from  punishment  1 
the  civil  tribunals  for  treason  to  the  Government.  But  treason  is  e 
offense  technically  defined  by  the  Constitution,  and  is  not  triable  1 
a military  commission ; nor  will  such  tribunal  try  or  punish  a soldi 
duly  enrolled  and  mustered  into  the  enemy’s  sendee  by  proper  autlio 
ity  for  taking  life  in  battle  or  according  to  the  rules  of  modern  wa 
fare.  But  it  is  a well-established  principle  that  insurgents  and  m 
rauding,  predatory,  and  guerrilla  bands  are  not  entitled  to  this  exem 
tion.  Such  men  are,  by  the  laws  of  war,  regarded  as  no  more  nor  le 
than  murderers,  robbers,  and  thieves.  The  military  garb  and  nan 
cannot  change  the  character  of  their  offenses  nor  exempt  them  fro 
punishment.  Moreover,  if  a prisoner  of  war  has  committed  acts  : 
violation  of  the  laws  of  war,  such  as  murder,  robbery,  arson,  &c.,  tJ 
fact  of  his  being  a prisoner  of  war  does  not  exempt  him  from  trial  ai 
punishment  by  a military  commission.  In  such  cases  the  charge  shou 
be  “ violation  of  the  laws  of  war,”  and  not  violation  of  the  “ Buies  ai 


iaf.  xvm.]  CORRESPONDENCE,  ETC. — UNION.  823 

rticles  of  War,”  wliicli  are  statutory  provisions,  modifying  the  laws  of 
ar  only  in  the  particular  cases  to  which  these  provisions  apply.  In 
I cases  not  embraced  in  this  statutory  law,  and  not  made  triable  by 
le  courts  which  it  creates,  we  must  recur  to  the  general  code  of  war 
id  try  by  a military  commission. 

A military  commission  will  be  immediately  ordered  to  assemble  at

roperly  drawn  up.

r — that  is,  taken  in  arms  or  in  the  enemy’s  service — should  be  held  as

release.

i The  difficulty  with  the  Germans  results  from  two  causes : 1st,  the 
ant  of  pay,  the  pay  department  here  being  out  of  funds,  which  fact

All  these  difficulties  are  being  satisfactorily  arranged.  A firm  and

ands.  Being  a German  myself  by  descent,  I know  something  of  the 
erman  character,  and  I am  confident  that  in  a few  weeks,  if  the  Gov- 
nment  does  not  interfere,  I can  reduce  these  disaffected  elements  to 
der  and  discipline. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  W.  HALLECK,

Washington  City, 

March  22,  1S62. 

General  H.  W.  Halleck,  ffic.,  Saint  Louis  : 

My  Dear  General:  I have  just  left  the  Secretary  (late  in  the  eve 
in  a).  When  about  to  bid  him  good  evening  he  conversationally  M 
me  that  Jim  Lane  had  been  to  him  to-day  with  an  order  from  the  P* 
dent  for  you  not  to  put  Denver  in  command  in  Kansas,  but  that  Dav] 
(a  recent  appointment  from  New  York,  a brother  of  Tush,  younger)  w 
to  be  assigued  to  that  command. 


AP.  XVffl.] 


CORRESPONDENCE,  ETC. UNION. 


833 


He  told  me  that  his  answer  to  Lane  was  a positive  refusal  to  attend 
any  such  order,  and  if  its  enforcement  should  be  attempted  he  would 
live  the  office.  He  said  so  many  right-minded  things  about  your  right 
make  your  own  assignments  within  your  own  command,  expressing 
s active  confidence  in  you,  that  I finally  asked  him  if  he  had  any  ob- 
stions  to  my  writing  you  a private  note  that  you  might  feel  assured 
proper  support  here.  He  said  he  had  none,  and  then  went  on  at  some 
ngth,  expressing  his  determination  to  allow  no  improper  interference 
Lth  you  while  he  continued  in  the  department. 

He  then  added  that  I might  say  that  he  had  called  upon  the  Secre- 
ry  of  the  Treasury  for  the  money  you  need  for  the  payment  of  troops, 
id  had  been  told  that  eight  millions  would  soon  be  ready,  and  that  he 
tie  Secretary  of  War)  had  directed  that  the  first  payment  should  be 
ade  to  your  troops,  as  you  desired  (by  a telegram). 

I then  bid  the  Secretary  good  evening  and  left  him,  but  he  called  me 
tck,  and  added  that  if  I was  going  to  write  to  you  he  wished  me  to  convey 
s respects  and  his  entire  confidence  in  your  ability  and  patriotism,  ex- 
aining  that  he  had  been  employed  against  you  in  the  mine  case  in  Cali- 
rnia,  and  that  his  partner  had  some  difficulty  or  controversy  with  you 
a somewhat  personal  nature,  but  that  for  his  part  he  had  taken  no 
Iterest  in  it,  and  Jiad  never  had  any  other  than  the  highest  respect  for 
>u,  and  he  hoped  you  would  not  imagine  that  he  ever  had. 

The  Secretary  understands  the  importance  of  your  command  and  the 
I Sees  si  ty  of  your  being  the  commander  for  carrying  out  its  objects. 

My  writing  this  note,  general,  is  a motion  of  my  own,  not  his,  and  I 
ive  been  moved  to  it  only  because  of  the  very  sensible  and  proper  re- 
arks  of  the  Secretary,  made  without  any  thought  of  their  being  com- 
unicated. 

I have  constituted  myself  a sort  of  temporary  aide-de-camp  to  the 
beretary  for  a short  time.  I do  not  expect  or  desire  to  remain  here, 
id  shall  be  more  willing  to  go  than  any  one  to  have  me  go. 

I remain,  very  truly,  yours, 

E.  A.  HITCHCOCK.

III.  In  view  of  the  rapid  extension  of  steamboat  navigation  into  di 
loyal  States,  and  the  importance  of  having  the  boats  engaged  in  sut 
navigation  controlled  by  loyal  citizens,  it  is  ordered  that  all  licenses 
pilots  and  engineers  navigating  the  waters  of  this  military  departmei 
be  revoked  from  and  after  the  15th  proximo,  and  that  said  pilots  ai 
engineers  take  out  new  licenses  from  the  u supervising  inspector,”  wl 
will  only  grant  licenses  to  persons  of  approved  loyalty;  or,  in  case 
doubt,  will  require  bond  with  security  for  the  loyal  conduct  of  such  e 
gineers  and  pilots.

I.  Commanders  of  army  corps,  divisions,  and  brigades,  and  of  inij 
tary  districts,  where  their  commands  are  equal  to  a brigade,  are  autho 
ized  to  order  military  commissions  to  try  offenses  against  the  laws  < 
war,  which  are  not  triable  by  general  court-martial;.  but  all  sentenc< 
of  such  commissions  extending  to  loss  of  life,  or  confiscation  of  propert, 
or  imprisonment  exceeding  the  term  of  thirty  days,  must  be  confirme 
by  the  commanding  general  of  the  department. 

II.  The  attention  of  all  such  commanders,  and  of  all  officers  of  mil 
taTy  commissions,  is  called  to  General  Orders,  No.  1,  of  1862,  Depar 
ment  of  the  Missouri,  in  relation  to  the  powers  and  duties  of  commi 
sions  as  distinguished  from  courts-martial.
